passages.title: Terminal voltage of a battery pack
text: A group of students investigated how the voltage available from a small rechargeable battery pack depends on the current drawn from it. The pack was connected to a resistance box, with an ammeter in series and a voltmeter across the pack's terminals. For each setting of the resistance box the students waited until both readings were steady, then recorded the current I and the terminal voltage V (Table 1). The voltmeter's own resistance was large enough that the current it drew could be ignored, and the pack was allowed to rest between readings so that its temperature stayed close to room temperature.

The students modelled the pack as an ideal source of emf ε in series with a fixed internal resistance r, so that the terminal voltage is V = ε − Ir. Figure 1 plots the terminal voltage against the current. The students also calculated the power delivered to the resistance box, P = I²R, for each setting (last column of Table 1).

After the run at the smallest resistance, the students noticed that the pack was slightly warm to the touch. One student proposed that the internal resistance had risen during that measurement. Another argued that warmth alone did not show this, because the pack dissipates heat at a rate I²r even if r does not change, and the last point still lay on the same straight line as the others.

figures.caption: Table 1. Resistance-box setting R, measured current I and terminal voltage V, and the calculated power P delivered to the box.
figures.alt: Table with five rows. R 11.5 ohms: I 0.50 A, V 5.75 V, P 2.9 W. R 5.5 ohms: I 1.00 A, V 5.50 V, P 5.5 W. R 3.5 ohms: I 1.50 A, V 5.25 V, P 7.9 W. R 2.5 ohms: I 2.00 A, V 5.00 V, P 10.0 W. R 1.5 ohms: I 3.00 A, V 4.50 V, P 13.5 W.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Terminal voltage V against current I for the five settings in Table 1.
figures.alt: Line graph of terminal voltage in volts against current in amperes. Five points fall on a straight line sloping downward: 0.50 A at 5.75 V, 1.00 A at 5.50 V, 1.50 A at 5.25 V, 2.00 A at 5.00 V and 3.00 A at 4.50 V. Extended to zero current the line would reach 6.0 V.

passages.source: Hypothetical experiment written for this app; the physics follows OpenStax College Physics 2e, 21.2 Electromotive Force: Terminal Voltage.

passages.title: Growth of two Escherichia coli strains in ampicillin
text: Students compared two strains of Escherichia coli. Strain W is a laboratory wild type. Strain R is the same strain carrying a plasmid, pBLA, that encodes a β-lactamase, an enzyme that hydrolyses the β-lactam ring of penicillin-type antibiotics. Each strain was grown overnight, diluted into fresh broth to an optical density at 600 nm (OD600) of 0.05, and incubated at 37 °C with shaking, with or without ampicillin (100 µg/mL). OD600 was recorded every 30 minutes for 3 hours (Table 1 and Figure 1). Over this range OD600 is roughly proportional to the number of cells per millilitre; the students estimated that an OD600 of 1.0 corresponded to about 1 × 10⁹ cells/mL.

In a second experiment, the students tested how resistance could spread. Strain R is sensitive to streptomycin, whereas a third strain, S, carries a chromosomal mutation that makes it resistant to streptomycin but is sensitive to ampicillin. Equal numbers of R and S cells were mixed in broth without antibiotics for 2 hours and then spread on agar containing both ampicillin and streptomycin. Several hundred colonies grew. No colonies grew when either strain was plated alone on the double-antibiotic agar. Adding DNase, which destroys free DNA, to the broth during mixing did not reduce the number of colonies. When the two strains were kept in the same flask but separated by a membrane filter whose pores let broth and DNA pass but not cells, no colonies grew.

At the end of the first experiment the students diluted the 180-minute culture of strain W (no ampicillin) by a factor of 10⁶ in sterile saline, spread 0.1 mL of this dilution on antibiotic-free agar, and counted 120 colonies the next day.

figures.caption: Table 1. OD600 of each culture at 30-minute intervals. Amp = ampicillin 100 µg/mL.
figures.alt: Table of OD600 readings at 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150 and 180 minutes. Strain W without ampicillin: 0.05, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.40, 0.80, 1.20. Strain W with ampicillin: 0.05, 0.05, 0.05, 0.04, 0.03, 0.03, 0.03. Strain R without ampicillin: 0.05, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.40, 0.80, 1.20. Strain R with ampicillin: 0.05, 0.05, 0.09, 0.18, 0.36, 0.72, 1.15.

figures.caption: Figure 1. OD600 against time for the four cultures in Table 1.
figures.alt: Line graph of OD600 against time in minutes for four cultures. Strain W and strain R without ampicillin follow the same curve: flat at 0.05 for 30 minutes, then doubling every 30 minutes to 0.80 at 150 minutes and 1.20 at 180 minutes. Strain R with ampicillin follows just below them, reaching 1.15 at 180 minutes. Strain W with ampicillin stays flat then falls slightly to 0.03.

passages.source: Hypothetical experiment written for this app; the biology follows OpenStax Microbiology, 9.1 How Microbes Grow, 11.6 How Asexual Prokaryotes Achieve Genetic Diversity, and 14.3 Mechanisms of Antibacterial Drugs.

passages.title: Rereading versus retrieval practice
text: Researchers tested whether the way students study a text affects how much of it they remember later. In a hypothetical experiment, 128 undergraduates read a 600-word passage about tidal ecosystems for 6 minutes. They were then randomly assigned to one of two study conditions. In the rereading condition, participants read the passage twice more, 6 minutes each time. In the retrieval-practice condition, participants spent the same two 6-minute periods writing down from memory as much of the passage as they could, with no feedback. Immediately afterward every participant predicted, on a 0–100 scale, what percentage of the passage they would remember in one week.

Within each study condition, half of the participants (32 per group) took a final free-recall test 5 minutes later and half took it one week later. Two raters, blind to condition, scored each recall protocol for the percentage of the passage's 25 idea units it contained (inter-rater agreement r = 0.91). Figure 1 shows the mean percentage recalled in each of the four groups; standard deviations were about 11 points in every group.

A 2 × 2 analysis of variance found a main effect of retention interval, F(1, 124) = 139.9, p < .001, and an interaction between study condition and retention interval, F(1, 124) = 16.9, p < .001. The main effect of study condition was not significant (F < 1). Participants in the rereading condition predicted that they would recall 70% of the passage after one week; those in the retrieval-practice condition predicted 50%.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Mean percentage of idea units recalled, by study condition and retention interval (standard deviations about 11 points in every group).
figures.alt: Bar chart with two pairs of bars. After 5 minutes: rereading 71 percent, retrieval practice 63 percent. After one week: rereading 40 percent, retrieval practice 48 percent.

passages.source: Hypothetical experiment written for this app. Its design resembles published retrieval-practice studies (e.g., Roediger HL, Karpicke JD. Test-enhanced learning. Psychological Science. 2006;17:249–255); the numbers are invented.

text: Every few decades a famous painting goes behind scaffolding and comes back brighter. The public response follows a script. Some viewers are delighted to see colours they never suspected; others complain that a familiar face has been scrubbed of its mystery. Both reactions assume that there is a single correct state of the picture, the one the artist left on the easel, and that the conservator's job is to find it. I want to suggest that this assumption, however natural, cannot bear the weight placed on it.

Consider what a conservator actually confronts. Varnish yellows; pigments shift as they age, some fading and others darkening; earlier restorers have added paint of their own, sometimes to hide damage and sometimes to improve on what they found. Beneath all this lies a surface that the artist may have altered several times before declaring it finished, and that the artist expected to be seen under candlelight, or in a chapel, or, as some have argued, through a tinted varnish applied on the day of delivery. There is no layer at which the picture is simply itself. To choose a layer is to make an argument about what mattered most, and arguments can be good or bad, but they cannot be neutral.

The usual reply is that science settles the matter. Cross-sections, infrared imaging and pigment analysis can tell us, often with great precision, what was applied and in what order. I do not doubt this. But knowing what is on the canvas does not tell us what to do about it. Analysis can establish that a glaze was added a century after the artist's death; whether to remove it depends on whether we value the painting as an object made by one person at one moment or as something that has lived in the world and been altered by it. That is a question of value, and no microscope can answer it.

None of this means that anything goes. A restoration can be careless, dishonest, or irreversible, and those are real faults. The best conservators I know are not timid; they clean, retouch, and consolidate. What distinguishes them is that they treat each intervention as a claim that must be defended in writing, that can be undone by a successor, and that leaves visible, to anyone who looks closely, the boundary between the artist's hand and their own. Restoration done this way is less like recovering a lost original than like editing a text whose author is dead: one does one's best, says what one did, and expects to be corrected.

The critic who protests that a cleaned painting no longer looks like itself is therefore not simply wrong. He is reporting the loss of something he valued, the picture as it had looked for as long as anyone could remember, and that is a loss, even if it was also the removal of grime. What he cannot claim is that his preferred state was the true one and the conservator's a fabrication. Both are versions. The honest position is not that we must never touch old paintings, but that we must stop pretending that touching them returns them to a state that exists somewhere, waiting to be found.
passages.source: Original essay written for this app (humanities: art conservation); not adapted from any published text.

text: A number between zero and one hundred now attaches to almost every address in the United States. It is meant to tell you how easily you could live there without a car, and it is consulted by renters, by property websites, and increasingly by the planners whose decisions shape the places being scored. The index is computed mostly from distances: how far the nearest grocery store is, the nearest school, the nearest park, with closer destinations earning more points. Its appeal is obvious. It is cheap, it is comparable across cities, and it turns a vague virtue into a figure that can be ranked.

The trouble begins with the word nearest. A supermarket four hundred metres away raises a score whether or not the residents can afford to shop in it, whether the route passes along a lit sidewalk or the shoulder of a four-lane road, and whether the store will still be there next year. The index measures the presence of destinations, not access to them, and it treats a neighbourhood as a set of points on a map rather than as a place where particular people, with particular incomes, schedules and bodies, try to get through the day.

Sociologists who have gone and asked those people find a different geography. Picture a study of a dense inner-city district with an enviable score: residents report walking less than residents of a lower-scoring suburb, and say why. They do not feel safe after dark, the crossings are timed for cars, and the shops that count toward the score sell things they do not buy. The number has described a neighbourhood that is walkable for someone, but not for them. A measure that cannot see this is not merely incomplete; it can mislead, because a high score becomes a reason not to invest in the very things that would make walking possible.

It would be unfair to blame the index for everything done in its name. Before such measures existed, the case for walkable neighbourhoods was made in prose, and prose is easy for a budget committee to ignore. The score gave the idea a seat at the table. Nor is the solution to abandon measurement. It is to measure what matters: not the distance to a grocery store but the share of households that reach one on foot each week; not the existence of a crossing but the time a person has to wait at it; not the average but the experience of those for whom walking is not a lifestyle choice but the only option.

Such measures are harder to collect. They require asking people rather than consulting a map, and they vary from one group to the next in ways a single number conceals. That is exactly why they are needed. An index that is easy to compute is easy to game, and a city can raise its score by permitting a convenience store near every apartment block while its residents go on driving to the places they actually need. The question a good measure should answer is not whether a neighbourhood looks walkable from above, but whether it is walked, by whom, and at what cost.
passages.source: Original essay written for this app (social sciences: urban sociology); the study it pictures is illustrative, not a citation.

passages.title: Pressure and flow across a carotid stenosis
text: In a hypothetical catheter study, investigators measured pressure and blood speed along a 50 mm length of a common carotid artery that contained a short, concentric atherosclerotic plaque. Along the healthy proximal and distal segments the lumen radius was 3.0 mm; within the plaque, which extended from x = 20 mm to x = 30 mm, the radius was 1.5 mm (a 50% reduction in diameter). A Doppler wire recorded the mean and peak systolic blood speeds in the proximal and distal segments (Table 1) but could not be positioned inside the narrowed segment. A pressure wire was then withdrawn slowly from the distal to the proximal end, recording the mean pressure at each position (Figure 1). A stethoscope placed over the plaque detected a bruit (a murmur) that was present only during systole.

For the analysis the investigators treated blood as an incompressible fluid of density 1.06 × 10³ kg/m³ and viscosity 3.0 × 10⁻³ Pa·s, took the vessel as horizontal, and used 1 mmHg = 133 Pa and g = 9.8 m/s². They applied the continuity equation and Bernoulli's equation to the entry of the narrowed segment, Poiseuille's law to the flow along it, and the Reynolds number, N_R = 2ρvr/η, to the onset of turbulence (laminar below about 2000, turbulent above about 3000).

Because the plaque was concentric and the flow steady on average, the pressure wire data were interpreted in three parts: an abrupt fall at the entry of the narrowed segment, a gradual decline along it, and a partial recovery just beyond its exit, where the fast jet slows and loses part of its energy to eddies. After the measurements the segment was dilated with a balloon so that its radius returned to 3.0 mm, and the pressure and Doppler recordings were repeated.

figures.caption: Table 1. Lumen radius r and Doppler blood speeds (mean and peak systolic) in each segment before dilation.
figures.alt: Table with three rows. Proximal segment: radius 3.0 mm, mean speed 0.30 m/s, peak systolic speed 0.75 m/s. Narrowed segment: radius 1.5 mm, speeds not measured. Distal segment: radius 3.0 mm, mean speed 0.30 m/s, peak systolic speed 0.75 m/s.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Mean pressure recorded by the pressure wire against position along the vessel before dilation. The narrowed segment runs from x = 20 mm to x = 30 mm.
figures.alt: Line graph of mean pressure in millimetres of mercury against position in millimetres. The pressure is 90.0 mmHg from 0 to 19 mm, drops abruptly to 84.6 mmHg at 20 mm, the entry of the narrowed segment, declines steadily to 84.1 mmHg at 25 mm and 83.6 mmHg at 30 mm, the exit, then rises to 87.0 mmHg at 31 mm just beyond the exit and stays at 87.0 mmHg to 50 mm.

passages.source: Hypothetical experiment written for this app. Physics from OpenStax College Physics 2e, 12.1 Flow Rate and Its Relation to Velocity, 12.2 Bernoulli's Equation, 12.4 Viscosity and Laminar Flow; Poiseuille's Law, and 12.5 The Onset of Turbulence (2022). Blood density 1.05–1.06 × 10³ kg/m³ (OpenStax College Physics 2e Table 11.1); whole-blood viscosity at 37 °C spans about 2–4 mPa·s across sources (OpenStax Table 12.1 lists 2.084; measured high-shear values near 3.3–3.5 mPa·s), so the passage states the value it uses. Normal common carotid diameter about 6 mm and peak systolic speed about 0.9 m/s (The Ultrasound Journal, 2010, Table 1).

passages.title: Blood gases in metabolic acidosis
text: A hospital laboratory calibrates its blood-gas analyser each morning. The analyser measures arterial pH and the partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PCO₂) with electrodes thermostatted at 37 °C, and then reports the bicarbonate concentration from the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation for the bicarbonate buffer, pH = pKa′ + log([HCO₃⁻]/(0.03 × PCO₂)), with [HCO₃⁻] in mmol/L, PCO₂ in mmHg, 0.03 mmol·L⁻¹·mmHg⁻¹ as the solubility coefficient of CO₂ in plasma at 37 °C, and pKa′ = 6.1, the apparent pKa of carbonic acid in plasma at 37 °C when dissolved CO₂ is counted as the acid. The ion product of water at 37 °C is Kw = 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁴.

In a hypothetical morning, samples from three patients were analysed (Table 1). Patient 1 was a healthy volunteer. Patient 2 had diabetic ketoacidosis and was breathing rapidly and deeply. Patient 3 had been found unresponsive after an overdose that depressed breathing; the pH electrode failed during this sample, so the analyser recorded PCO₂ and the laboratory measured [HCO₃⁻] directly by a separate enzymatic method.

To check the pKa′ programmed into the analyser, the laboratory titrated 100.0 mL of a 20 mmol/L solution of dissolved CO₂ (carbonic acid) in 0.15 mol/L NaCl with 0.200 mol/L NaOH at 37 °C in a sealed cell, so that no CO₂ could escape, recording the pH after each addition (Figure 1). The volume of titrant was small compared with the sample, and dilution was ignored. The titration was carried only to the first equivalence point, at 10.0 mL, where essentially all of the carbonic acid had been converted to bicarbonate; the second proton (pKa₂′ about 10) was not titrated.

figures.caption: Table 1. Arterial blood-gas results for the three patients (reference range for a healthy adult: pH 7.35–7.45, PCO₂ 35–45 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 22–26 mmol/L).
figures.alt: Table with three rows. Patient 1: pH 7.40, PCO2 40 mmHg, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L. Patient 2: pH 7.10, PCO2 20 mmHg, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L. Patient 3: pH not recorded, PCO2 80 mmHg, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L.

figures.caption: Figure 1. pH of 100.0 mL of 20 mmol/L carbonic acid (dissolved CO₂) in 0.15 mol/L NaCl at 37 °C against the volume of 0.200 mol/L NaOH added, in a sealed cell. The first equivalence point is at 10.0 mL.
figures.alt: Titration curve of pH against volume of sodium hydroxide added in millilitres. The curve starts at pH 3.9 with no base, rises to pH 5.5 at 2 mL, 5.9 at 4 mL, 6.1 at 5 mL, 6.3 at 6 mL, 6.7 at 8 mL and 7.05 at 9 mL, then climbs steeply through pH 8.05 at 10 mL (the equivalence point) to 8.7 at 10.5 mL, 9.0 at 11 mL and 9.4 at 12 mL. The gentlest slope is around 5 mL, halfway to equivalence.

passages.source: Hypothetical experiment written for this app. Henderson–Hasselbalch form, pKa′ 6.1 at 37 °C and the solubility coefficient 0.03 mmol/L per mmHg from Acid-Base Physiology (Brandis), 2.2 Buffering (anaesthesiamcq.com; Medicine LibreTexts mirror); 20:1 bicarbonate to carbonic acid ratio from OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 26.4 Acid-Base Balance (2022); half-equivalence pH = pKa from OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 14.7 Acid-Base Titrations (2019); Kw at 37 °C = 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁴ (neutral pH 6.81) from University of Waterloo Chem 13 News, Tough questions series, 2014 exam; carbonic acid Ka₁ 4.3 × 10⁻⁷ at 25 °C in pure water from OpenStax Chemistry 2e Appendix H. The curve was computed from the stated concentrations with pKa₁′ = 6.1 and pKa₂′ = 10.0 (review/chem_phys_batch_01_check.py).

passages.title: Screening an inhibitor of a protein kinase
text: Protein kinases transfer the terminal (γ) phosphate of ATP to a serine, threonine or tyrosine side chain of a protein substrate. In the cell, ATP exists almost entirely as its complex with Mg²⁺, and kinase assays therefore include MgCl₂ in excess of ATP. In a hypothetical screen, a purified kinase was assayed at 30 °C, pH 7.5, with 1.0 mmol/L ATP, 5.0 mmol/L MgCl₂, a fixed amount of enzyme, and a short peptide substrate whose phosphorylated product was quantified after 2 minutes. The initial rate v₀ was measured at six peptide concentrations [S], first without and then with a candidate inhibitor at 20 µmol/L (Table 1).

Fitting the uninhibited data to the Michaelis–Menten equation, v₀ = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]), gave the enzyme's Km and Vmax. Fitting the inhibited data gave the same Vmax, within error, and an apparent Km of 60 µmol/L.

To test whether the inhibitor binds reversibly, the enzyme was incubated with 20 µmol/L inhibitor for 30 minutes and then dialysed for 12 hours against a large volume of inhibitor-free assay buffer through a membrane that retains the enzyme but passes small molecules. The dialysed enzyme was then assayed at [S] = 20 µmol/L: its rate was 51 nmol/min, 85% of the 60 nmol/min given by untreated enzyme at the same substrate concentration (with inhibitor present, the rate at this concentration was 30 nmol/min, Table 1). No other samples were dialysed.

figures.caption: Table 1. Initial rate v₀ of the kinase (nmol/min) at six peptide concentrations, without and with 20 µmol/L inhibitor.
figures.alt: Table with six rows of peptide concentration and two rate columns in nanomoles per minute. At 5 micromolar: 24 without inhibitor, 9 with. At 10: 40 and 17. At 20: 60 and 30. At 40: 80 and 48. At 200: 109 and 92. At 2000: 119 and 117.

passages.source: Hypothetical experiment written for this app. Michaelis–Menten kinetics, Km and Lineweaver–Burk intercepts from Biology LibreTexts, Biochemistry Free For All (Ahern, Rajagopal, Tan), 4.1 Basic Principles of Catalysis; competitive, non-competitive, uncompetitive and irreversible inhibition from the same book, 4.2 Control of Enzymatic Activity; cofactors such as Mg²⁺ from OpenStax Biology 2e, 6.5 Enzymes (2018); the Mg²⁺–ATP complex as the true substrate of ATP-using enzymes (dissociation constant about 0.1 mmol/L) from Berg, Tymoczko and Stryer, Biochemistry, 5th ed. (2002), section 9.4. Table values were generated from Vmax = 120 nmol/min, Km = 20 µmol/L and an apparent Km of 60 µmol/L (review/chem_phys_batch_01_check.py).

passages.title: Calibrating a fluorine-18 dose for PET
text: Positron emission tomography (PET) most often uses fluorine-18 attached to a glucose analogue, ¹⁸F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG), which accumulates in tissues that take up glucose rapidly. Fluorine-18 (Z = 9, A = 18) decays with a half-life of 110 minutes, mainly by positron emission; the positron travels about a millimetre in tissue, slows, and annihilates with an electron. The rest energy of an electron (and of a positron) is 511 keV. The scanner's ring of detectors registers only pairs of photons that arrive at the same moment at two detectors, and reconstructs the line along which the annihilation occurred.

In a hypothetical morning at a PET centre, a vial of FDG was delivered from the cyclotron at 08:00 and its activity measured in a dose calibrator at four times while it waited for patients (Table 1). A patient's prescribed dose was to be drawn from the vial so that the activity injected would be close to 250 MBq, and the volume drawn was adjusted for the time of injection. A second vial from the same batch, calibrated at 1200 MBq at 08:00, was reserved for an afternoon patient injected at 15:20.

Constants used by the centre: Planck's constant h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, speed of light c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s, 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (so that hc = 1240 eV·nm), ln 2 = 0.693, and 1 MBq = 10⁶ decays per second.

figures.caption: Table 1. Activity of the first FDG vial measured in the dose calibrator.
figures.alt: Table with four rows. 08:00, 0 minutes after delivery: 800 MBq. 09:50, 110 minutes: 400 MBq. 11:40, 220 minutes: 200 MBq. 13:30, 330 minutes: 100 MBq.

passages.source: Hypothetical scenario written for this app. Fluorine-18 half-life 109.77 min, decay to oxygen-18 by positron emission with a small electron-capture branch (NNDC NuDat as reproduced by the KAERI nuclide table; TUNL Nuclear Data Evaluation, A = 18). Electron rest energy 0.510 998 950 69 MeV and h = 6.626 070 15 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s from NIST CODATA 2022. Positron decay and annihilation from OpenStax College Physics 2e, 31.4 Nuclear Decay and Conservation Laws; half-life and activity from 31.5 Half-Life and Activity; PET (two 0.511 MeV photons moving directly away from one another) from 32.1 Diagnostics and Medical Imaging; hc = 1240 eV·nm from 29.3 Photon Energies and the Electromagnetic Spectrum (2022).

passages.title: Conduction in myelinated and demyelinated axons
text: Electrically, an axon is a long, leaky cable: the axoplasm is a resistor, the membrane a capacitor in parallel with its ion channels. In a hypothetical study, investigators recorded from single motor axons dissected from rat sciatic nerve at 37 °C. Every axon rested at −70 mV and fired an action potential when depolarized to a threshold of about −55 mV. In the myelinated axons the voltage-gated Na⁺ channels were confined to the nodes of Ranvier, bare gaps about 1 µm long spaced 1.0 mm apart; between nodes, each internode was wrapped in a sheath so that the axoplasm was separated from the extracellular fluid by a stack of n membrane bilayers in series (n = 1 for a bare axon; n = 100 in the intact fibres, the axon's own membrane plus the wraps of the sheath).

The investigators modelled each internode as the axial resistance of its axoplasm, R = ρL/A, where ρ = 1.0 Ω·m, L = 1.0 mm is the internode length and A is the cross-sectional area of the axon, in series with the capacitance C of the internodal membrane together with its sheath. A single bilayer has a capacitance of 1.0 × 10⁻² F per square metre of surface (1 µF/cm²), and a stack of n bilayers has 1/n of that, so C = (1.0 × 10⁻² F/m²)(πdL)/n for an axon of diameter d. Current entering at an active node must charge the next internode before the following node reaches threshold; the time this takes scales with τ = RC, and in the model the conduction velocity is approximately L/τ. Table 1 lists the model values and the measured conduction velocity for four fibres: two intact fibres of different diameter, a 10 µm fibre after a treatment that had thinned its sheath to 20 bilayers along every internode, and a 10 µm fibre whose internodes had been stripped bare.

In the bare fibre the action potential at the last intact node failed to bring the next node to threshold and conduction stopped; the exposed internodal membrane contained almost no voltage-gated Na⁺ channels. In a second part of the study, rats were given the demyelinating agent systemically and their sciatic nerve conduction velocity, recorded with surface electrodes, was 40% lower than in a group given the vehicle alone; the axons of the treated nerves had not been examined under the microscope.

figures.caption: Table 1. The four fibres: 1 and 2 intact, 3 with a thinned sheath, 4 bare; axon diameter d = 10 µm for fibres 1, 3 and 4 and 5 µm for fibre 2. n = number of bilayers, C = model capacitance per 1.0 mm internode, τ = RC (model), v = measured conduction velocity.
figures.alt: Table with four rows. Fibre 1 (intact, axon diameter 10 micrometres): 100 bilayers, capacitance per internode 3.14 picofarads, time constant 40 microseconds, measured velocity 24 metres per second. Fibre 2 (intact, 5 micrometres): 100 bilayers, 1.57 picofarads, 80 microseconds, 12 metres per second. Fibre 3 (thinned sheath, 10 micrometres): 20 bilayers, 15.7 picofarads, 200 microseconds, 4.8 metres per second. Fibre 4 (bare, 10 micrometres): 1 bilayer, 314 picofarads, 4,000 microseconds, conduction failed.

passages.source: Hypothetical experiment written for this app. Resting potential −70 mV, threshold −55 mV, Na⁺ entry at threshold, nodes of Ranvier and saltatory conduction from OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 12.4 The Action Potential (2022). The cable model follows Tasaki and Matsumoto, On the Cable Theory of Nerve Conduction, Bulletin of Mathematical Biology 64:1069–1082 (2002): in the internode the potential spreads as ∂V/∂t = (1/(c_m r_i)) ∂²V/∂x², the time for a point to reach a given potential is proportional to x² c_m r_i, and the internodal conduction time is set by this spread; their measured frog motor fibre values (myelin capacitance 1.6 × 10⁻¹¹ F/cm, axoplasm resistance 1.45 × 10⁸ Ω/cm, 20–25 m/s) are of the same order as the model values here. Myelin lowers the capacitance and raises the resistance of the internodal membrane (Stony Brook Cellular Neurophysiology, 4.6 Conduction of Action Potentials along Axons; OpenStax College Physics 2e, 20.7 Nerve Conduction). Bare-membrane capacitance 1 µF/cm² is the standard value; axoplasm resistivity is quoted between about 70 Ω·cm (Tarotin, Aristovich and Holder, Simulation of impedance changes with a FEM model of a myelinated nerve fibre, arXiv:1903.04948, 2019, 150 lamellae, 65 m/s) and 110 Ω·cm (MIT OpenCourseWare 6.021J, 2004, problem set 8, 150 lamellae), so the passage states the value it uses (1.0 Ω·m = 100 Ω·cm). Sheaths of up to about 100 layers: Frontiers in Chemistry 10:1041961 (2022). Conduction block when a demyelinated internode lacks Na⁺ channels: Waxman and Brill, J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 41:408–416 (1978); a simulation study in Restorative Neurology and Neuroscience, vol. 3 (1991). Table values generated in review/chem_phys_batch_02_check.py; the measured velocities are set 4% below L/τ.

passages.title: pH, pKa and the oral absorption of four drugs
text: Most drugs are weak acids or weak bases. A drug crosses the lipid bilayers of the gut epithelium chiefly as its un-ionized (neutral) form; the ionized form is hydrated and crosses far more slowly. The ratio of the two forms at a given pH follows from the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation: for a weak acid HA, log([A⁻]/[HA]) = pH − pKa, and for a weak base B, log([BH⁺]/[B]) = pKa − pH, where pKa is that of the conjugate acid BH⁺. Once the neutral form has crossed a membrane it re-equilibrates at the pH of the new compartment, which can hold the drug there as its ion (ion trapping).

In a hypothetical study, four candidate drugs (W, X, Y and Z; Table 1) were characterized. Each drug's octanol–water partition coefficient was measured by shaking a solution of the drug between n-octanol and an aqueous buffer held at a pH at which the drug was more than 99% un-ionized, and was reported as log P, the logarithm of the ratio of the drug's concentration in the octanol layer to that in the water layer. The investigators treated a log P between about 1 and 3 as favourable for passive diffusion across membranes; a compound with log P below 0 partitions poorly into the bilayer however small its ionized fraction. The percentage of each drug in its un-ionized form was calculated for gastric fluid (pH 2.0) and for the fluid of the upper small intestine (pH 6.0) (Figure 1). The absorptive surface of the small intestine is many times that of the stomach.

Drug W was then prepared as two tablets of equal dose (1.0 mmol): one containing the free acid and one its sodium salt. In a dissolution test in 900 mL of simulated gastric fluid at pH 2.0 and 37 °C, 85% of the dose had dissolved from the sodium-salt tablet after 10 minutes but only 15% from the free-acid tablet. In volunteers, the peak plasma concentration was reached at 0.5 h after the salt and at 2 h after the free acid, with the same total exposure to the drug. Once in solution at pH 2.0, the drug from either tablet is in the same equilibrium between the un-ionized acid and its anion.

passages.title: Purifying a His-tagged zinc hydrolase
text: In a hypothetical purification, a zinc-dependent hydrolase from a thermophilic bacterium was expressed in Escherichia coli with a six-histidine (His₆) tag at its N-terminus; the mass of the polypeptide predicted from its sequence is 50 kDa. The cells were lysed and the debris removed by centrifugation (step 1, cleared lysate). The lysate was applied to a column of agarose beads carrying Ni²⁺ held by a chelating group; after a wash with buffer containing 20 mmol/L imidazole, the enzyme was eluted with 250 mmol/L imidazole (step 2). The eluate was passed through a gel-filtration (size-exclusion) column equilibrated in 50 mmol/L Tris, pH 7.5, 150 mmol/L NaCl, a buffer containing no nickel (step 3); against globular protein standards the enzyme eluted at a position corresponding to about 100 kDa. Finally, to remove any Ni²⁺ that had leached from the column, the pooled fractions were dialysed overnight at 4 °C against the same buffer containing 5 mmol/L EDTA (step 4); the EDTA remained in the sample.

At each step the total protein was measured by the Bradford dye-binding assay and the enzyme activity by the rate of hydrolysis of a chromogenic substrate at 37 °C; one unit (U) hydrolyses 1 µmol of substrate per minute (Table 1). Samples from each step were heated in SDS, with and without the reducing agent dithiothreitol (DTT), and run on SDS-PAGE. The lysate lane showed many bands; the lanes from steps 2, 3 and 4 each showed a single band at 50 kDa whether or not DTT had been added, and a Western blot with an antibody against the His tag stained this band. When the step 4 sample was run again on the gel-filtration column, the enzyme still eluted at about 100 kDa.

The investigators noted that the specific activity had risen at every step but the last, and considered two explanations for the fall at step 4: that EDTA had removed a metal ion the enzyme requires, or that the enzyme had been denatured during the overnight dialysis.

figures.caption: Table 1. Total protein and total activity at each step of the purification.
figures.alt: Table with four rows. Step 1, cleared lysate: 500 milligrams of protein, 2,000 units of activity. Step 2, nickel affinity eluate: 10 milligrams, 1,600 units. Step 3, gel filtration pool: 4.0 milligrams, 1,200 units. Step 4, after dialysis with EDTA: 3.8 milligrams, 760 units.

SDS-PAGE (SDS coats proteins so that charge is proportional to mass and they move at speeds inversely related to size; mercaptoethanol or DTT breaks disulfide bonds; native gels separate by charge and mass) from the same book, 8.3 Electrophoresis. Quaternary structure from OpenStax Biology 2e, 3.4 Proteins (2018). Purification-table conventions (specific activity = total activity/total protein; fold purification relative to the lysate; yield = activity recovered) from the Colorado State University handout Preparing a Summary Purification Table and the standard layout of purification tables in the literature. Zinc as an enzyme cofactor from OpenStax Biology 2e, 6.5 Enzymes; chelators strip zinc from carbonic anhydrase and Zn²⁺ restores the apoenzyme's activity (Lindskog and Malmström, J Biol Chem 237:1129 (1962); Udom and Brady, Biochem J 187:329–335 (1980)). passages.title: Doppler ultrasound of the umbilical cord
text: An ultrasound transducer contains a piezoelectric crystal that changes thickness when a voltage is applied across it and produces a voltage when a returning pressure wave compresses it, so the same crystal transmits sound and receives echoes. Echoes arise wherever the acoustic impedance (the product of density and speed of sound) changes; red blood cells scatter a small fraction of the beam back toward the probe. Sound is attenuated as it travels through tissue, and higher frequencies are attenuated more strongly over the same path. In a hypothetical examination at 36 weeks of gestation, a probe transmitting a continuous 3.00 MHz beam was placed over the mother's abdomen and aimed at loops of the umbilical cord. The speed of sound in soft tissue and blood was taken as 1,540 m/s.

Red cells moving relative to the probe shift the frequency of the echo. A cell moving toward the probe first meets wavefronts more often than a stationary reflector would, as a moving observer, and then re-emits the sound as a moving source, shortening the wavelength of the returning wave. For blood speeds v far below the speed of sound c the two shifts add, giving Equation 1, in which f₀ is the transmitted frequency and θ is the angle between the beam and the direction of flow. The scanner obtains Δf as the beat frequency between the transmitted and received signals and records it as positive for flow toward the probe.

The cord's artery and vein were examined in a loop lying along the beam (θ = 0°) and in a second loop crossing the beam at θ = 60° (Table 1). Arterial flow in the cord runs from the fetus to the placenta and is pulsatile; venous flow runs from the placenta to the fetus and is steady. In both loops the arterial blood was moving toward the probe and the venous blood away from it. The values for the artery are the peak systolic shifts.

figures.caption: Equation 1. The Doppler shift of an echo from blood moving at speed v.
figures.alt: Delta f equals f received minus f zero, equals two f zero v cosine theta divided by c.

figures.caption: Table 1. Doppler shifts recorded with the 3.00 MHz probe (artery: peak systolic; vein: steady flow).
figures.alt: Table with four rows. Umbilical artery in loop 1, angle 0 degrees, shift plus 2,000 hertz. Umbilical vein in loop 1, angle 0 degrees, shift minus 600 hertz. Umbilical artery in loop 2, angle 60 degrees, shift plus 1,000 hertz. Umbilical vein in loop 2, angle 60 degrees, shift minus 300 hertz.

The angle-corrected form Δf = 2 f₀ v cos θ / c and the practice of keeping θ below 60° from the British Medical Ultrasound Society teaching notes, Concepts of Doppler. passages.title: Bomb calorimetry of a meal bar
text: A bomb calorimeter measures the energy released when a sample burns completely. A weighed sample is sealed in a steel bomb under about 30 atm of oxygen, the bomb is submerged in a known mass of water, and the sample is ignited by a fuse wire. The temperature of the whole assembly (bomb, water and bucket) rises, and the heat released is q = CΔT, where C is the heat capacity of the assembly. C cannot be calculated from the parts with enough accuracy, so it is found by calibration, either by burning a reference material of certified heat of combustion or by delivering a measured quantity of electrical energy from a heater inside the bucket. Because the bomb's volume is fixed, the heat it releases equals the decrease in the internal energy of its contents; for foods the difference between this and the enthalpy change is well under 1% and is ignored.

In a hypothetical study, a nutrition laboratory measured the gross energy of a 50 g meal bar. The assembly was first calibrated electrically: a heater delivering a constant 110 W was switched on at t = 60 s and off at t = 360 s while the temperature was recorded (Figure 1). It was then calibrated chemically by burning a 1.000 g pellet of benzoic acid, a certified reference material with a heat of combustion of 26.4 kJ/g (Table 1). Finally a 1.000 g sample of the dried, ground bar was burned under identical conditions (Table 1). The small corrections for the fuse wire were applied before the values in Table 1 were recorded.

Food labels do not report gross energy. The Atwater general factors (Table 2) estimate the metabolizable energy: the gross energy less the energy lost in faeces and urine. Fat and available carbohydrate are oxidized in the body to the same final products as in the bomb, carbon dioxide and water, so for them only incomplete digestion is deducted. Protein is different: in the bomb its nitrogen ends up mainly as N₂, whereas the body excretes nitrogen chiefly as urea, which still has combustion energy, so protein's gross energy of about 23.6 kJ/g is reduced to 17 kJ/g. Dietary fibre is not digested by human enzymes and is only partly fermented by colonic bacteria. Because enthalpy is a state function, the energy released when glucose is oxidized to carbon dioxide and water is the same whether it burns in the bomb in a fraction of a second or passes through glycolysis, the citric acid cycle and the electron transport chain. To compare pathways, the investigators used rounded standard enthalpies of combustion of −2,800 kJ/mol for glucose and −1,360 kJ/mol for lactic acid.

figures.alt: Line graph of temperature in degrees Celsius against time in seconds. The temperature is 25.00 °C from 0 to 60 s, rises in a straight line while the heater runs, reaching 25.60 at 120 s, 26.20 at 180 s, 26.80 at 240 s, 27.40 at 300 s and 28.00 °C at 360 s, then stays at 28.00 °C to 480 s.

figures.alt: Table with two rows. Calibration run: benzoic acid, 1.000 g, temperature rise 2.40 K. Sample run: meal bar, 1.000 g, temperature rise 2.00 K.

passages.title: Mass spectrometry of a tryptic peptide
text: In matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization (MALDI) mass spectrometry, the sample is co-crystallized with a matrix, an aromatic acid that absorbs the laser's wavelength. A laser pulse vaporizes a little of the crystal, and the matrix transfers a proton to most sample molecules, giving [M + H]⁺ ions; a few molecules gain two protons. The ions are accelerated through a potential difference V, so a singly charged ion acquires kinetic energy eV, where e is the elementary charge, and an ion of charge number z acquires zeV. They then drift down a field-free tube of length L and reach the detector after a time t = L/v, the time of flight. The spectrum plots detector signal against m/z, the mass in daltons (1 Da = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) divided by the charge number. The most intense peak of a small peptide is its monoisotopic peak, in which every atom is the lightest isotope; the peak one unit higher comes from molecules containing one heavy atom, mostly carbon-13, whose natural abundance the investigators took as 1.1%.

In a hypothetical study, a 21 kDa recombinant protein expressed in insect cells was suspected of carrying a post-translational modification. The protein was digested with trypsin, which cleaves on the carboxyl side of lysine and arginine, and the peptides were analysed by MALDI time-of-flight at V = 20 kV with L = 2.0 m; singly charged ions of m/z 900 reached the detector 30.5 µs after the laser pulse. Five peptides were detected (Figure 1). Four of them, T1, T2, T4 and T5, matched the masses predicted from the gene sequence within 0.1 Da. T3, whose predicted sequence is Ala-Tyr-Ser-Leu-Gln-Asp-Val-Phe-Lys with a predicted [M + H]⁺ of 1,070.55, instead appeared at 1,150.52, a difference of 79.97 Da. Phosphorylation of a serine, threonine or tyrosine side chain adds HPO₃, 79.97 Da, and the investigators adopted this as their working hypothesis.

To locate the modification, T3 ions were selected, fragmented along the peptide backbone, and the fragments were analysed in a second stage. Fragments that retain the C-terminal lysine (the y series) form a ladder in which each member differs from the next by the mass of one amino acid residue (Table 2; residue masses in Table 1). The neutral mass of any peptide is the sum of its residue masses plus the mass of water (18.01 Da) for the two termini, and the [M + H]⁺ ion is one unit heavier still. A second sample of the protein was digested with chymotrypsin, which cleaves on the carboxyl side of phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan, and its peptides were analysed in the same way.

passages.title: Presbyopia and reading lenses
text: The cornea and the lens of the eye together form a real, inverted image on the retina, about 2.0 cm behind the lens. Light is bent at each boundary according to Snell's law, n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, where the refractive indices are about 1.00 for air, 1.38 for the cornea, 1.34 for the aqueous humour in front of the lens, 1.41 for the lens itself and 1.34 for the vitreous humour behind it. The power of a lens is P = 1/f, in diopters (D) when the focal length f is in metres, and the powers of thin lenses in contact add. The relaxed eye has a total power of about 50 D; to focus an object 25 cm away it must reach about 54 D, which it does by accommodation, the ciliary muscle thickening the lens. The far point is the greatest distance at which an object is seen sharply with the eye relaxed (infinity for a normal eye) and the near point the smallest distance at which it is seen sharply with full accommodation. The amplitude of accommodation, in diopters, is 1/(near point) − 1/(far point), with distances in metres. With age the lens stiffens, the amplitude falls and the near point recedes beyond comfortable reading distance: presbyopia.

In a hypothetical clinic study, the near point and far point of three patients were measured without lenses (Table 1). The clinic takes 25 cm as the standard reading distance and treats a spectacle lens as a thin lens placed at the eye, neglecting the small separation between them. Lenses are prescribed with the thin-lens equation 1/dₒ + 1/dᵢ = 1/f, in which a virtual image, formed on the same side of the lens as the object, has a negative image distance. A reading lens must form a virtual image of the page, held at 25 cm, at the patient's near point, where the eye can focus it; a distance lens must form a virtual image of a distant object at the patient's far point.
Patient C, who is myopic, reported reading comfortably without spectacles but seeing distant objects blurred.

figures.caption: Table 1. Near point and far point, in centimetres, of the three patients, measured with the eye unaided (∞ = infinity).
figures.alt: Table with three rows. Patient A, age 48, near point 50 cm, far point infinity. Patient B, age 58, near point 100 cm, far point infinity. Patient C, age 50, near point 25 cm, far point 50 cm.

Correction of myopia with a diverging lens that forms a virtual image at the far point, of hyperopia with a converging lens that forms a virtual image at the near point, the sign convention (virtual image distance negative) and the use of P = 1/dₒ + 1/dᵢ from OpenStax College Physics 2e, 26.2 Vision Correction (Examples 26.3 and 26.4; the clinic in this passage neglects the 1.5 cm lens–eye separation those examples include, and says so). passages.title: An electrochemical glucose test strip
text: Glucose oxidase is a flavoprotein oxidoreductase: each subunit holds one tightly bound flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD). It oxidizes β-D-glucose at C1 to D-glucono-1,5-lactone in two half-steps. First, glucose reduces the enzyme's FAD: glucose + GOx·FAD → gluconolactone + GOx·FADH₂. Second, the natural electron acceptor, oxygen, re-oxidizes the flavin: GOx·FADH₂ + O₂ → GOx·FAD + H₂O₂. First-generation glucose sensors oxidized the hydrogen peroxide at a platinum electrode held near +0.6 V against a reference electrode and measured the current, but the reading depended on the oxygen content of the sample, and at that potential ascorbate, urate and acetaminophen in blood are also oxidized.

In a hypothetical second-generation strip, glucose oxidase and a large excess of potassium ferricyanide, K₃Fe(CN)₆, are dried onto a carbon working electrode. A 1 µL drop of blood rehydrates the layer. Glucose reduces the enzyme's FAD as before, but ferricyanide now takes the electrons: GOx·FADH₂ + 2 Fe(CN)₆³⁻ → GOx·FAD + 2 Fe(CN)₆⁴⁻ + 2 H⁺. After a 5.0 s incubation the meter applies +0.3 V between the working electrode and the reference electrode, re-oxidizing the ferrocyanide formed, Fe(CN)₆⁴⁻ → Fe(CN)₆³⁻ + e⁻, and records the current for 5.0 s; each glucose molecule therefore delivers two electrons to the electrode. For a calibration sample the average current over the measurement was 10 µA. Table 1 lists the standard reduction potentials at pH 7 that the investigators used; for FAD they used the value for the free coenzyme, noting that the potential of enzyme-bound FAD differs.

The investigators also made open-circuit measurements, in which no current flows and the electrode potential follows the Nernst equation for the ferricyanide/ferrocyanide couple: E = E°′ − (0.0592 V) log([Fe(CN)₆⁴⁻]/[Fe(CN)₆³⁻]). In a fresh strip the ferrocyanide:ferricyanide ratio is about 1:100. Dissolved oxygen can still compete with ferricyanide for the reduced enzyme, diverting electrons into hydrogen peroxide, which is not oxidized at +0.3 V; the ferricyanide is loaded in excess so that it outcompetes oxygen, and the investigators planned a test of the residual interference. Venous blood carries less oxygen than arterial blood, and capillary blood from a fingertip lies between the two.

figures.caption: Table 1. Standard reduction potentials at pH 7 and 25 °C used by the investigators, in volts against the standard hydrogen electrode. The FAD value is that of the free coenzyme.
figures.alt: Table with three rows. Oxygen plus two protons plus two electrons to hydrogen peroxide, plus 0.30 V. Ferricyanide plus one electron to ferrocyanide, plus 0.36 V. FAD plus two protons plus two electrons to FADH₂ (free coenzyme), minus 0.22 V.

passages.source: Hypothetical study written for this app. Glucose oxidase reaction β-D-glucose + O₂ = D-glucono-1,5-lactone + H₂O₂ from ExPASy ENZYME entry EC 1.1.3.4; the two half-steps with GOx/FAD and GOx/FADH₂, the oxygen dependence of first-generation H₂O₂-detecting electrodes, second-generation mediated electrodes that are 'relatively insensitive to changes in dioxygen tension' and run at lower potentials, and ascorbate interference from Lowry, McAteer, El Atrash, Duff and O'Neill, Characterization of glucose oxidase-modified poly(phenylenediamine)-coated electrodes in vitro and in vivo, Analytical Chemistry 66:1754–1761 (1994). The three generations of biosensors, the mediated scheme glucose + GOD(ox) → gluconolactone + GOD(red) + 2H⁺, GOD(red) + 2 mediator(ox) → GOD(ox) + 2 mediator(red), mediator re-oxidation at the electrode, ferricyanide and ferrocene as mediators, the requirement that a mediator 'should not react with oxygen', and the H₂O₂ oxidation potential of about +0.65 V from Eggins, Chemical Sensors and Biosensors (Wiley 2002), chapter 5, Amperometric biosensors. Standard reduction potential of Fe(CN)₆³⁻/Fe(CN)₆⁴⁻ +0.356 V from Chemistry LibreTexts, P1: Standard Reduction Potentials by Element (rounded to +0.36; the formal potential depends on the medium and is quoted as high as +0.45 V in some biosensor tables, so the passage states the value it uses). FAD/FADH₂ (free coenzyme) −0.22 V and O₂/H₂O₂ +0.30 V at pH 7 from the standard reduction potential table in Jakubowski, Biochemistry Online (CSB/SJU), Oxidative Phosphorylation: Dehydrogenases (free FAD is −0.219 V in other biochemistry tables; enzyme-bound FAD ranges from about 0.00 to −0.09 V, as the passage notes; O₂/H₂O₂ is +0.695 V at pH 0 in the LibreTexts table, which gives +0.28 V when shifted to pH 7). Nernst equation at 25 °C, E = E° − (0.0592 V/n) log Q, and ΔG° = −nFE° from OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 17.4 Potential, Free Energy, and Equilibrium (2019); Q = It and n = Q/F with F = 96,485 C/mol from OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 17.7 Electrolysis; Faraday constant 96,485.332 C/mol from NIST CODATA 2022. Every potential and charge in the items is re-derived in review/chem_phys_batch_03_check.py.

items.stem: A block of wood with a density of 600 kg/m³ and a volume of 0.020 m³ floats at rest in fresh water (density 1,000 kg/m³). The volume of the block that is above the waterline is:
why_correct: A floating object displaces its own weight of fluid. Weight of block = buoyant force: ρ_wood V g = ρ_water V_sub g, so the submerged fraction is V_sub/V = ρ_wood/ρ_water = 600/1,000 = 0.60.
Submerged volume = 0.60 × 0.020 m³ = 0.012 m³, so the part above water is 0.020 − 0.012 = 0.008 m³.
Sense check: a block less dense than water floats with a fraction equal to its relative density under water; 60% under, 40% above.

why_wrong.B: 0.012 m³ is the volume below the waterline (60% of the block), not the volume above it.
why_wrong.C: 0.020 m³ is the whole block; a floating block must have part of its volume submerged to displace enough water to support its weight.
why_wrong.D: 0.033 m³ comes from inverting the density ratio (1,000/600 × 0.020); the submerged volume cannot exceed the block's volume.

error_types.B: reversed relationship: submerged volume given instead of the exposed volume
error_types.C: wrong formula: no displacement considered
error_types.D: reversed relationship: density ratio inverted

items.takeaway: For a floating object, the submerged fraction equals the ratio of its density to the fluid's density.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 11.7 Archimedes' Principle (2022): a floating object displaces a weight of fluid equal to its own weight; fraction submerged = ρ_object/ρ_fluid.

items.stem: A pressure sensor lowered into a lake records absolute pressures of 101 kPa at the surface, 150 kPa at 5.0 m, 199 kPa at 10.0 m and 248 kPa at 15.0 m. Taking g = 9.8 m/s², the density of the lake water is closest to:
why_correct: Pressure in a fluid at rest rises linearly with depth: P = P₀ + ρgh. The readings rise by 49 kPa for every 5.0 m, a slope of 9.8 kPa/m, and the constant slope confirms the linear model.
Check one point: 101 kPa + 1,000 × 9.8 × 10.0 = 101 + 98 = 199 kPa, as recorded.

why_wrong.A: 100 kg/m³ would give only 4.9 kPa per 5 m; the readings rise ten times faster.
why_wrong.C: 1,025 kg/m³ is typical of sea water; it would give 50.2 kPa per 5 m, and the data (49.0 kPa per 5 m) fit fresh water, as expected for a lake.
why_wrong.D: 9,800 is the slope in Pa/m, that is, ρg; dividing by g is still needed to get the density.

error_types.A: sign or unit error: a factor of ten lost converting kPa/m to Pa/m
error_types.C: true but irrelevant: a sea-water value applied to a lake
error_types.D: wrong formula: ρg reported as ρ

items.takeaway: Gauge pressure in a static fluid is ρgh: the slope of pressure against depth is ρg.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 11.4 Variation of Pressure with Depth in a Fluid (2022): P = hρg for a fluid of uniform density; fluid pressures add.
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 11.6 Gauge Pressure, Absolute Pressure, and Pressure Measurement (2022): absolute pressure = gauge pressure + atmospheric pressure.

items.stem: Blood flows through an arteriole under a fixed pressure difference. If smooth-muscle contraction reduces the arteriole's radius by 20% while its length and the blood's viscosity stay the same, the volume flow rate becomes about:
why_correct: Poiseuille's law for laminar flow: Q = πr⁴ΔP/(8ηL). With ΔP, η and L fixed, Q is proportional to r⁴.
The new radius is 0.80 r, so Q_new/Q_old = 0.80⁴ = 0.64 × 0.64 = 0.41. The flow falls to about 41%.
This fourth-power dependence is why small changes in arteriolar radius give the body powerful control over blood flow and resistance.

why_wrong.B: 64% is 0.80², the change in cross-sectional area; flow through a tube depends on the fourth power of the radius, not the second.
why_wrong.C: 80% assumes flow is proportional to radius; it is proportional to r⁴.
why_wrong.D: 125% is 1/0.80, as if a narrower vessel carried more flow at the same pressure difference; narrowing raises resistance and lowers flow.

error_types.B: wrong formula: r² (area) used instead of r⁴
error_types.C: wrong formula: linear dependence on r assumed
error_types.D: reversed relationship: flow taken to rise when the vessel narrows

items.takeaway: Laminar flow through a tube scales with r⁴ (Poiseuille): a 20% narrowing cuts flow to about 41% at the same pressure difference.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 12.4 Viscosity and Laminar Flow; Poiseuille's Law (2022): Q = (P₂ − P₁)πr⁴/(8ηl); resistance varies as 1/r⁴, which is how the body regulates blood flow.

items.stem: Water flows steadily through a horizontal pipe whose diameter narrows from 4.0 cm to 2.0 cm. If the speed in the wide section is 1.0 m/s, the speed in the narrow section is:
why_correct: For an incompressible fluid the volume flow rate is the same everywhere along the pipe: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ (the continuity equation).
Area scales with the square of the diameter, so halving the diameter divides the area by 4 and the speed must rise by 4: v₂ = 1.0 m/s × (4.0/2.0)² = 4.0 m/s.
Check: Q = A₁v₁ = π(0.020 m)² × 1.0 m/s ≈ 1.26 × 10⁻³ m³/s, and π(0.010 m)² × 4.0 m/s gives the same value.

why_wrong.A: 0.25 m/s would be the speed if the pipe widened by this ratio; the narrow section must carry the same flow through a smaller area, so the fluid speeds up.
why_wrong.B: 2.0 m/s uses the ratio of diameters rather than of areas; area goes as diameter squared.
why_wrong.D: 8.0 m/s uses the cube of the diameter ratio; area, not volume, sets the speed.

error_types.A: reversed relationship: speed decreased in the narrower section
error_types.B: wrong formula: diameter ratio used instead of area ratio
error_types.D: wrong formula: diameter ratio cubed

items.takeaway: Continuity: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, and area scales with diameter squared, so halving the diameter quadruples the speed.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 12.1 Flow Rate and Its Relation to Velocity (2022): Q = Av; for an incompressible fluid A₁v₁ = A₂v₂.

items.stem: A student records readings along a horizontal pipe carrying water (density 1,000 kg/m³): in section 1 the pressure is 150 kPa and the speed 1.0 m/s; in section 2 the speed is 5.0 m/s. Assuming ideal flow, the pressure in section 2 is closest to:
why_correct: Bernoulli's equation for a horizontal pipe (no height change): P₁ + ½ρv₁² = P₂ + ½ρv₂².
Sense check: the fluid speeds up in section 2, so its pressure must be lower there; the drop in pressure is what accelerates the water.

why_wrong.A: 126 kPa subtracts 24 kPa, leaving out the factor of ½ in the kinetic-energy term.
why_wrong.C: 150 kPa assumes the pressure is unchanged; where the speed rises, the pressure falls.
why_wrong.D: 162 kPa adds the kinetic term instead of subtracting it, as if the faster section were at higher pressure.

error_types.A: wrong formula: the ½ dropped from ½ρv²
error_types.C: wrong formula: pressure assumed constant along a pipe with changing speed
error_types.D: reversed relationship: sign of the pressure change reversed

items.takeaway: Along a horizontal streamline, P + ½ρv² is constant: faster flow means lower pressure.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 12.2 Bernoulli's Equation (2022): P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant; for constant height, P₁ + ½ρv₁² = P₂ + ½ρv₂².

items.stem: According to the Reynolds number for flow in a tube, which single change makes the onset of turbulence in a blood vessel more likely?

options.A: A decrease in the flow speed
options.B: An increase in the viscosity of the blood
options.C: An increase in the vessel's diameter at the same flow speed
options.D: A decrease in the density of the blood

why_correct: The Reynolds number for flow in a tube is Re = 2ρvr/η (ρ density, v mean speed, r radius, η viscosity). Flow is laminar below about 2,000 and turbulent above about 3,000.
Re grows with density, speed and radius and falls with viscosity, so a wider vessel at the same speed raises Re and favours turbulence.

This is why turbulence (and the sounds it makes) appears in the aorta and at narrowings or damaged valves rather than in capillaries; because anaemia lowers blood viscosity, it also makes turbulent flow more likely.

why_wrong.A: Lower speed lowers Re and makes laminar flow more likely.
why_wrong.B: Higher viscosity is in the denominator of Re; thicker fluid damps turbulence.
why_wrong.D: Lower density lowers Re, since inertial forces, which drive turbulence, scale with density.

error_types.A: reversed relationship: speed lowers Re, not raises it
error_types.B: reversed relationship: viscosity opposes turbulence
error_types.D: reversed relationship: density favours turbulence

items.takeaway: Re = 2ρvr/η: turbulence is favoured by high density, speed and radius and by low viscosity.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 12.5 The Onset of Turbulence (2022): Reynolds number N_R = 2ρvr/η; laminar below 2,000, turbulent above 3,000; turbulence in blood flow and its sounds.
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 20.2 Blood Flow, Blood Pressure, and Resistance (2022): conditions such as anemia or polycythemia change blood viscosity.

items.stem: The combined cross-sectional area of all the body's capillaries is roughly 1,000 times the cross-sectional area of the aorta. If blood leaves the heart through the aorta at a mean speed of about 30 cm/s, the mean speed of blood in a capillary is about:
why_correct: The volume flow rate is conserved: all the blood that passes through the aorta each second passes through the capillaries together. Continuity gives A_aorta v_aorta = A_cap v_cap.
v_cap = v_aorta × (A_aorta/A_cap) = 30 cm/s ÷ 1,000 = 0.03 cm/s, about 0.3 mm/s.
The slow capillary flow gives time for exchange of gases and nutrients across the capillary wall; the speed rises again in the veins as the total area falls.

why_wrong.B: 0.3 cm/s would need an area ratio of 100, ten times smaller than stated.
why_wrong.C: 3 cm/s divides by only 10; the question states a factor of 1,000.
why_wrong.D: 30 cm/s assumes the speed is unchanged; the same flow spread over a far larger area must move much more slowly.

error_types.B: sign or unit error: a factor of 10 lost
error_types.C: sign or unit error: a factor of 100 lost
error_types.D: wrong formula: continuity ignored

items.takeaway: Blood speed is inversely proportional to total cross-sectional area; it is slowest in the capillaries, where the total area is greatest.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 12.1 Flow Rate and Its Relation to Velocity (2022): the continuity equation applied to branching vessels; flow speed falls as total cross-sectional area rises.

OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 20.2 Blood Flow, Blood Pressure, and Resistance (2022): the total cross-sectional area of the capillary beds is far greater than that of any other vessel type; blood velocity falls dramatically from arteries to capillaries, allowing time for exchange, and rises again in the veins as total area falls.

items.stem: A 2.0 L sample of an ideal gas at 300 K and 2.0 atm is warmed to 450 K while its pressure is reduced to 1.0 atm. The amount of gas is unchanged. Its new volume is:
why_correct: For a fixed amount of ideal gas, PV/T is constant (combined gas law): V₂ = V₁ × (P₁/P₂) × (T₂/T₁).
Both changes expand the gas: halving the pressure doubles the volume and raising the absolute temperature by half enlarges it by half again.

why_wrong.A: 0.67 L inverts both ratios, as if higher temperature and lower pressure both shrank the gas.
why_wrong.B: 1.5 L applies the pressure ratio upside down (1.0/2.0) and keeps the temperature ratio right.
why_wrong.C: 3.0 L accounts for the temperature rise but ignores the halving of the pressure.

error_types.A: reversed relationship: both ratios inverted
error_types.B: reversed relationship: pressure ratio inverted
error_types.C: wrong formula: pressure change omitted

items.takeaway: Combined gas law: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ with temperatures in kelvin; lower pressure and higher temperature both increase volume.
sources: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 9.2 Relating Pressure, Volume, Amount, and Temperature: The Ideal Gas Law (2019): combined gas law P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂.

items.stem: At the same temperature, the root-mean-square speed of hydrogen molecules (H₂, molar mass 2 g/mol) compared with that of oxygen molecules (O₂, molar mass 32 g/mol) is:
why_correct: Kinetic theory gives the same average translational kinetic energy, (3/2)kT, to every molecule at a given temperature, so lighter molecules move faster: v_rms = √(3RT/M).
The same √(1/M) dependence underlies Graham's law of effusion: hydrogen effuses four times as fast as oxygen.

why_wrong.A: 1/16 inverts the ratio and also forgets the square root.
why_wrong.B: 1/4 has the right size but the wrong direction; the lighter gas is the faster one.
why_wrong.D: 16 is the molar-mass ratio itself; speed depends on the square root of the mass ratio.

error_types.A: reversed relationship: inverted and square root omitted
error_types.B: reversed relationship: lighter molecules are faster, not slower
error_types.D: wrong formula: square root omitted

items.takeaway: v_rms = √(3RT/M): at equal temperature, speeds scale with 1/√M, so H₂ moves four times as fast as O₂.
sources: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 9.5 The Kinetic-Molecular Theory (2019): u_rms = √(3RT/M); molecules of lighter gases have higher speeds at the same temperature; Graham's law.
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 13.4 Kinetic Theory: Atomic and Molecular Explanation of Pressure and Temperature (2022): average kinetic energy (3/2)kT; v_rms = √(3kT/m).

items.stem: A researcher wants to test the hypothesis that the rate at which oxygen dissolves into a stirred solution depends on the partial pressure of O₂ above it and not on the total gas pressure. Which pair of conditions most directly tests whether total pressure has an effect of its own?

options.A: Pure O₂ at 1.0 atm versus air (21% O₂) at 1.0 atm
options.B: Air at 1.0 atm versus a 21% O₂ in helium mixture at 1.0 atm
options.C: Air at 1.0 atm versus air at 5.0 atm
options.D: Air at 1.0 atm versus a 4.2% O₂ in nitrogen mixture at 5.0 atm

why_correct: To show that partial pressure, not total pressure, is what matters, hold the partial pressure of O₂ fixed while changing the total pressure. By Dalton's law P_O₂ = x_O₂ × P_total: air at 1.0 atm gives 0.21 × 1.0 = 0.21 atm, and 4.2% O₂ at 5.0 atm gives 0.042 × 5.0 = 0.21 atm.
If the dissolution rate is the same in both, total pressure has no effect of its own and the hypothesis survives; if it differs, total pressure matters.
This is the logic of a controlled comparison: change only the variable you want to rule out.

why_wrong.A: This changes the O₂ partial pressure (1.0 versus 0.21 atm) at constant total pressure. It can show that partial pressure matters, but it never varies total pressure, so it cannot test whether total pressure matters too.
why_wrong.B: Both mixtures have the same O₂ partial pressure and the same total pressure; this tests whether the other gas (nitrogen versus helium) matters, not the role of total pressure.
why_wrong.C: Raising the total pressure of air five-fold also raises the O₂ partial pressure five-fold, so the two variables change together and cannot be separated.

error_types.A: true but irrelevant: tests the first half of the hypothesis only
error_types.B: out of scope: varies the diluent gas, not the pressures
error_types.C: wrong formula: P_O₂ treated as independent of total pressure

items.takeaway: Dalton's law: P_gas = mole fraction × P_total; to isolate partial pressure, vary total pressure while holding the partial pressure fixed.
sources: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 9.3 Stoichiometry of Gaseous Substances, Mixtures, and Reactions (2019): Dalton's law of partial pressures, P_A = X_A × P_total.

OpenStax Biology 2e, 1.1 The Science of Biology (2018): a control group has every feature of the experimental group except the hypothesized manipulation, so any difference must come from that manipulation.

items.stem: A nurse lifts a 2.0 kg infusion pump from the floor onto a shelf 1.5 m high, moving it at constant speed. Taking g = 9.8 m/s², the work the nurse does against gravity is closest to:
why_correct: At constant speed the lifting force just balances the weight, so the work against gravity equals the gain in gravitational potential energy: W = mgh.
W = (2.0 kg)(9.8 m/s²)(1.5 m) = 29.4 J, which rounds to 30 J. Estimate: 2 × 10 × 1.5 = 30 J. Check the units: kg·m/s²·m = N·m = J.
Second route: the weight is 2.0 × 9.8 ≈ 20 N; a 20 N force through 1.5 m does 30 J of work.

why_wrong.A: 3 J is m × h without g: 2.0 × 1.5. Weight is mg, not m, so this answer is off by a factor of about 10.
why_wrong.B: 15 J is half the correct value, as if the lift stored ½mgh. The ½ belongs to kinetic energy (½mv²) and spring energy (½kx²), not to gravitational potential energy.
why_wrong.D: 60 J doubles the correct value, which would follow from using g ≈ 20 m/s² or counting the weight twice.

error_types.A: sign or unit error: dropped g, multiplying mass by height
error_types.B: wrong formula: applied the ½ from kinetic energy to mgh
error_types.D: wrong formula: doubled g or counted the force twice

items.takeaway: Work against gravity at constant speed equals mgh; with g ≈ 10 m/s² a 2 kg mass lifted 1.5 m takes about 30 J.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 7.3 Gravitational Potential Energy (2022): ΔPE_g = mgh for a mass raised a height h near Earth's surface.
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 7.1 Work: The Scientific Definition (2022): W = Fd cos θ with the lifting force parallel to the displacement.

items.stem: In a bench-top electrophoresis power circuit, a 10 Ω resistor and a 15 Ω resistor are connected in parallel, and that pair is connected in series with a 3 Ω resistor across an 18 V supply of negligible internal resistance. What current does the supply deliver?
why_correct: Reduce the parallel pair first: 1/R = 1/10 + 1/15 = 3/30 + 2/30 = 5/30, so R = 6 Ω. A parallel combination is always smaller than its smallest member, so 6 Ω is sensible.
That 6 Ω sits in series with 3 Ω, giving a total of 9 Ω. Ohm's law: I = V/R = 18 V / 9 Ω = 2 A.
Second route: the 2 A through the 3 Ω resistor drops 6 V, leaving 12 V across the parallel pair; 12 V/10 Ω + 12 V/15 Ω = 1.2 A + 0.8 A = 2 A, consistent.

why_wrong.A: 0.6 A comes from adding all three resistors in series (28 Ω) and dividing 18 V by 28 Ω. The 10 Ω and 15 Ω resistors share the same voltage, so they are in parallel, not series.
why_wrong.C: 3 A is 18 V divided by the 6 Ω parallel combination alone, ignoring the 3 Ω resistor in series with it.
why_wrong.D: 6 A is 18 V divided by the 3 Ω resistor alone, ignoring the parallel pair that adds 6 Ω to the path.

error_types.A: wrong formula: treated the parallel pair as series resistors
error_types.C: wrong formula: dropped the series resistor from the total resistance
error_types.D: wrong formula: dropped the parallel pair from the total resistance

items.takeaway: Collapse parallel groups first (reciprocals add), then add series resistances, then apply I = V/R once.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 21.1 Resistors in Series and Parallel (2022): R_s = R₁ + R₂ + …; 1/R_p = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …; combinations are reduced in stages.
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 20.2 Ohm's Law: Resistance and Simple Circuits (2022): I = V/R.

items.stem: The glass core of an endoscope's optical fibre has a refractive index of 1.60 and is surrounded by a cladding of index 1.28. Light inside the core is totally internally reflected at the core–cladding boundary when its angle of incidence, measured from the normal, is greater than approximately:
why_correct: Total internal reflection occurs only when light travels from a higher-index medium toward a lower-index one, and the critical angle satisfies sin θc = n₂/n₁.
sin θc = 1.28/1.60 = 0.80. The 3-4-5 triangle gives sin 53° ≈ 0.80, so θc ≈ 53°; any incidence angle larger than that is reflected completely.

Second route: Snell's law with the refracted ray at 90°: 1.60 sin θc = 1.28 sin 90° = 1.28, so sin θc = 0.80, as before. Check: 0.80 lies between sin 45° (0.71) and sin 60° (0.87), so the answer must be between 45° and 60°.

why_wrong.A: 37° is the complement of 53° (cos 53° = 0.60). It would follow from measuring the angle from the boundary surface instead of from the normal, or from reading sin and cos backward.
why_wrong.B: 45° corresponds to a ratio of 0.71, which would need a cladding index of about 1.13 with this core.
why_wrong.D: 60° corresponds to a ratio of 0.87; it would also result from using 1.28/1.60 with a wrong value of sin 60°.

error_types.A: reversed relationship: angle taken from the surface rather than the normal (sin and cos swapped)
error_types.B: wrong formula: guessed the 45° value instead of computing n₂/n₁
error_types.D: misread graph: wrong trigonometric value for the 0.80 ratio

items.takeaway: Critical angle: sin θc = n₂/n₁ (lower index over higher); a ratio of 0.80 means about 53°.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 25.4 Total Internal Reflection (2022): θc = sin⁻¹(n₂/n₁) for n₁ > n₂; fibre optics use a core of higher index than the cladding.
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 25.3 The Law of Refraction (2022): n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂.

items.stem: Technetium-99m, used in nuclear medicine imaging, has a half-life of about 6.0 hours. A syringe is calibrated to contain 800 MBq at 8:00 a.m. If the dose is not used until 8:00 p.m. the same day, the activity remaining is closest to:
why_correct: Radioactive decay is first-order: after each half-life the activity halves. From 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. is 12 hours, which is 12/6 = 2 half-lives.
800 MBq → 400 MBq after the first half-life → 200 MBq after the second. In one step: A = A₀(½)ⁿ = 800 × ¼ = 200 MBq.
Second route: the decay constant is λ = 0.693/6.0 h ≈ 0.116 h⁻¹; λt = 0.116 × 12 ≈ 1.39, and e⁻¹·³⁹ ≈ 0.25, giving 800 × 0.25 = 200 MBq.

why_wrong.A: 100 MBq would need three half-lives (18 hours), that is, 2:00 a.m. the next day.
why_wrong.C: 400 MBq is one half-life's worth of decay, which would be the activity at 2:00 p.m., not 8:00 p.m. Twelve hours is two half-lives, not one.
why_wrong.D: 570 MBq comes from inverting the exponent: 800 × (½)^(6/12) = 800 × 0.71. The number of half-lives is elapsed time ÷ half-life = 12/6 = 2, not 6/12.

error_types.A: wrong formula: used three half-lives instead of two
error_types.C: sign or unit error: counted the 12-hour interval as one half-life
error_types.D: wrong formula: inverted the exponent (half-life ÷ time instead of time ÷ half-life)

items.takeaway: Count half-lives (elapsed time ÷ half-life) and halve the activity that many times; two half-lives leave one-quarter.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 31.5 Half-Life and Activity (2022): N = N₀e^(−λt), t½ = 0.693/λ, and the activity falls by half each half-life.
OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 21.5 Uses of Radioisotopes (2019): the ubiquitous Tc-99m has a half-life of 6.01 hours.
Brookhaven National Laboratory, NuDat 3 / ENSDF (accessed 2026): Tc-99m half-life 6.0072 h (DDEP/LNHB recommends 6.0067 h).

items.stem: A researcher prepares a phosphate buffer for an enzyme assay that contains 20 mM HPO₄²⁻ and 2 mM H₂PO₄⁻. The pKa of H₂PO₄⁻ is 7.2. The pH of the buffer is closest to:
why_correct: H₂PO₄⁻ is the acid of this pair and HPO₄²⁻ its conjugate base. Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([base]/[acid]) = 7.2 + log(20/2) = 7.2 + log 10 = 7.2 + 1 = 8.2.
Sense check: there is ten times more base than acid, so the pH must sit one unit above the pKa, on the basic side. A buffer this lopsided is near the edge of its useful range (about pKa ± 1).
Second route: Ka = [H⁺][HPO₄²⁻]/[H₂PO₄⁻], so [H⁺] = Ka × (2/20) = Ka/10 = 10⁻⁷·² /10 = 10⁻⁸·², giving pH 8.2.

why_wrong.A: 6.2 results from inverting the ratio, log(2/20) = −1, treating HPO₄²⁻ as the acid. The species with the extra proton (H₂PO₄⁻) is the acid.
why_wrong.B: 7.2 is the pKa, which equals the pH only when acid and base are present in equal amounts. Here they differ tenfold.
why_wrong.C: 7.7 would correspond to a base:acid ratio of about 3:1 (log 3 ≈ 0.5), not 10:1.

error_types.A: reversed relationship: acid and conjugate base swapped in the ratio
error_types.B: true but irrelevant: pH equals pKa only at a 1:1 ratio
error_types.C: wrong formula: log of the ratio miscomputed (log 10 = 1, not 0.5)

items.takeaway: pH = pKa + log(base/acid); each tenfold excess of base adds one pH unit above the pKa.
sources: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 14.6 Buffers (2019): Henderson–Hasselbalch equation pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]).
Chemistry LibreTexts, Henderson–Hasselbalch Approximation (2023): the effective buffer range spans about two pH units centred on the pKa.
OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Appendix H (2019): Ka₂ of phosphoric acid (H₂PO₄⁻) = 6.2 × 10⁻⁸, pKa ≈ 7.2.

items.stem: A student measures the initial rate of a digestive enzyme at pH 5, 7, and 9 with the substrate at saturating concentration and finds the rate highest at pH 7. The student concludes that the enzyme's optimum pH is 7. Which additional measurement would most strengthen this conclusion?

options.A: Measuring the rate at pH 6 and pH 8 under the same conditions
options.B: Repeating the pH 7 trial with twice as much enzyme
options.C: Measuring the rate at pH 7 with half the substrate concentration
options.D: Measuring the rate at pH 7 at a higher temperature

why_correct: Three widely spaced pH values can only show that 7 beats 5 and 9; the true optimum could lie anywhere between about 5 and 9. Sampling pH 6 and 8 narrows the peak and tests whether 7 really is the maximum rather than a point on a slope.
Keeping substrate saturating and everything else the same isolates pH as the only variable, which is what the conclusion is about.
Design principle: to locate an optimum, sample more densely around the apparent peak while holding other variables fixed.

why_wrong.B: Doubling the enzyme raises the rate at every pH proportionally and says nothing about where the optimum lies.
why_wrong.C: Lowering substrate below saturation changes the rate for kinetic reasons unrelated to pH and would confound the comparison.
why_wrong.D: Changing temperature introduces a second variable; it would test temperature dependence, not pin down the pH optimum.

error_types.B: true but irrelevant: enzyme amount scales rate without locating the optimum
error_types.C: true but irrelevant: substrate concentration is a different variable
error_types.D: true but irrelevant: adds a second variable instead of resolving the first

items.takeaway: To pin down an optimum, measure more points around the apparent peak while holding every other variable constant.
sources: OpenStax Biology 2e, 6.5 Enzymes (2018): each enzyme has an optimal pH and temperature; activity falls away from the optimum as the active site's shape and charges change.
OpenStax Biology 2e, 1.1 The Science of Biology (2018): a controlled experiment changes one variable between the experimental and control groups and holds the rest constant.

items.stem: In aqueous solution, D-glucose exists mostly as a six-membered ring (glucopyranose). The ring forms when one of the sugar's own hydroxyl groups adds to its aldehyde carbon. Which hydroxyl attacks, and what functional group is produced at C1?
why_correct: An alcohol adding once to an aldehyde gives a hemiacetal: a carbon bearing one –OH and one –OR. In glucose the attacking alcohol is the C5 hydroxyl, so the ring contains C1 through C5 plus the ring oxygen, six atoms, a pyranose.
C1 therefore ends up with the ring oxygen (the –OR part) and a free hydroxyl (the anomeric –OH), which can point either way, giving the α and β anomers that interconvert by mutarotation.
An acetal would require a second alcohol to replace that anomeric –OH; that happens when glucose bonds to another sugar or alcohol (a glycoside), not when it simply cyclizes.
