why_wrong.A: The C2 hydroxyl would make a three-membered ring, which is far too strained; and a single addition gives a hemiacetal, not an acetal.
why_wrong.B: The C5 hydroxyl is the right nucleophile, but one addition produces a hemiacetal; an acetal needs a second –OR in place of the anomeric –OH.
why_wrong.C: The C6 hydroxyl would give a seven-membered ring, which glucose does not favour; the six-membered pyranose uses C5.

error_types.A: wrong formula: wrong ring size and the acetal/hemiacetal distinction confused
error_types.B: wrong formula: hemiacetal (one addition) confused with acetal (two)
error_types.C: wrong formula: wrong hydroxyl, giving a seven-membered ring

items.takeaway: Cyclic glucose is a hemiacetal formed by the C5 –OH attacking C1; a glycosidic bond converts it to an acetal.
sources: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 25.5 Cyclic Structures of Monosaccharides: Anomers (2023): glucose forms its pyranose ring by addition of the C5 –OH to the C1 carbonyl, producing a cyclic hemiacetal with a new anomeric centre.
OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 19.10 Nucleophilic Addition of Alcohols: Acetal Formation (2023): one equivalent of alcohol gives a hemiacetal; a second, with acid, gives an acetal.

items.stem: A candidate drug is tested against a kinase. Without the drug, the enzyme shows Vmax = 100 µmol/min and Km = 3 mM. With the drug present, Vmax = 100 µmol/min and Km = 9 mM. Based on these data, the drug is most likely a:
why_correct: The drug left Vmax unchanged and raised the apparent Km threefold. That is the signature of competitive inhibition: the inhibitor competes with substrate for the active site, so more substrate is needed to reach half-maximal rate, but enough substrate can still drive the enzyme to the same Vmax.
Quantitatively, Km,app = Km(1 + [I]/Ki); a threefold rise means [I]/Ki = 2.
On a Lineweaver–Burk plot these two conditions would give lines crossing on the y-axis (same 1/Vmax) with different x-intercepts.

why_wrong.B: A noncompetitive inhibitor lowers Vmax and leaves Km unchanged, the reverse of what was observed.
why_wrong.C: An uncompetitive inhibitor binds only the enzyme–substrate complex and lowers both Vmax and Km; here Vmax did not change and Km rose.
why_wrong.D: An irreversible inhibitor removes active enzyme permanently, which shows up as a lower Vmax (less working enzyme), not a higher Km with unchanged Vmax.

error_types.B: reversed relationship: swapped the effects on Km and Vmax
error_types.C: misread graph: uncompetitive lowers both constants
error_types.D: wrong formula: irreversible inhibition reduces Vmax

items.takeaway: Competitive inhibition raises apparent Km and leaves Vmax alone; noncompetitive lowers Vmax and leaves Km alone; uncompetitive lowers both.
sources: Biology LibreTexts, Biochemistry Free For All (Ahern, Rajagopal, Tan), 4.2 Control of Enzymatic Activity (2019): competitive inhibitors raise apparent Km with Vmax unchanged; noncompetitive lower Vmax with Km unchanged; uncompetitive lower both.
OpenStax Biology 2e, 6.5 Enzymes (2018): competitive inhibitors bind the active site and can be overcome by substrate.

items.stem: A Lineweaver–Burk plot (1/v₀ against 1/[S]) for a purified enzyme is a straight line that crosses the x-axis at −0.5 mM⁻¹ and the y-axis at 0.01 min·µmol⁻¹. The enzyme's Km and Vmax are:
why_correct: The double-reciprocal form of the Michaelis–Menten equation is 1/v₀ = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax. The y-intercept is 1/Vmax and the x-intercept is −1/Km.
y-intercept 0.01 min/µmol means Vmax = 1/0.01 = 100 µmol/min. x-intercept −0.5 mM⁻¹ means −1/Km = −0.5 mM⁻¹, so Km = 1/0.5 = 2 mM.
Check with the slope: Km/Vmax = 2/100 = 0.02 min·mM/µmol; rise over run from the x-intercept to the y-intercept is 0.01/0.5 = 0.02, consistent.

why_wrong.A: 0.5 mM is the magnitude of the x-intercept itself, not its reciprocal; Km is 1 divided by that value.
why_wrong.C: 0.01 is the y-intercept, which is 1/Vmax; Vmax is its reciprocal, 100, not 0.01.
why_wrong.D: Both constants are read directly from the intercepts instead of inverting them.

error_types.A: misread graph: x-intercept not inverted to get Km
error_types.C: misread graph: y-intercept not inverted to get Vmax
error_types.D: misread graph: neither intercept inverted

items.takeaway: On a Lineweaver–Burk plot, Vmax is the reciprocal of the y-intercept and Km is the negative reciprocal of the x-intercept.
sources: Biology LibreTexts, Biochemistry Free For All (Ahern, Rajagopal, Tan), 4.1 Basic Principles of Catalysis (2019): Lineweaver–Burk plot intercepts 1/Vmax (y) and −1/Km (x).
OpenStax Biology 2e, 6.5 Enzymes (2018): qualitative relationship between substrate concentration and reaction rate, and the effect of inhibitors.

items.stem: A single-nucleotide substitution in a gene changes the codon UGG, which encodes tryptophan, to UGA in the middle of the coding sequence. The most likely effect on the protein is:

options.A: No change, because the substitution is silent
options.B: A single amino acid replaced by another
options.C: A shifted reading frame from the mutation onward
options.D: A truncated protein, because translation stops early

why_correct: UGA is one of the three stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA). No tRNA reads it; instead a release factor ends translation, so the ribosome stops in the middle of the message.
A codon changed to a stop is a nonsense mutation. The protein made is shorter than normal, usually unfolded and nonfunctional, and the mRNA is often destroyed by nonsense-mediated decay.
The reading frame is unaffected because one nucleotide replaced another; no bases were added or removed.

why_wrong.A: A silent mutation changes a codon to another codon for the same amino acid. Tryptophan has only one codon (UGG), and UGA encodes no amino acid at all.
why_wrong.B: That describes a missense mutation, in which the new codon specifies a different amino acid. UGA specifies none; it signals stop.
why_wrong.C: Frameshifts come from insertions or deletions that are not multiples of three. A substitution keeps the frame intact.

error_types.A: wrong formula: UGA is a stop codon, not a synonymous codon
error_types.B: wrong formula: missense requires a new amino acid, not a stop
error_types.C: wrong formula: frameshifts need insertions or deletions

items.takeaway: A substitution that creates UAA, UAG, or UGA is a nonsense mutation and truncates the protein without shifting the frame.
sources: OpenStax Microbiology, 11.4 Protein Synthesis (Translation) (2016): UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons, recognized by release factors rather than a tRNA.

OpenStax Microbiology, 11.5 Mutations (2016): silent, missense and nonsense substitutions; nonsense mutations give shorter, usually non-functional proteins; insertions and deletions cause frameshifts.
OpenStax Biology 2e, 15.1 The Genetic Code (2018): codon table (tryptophan has the single codon UGG).
Hwang J, Kim YK. When a ribosome encounters a premature termination codon. BMB Reports. 2013;46(1):9–16: nonsense-mediated decay of transcripts with premature stop codons.

items.stem: An autosomal recessive metabolic disorder affects 1 newborn in 10,000 in a large, randomly mating population. Assuming Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, the fraction of the population that carries one copy of the disease allele is closest to:
why_correct: Affected newborns are homozygous recessive, so q² = 1/10,000 = 0.0001. Taking the square root, q = 0.01 (1 in 100) is the allele frequency, and p = 1 − q = 0.99.
Carriers are heterozygotes: 2pq = 2 × 0.99 × 0.01 ≈ 0.0198, about 0.02, which is 1 in 50.
Shortcut for rare recessive traits: the carrier frequency is about 2q, twice the allele frequency, because p is nearly 1.

why_wrong.A: 1 in 10,000 is the frequency of affected individuals (q²), not of carriers.
why_wrong.B: 1 in 100 is the allele frequency q. Each carrier has two alleles and can carry the disease allele on either, so the carrier frequency is about twice this.
why_wrong.D: 1 in 25 (0.04) would require q = 0.02, that is, an affected frequency of 1 in 2,500.

error_types.A: true but irrelevant: reported the affected frequency instead of the carriers
error_types.B: wrong formula: stopped at the allele frequency q instead of 2pq
error_types.D: wrong formula: doubled twice (4q instead of 2q)

items.takeaway: For a rare recessive disease: q = √(affected frequency), and carriers ≈ 2q.
sources: OpenStax Biology 2e, 19.1 Population Evolution (2018): Hardy–Weinberg equation p² + 2pq + q² = 1; heterozygote frequency 2pq.
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 28.7 Patterns of Inheritance (2022): autosomal recessive disorders appear only in homozygous recessive individuals; heterozygotes are carriers.

items.stem: One molecule of acetyl-CoA enters the citric acid cycle and is fully processed through one turn. Which set of energy-carrying products does that single turn generate?
why_correct: In one turn the two carbons of the acetyl group are oxidized and released as two CO₂ while four pairs of electrons are captured: three by NAD⁺ (isocitrate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, malate dehydrogenase) and one by FAD (succinate dehydrogenase).
One substrate-level phosphorylation, at succinyl-CoA synthetase, makes one GTP (ATP in some tissues).
Per glucose, which gives two acetyl-CoA, the totals double to 6 NADH, 2 FADH₂, 2 GTP, and 4 CO₂; option D lists those per-glucose numbers, not the per-turn numbers asked for.

why_wrong.B: No step of the cycle makes two FADH₂, and the cycle's substrate-level phosphorylation yields one nucleotide triphosphate per turn, not two.
why_wrong.C: Only three dehydrogenases in the cycle use NAD⁺, and there is one substrate-level phosphorylation per turn, not two.
why_wrong.D: These are the yields for two turns, that is, per glucose molecule, not per acetyl-CoA.

error_types.B: wrong formula: miscounted the electron carriers and phosphorylations
error_types.C: wrong formula: one NADH and one GTP too many
error_types.D: true but irrelevant: per-glucose totals given for a per-acetyl-CoA question

items.takeaway: Each turn of the citric acid cycle yields 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP, and 2 CO₂; double everything for one glucose.
sources: OpenStax Biology 2e, 7.3 Oxidation of Pyruvate and the Citric Acid Cycle (2018): each turn produces 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂ and 1 ATP or GTP, with two carbons released as CO₂.
OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 29.7 The Citric Acid Cycle (2023): the eight steps and the dehydrogenase and substrate-level phosphorylation steps.

items.stem: Normal saline (0.9% NaCl) has about the same osmolarity as blood plasma. If red blood cells are placed in a solution of 0.45% NaCl, the cells will most likely:

options.A: shrink and crenate as water leaves them
options.B: swell, and some will burst, as water enters them
options.C: keep their shape, because NaCl crosses the membrane freely
options.D: shrink at first and then return to normal size

why_correct: Osmosis moves water across a selectively permeable membrane toward the side with the higher concentration of non-penetrating solute. The cell interior matches 0.9% NaCl; a 0.45% solution has half that solute, so it is hypotonic to the cell.
Water therefore flows into the cells. Red cells have no wall to resist the pressure, so they swell and, if the gradient is large enough, lyse (hemolysis).
Numbers: 0.9% NaCl is about 0.15 M and, since each NaCl gives two particles, about 300 mOsm, like plasma; 0.45% is about 150 mOsm, clearly hypotonic.

why_wrong.A: Shrinking (crenation) happens in a hypertonic solution such as 3% NaCl, where water leaves the cell.
why_wrong.C: The red cell membrane is not freely permeable to Na⁺ and Cl⁻, so NaCl is a non-penetrating solute and the gradient drives water movement.
why_wrong.D: There is no mechanism for an initial loss of water in a hypotonic solution; the gradient favours water entry from the start.

error_types.A: reversed relationship: hypotonic and hypertonic effects swapped
error_types.C: wrong formula: treats NaCl as a solute that crosses the membrane freely
error_types.D: wrong formula: invented a two-phase response with no basis

items.takeaway: Cells in a hypotonic solution gain water and swell (red cells lyse); in a hypertonic solution they lose water and shrink.
sources: OpenStax Biology 2e, 5.2 Passive Transport (2018): osmosis, tonicity, and the behaviour of red blood cells in hypotonic, isotonic and hypertonic solutions.

OpenStax Biology 2e, 41.1 Osmoregulation and Osmotic Balance (2018): body fluids are about 280–300 mOsm; OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 11.4 Colligative Properties (2019): hemolysis in hypotonic and crenation in hypertonic solutions; a 0.9% NaCl solution is isotonic with serum.

items.stem: A human somatic cell has completed S phase and is in G₂ of the cell cycle. At this point the cell contains:
why_correct: Chromosomes are counted by centromeres. A human somatic cell has 46 chromosomes throughout interphase and mitosis until anaphase, when sister chromatids separate.
During S phase each chromosome is replicated into two sister chromatids joined at one centromere, so after S phase (in G₂) there are 46 chromosomes made of 92 chromatids.
At anaphase the 92 chromatids separate and each becomes a chromosome in its own right, so each daughter cell receives 46.

why_wrong.A: 23 is the haploid number found in gametes; a somatic cell is diploid with 46.
why_wrong.B: 46 chromosomes of one chromatid each describes a cell in G₁, before DNA replication.
why_wrong.C: 92 chromosomes would only be reached if the replicated chromatids were already counted as separate chromosomes, which happens at anaphase, after which they are divided between the two daughter cells.

error_types.A: wrong formula: haploid number used for a somatic cell
error_types.B: reversed relationship: pre-replication count given for a post-replication cell
error_types.C: wrong formula: chromatids counted as chromosomes before anaphase

items.takeaway: Count chromosomes by centromeres: a human cell in G₂ has 46 chromosomes and 92 chromatids.
sources: OpenStax Biology 2e, 10.2 The Cell Cycle (2018): DNA is replicated in S phase, producing sister chromatids held at the centromere; chromosome number does not change until anaphase.
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 3.5 Cell Growth and Division (2022): human cells have 46 chromosomes; after replication each consists of two sister chromatids.

items.stem: Tetrodotoxin, the pufferfish toxin, selectively blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels in neurons. A neuron exposed to tetrodotoxin would be expected to:

options.A: maintain its resting potential but be unable to fire action potentials
options.B: depolarize to about 0 mV and stay there
options.C: fire action potentials that cannot repolarize
options.D: fire larger action potentials than normal

why_correct: The resting potential depends on K⁺ leak channels and the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, neither of which tetrodotoxin touches, so the membrane stays near −70 mV.

The rising phase of the action potential is the inrush of Na⁺ through voltage-gated Na⁺ channels. With those blocked, a stimulus can still produce a small graded depolarization, but it cannot regenerate into an all-or-none spike, so the neuron is silenced.
This is why tetrodotoxin poisoning causes paralysis and numbness: sensory and motor neurons stop conducting while the cells themselves remain alive.

why_wrong.B: A sustained depolarization would require Na⁺ channels stuck open, the opposite of blockade; blocking them removes the main depolarizing current.
why_wrong.C: Repolarization is carried by voltage-gated K⁺ channels, which the toxin does not affect; but no action potential starts in the first place.
why_wrong.D: Action potential amplitude depends on the Na⁺ gradient and the number of channels that open; blocking channels cannot make the spike larger.

error_types.B: reversed relationship: blockade confused with channels held open
error_types.C: wrong formula: repolarization is carried by K⁺ channels, not Na⁺
error_types.D: reversed relationship: fewer working channels cannot increase amplitude

items.takeaway: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels generate the action potential's rising phase; block them and the neuron keeps its resting potential but cannot fire.
sources: OpenStax Biology 2e, 35.2 How Neurons Communicate (2018): the resting potential arises from K⁺ leak and the Na⁺/K⁺ pump; the action potential's depolarization is due to voltage-gated Na⁺ channels and repolarization to voltage-gated K⁺ channels.

Geffeney SL, Ruben PC. The structural basis and functional consequences of sodium channel pharmacology. Marine Drugs. 2006; and Lago J et al. Tetrodotoxin, an extremely potent marine neurotoxin. Marine Drugs. 2015;13(10):6384–6406: tetrodotoxin binds the outer pore of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, blocking action-potential propagation and causing numbness and paralysis.
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 12.4 The Action Potential (2022): all action potentials peak at the same voltage, so one cannot be larger than another.

items.stem: Researchers hypothesize that a new compound stimulates antidiuretic hormone (ADH) release. They inject the compound dissolved in saline into rats with free access to water and measure urine osmolarity two hours later. To test the hypothesis, the most appropriate comparison group is rats that:

options.A: receive no injection and have free access to water
options.B: receive twice the dose of the compound
options.C: receive an injection of the same volume of saline by the same route
options.D: are deprived of water for the two hours

why_correct: The experimental variable is the compound. A proper control matches everything else, the injection itself, its volume, route, timing, and handling stress, and omits only the compound; that is the vehicle (saline) control.

If the compound raises ADH, its rats should produce more concentrated urine (higher osmolarity, lower volume) than the vehicle group because ADH inserts aquaporins in the collecting duct and water is reabsorbed.
Handling and the injection itself could alter hormone levels or urine output, so an uninjected group would leave that confound in place.

why_wrong.A: Uninjected rats differ from the treated rats in two ways, the compound and the injection procedure, so any difference could be due to handling or stress rather than the compound.
why_wrong.B: A higher dose tests dose dependence, which is useful later, but without a no-compound baseline it cannot show that the compound has any effect at all.
why_wrong.D: Water deprivation raises ADH on its own; it is a positive control for the measurement, not the comparison that isolates the compound's effect.

error_types.A: true but irrelevant: leaves the injection procedure as a confounding difference
error_types.B: out of scope: dose–response is a different question from whether there is an effect
error_types.D: reversed relationship: a positive control cannot serve as the negative (vehicle) control

items.takeaway: The right control differs from the treatment in exactly one way: here, the vehicle injection without the compound.
sources: OpenStax Biology 2e, 41.5 Hormonal Control of Osmoregulatory Functions (2018): ADH increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct, concentrating the urine.
OpenStax Psychology 2e, 2.3 Analyzing Findings (2020): the experimental group receives the manipulation and the control group does not; placebo controls.

items.stem: A participant holding a 100 g weight can just notice when it is replaced by a 102 g weight. According to Weber's law, the smallest increase the same participant could notice when holding a 500 g weight is about:
why_correct: Weber's law says the just noticeable difference is a constant fraction of the starting stimulus: ΔI/I = k. From the first pair, k = 2 g / 100 g = 0.02, two percent.
At 500 g the just noticeable difference is 0.02 × 500 g = 10 g. The participant needs 510 g before the change registers.
Second route: 500 g is five times 100 g, so the difference threshold is five times 2 g, which is 10 g.

why_wrong.A: 2 g assumes the difference threshold is a fixed amount regardless of the standard; Weber's law says it scales with the standard.
why_wrong.C: 20 g is four percent of 500 g, double the fraction found at 100 g.
why_wrong.D: 50 g is ten percent, which would need a Weber fraction five times larger than the one measured.

error_types.A: wrong formula: treated the threshold as a constant amount instead of a constant fraction
error_types.C: wrong formula: used double the Weber fraction
error_types.D: wrong formula: multiplied the threshold by the ratio of weights twice

items.takeaway: Weber's law: the just noticeable difference is a constant proportion of the stimulus, so heavier standards need bigger changes.
sources: OpenStax Psychology 2e, 5.1 Sensation versus Perception (2020): Weber's law, the just noticeable difference is a constant proportion of the original stimulus.

items.stem: A student who studied Spanish for three years begins learning Italian. When trying to recall Italian vocabulary, Spanish words keep coming to mind instead. This difficulty is best described as:
why_correct: Interference is forgetting caused by competing memories. In proactive interference, older learning disrupts the retrieval of newer learning: the earlier Spanish gets in the way of the later Italian.
The direction is the key: 'pro' means the old material acts forward onto the new.
If the student later found that Italian had begun to crowd out their Spanish, that would be retroactive interference, the new disrupting the old.

why_wrong.A: Retroactive interference runs the other way: newly learned material disrupts recall of what was learned earlier.
why_wrong.B: Decay is the fading of a memory trace with disuse over time; here the Spanish is being recalled all too well.
why_wrong.D: A source monitoring error is misattributing where a memory came from, not competition between two sets of words.

error_types.A: reversed relationship: direction of interference swapped
error_types.B: wrong formula: decay is loss with time, not competition
error_types.D: out of scope: concerns the origin of a memory, not retrieval competition

items.takeaway: Proactive interference: old learning blocks new; retroactive interference: new learning blocks old.
sources: OpenStax Psychology 2e, 8.3 Problems with Memory (2020): proactive interference (old information hinders recall of new) and retroactive interference (new information hinders recall of old).
Johnson MK, Hashtroudi S, Lindsay DS. Source monitoring. Psychological Bulletin. 1993;114(1):3–28 (OpenStax 8.3 calls the same error misattribution).

items.stem: In a classic experiment, participants were injected with epinephrine (adrenaline) but not told what effects to expect. Those who then waited with a playful confederate reported feeling happier and joined in, while those who waited with an angry confederate behaved more angrily, despite comparable physiological arousal. These findings most directly support which theory of emotion?
why_correct: Two-factor theory holds that an emotion is produced by physiological arousal plus a cognitive label for it drawn from the situation. The same epinephrine-induced arousal was expressed as happiness in one context and anger in another, which is exactly what the theory predicts.
Participants who were told what the injection would do had an explanation for their arousal and were less influenced by the confederate, again as the theory predicts.

The experiment separated arousal (comparable across groups) from interpretation (varied), showing that interpretation shapes which emotion is felt and shown. In the anger condition the difference appeared in behaviour rather than in self-report, which the authors attributed to participants' reluctance to admit anger to the experimenter.

why_wrong.B: James–Lange holds that distinct bodily responses produce distinct emotions; comparable arousal producing different emotions is a problem for that view, not support for it.
why_wrong.C: Cannon–Bard holds that arousal and emotion occur at the same time and independently; it does not predict that the social context will decide which emotion is felt.
why_wrong.D: The Yerkes–Dodson law relates arousal level to task performance, not to which emotion a person experiences.

error_types.B: reversed relationship: the finding contradicts a one-to-one arousal–emotion mapping
error_types.C: wrong formula: simultaneous-but-independent theory does not involve labelling
error_types.D: out of scope: a performance law, not a theory of emotion

items.takeaway: Two-factor theory: emotion = physiological arousal + a cognitive label supplied by the situation.
sources: OpenStax Psychology 2e, 10.4 Emotion (2020): Schachter–Singer two-factor theory, with the epinephrine and confederate experiment, and the contrast with James–Lange and Cannon–Bard; the Yerkes–Dodson law is in 10.1 Motivation.

Schachter S, Singer JE. Cognitive, social, and physiological determinants of emotional state. Psychological Review. 1962;69(5):379–399: euphoria self-report differed by condition (Table 2); anger appeared on the behavioural index (Table 5), not in self-report (Table 4).

items.stem: A physiotherapy clinic gives patients a small gift each time they complete five supervised exercise sessions. Which schedule of reinforcement is the clinic using?
why_correct: Ratio schedules reinforce after a number of responses; interval schedules reinforce the first response after a period of time. The gift depends on a count of sessions, so it is a ratio schedule.
The count is always five, so the ratio is fixed: a fixed-ratio (FR-5) schedule.
Fixed-ratio schedules produce a high, steady response rate with a brief pause after each reinforcer, which is why some patients slow down right after collecting a gift.

why_wrong.A: A fixed-interval schedule would give the gift for the first session completed after a set time (say, every month) regardless of how many sessions were done.
why_wrong.B: A variable-interval schedule rewards after unpredictable amounts of time, as when a supervisor drops in at random.
why_wrong.C: A variable-ratio schedule rewards after an unpredictable number of responses, as a slot machine does; here the number is always five.

error_types.A: wrong formula: time-based schedule chosen for a count-based rule
error_types.B: wrong formula: time-based and unpredictable, neither of which applies
error_types.C: reversed relationship: a fixed count read as a variable one

items.takeaway: Ratio = number of responses, interval = time; fixed = constant, variable = unpredictable. A gift every five sessions is fixed-ratio.
sources: OpenStax Psychology 2e, 6.3 Operant Conditioning (2020): fixed-ratio, variable-ratio, fixed-interval and variable-interval schedules with examples and response patterns.

items.stem: In a hypothetical study, a researcher wants to know whether a daily meditation program reduces stress in medical students. Students are invited to join; those who accept form the meditation group and those who decline form the comparison group. After eight weeks the meditation group reports lower stress. The most serious threat to concluding that meditation caused the reduction is:

options.A: the sample is too small to detect a difference
options.B: the groups were not formed by random assignment
options.D: the researcher knew which group each student was in

why_correct: Students chose their own group. Those who accept a meditation program may already differ from those who decline, in baseline stress, motivation, free time, or beliefs about meditation, and any of those differences could produce the result.

Random assignment is what makes the groups equivalent on average before treatment, so that the only systematic difference is the program. Without it the design is a quasi-experiment and the result is a correlation, not evidence of cause.
A fix would be to randomize willing volunteers to meditate now or to a waiting list, and compare them.

why_wrong.A: A small sample makes it harder to find a difference, but a difference was found; sample size does not explain away the self-selection problem.
why_wrong.C: The stem implies stress was measured by self-report, which is an operational definition, even if an imperfect one; it is not the main threat to the causal claim.
why_wrong.D: Researcher awareness could bias measurement, but it is not the design flaw at issue: even a blinded researcher would be left with self-selected groups.

error_types.A: true but irrelevant: power concerns a missed effect, not a found one
error_types.C: out of scope: a measurement issue, not the design flaw that blocks causal inference
error_types.D: true but irrelevant: a measurement bias that would remain even after blinding

items.takeaway: Without random assignment, group differences that existed before the treatment can explain the outcome; self-selected groups cannot support a causal claim.
sources: OpenStax Psychology 2e, 2.3 Analyzing Findings (2020): random assignment makes systematic differences between groups unlikely; quasi-experimental designs cannot support cause-and-effect claims.
OpenStax Introductory Statistics 2e, 1.4 Experimental Design and Ethics (2023): random assignment to treatment groups controls lurking variables.

items.stem: A driver who is cut off in traffic concludes that the other driver is reckless and selfish. Later that day the same driver cuts someone off and explains it by the confusing lane markings at that junction. This pattern of explanation best illustrates:
why_correct: The driver explains another person's behaviour by disposition (reckless, selfish) but their own identical behaviour by the situation (bad lane markings). That asymmetry, dispositional attributions for others and situational attributions for oneself, is the actor–observer bias.
It arises partly because we see our own circumstances in detail but see other people as the most salient thing in their scene.
The first half alone, blaming the other driver's character, is the fundamental attribution error; the contrast with the self-explanation is what makes it actor–observer.

why_wrong.A: The self-serving bias is attributing one's successes to oneself and one's failures to circumstances; this scenario involves no success, only two explanations of the same misbehaviour.
why_wrong.B: The just-world hypothesis is the belief that people get what they deserve, leading to blaming victims; nobody here is judged to deserve a misfortune.
why_wrong.D: The false consensus effect is overestimating how many others share one's own views or behaviour, which is not what is described.

error_types.A: wrong formula: the self-serving bias concerns success versus failure
error_types.B: out of scope: no judgement about deserved outcomes is made
error_types.D: out of scope: no estimate of others' agreement is involved

items.takeaway: Actor–observer bias: my behaviour is due to the situation, yours is due to your character.
sources: OpenStax Psychology 2e, 12.1 What Is Social Psychology? (2020): fundamental attribution error, actor–observer bias, self-serving bias and the just-world hypothesis.
Ross L, Greene D, House P. The false consensus effect. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology. 1977;13(3):279–301 (people overestimate how far others share their beliefs and behaviour).

items.stem: A sociologist argues that the traditional hierarchy of physicians over nurses in hospitals persists because it protects the income and authority of the more powerful group, and that it will change only when nurses organize to contest it. This analysis is most characteristic of:
why_correct: Conflict theory views social arrangements as the outcome of competition between groups with unequal power, sees institutions as serving the interests of the dominant group, and expects change to come from struggle. Every element of the argument fits: an arrangement that benefits the powerful, maintained by power, changed by organized contest.
A functionalist would instead ask what the hierarchy contributes to the smooth running of the hospital; an interactionist would study how the hierarchy is enacted in daily encounters.
The macro scale (an institution-wide arrangement) and the focus on power and inequality are the markers of the conflict perspective.

why_wrong.B: Functionalism explains institutions by the functions they serve for the whole system and emphasizes stability and consensus, not the interests of a dominant group or change through struggle.
why_wrong.C: Symbolic interactionism is a micro perspective on how meaning is created in face-to-face interaction; it would examine how deference is performed, not why the structure persists.
why_wrong.D: Exchange theory treats interaction as the trading of rewards and costs between individuals; it does not frame institutions as instruments of group power.

error_types.B: reversed relationship: a consensus perspective offered for a power-based argument
error_types.C: out of scope: a micro perspective for a macro question
error_types.D: wrong formula: individual cost–benefit framing for a group-power argument

items.takeaway: Arguments about who benefits, power, and change through struggle are conflict theory; arguments about what an arrangement does for the system are functionalist.
sources: OpenStax Introduction to Sociology 3e, 1.3 Theoretical Perspectives in Sociology (2021): functionalism, conflict theory and symbolic interactionism compared.
OpenStax Introduction to Sociology 3e, 19.5 Theoretical Perspectives on Health and Medicine (2021): conflict theory applied to the health care system.
Social Sci LibreTexts, Sociology (Boundless), 5.2B Exchange (2021): exchange theory treats interaction as a trade of rewards and costs between individuals.

items.stem: A hypothetical survey reports the following age-adjusted rates of type 2 diabetes among adults, per 1,000 people, by annual household income: under $25,000: 120; $25,000–$49,999: 95; $50,000–$99,999: 70; $100,000 and above: 50. Which conclusion do these data best support?

options.A: Low income causes type 2 diabetes in the population surveyed
options.B: Diabetes is concentrated almost entirely in households earning under $25,000
options.C: Above $25,000, income has little relationship with diabetes rates
options.D: Diabetes rates fall at every step up the income scale

why_correct: Read the table: 120 → 95 → 70 → 50. The rate drops at every income step, not only at the poverty line, and the drop continues well into the highest bracket. That stepwise pattern is what health researchers call the socioeconomic gradient in health.
Age adjustment rules out the explanation that the pattern arises just because poorer groups are older, which strengthens the comparison across income groups.
The data are observational and describe a relationship; they do not identify its cause.

why_wrong.A: A survey correlation cannot establish cause. Illness can also lower income (reverse causation), and factors such as education, neighbourhood, and access to care could drive both.
why_wrong.B: The lowest-income group has the highest rate, but the rates in the other three groups (95, 70 and 50 per 1,000) are far from negligible, so diabetes is clearly not confined to the lowest bracket.
why_wrong.C: The rate falls from 95 to 70 to 50 above $25,000, a substantial and consistent relationship.

error_types.A: reversed relationship: causation inferred from correlational data
error_types.B: too extreme: 'almost entirely' is not supported by the other groups' rates
error_types.C: misread graph: the decline above $25,000 is large and consistent

items.takeaway: A health gradient means risk changes at every step of socioeconomic status, not only below a poverty threshold; survey data show the pattern but not its cause.
sources: OpenStax Introduction to Sociology 3e, 19.3 Health in the United States (2021): socioeconomic status is one of the strongest and most consistent predictors of morbidity and mortality.
Adler NE et al. Socioeconomic status and health: the challenge of the gradient. American Psychologist. 1994;49(1):15–24: the association is graded across the whole SES range, not confined to poverty.

CDC, National Diabetes Statistics Report, Appendix Table 3 (NHIS 2019–2021): age-adjusted diagnosed diabetes 13.1% below the poverty level, 10.3% at 100–299%, 7.7% at 300–499%, 5.1% at 500% and above (the stem's figures are hypothetical but of this order).
OpenStax Introductory Statistics 2e, 12.3 The Regression Equation and 1.4 Experimental Design and Ethics (2023): correlation does not imply causation; observational studies cannot establish cause.

items.stem: According to Figure 1, the emf and the internal resistance of the battery pack are closest to:
why_correct: The passage's model, V = ε − Ir, is a straight line whose intercept on the voltage axis is the emf ε and whose slope is −r. Extending the line in Figure 1 back to I = 0 gives 6.0 V.
Check with any row of Table 1: at 2.00 A, 6.0 V − 2.00 A × 0.50 Ω = 5.0 V, as measured.

why_wrong.A: 4.5 V is the terminal voltage at the largest current, not the intercept at zero current; the emf is what the pack would show with no current flowing.
why_wrong.B: 5.75 V is simply the first measured voltage, and 0.25 Ω comes from dividing the 0.25 V drop between the first two rows by a current change of 1.0 A; the current actually changed by only 0.50 A, so the slope magnitude is 0.50 Ω.
why_wrong.D: 2.0 Ω is the reciprocal of the slope magnitude (ΔI/ΔV = 2.0 A/V); the internal resistance is ΔV/ΔI, in volts per ampere.

error_types.A: misread graph: an end point read as the intercept
error_types.B: misread graph: the current change between points misread
error_types.D: wrong formula: slope inverted

items.takeaway: On a terminal-voltage versus current graph, the intercept is the emf and the slope magnitude is the internal resistance (V = ε − Ir).
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 21.2 Electromotive Force: Terminal Voltage (2022): V = emf − Ir; the internal resistance causes the terminal voltage to fall as current rises.

items.stem: With the resistance box set to 2.5 Ω, the power dissipated inside the battery pack itself is closest to:
why_correct: Table 1 gives I = 2.00 A at this setting, and from Figure 1 the internal resistance is r = 0.50 Ω. Power dissipated in a resistance is I²r = (2.00 A)² × 0.50 Ω = 4.0 × 0.50 = 2.0 W.
Energy check: the emf supplies εI = 6.0 V × 2.00 A = 12 W in total; the box receives 10.0 W (Table 1) and the remaining 2.0 W is lost inside the pack, consistent.
The same 2.0 W follows from the internal voltage drop: (ε − V) × I = (6.0 − 5.0) V × 2.00 A = 2.0 W.

why_wrong.A: 1.0 W is the number you get from I × r = 2.00 × 0.50, which is the internal voltage drop in volts, not a power; power needs the current squared (I²r) or the drop times the current.
why_wrong.C: 10 W is the power delivered to the 2.5 Ω box (I²R, last column of Table 1), not the power lost inside the pack.
why_wrong.D: 12 W is the total power supplied by the emf (εI); only the part not delivered to the box, 12 − 10 = 2 W, is dissipated inside the pack.

error_types.A: wrong formula: current not squared (Ir is a voltage, not a power)
error_types.C: true but irrelevant: load power given for an internal-power question
error_types.D: wrong formula: total power from the emf instead of the internal share

items.takeaway: Power lost inside a source is I²r, the difference between the power the emf supplies (εI) and the power the load receives (I²R).
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 21.2 Electromotive Force: Terminal Voltage (2022): V = emf − Ir and I = emf/(R + r); the internal resistance dissipates energy as the current passes through it.
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 20.4 Electric Power and Energy (2022): the power dissipated in any resistance is P = I²R, so the internal loss is I²r.
OpenStax University Physics Volume 2, 10.1 Electromotive Force (2016): power dissipated by the internal resistance can overheat a battery driving a large current.

items.stem: If the students could set the resistance box to any value, the power delivered to the box would be greatest when its resistance is set to:
why_correct: The load power is P = I²R with I = ε/(R + r), so P = ε²R/(R + r)². This is largest when the load resistance equals the internal resistance, R = r (the maximum-power condition): making R smaller than r raises the current but an ever larger share of the power is lost inside the source, and making R larger cuts the current faster than it raises R.

No calculus is needed to see it with numbers. At R = 0.50 Ω: I = 6.0/1.0 = 6.0 A and P = 36 × 0.50 = 18 W. At R = 0.25 Ω: I = 6.0/0.75 = 8.0 A and P = 64 × 0.25 = 16 W. At R = 1.5 Ω (Table 1): 13.5 W. The peak is at 0.50 Ω, the internal resistance found from Figure 1.
At that setting only half the emf appears across the box (3.0 V), so maximum power transfer is not the same as maximum efficiency.

why_wrong.B: 1.5 Ω gives the largest power in Table 1 (13.5 W), but the table stops there; a lower setting, down to R = r, delivers more.
why_wrong.C: 2.5 Ω delivers 10.0 W, less than the 13.5 W at 1.5 Ω and the 18 W available at 0.50 Ω.
why_wrong.D: 11.5 Ω gives the highest terminal voltage but the smallest current, and the power (2.9 W) is the lowest in the table; a high voltage reading is not the same as high power.

error_types.B: true but irrelevant: the table's maximum is not the physical maximum
error_types.C: misread graph: a mid-table value chosen without checking the trend
error_types.D: reversed relationship: highest voltage mistaken for highest power

items.takeaway: A source delivers maximum power to a load when the load resistance equals the source's internal resistance (P = ε²R/(R + r)² peaks at R = r).
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 21.2 Electromotive Force: Terminal Voltage (2022): current I = emf/(R + r); terminal voltage and internal losses.
Physics LibreTexts, Tatum, Electricity and Magnetism, 4.8 Power Delivered to an External Resistance (2022): P = E²R/(R + r)², greatest (E²/4r) when R = r.
OpenStax University Physics Volume 2, Chapter 10 exercises (2016): show that the power dissipated by the load is maximum when the load resistance equals the internal resistance.

items.stem: Two identical battery packs are connected in series and used to drive the resistance box at its 5.5 Ω setting. The current is closest to:
why_correct: Sources in series add their emfs and their internal resistances: ε = 2 × 6.0 = 12 V and r = 2 × 0.50 = 1.0 Ω.
Sense check: the current is less than double the single-pack value (1.00 A) because the extra internal resistance is now a larger share of the circuit's total resistance.

why_wrong.A: 0.92 A is 6.0 V / 6.5 Ω: the internal resistance was doubled but the emf was left at 6.0 V. Series packs add both.
why_wrong.B: 1.0 A is the single-pack current from Table 1; a second pack in series doubles the driving emf.
why_wrong.D: 2.2 A is 12 V / 5.5 Ω, ignoring the 1.0 Ω of internal resistance that the two packs add.

error_types.A: wrong formula: internal resistance doubled but not the emf
error_types.B: true but irrelevant: the single-pack value reused
error_types.D: wrong formula: internal resistance dropped

items.takeaway: Cells in series add emfs and add internal resistances; the current is the total emf over the total resistance, load plus internal.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 21.2 Electromotive Force: Terminal Voltage (2022): multiple voltage sources in series add emfs and internal resistances.
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 21.1 Resistors in Series and Parallel (2022): resistances in series add.

items.stem: The terminal voltage of a real battery falls as the current drawn from it rises because:

options.A: the battery's emf decreases in proportion to the current
options.B: the external resistance rises as the circuit warms
options.C: the ammeter adds resistance in series with the battery
options.D: part of the emf is used to drive the current through the battery's own internal resistance

why_correct: A real source behaves like an ideal emf in series with an internal resistance r. The current must pass through r, which costs a voltage Ir, so the voltage left at the terminals is V = ε − Ir and falls linearly with current.
This is the model the students used and Figure 1 confirms it: the points lie on a straight line of slope −r.
The lost voltage shows up as heat inside the source (I²r), which is why the pack felt warm after the high-current run.

why_wrong.A: The emf is set by the chemistry of the cells and is treated as constant; what falls with current is the terminal voltage, not the emf.
why_wrong.B: The external resistance is whatever the resistance box is set to; in this experiment it was deliberately decreased, and the drop in terminal voltage is explained without any change in it.
why_wrong.C: A good ammeter has very small resistance and simply forms part of the external circuit; it would not make the voltage measured across the pack's own terminals depend on current.

error_types.A: wrong formula: emf confused with terminal voltage
error_types.B: reversed relationship: the change is in the source, not the load
error_types.C: true but irrelevant: meter resistance does not create the Ir drop

items.takeaway: Terminal voltage = emf − Ir: the drop with current comes from the source's own internal resistance.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 21.2 Electromotive Force: Terminal Voltage (2022): a source has an emf and an internal resistance; V = emf − Ir.

items.stem: Based on Table 1, the generation (doubling) time of strain W without ampicillin during its exponential phase is closest to:
why_correct: Read the W, no amp column after the lag: 0.10 at 60 min, 0.20 at 90 min, 0.40 at 120 min, 0.80 at 150 min. The OD, and so the cell number, doubles every 30 minutes.
The first 30 minutes (0.05 to 0.05) are a lag phase, when cells adapt to fresh medium without dividing, and must be excluded from the estimate.
Check: three doublings from 60 to 150 min should give 2³ = 8 times the OD, and 0.10 × 8 = 0.80, as observed.

why_wrong.A: A 15-minute generation time would give four doublings (16-fold) every hour; the OD rose only 4-fold per hour (two doublings).
why_wrong.C: 60 minutes is how long it took to get from 0.05 to 0.10, but that interval includes the 30-minute lag; during exponential growth the OD doubles twice an hour.
why_wrong.D: 90 minutes is the time from the start to the first reading of 0.20, which spans the lag plus two doublings, not one.

error_types.A: misread graph: doublings per hour overcounted
error_types.C: misread graph: lag phase included in the doubling interval
error_types.D: misread graph: elapsed time from inoculation used instead of one doubling

items.takeaway: Generation time is read from the exponential phase only, as the interval over which cell number (or OD) doubles.
sources: OpenStax Microbiology, 9.1 How Microbes Grow (2016): lag, log (exponential), stationary and death phases; generation time; turbidity (OD) as a measure of growth.

items.stem: During its exponential phase, the number of strain W cells (no ampicillin) at 150 minutes compared with the number at 60 minutes was about:
why_correct: From 60 to 150 minutes is 90 minutes, which at a 30-minute generation time is 90/30 = 3 generations.
Each generation doubles the population, so N = N₀ × 2ⁿ = N₀ × 2³ = 8 N₀.
The table agrees: OD 0.10 at 60 min and 0.80 at 150 min, an 8-fold increase.

why_wrong.A: 3 is the number of generations, not the growth factor; each generation multiplies the population by 2, giving 2³ = 8.
why_wrong.B: 4-fold corresponds to two generations (60 minutes), not the three that fit in 90 minutes.
why_wrong.D: 16-fold would need four generations (120 minutes); only 90 minutes elapsed.

error_types.A: wrong formula: generations counted instead of doublings applied
error_types.B: wrong formula: one generation too few
error_types.D: wrong formula: one generation too many

items.takeaway: Exponential growth: N = N₀ × 2ⁿ, where n is elapsed time divided by the generation time.
sources: OpenStax Microbiology, 9.1 How Microbes Grow (2016): N = N₀ × 2ⁿ for n generations of binary fission.

items.stem: The DNase added to the broth in the second experiment was included to rule out transfer of the resistance gene by:
why_correct: Transformation is the uptake of free DNA from the surroundings. If cells of strain S had become ampicillin-resistant by taking up pBLA DNA released from dead R cells, destroying that free DNA with DNase would have cut the number of resistant colonies.

The colony count was unchanged, so free DNA was not the vehicle. Together with the filter result (no transfer without cell contact), this points to conjugation, the plasmid moving through direct cell-to-cell contact.

The double-antibiotic plate selects only S cells that received the plasmid (streptomycin resistance from their own chromosome, ampicillin resistance from pBLA); neither parent alone can grow, as the controls showed.

why_wrong.B: Transduction moves DNA inside a bacteriophage, where it is protected from DNase; a DNase control cannot rule it out. The filter experiment argues against transduction, since phage particles would pass through the pores.
why_wrong.C: Conjugation transfers DNA through direct contact between cells, so DNase in the medium has no effect on it; the DNase control is not aimed at conjugation.
why_wrong.D: Transposition is the movement of a DNA segment within a cell's own genome; it does not move genes between cells and is not tested by DNase.

error_types.B: reversed relationship: DNase-protected transfer mistaken for DNase-sensitive transfer
error_types.C: reversed relationship: the mechanism the control leaves standing, not the one it excludes
error_types.D: true but irrelevant: a real process, but intracellular, so not a transfer between cells

items.takeaway: DNase-insensitive, contact-dependent gene transfer is conjugation; DNase-sensitive transfer is transformation; phage-mediated transfer is transduction.
sources: OpenStax Microbiology, 11.6 How Asexual Prokaryotes Achieve Genetic Diversity (2016): transformation (free DNA), transduction (phage) and conjugation (direct contact via a pilus); F plasmids and R plasmids.
OpenStax Biology 2e, 22.2 Structure of Prokaryotes: Bacteria and Archaea (2018): horizontal gene transfer by transformation, transduction and conjugation.

items.stem: The fall in OD600 of strain W in ampicillin (Table 1) is best explained by ampicillin:

options.A: blocking transcription, so that cells stop making protein and shrink
options.B: dissolving the plasma membrane in the manner of a detergent
options.C: inhibiting DNA gyrase, so that chromosome replication stalls
options.D: preventing cross-linking of peptidoglycan, so that growing cells lyse

why_correct: Ampicillin is a β-lactam. β-Lactams bind the penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases) that cross-link peptidoglycan, so new cell wall is laid down without cross-links.

Cells trying to grow in a hypotonic broth then cannot withstand their own turgor pressure and burst. Lysed cells no longer scatter light, which is why the OD fell below its starting value rather than simply staying flat.
The passage's own clue is consistent: strain R survives because its plasmid-encoded β-lactamase opens the β-lactam ring before the drug reaches its target.

why_wrong.A: Rifampin-type drugs block bacterial RNA polymerase; a transcription block halts growth but does not break cells open, and ampicillin does not act on transcription.
why_wrong.B: Membrane-disrupting agents such as polymyxins act on the lipid bilayer; ampicillin's target is the cell wall, and the lysis is a consequence of a weakened wall, not of dissolved membrane.
why_wrong.C: Fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase; ampicillin does not, and a replication block would stop division rather than cause lysis.

error_types.A: true but irrelevant: rifampin's mechanism, not ampicillin's
error_types.B: true but irrelevant: polymyxins' mechanism, not ampicillin's
error_types.C: true but irrelevant: fluoroquinolones' mechanism, not ampicillin's

items.takeaway: β-Lactams block peptidoglycan cross-linking; growing bacteria lyse, and β-lactamases confer resistance by hydrolysing the ring.
sources: OpenStax Microbiology, 14.3 Mechanisms of Antibacterial Drugs (2016): β-lactams inhibit transpeptidase cross-linking of peptidoglycan, leading to lysis; polymyxins target membranes, rifampin targets RNA polymerase, fluoroquinolones target DNA gyrase.
OpenStax Microbiology, 14.5 Drug Resistance (2016): β-lactamases hydrolyse the β-lactam ring; resistance genes are often carried on plasmids.

items.stem: From the plate count described in the final paragraph, the concentration of viable cells in the undiluted 180-minute culture of strain W was about:
why_correct: Each colony grew from one viable cell. 120 colonies came from 0.1 mL of the diluted sample, so the diluted sample held 120 / 0.1 = 1,200 cells per mL.
The sample had been diluted 10⁶-fold, so the original culture held 1,200 × 10⁶ = 1.2 × 10⁹ cells/mL.
Consistency check: the culture's OD600 was 1.20, and the passage says OD600 1.0 corresponds to about 10⁹ cells/mL, so 1.2 × 10⁹ is the expected order of magnitude.

why_wrong.A: 1.2 × 10⁷ treats the dilution as 10⁵ and ignores the plating volume; both the 10⁶ dilution and the 0.1 mL must be undone.
why_wrong.B: 1.2 × 10⁸ undoes the dilution (120 × 10⁶) but forgets that only 0.1 mL was plated, which adds another factor of 10.
why_wrong.D: 1.2 × 10¹⁰ multiplies by an extra factor of 10, as if 0.01 mL had been plated.

error_types.A: sign or unit error: dilution factor and plating volume both mishandled
error_types.B: sign or unit error: plating volume (0.1 mL) not converted to per-millilitre
error_types.D: sign or unit error: an extra factor of 10

items.takeaway: Viable count per mL = colonies ÷ volume plated × dilution factor; check it against the OD.
sources: OpenStax Microbiology, 9.1 How Microbes Grow (2016): serial dilution and plate counts; colony-forming units per millilitre = colonies × dilution factor ÷ volume plated; turbidity as an indirect measure.

items.stem: The independent variables in the experiment are:

options.B: study condition and percentage of idea units recalled

why_correct: An independent variable is one the researchers set. They assigned participants to a study condition (rereading or retrieval practice) and to a retention interval (5 minutes or one week), giving a 2 × 2 design with four groups.
Percentage recalled is the dependent variable, measured to see the effect of those manipulations; predicted recall is an additional measured variable.
The passage's own analysis confirms the structure: the ANOVA tests the effects of study condition, retention interval, and their interaction.

why_wrong.B: Percentage recalled was measured, not manipulated; it is the dependent variable.
why_wrong.C: Predicted recall was a rating participants gave, not something the researchers assigned.
why_wrong.D: Both of these are outcomes recorded from participants; neither was manipulated.

error_types.B: reversed relationship: a dependent variable listed as independent
error_types.C: reversed relationship: a measured rating treated as a manipulation
error_types.D: reversed relationship: two measured outcomes treated as manipulations

items.takeaway: Independent variables are the ones the experimenter manipulates; what is measured afterward is the dependent variable.
sources: OpenStax Psychology 2e, 2.3 Analyzing Findings (2020): independent variable (manipulated by the experimenter) versus dependent variable (measured); random assignment.

items.stem: Which statement best describes the pattern of results in Figure 1?

options.A: Retrieval practice produced better recall at both intervals
options.B: Rereading produced better recall at both intervals
options.C: Rereading was better after 5 minutes, but retrieval practice was better after one week
options.D: The two study methods did not differ at either interval

why_correct: Read the bars: at 5 minutes rereading (71%) is above retrieval practice (63%); at one week the order reverses, retrieval practice (48%) above rereading (40%).
This crossover is what the significant interaction in the passage reports: the effect of study method depends on when memory is tested.

The non-significant main effect of study condition fits too: averaged over both intervals the methods come out equal (55.5% each), because the 8-point advantage runs in opposite directions at the two intervals.

why_wrong.A: At 5 minutes the rereading group recalled more (71% versus 63%), so retrieval practice was not better at both intervals.
why_wrong.B: At one week the rereading group recalled less (40% versus 48%).
why_wrong.D: The groups differed by 8 points at each interval, in opposite directions, and the interaction was significant.

error_types.A: misread graph: the 5-minute bars reversed
error_types.B: misread graph: the one-week bars reversed
error_types.D: misread graph: clear differences ignored

items.takeaway: A crossover between conditions across levels of a second variable is an interaction: the effect of one variable depends on the other.
sources: OpenStax Psychology 2e, 2.3 Analyzing Findings (2020): reading experimental results; interpreting group differences.
OpenStax Introductory Statistics 2e, 13.1 One-Way ANOVA (2023): analysis of variance compares group means using an F statistic.

items.stem: The gap between what the rereading group predicted (70%) and what it actually recalled after one week (40%) best illustrates:

options.B: a metacognitive illusion in which the fluency of rereading is mistaken for durable learning
options.D: proactive interference from the first reading

why_correct: Rereading makes a text feel familiar and easy to process. People read that fluency as a sign that the material is well learned, and so they overestimate how much will survive a delay.
The retrieval-practice group, who had just struggled to recall the passage, had direct evidence of what they did not know; their prediction (50%) was close to their actual one-week recall (48%).
Judgements of learning that track familiarity rather than retrievability are a well-documented source of poor study choices.

why_wrong.A: The spacing effect is better retention when study sessions are spread out over time; the sessions here were back to back in both conditions, and the gap concerns prediction versus performance.
why_wrong.C: State-dependent memory is better recall when a person's internal state at retrieval matches the state at encoding; nothing in the design manipulated internal state.
why_wrong.D: Proactive interference is older material hindering recall of newer material; rereading the same passage does not create competing content, and interference would not explain an over-confident prediction.

error_types.A: out of scope: a scheduling effect, not a judgement error
error_types.C: out of scope: no state manipulation in the design
error_types.D: wrong formula: interference requires competing material

items.takeaway: Ease of processing during restudy inflates judgements of learning; retrieval practice gives more accurate self-assessment and better long-term retention.
sources: OpenStax Psychology 2e, 8.4 Ways to Enhance Memory (2020): rehearsal, practice quizzes and spaced study as memory strategies.

Koriat A, Bjork RA. Illusions of competence in monitoring one's knowledge during study. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition. 2005;31(2):187–194: judgements of learning made while the material is in view instil an unwarranted sense of competence.

Roediger HL, Karpicke JD. Test-enhanced learning: taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science. 2006;17(3):249–255: repeated study produced higher predicted recall but lower delayed recall than repeated testing.

items.stem: The reported interaction, F(1, 124) = 16.9, p < .001, means that:

options.A: the effect of study method depended on the retention interval, and a difference in pattern this large would be very unlikely if there were no true interaction
options.B: the probability that the null hypothesis is true is less than 0.001
options.C: retrieval practice improved recall by 16.2 percentage points
options.D: the result would be obtained in 99.9% of replications

why_correct: An interaction term tests whether the effect of one independent variable differs across levels of the other. Here the study-method difference reversed between 5 minutes and one week.
The p-value is the probability of observing an interaction at least this strong if, in the population, there were none. Below .001, the observed crossover is very unlikely to be a chance pattern.
The F statistic is a ratio of the variance explained by the interaction to the error variance; it is not a percentage or an effect size.

why_wrong.B: A p-value is the probability of the data (or more extreme data) given the null hypothesis, not the probability that the null hypothesis is true; the latter would require a Bayesian analysis with prior probabilities.
why_wrong.C: F = 16.9 is a variance ratio, not a difference in recall; the one-week advantage of retrieval practice in Figure 1 is 8 points, and averaged across intervals the two methods tie.
why_wrong.D: A p-value says nothing about the probability of replication; replication depends on effect size, sample size and the study's design.

error_types.B: reversed relationship: the conditional probability inverted
error_types.C: misread graph: a test statistic read as an effect size
error_types.D: wrong formula: p-value confused with replication probability

items.takeaway: p is the chance of data this extreme if the null were true; it is not the chance the null is true, an effect size, or a replication rate.
sources: OpenStax Introductory Statistics 2e, 9.4 Rare Events, the Sample, and the Decision and Conclusion (2023): the p-value is the probability, if the null hypothesis is true, of a sample result at least as extreme as the one observed.
OpenStax Introductory Statistics 2e, 13.2 The F Distribution and the F-Ratio (2023): F is the ratio of between-group to within-group variance.
OpenStax Psychology 2e, 2.3 Analyzing Findings (2020): statistical significance.

items.stem: The decline in recall between 5 minutes and one week seen in both study conditions is best described as:

options.A: retroactive interference caused by the final test
options.B: encoding failure, because the passage never entered long-term memory
options.C: anterograde amnesia for material learned in the laboratory
options.D: normal forgetting of the kind described by the forgetting curve

why_correct: Memory for newly learned material drops quickly in the hours and days after learning and then declines more slowly, the pattern Ebbinghaus first charted as the forgetting curve. A week is long enough for much of that early loss.
Both groups show it; retrieval practice slowed the loss (63% to 48%) more than rereading did (71% to 40%), but did not prevent it.
The decline is ordinary storage decay plus interference from everything learned in the intervening week, not a defect of the participants or the design.

why_wrong.A: Retroactive interference is newer learning hindering recall of older material; the final test is the measurement itself, taken once, and cannot interfere with what it measures.
why_wrong.B: Participants recalled 40–48% of the idea units a week later, so much of the passage clearly did enter long-term memory; encoding failure would mean the material was never stored.
why_wrong.C: Anterograde amnesia is an inability to form new long-term memories after brain injury; healthy undergraduates forming and retaining memories over a week show normal forgetting, not amnesia.

error_types.A: wrong formula: the measurement cannot interfere with itself
error_types.B: too extreme: partial forgetting mistaken for no storage
error_types.C: out of scope: a clinical condition applied to normal forgetting

items.takeaway: Normal forgetting is fastest soon after learning and slows over time (the forgetting curve); good study methods flatten the curve, they do not abolish it.
sources: OpenStax Psychology 2e, 8.3 Problems with Memory (2020): Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve, storage decay, proactive and retroactive interference, encoding failure, anterograde and retrograde amnesia.

items.stem: The central claim of the passage is that:

options.A: old paintings should not be cleaned, because every cleaning destroys evidence of their history
options.B: scientific analysis has made disputes about restoration obsolete
options.C: a painting has no single original state for restoration to recover, so a restoration is a defensible choice rather than a discovery
options.D: critics who object to cleaned paintings are reacting to the loss of grime that they mistook for mystery

why_correct: The thesis is stated at the end of the first paragraph and restated at the end: the assumption of 'a single correct state of the picture' cannot bear the weight placed on it, and we must stop pretending that restoration 'returns them to a state that exists somewhere, waiting to be found.'
Paragraph 2 argues there is 'no layer at which the picture is simply itself'; paragraph 4 describes good restoration as a claim 'that must be defended in writing', that is, a choice to be argued for.
Every other paragraph serves this claim: science cannot settle a question of value (3), and the critic's preferred state is also only a version (5).

why_wrong.A: Too extreme. The author explicitly says the honest position 'is not that we must never touch old paintings' and praises conservators who 'clean, retouch, and consolidate.'
why_wrong.B: Reversed. Paragraph 3 concedes what science can establish and then argues that it 'does not tell us what to do about it.'
why_wrong.D: A distortion of a minor point. The author grants that the critic's loss is real and says he is 'not simply wrong'; the critic's reaction is discussed to show that his state is one version among others, not to dismiss it.

error_types.A: too extreme: forbids what the author permits
error_types.B: reversed relationship: the author argues the opposite
error_types.D: true but irrelevant: a supporting point mistaken for the thesis

items.takeaway: Find the sentence the whole passage returns to; here it is the denial of a single recoverable original.
sources: AAMC, What's on the MCAT Exam?, Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills section overview: Foundations of Comprehension (main idea and purpose).
Original passage written for this app.

items.stem: As used at the end of the second paragraph, 'neutral' most nearly means:

options.B: free of any judgement about what matters

why_correct: The sentence reads: 'To choose a layer is to make an argument about what mattered most, and arguments can be good or bad, but they cannot be neutral.' Neutral is contrasted with making an argument about what mattered most.
So a neutral choice would be one that involved no judgement of value, which the author says is impossible.
Paragraph 3 confirms the sense by calling the decision 'a question of value'.

why_wrong.A: The author allows that analysis can be accurate 'often with great precision'; accuracy is not what is denied. What cannot be avoided is a judgement about what matters.
why_wrong.C: Ageing is discussed earlier in the paragraph, but the sentence is about the conservator's choice of layer, not about the paint's physical stability.
why_wrong.D: Nothing in the sentence concerns visibility; later, in paragraph 4, the author wants the boundary of restoration to be visible, which is a different point.

error_types.A: out of scope: accuracy is not the contrast being drawn
error_types.C: out of scope: an earlier topic in the paragraph
error_types.D: out of scope: borrowed from a later paragraph

items.takeaway: Define a word from the clause it sits in and the contrast it completes, not from the surrounding topic.
sources: AAMC, What's on the MCAT Exam?, Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills section overview: Foundations of Comprehension (meaning of words and phrases in context).
Original passage written for this app.

items.stem: The author mentions cross-sections, infrared imaging and pigment analysis (paragraph 3) primarily in order to:

options.A: concede the power of technical analysis before arguing that it cannot settle a question of value
options.B: show that conservators now have the tools to identify a painting's original surface
options.C: argue that scientific methods of examining paintings are unreliable
options.D: explain why earlier restorers made so many mistakes

why_correct: The paragraph opens with an objection ('The usual reply is that science settles the matter'), grants it ('I do not doubt this'), and then turns: 'But knowing what is on the canvas does not tell us what to do about it.'
The list of techniques makes the concession concrete; its function is to set up the distinction between fact and value that the paragraph ends on.
This concede-then-limit structure is a standard move for anticipating a counterargument.

why_wrong.B: Reversed. The author's point is that even with these tools the choice of surface remains a judgement; paragraph 2 denies that there is an original surface to identify.
why_wrong.C: Too extreme and contradicted: 'often with great precision' and 'I do not doubt this'.
why_wrong.D: Out of scope. Earlier restorers are mentioned in paragraph 2 as part of what a conservator confronts; their mistakes are never explained.

error_types.B: reversed relationship: the concession read as the conclusion
error_types.C: too extreme: contradicts the author's explicit concession
error_types.D: out of scope: a topic the passage does not pursue

items.takeaway: When an author grants a point and then says 'but', the granted point is a concession; ask what the 'but' is setting up.
sources: AAMC, What's on the MCAT Exam?, Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills section overview: Reasoning Within the Text (function of a detail in the argument).
Original passage written for this app.

items.stem: The author's attitude toward the critic described in the final paragraph is best described as:

options.A: contemptuous of his ignorance of conservation science
options.B: fully in agreement with his objection
options.C: indifferent, because the question is purely technical
options.D: sympathetic to his sense of loss, but unwilling to grant his claim to authenticity

why_correct: The author grants the critic something real: he 'is therefore not simply wrong', and what he reports 'is a loss, even if it was also the removal of grime.'
The author then withholds the larger claim: 'What he cannot claim is that his preferred state was the true one and the conservator's a fabrication. Both are versions.'
That combination, partial sympathy with a firm limit, is the attitude of the whole paragraph.

why_wrong.A: Too extreme. Nothing in the paragraph mocks the critic or calls him ignorant; the author treats his loss as genuine.
why_wrong.B: Reversed in part. The author agrees that a loss occurred but rejects the critic's central assumption that the older appearance was the true one.
why_wrong.C: Contradicted. The author's whole argument is that restoration is a question of value, not a purely technical one, and the final paragraph engages the critic seriously.

error_types.A: too extreme: hostility the text does not show
error_types.B: reversed relationship: partial agreement read as full agreement
error_types.C: outside knowledge contradicting the passage: 'purely technical' is what the author denies

items.takeaway: Attitude questions often hinge on a 'yes, but' structure; the answer must capture both halves.
sources: AAMC, What's on the MCAT Exam?, Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills section overview: Reasoning Within the Text (author's tone and attitude).
Original passage written for this app.

items.stem: Which of the following practices would the author most likely endorse?

options.A: removing every later addition so that only paint applied by the artist remains
options.B: leaving old paintings untouched so that their full history is preserved
options.C: retouching losses with a material that can be dissolved later and publishing a record of each step
options.D: returning a painting to the appearance it had when the public first came to love it

why_correct: Paragraph 4 sets out the author's criteria: each intervention should be 'defended in writing', should be one 'that can be undone by a successor', and should leave the boundary between the artist's hand and the restorer's visible.
A reversible retouching material and a published record meet the first two criteria directly.
The author also describes the best conservators as ones who 'clean, retouch, and consolidate', so retouching itself is not objectionable.

why_wrong.A: This assumes there is a pure authorial layer to return to, which paragraph 2 denies, and it treats removal as the obvious choice, which paragraph 3 says is a question of value.
why_wrong.B: Too extreme. The author says the honest position 'is not that we must never touch old paintings' and criticises timidity.
why_wrong.D: This is the critic's preferred state, which the author says is only one version with no special claim to be the true one.

error_types.A: outside knowledge contradicting the passage: assumes a recoverable original
error_types.B: too extreme: forbids what the author permits
error_types.D: reversed relationship: the position the author rejects

items.takeaway: To apply an author's view, use the criteria the author states, not the position of the people the author argues against.
sources: AAMC, What's on the MCAT Exam?, Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills section overview: Reasoning Beyond the Text (applying the author's ideas to a new situation).
Original passage written for this app.

items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the argument of the second paragraph?

options.A: Modern synthetic varnishes do not yellow with age
options.B: Surveys show that most museum visitors prefer paintings that have been cleaned
options.C: Conservators can usually identify the moment the artist stopped work and recover the surface exactly as it then appeared
options.D: Earlier restorers rarely documented what they added

why_correct: Paragraph 2 argues that 'there is no layer at which the picture is simply itself', because the artist altered the surface repeatedly and expected it to be seen under particular conditions.
If a single moment of completion could usually be identified and its surface recovered exactly, the premise that there is no privileged layer would be in serious doubt.
The author would still have the value argument of paragraph 3, but the specific claim of paragraph 2 would be weakened.

why_wrong.A: Irrelevant to old paintings, whose varnishes have already yellowed; the paragraph concerns what has happened to them, not what new materials do.
why_wrong.B: Public preference has no bearing on whether there is a single original state; the author's point is about what exists on the canvas and what choosing among layers involves.
why_wrong.D: This would support the author's description of a layered, altered surface rather than weaken it.

error_types.A: out of scope: concerns new materials, not old paintings
error_types.B: true but irrelevant: preference does not bear on the premise
error_types.D: reversed relationship: strengthens rather than weakens

items.takeaway: To weaken an argument, attack the premise the paragraph rests on, not a nearby fact.
sources: AAMC, What's on the MCAT Exam?, Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills section overview: Reasoning Beyond the Text (assessing the effect of new information on the argument).
Original passage written for this app.

items.stem: The author's primary purpose is to:

options.A: argue that walkability indices should be abandoned
options.B: show that a popular index measures the presence of destinations rather than people's access to them, and to propose measuring use instead
options.C: explain how walkability scores are calculated
options.D: demonstrate that suburbs are more walkable than inner-city districts

why_correct: The diagnosis is stated in paragraph 2: 'The index measures the presence of destinations, not access to them'. The remedy is stated in paragraph 4: 'not the distance to a grocery store but the share of households that reach one on foot each week'.
Paragraphs 3 and 5 supply the evidence and the warning; paragraph 1 describes the index to set up the critique.
The passage ends by restating the purpose: a good measure should ask 'whether it is walked, by whom, and at what cost.'

why_wrong.A: Too extreme. The author says plainly, 'Nor is the solution to abandon measurement', and credits the index with giving the idea 'a seat at the table'.
why_wrong.C: The calculation is described in one sentence of paragraph 1 only as background; the passage is an argument, not an explanation.
why_wrong.D: The suburb in paragraph 3 is one illustrative case; the author does not generalise about suburbs, and the point of the example is that the score misdescribed both places.

error_types.A: too extreme: the author rejects abandoning measurement
error_types.C: true but irrelevant: background mistaken for purpose
error_types.D: too extreme: one example generalised

items.takeaway: Purpose questions ask what the whole passage does; a diagnosis plus a proposed remedy is a common shape.
sources: AAMC, What's on the MCAT Exam?, Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills section overview: Foundations of Comprehension (main idea and purpose).
Original passage written for this app.

items.stem: According to the passage, the index awards more points when:

options.A: destinations are closer to the address
options.C: the route to a destination has a lit sidewalk
options.D: residents can afford what nearby shops sell

why_correct: Paragraph 1: 'The index is computed from distances ... with closer destinations earning more points.'
That is the only input the passage describes; everything else the author discusses is what the index leaves out.
The question tests careful reading of the setup, not the argument.

why_wrong.B: Reported walking is what the sociologists in paragraph 3 measured, and what the author wants measured; the index does not use it.
why_wrong.C: Paragraph 2 says a destination raises the score 'whether the route passes along a lit sidewalk or the shoulder of a four-lane road'; the sidewalk does not count.
why_wrong.D: Paragraph 2 says a supermarket raises the score 'whether or not the residents can afford to shop in it'.

error_types.B: reversed relationship: the author's proposed measure, not the index's input
error_types.C: outside knowledge contradicting the passage: the passage says this is ignored
error_types.D: outside knowledge contradicting the passage: the passage says this is ignored

items.takeaway: Detail questions are answered by the sentence that states the fact; the author's criticisms list what the index does not do.
sources: AAMC, What's on the MCAT Exam?, Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills section overview: Foundations of Comprehension (locating stated information).
Original passage written for this app.

items.stem: The author's claim that a high score 'becomes a reason not to invest' (paragraph 3) serves to:

options.A: show that the index is not merely incomplete but actively harmful
options.B: argue that spending on walking infrastructure is usually wasted
options.C: praise the index for directing investment to the neighbourhoods that need it
