options.D: suggest that residents of high-scoring districts exaggerate their fears

why_correct: The sentence is introduced with 'A measure that cannot see this is not merely incomplete; it can mislead, because ...'. The clause explains how misleading turns into harm.
The harm is specific: a good number removes the case for fixing 'the very things that would make walking possible', so the index's blind spot perpetuates itself.
The paragraph thus escalates from a limitation (the index is incomplete) to a harm (it misleads and blocks investment).

why_wrong.B: Reversed. The author wants investment in crossings, lighting and the like; the complaint is that the score discourages it.
why_wrong.C: Reversed. The sentence criticises the index for steering investment away from where it is needed.
why_wrong.D: Nothing in the passage doubts the residents' reports; the author treats them as the better evidence.

error_types.B: reversed relationship: the author favours the investment
error_types.C: reversed relationship: criticism read as praise
error_types.D: reversed relationship: the residents' reports are the trusted evidence

items.takeaway: Ask what a sentence adds to the paragraph's movement; here it turns a limitation into a harm.
sources: AAMC, What's on the MCAT Exam?, Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills section overview: Reasoning Within the Text (function of a claim within the argument).
Original passage written for this app.

items.stem: It can be inferred that the author believes the suburb mentioned in paragraph 3:

options.A: has a higher walkability score than the inner-city district
options.B: is walked more by its residents despite its lower score
options.C: lacks a grocery store within walking distance
options.D: was scored incorrectly by the index

why_correct: Paragraph 3 says residents of the high-scoring district 'report walking less than residents of a lower-scoring suburb'. So the suburb scores lower and is walked more.
The author uses the comparison to show that the score and actual walking come apart, which is the passage's central complaint.
No claim is made that the suburb's score was miscalculated; the point is that the score measures the wrong thing.

why_wrong.A: Contradicted by the text: the suburb is 'lower-scoring'.
why_wrong.C: Not stated. The passage says nothing about the suburb's shops; the shops discussed are in the inner-city district.
why_wrong.D: The author's argument is that the index computed its distances correctly but measured the wrong thing; 'scored incorrectly' misstates the criticism.

error_types.A: reversed relationship: the comparison inverted
error_types.C: out of scope: a detail the passage does not give
error_types.D: outside knowledge contradicting the passage: the index is accurate but misdirected

items.takeaway: An inference must follow from what is stated; 'lower-scoring' and 'walking less' fix the comparison.
sources: AAMC, What's on the MCAT Exam?, Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills section overview: Reasoning Within the Text (drawing inferences).
Original passage written for this app.

items.stem: Which proposed measure is most consistent with the author's recommendation in paragraph 4?

options.A: the number of shops within 500 metres of each home
options.B: the average distance from homes to the nearest park
options.C: the total length of sidewalk per square kilometre
options.D: the proportion of residents over 65 who walk to a pharmacy at least once a week

why_correct: Paragraph 4 asks for measures of use rather than availability ('the share of households that reach one on foot each week') and for attention to 'the experience of those for whom walking is ... the only option.'
A weekly walking rate among older residents measures actual trips by a group with limited alternatives, matching both criteria.
The other options are all map-based counts of what exists, exactly the kind of measure the author criticises.

why_wrong.A: A count of nearby destinations is the index's own logic, 'the presence of destinations, not access to them'.
why_wrong.B: A distance to the nearest facility is precisely the input the author rejects in favour of 'the share of households that reach one on foot'.
why_wrong.C: Sidewalk length is infrastructure that exists, not evidence that anyone walks on it; the author warns that such measures are 'easy to game'.

error_types.A: reversed relationship: the index's logic, not the author's
error_types.B: reversed relationship: the input the author rejects
error_types.C: true but irrelevant: availability, not use

items.takeaway: Apply the author's stated criteria (use, not availability; the experience of those with no alternative) to each option.
sources: AAMC, What's on the MCAT Exam?, Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills section overview: Reasoning Beyond the Text (applying the author's ideas to new cases).
Original passage written for this app.

items.stem: Suppose a city raises its average score from 60 to 75 over five years while surveys show its residents walk no more than before. The author would most likely view this as:

options.A: evidence that the index works, because the scores improved
options.B: proof that the residents are behaving irrationally
options.C: irrelevant, because surveys of residents are unreliable
options.D: an example of the index being gamed, as warned in the final paragraph

why_correct: The final paragraph predicts this exact situation: 'a city can raise its score by permitting a convenience store near every apartment block while its residents go on driving to the places they actually need.'
A rising score with unchanged walking is the gap between 'looks walkable from above' and 'is walked' that the author says a good measure should expose.
The author trusts surveys of residents over map-based scores (paragraph 3), so the survey result would be taken as the real outcome.

why_wrong.A: Reversed. For the author, the score is the suspect measure; a higher score with no more walking is a failure of the index, not a success.
why_wrong.B: Nothing in the passage blames residents; their choices are treated as reasonable responses to their surroundings.
why_wrong.C: Contradicted. The author's preferred measures 'require asking people rather than consulting a map'.

error_types.A: reversed relationship: the score treated as the outcome
error_types.B: outside knowledge contradicting the passage: residents are not criticised
error_types.C: outside knowledge contradicting the passage: surveys are the author's preferred evidence

items.takeaway: When new information matches a scenario the author has already described, the author's stated reaction to that scenario is the answer.
sources: AAMC, What's on the MCAT Exam?, Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills section overview: Reasoning Beyond the Text (assessing new information).
Original passage written for this app.

items.stem: Based on Table 1, the mean blood speed inside the narrowed segment before dilation was closest to:
why_correct: Blood is treated as incompressible, so the volume flow rate Av is the same in every segment (continuity): A₁v₁ = A₂v₂.
The area of a circular lumen is πr², so v₂ = v₁ (r₁/r₂)² = 0.30 m/s × (3.0/1.5)² = 0.30 × 4 = 1.2 m/s.
Shortcut: halving the radius quarters the area, so the speed quadruples.

why_wrong.A: 0.075 m/s is 0.30 m/s divided by 4: the speed has been made proportional to the area instead of inversely proportional to it; a narrower tube carries the same flow faster, not slower.
why_wrong.B: 0.60 m/s doubles the speed because the radius halved, but the area, which is what continuity uses, falls with the square of the radius.
why_wrong.D: 4.8 m/s multiplies by 2⁴ = 16, the fourth-power dependence that belongs to Poiseuille's law for flow at a fixed pressure difference, not to continuity.

error_types.A: reversed relationship: speed taken as proportional to area
error_types.B: wrong formula: radius ratio used instead of its square
error_types.D: wrong formula: Poiseuille's r⁴ applied to continuity

items.takeaway: For an incompressible fluid, A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, so halving a vessel's radius quadruples the speed of the blood through it.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 12.1 Flow Rate and Its Relation to Velocity (2022): A₁v̄₁ = A₂v̄₂; speed is inversely proportional to the square of the tube radius.

items.stem: In Figure 1 the mean pressure at the entry of the narrowed segment (x = 20 mm) is lower than the proximal pressure. Using Table 1 and the constants in the passage, this difference is best accounted for by:

options.A: ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²), about 7 × 10² Pa, the kinetic energy per unit volume that the blood gains as it speeds up
options.B: ½ρ(v₂ − v₁)², about 4 × 10² Pa, the kinetic energy per unit volume associated with the change in speed
options.C: 8ηLv₂/r₂², about 1 × 10² Pa, the viscous pressure loss along the 10 mm narrowed segment
options.D: ρg × 0.020 m, about 2 × 10² Pa, the hydrostatic pressure change over the 20 mm the wire travelled

why_correct: Read the chart: the pressure falls from 90.0 mmHg (x ≤ 19 mm) to 84.6 mmHg at x = 20 mm, a drop of 5.4 mmHg, which is 5.4 × 133 ≈ 7.2 × 10² Pa.

Bernoulli's equation along a horizontal streamline: P₁ + ½ρv₁² = P₂ + ½ρv₂², so P₁ − P₂ = ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²). With v₁ = 0.30 m/s (Table 1) and v₂ = 1.2 m/s (continuity, four times faster), v₂² − v₁² = 1.44 − 0.09 = 1.35 m²/s², and ½ × 1060 × 1.35 ≈ 530 × 1.35 ≈ 7.2 × 10² Pa.

Shortcut: v₁² is only one sixteenth of v₂², so the drop is about 15/16 of ½ρv₂² ≈ 0.94 × 760 ≈ 7.2 × 10² Pa. The drop occurs abruptly where the speed changes, which is the signature of a kinetic (Bernoulli) effect rather than a loss that accumulates with length.

why_wrong.B: The Bernoulli terms are ½ρv² for each speed; their difference is ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²), not ½ρ(v₂ − v₁)². The wrong expression gives 530 × 0.81 ≈ 4.3 × 10² Pa (3.2 mmHg), which does not match the 5.4 mmHg drop in Figure 1.
why_wrong.C: The viscous (Poiseuille) loss along the narrowed segment is real but is the gentle decline from x = 20 mm to x = 30 mm in Figure 1 (about 1 mmHg, or 1.3 × 10² Pa); it accumulates with length and cannot produce the abrupt fall at the entry.
why_wrong.D: The vessel is horizontal in the analysis, so there is no hydrostatic term along it; ρgh with h = 0.020 m would be about 2.1 × 10² Pa, which neither matches the drop nor applies here.

error_types.B: wrong formula: difference of speeds squared instead of difference of squared speeds
error_types.C: true but irrelevant: the viscous loss is the gradual decline, not the entry drop
error_types.D: wrong formula: a hydrostatic term applied to a horizontal vessel

items.takeaway: Where a vessel narrows, the pressure falls by ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²) over the short entry region; viscous losses, by contrast, grow with the length of the segment.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 12.2 Bernoulli's Equation (2022): P₁ + ½ρv₁² + ρgh₁ = P₂ + ½ρv₂² + ρgh₂; pressure drops in a rapidly moving fluid.
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 12.4 Viscosity and Laminar Flow; Poiseuille's Law (2022): Q = (P₂ − P₁)πr⁴/(8ηl), so the viscous pressure loss grows with tube length.

items.stem: Consider the 10 mm segment on its own, with laminar flow and the same pressure difference maintained between its two ends. Compared with the flow through the segment before the plaque formed (radius 3.0 mm), the flow with the plaque in place (radius 1.5 mm) is:
why_correct: Poiseuille's law for laminar flow through a tube: Q = πr⁴ΔP/(8ηL). With ΔP, η and L fixed, Q is proportional to r⁴.
Halving the radius multiplies the flow by (1/2)⁴ = 1/16.
This is why small changes in vessel radius, by plaque or by smooth-muscle tone, have such large effects on flow: a 50% narrowing cuts flow at a given pressure difference by about 94%.

why_wrong.B: 1/8 corresponds to a cubic dependence (r³), which is not the exponent in Poiseuille's law.
why_wrong.C: 1/4 is the change in cross-sectional area (r²); at a fixed pressure difference the flow falls much faster than the area, because the fluid near the walls moves slowly and a narrower tube is wall-dominated.
why_wrong.D: 1/2 treats flow as proportional to the radius itself; it is proportional to the fourth power.

error_types.B: wrong formula: r³ instead of r⁴
error_types.C: wrong formula: area (r²) instead of r⁴
error_types.D: wrong formula: flow taken as proportional to r

items.takeaway: At a fixed pressure difference, laminar flow through a tube scales with r⁴, so halving the radius cuts the flow sixteenfold.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 12.4 Viscosity and Laminar Flow; Poiseuille's Law (2022): Q = (P₂ − P₁)πr⁴/(8ηl), with r raised to the fourth power.

items.stem: The bruit heard over the plaque was present only during systole. Which of the following best explains this observation?

options.A: During systole the pressure inside the narrowed segment rises above the proximal pressure, and that pressure difference vibrates the vessel wall.
options.B: Only at peak systolic speed does the Reynolds number in the narrowed segment rise past the laminar range, so eddies form and make noise.
options.C: Blood viscosity falls during systole, which lowers the Reynolds number in the narrowed segment and lets the flow separate from the wall.
options.D: Surface tension at the surface of the plaque is overcome only at the systolic pressure peak, releasing bubbles that are heard as a murmur.

why_correct: Governing principle: N_R = 2ρvr/η. In a tube the flow is laminar below about 2000 and turbulent above about 3000; between those values it is unstable.

In the narrowed segment, at mean flow v = 1.2 m/s and r = 1.5 mm: N_R = 2 × 1060 × 1.2 × 1.5 × 10⁻³ / 3.0 × 10⁻³ ≈ 1.3 × 10³ (laminar). At peak systole the speed is four times the proximal peak, 4 × 0.75 = 3.0 m/s, so N_R ≈ 2 × 1060 × 3.0 × 1.5 × 10⁻³ / 3.0 × 10⁻³ ≈ 3.2 × 10³, above the turbulent threshold. In the proximal segment even the peak value (v = 0.75 m/s, r = 3.0 mm) is only about 1.6 × 10³.

Turbulent flow is noisy: the same physics produces Korotkoff sounds under a blood-pressure cuff and the murmurs of narrowed valves. Since the Reynolds number scales with speed, the threshold is crossed only at the systolic peak, so the bruit comes and goes with each heartbeat.

why_wrong.A: Bernoulli's equation gives the opposite: where the blood moves faster, inside the narrowing, the pressure is lower than proximally (Figure 1 shows the fall).
why_wrong.C: The Reynolds number rises, not falls, when viscosity falls (η is in the denominator), and blood viscosity does not change meaningfully within one heartbeat.
why_wrong.D: Surface tension concerns liquid–gas interfaces and there is no gas phase in the artery; the murmur is sound generated by turbulent liquid flow.

error_types.A: reversed relationship: pressure taken to rise where speed rises
error_types.C: reversed relationship: lower viscosity lowers rather than raises N_R, and the premise is false
error_types.D: out of scope: surface tension has no role in single-phase arterial flow

items.takeaway: N_R = 2ρvr/η rises with speed; a stenosis pushes the systolic Reynolds number past the laminar range, and the resulting turbulence is heard as a bruit.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 12.5 The Onset of Turbulence (2022): N_R = 2ρvr/η; laminar below about 2000, unstable between 2000 and 3000, turbulent above about 3000; turbulence is noisy (Korotkoff sounds).
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 12.2 Bernoulli's Equation (2022): pressure drops in a rapidly moving fluid.

items.stem: The investigators proposed that the plaque was responsible for the lower pressure in the distal segment (87.0 mmHg against 90.0 mmHg proximally). Which finding after balloon dilation would provide the strongest support for this proposal?

options.A: The proximal pressure rises above 90.0 mmHg.
options.B: The mean speed in the treated segment is about 0.30 m/s, a quarter of the value calculated for the narrowed segment before dilation.
options.C: The bruit over the treated segment disappears.
options.D: The distal pressure returns to within about 1 mmHg of the proximal pressure.

why_correct: The proposal is about the pressure drop across the plaque. The direct test is to remove the plaque's narrowing and see whether the pressure difference disappears: if the distal pressure returns to nearly the proximal value, the drop depended on the narrowing.

Flow in the circulation follows Q = ΔP/R; the arterial pressure that reaches the tissues downstream depends on the resistance of the segments upstream. A focal narrowing adds resistance and dissipates energy (Figure 1 shows the drop and the incomplete recovery). Restoring the radius removes that resistance, so the pressure downstream should recover.
This is the logic of a within-subject before-and-after comparison: the same vessel, with and without the narrowing.

why_wrong.A: A change in proximal pressure says nothing about the pressure lost across the plaque; the proposal concerns the difference between proximal and distal segments, and proximal pressure is set largely by the heart and the rest of the circulation.
why_wrong.B: A fall in speed inside the dilated segment is required by continuity whenever the radius returns to 3.0 mm; it would happen whether or not the plaque had reduced distal pressure, so it does not test the proposal.
why_wrong.C: Loss of the bruit shows that the flow is no longer turbulent, but turbulence and the pressure loss are different consequences of the narrowing; a bruit could vanish while a smaller residual pressure drop persists, so this is weaker evidence than measuring the pressure itself.

error_types.A: true but irrelevant: proximal pressure is not the quantity in question
error_types.B: true but irrelevant: follows from continuity regardless of the hypothesis
error_types.C: true but irrelevant: measures turbulence, not perfusion pressure

items.takeaway: To show that a narrowing caused a downstream pressure loss, remove the narrowing and measure the same pressure difference again: Q = ΔP/R, and a focal stenosis is added resistance.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 20.2 Blood Flow, Blood Pressure, and Resistance (2022): blood flow is proportional to the pressure difference and inversely proportional to resistance; vessel radius is the main determinant of resistance.
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 12.4 Viscosity and Laminar Flow; Poiseuille's Law (2022): Q = (P₂ − P₁)/R with R = 8ηl/(πr⁴).

items.stem: Using the analyser's equation and the values in Table 1, the arterial pH of Patient 3 was closest to:
why_correct: Passage: pH = pKa′ + log([HCO₃⁻]/(0.03 × PCO₂)) with pKa′ = 6.1. For Patient 3, [HCO₃⁻] = 12 mmol/L and PCO₂ = 80 mmHg.

Check against Patient 1: 24/(0.03 × 40) = 24/1.2 = 20, log 20 = 1.30, pH = 7.40, as in the table. Patient 3 has both a low bicarbonate (metabolic acidosis) and a high PCO₂ from depressed breathing (respiratory acidosis), so the ratio is far below 20 and the pH is severely low.

why_wrong.A: 5.3 comes from taking the ratio 12/80 = 0.15 without converting PCO₂ in mmHg to dissolved CO₂ in mmol/L (log 0.15 ≈ −0.82): the two quantities in the ratio must be in the same units.
why_wrong.C: 7.1 results from using a normal PCO₂ of 40 mmHg (ratio 12/1.2 = 10, log 10 = 1): the table gives 80 mmHg for this patient.
why_wrong.D: 7.4 assumes the patient is normal or that respiratory compensation has restored the ratio to 20; with [HCO₃⁻] = 12 that would need PCO₂ = 20 mmHg, the opposite of the measured 80.

error_types.A: sign or unit error: PCO₂ not converted with the 0.03 solubility coefficient
error_types.C: misread graph: PCO₂ read as the reference value instead of the table value
error_types.D: true but irrelevant: the normal pH, not this patient's

items.takeaway: For blood, pH = 6.1 + log([HCO₃⁻]/(0.03 × PCO₂)); a ratio of 20 gives 7.4, and each halving of the ratio lowers the pH by 0.30.
sources: Acid-Base Physiology (Brandis), 2.2 Buffering (anaesthesiamcq.com): pH = 6.1 + log{[HCO₃⁻]/(0.03 × PCO₂)}, pKa′ 6.1 at 37 °C, 0.03 mmol/L per mmHg.
OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 14.6 Buffers (2019): Henderson–Hasselbalch equation.

items.stem: The analyser's electrodes are held at 37 °C, where Kw = 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁴. A sample of pure water at 37 °C is best described as:

options.A: neutral, with a pH slightly below 7
options.B: slightly acidic, because its pH is below 7
options.C: neutral, with a pH of exactly 7.00, because only [OH⁻] changes with temperature
options.D: slightly basic, because the extra ionization at 37 °C produces more OH⁻ than H₃O⁺

why_correct: Water self-ionizes, 2 H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻, producing the two ions in equal numbers, so pure water is always neutral: [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻] whatever the temperature.
Neutral means [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻], not pH 7; pH 7 is neutral only at 25 °C, where Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴. Self-ionization is endothermic, so Kw grows with temperature and the neutral pH falls.

why_wrong.B: A pH below 7 does not make a solution acidic unless [H₃O⁺] exceeds [OH⁻]; in pure water they are equal at every temperature.
why_wrong.C: The ions are produced together, so [H₃O⁺] and [OH⁻] rise together; neither can change alone, and pH 7.00 is neutral only when Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴.
why_wrong.D: Self-ionization produces one OH⁻ for every H₃O⁺, so the extra ionization cannot create an excess of either.

error_types.B: wrong formula: neutrality equated with pH 7 rather than [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻]
error_types.C: wrong formula: one ion assumed to change without the other
error_types.D: reversed relationship: ionization produces the ions in equal numbers

items.takeaway: Neutral means [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻] = √Kw; because Kw rises with temperature, neutral water at 37 °C has pH about 6.8, not 7.
sources: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 14.1 Brønsted-Lowry Acids and Bases (2019): autoionization is endothermic and Kw increases with temperature; in pure water [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻].
University of Waterloo, Chem 13 News, Tough questions series, 2014 exam: Kw at 37 °C = 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁴, [H₃O⁺] = 1.5 × 10⁻⁷ mol/L, pH 6.81.

items.stem: According to Figure 1, the apparent pKa of carbonic acid under the conditions of the titration is closest to:
why_correct: For a weak acid titrated with strong base, pH = pKa at the half-equivalence point, where half of the acid has been converted to its conjugate base so that [A⁻] = [HA] and the log term in the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation is zero.

Equivalence check: 100.0 mL × 20 mmol/L = 2.0 mmol of carbonic acid, which needs 2.0 mmol of OH⁻, that is 2.0 mmol ÷ 0.200 mmol/mL = 10.0 mL of NaOH, as the passage states. Half-equivalence is therefore at 5.0 mL.
Reading Figure 1 at half of the equivalence volume, 5.0 mL, gives pH 6.1, which matches the pKa′ the analyser uses. The curve is flattest there, the centre of the buffer region, as expected.

why_wrong.B: 7.4 is the normal arterial pH, which lies in the buffer region of the curve (about 9.5 mL) but is not the pKa; the bicarbonate system holds blood far from its pKa because the lungs and kidneys keep the ratio near 20:1.
why_wrong.C: 8.1 is the pH at the equivalence point (10.0 mL), where the solution is essentially sodium bicarbonate; the equivalence pH of a weak acid is above 7, but it is not the pKa.
why_wrong.D: 10.0 is roughly the second pKa (bicarbonate losing its proton), which the passage says was not titrated; it cannot be read from a curve that stops at the first equivalence point.

error_types.B: true but irrelevant: physiological pH is not a feature of the curve
error_types.C: misread graph: equivalence point read instead of half-equivalence
error_types.D: out of scope: the second proton was not titrated

items.takeaway: On a weak-acid titration curve, pH equals pKa at half the equivalence volume, the flattest part of the curve.
sources: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 14.7 Acid-Base Titrations (2019): pH = pKa at the half-equivalence point in a titration of a weak acid.
OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 14.6 Buffers (2019): Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]).

items.stem: Based on Table 1, whose blood has the least remaining capacity for the bicarbonate buffer to take up additional acid (H⁺) produced by metabolism?

options.A: Patient 1, because a ratio of 20:1 is far from the ideal buffer ratio of 1:1
options.B: Patient 2, because the bicarbonate concentration, the base that accepts H⁺, is lowest
options.C: Patient 3, because the pH is lowest
options.D: Patients 2 and 3 equally, because both have a bicarbonate-to-CO₂ ratio below 20

why_correct: Added H⁺ is removed by the base of the pair: H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ → H₂CO₃ → CO₂ + H₂O. The capacity to absorb more acid is set by how much HCO₃⁻ remains, since the CO₂ formed is breathed off and does not accumulate.

Table 1: [HCO₃⁻] is 24 mmol/L (Patient 1), 6 mmol/L (Patient 2) and 12 mmol/L (Patient 3). Patient 2 has only a quarter of the normal bicarbonate left; a further acid load of 6 mmol/L would exhaust the buffer entirely.
Patient 2's pH (7.10) is less severe than Patient 3's (6.80) only because rapid deep breathing has lowered PCO₂ to 20 mmHg; that compensation hides how little bicarbonate reserve remains.

why_wrong.A: Patient 1 has the largest bicarbonate reserve. The 20:1 ratio is far from the 1:1 ideal for a closed buffer, but the bicarbonate system is open (CO₂ is exhaled), and the reserve against acid is the amount of HCO₃⁻, which is normal here.
why_wrong.C: pH reports the current ratio, not the reserve; Patient 3's low pH is driven largely by a high PCO₂ (the acid side), while twice as much bicarbonate remains as in Patient 2.
why_wrong.D: A ratio below 20 shows that both patients are acidaemic, but capacity for more acid depends on the absolute bicarbonate concentration, which is 6 mmol/L in one and 12 mmol/L in the other.

error_types.A: reversed relationship: the normal patient has the most reserve
error_types.C: misread graph: pH taken as a measure of remaining capacity
error_types.D: too extreme: equal ratios below 20 treated as equal reserves

items.takeaway: A buffer's reserve against added acid is the amount of its base form; in blood that is [HCO₃⁻], and respiratory compensation can normalise pH while the reserve stays dangerously low.
sources: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 14.6 Buffers (2019): buffer capacity depends on the amounts of the weak acid and its conjugate base; added strong acid is consumed by the conjugate base.
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 26.4 Acid-Base Balance (2022): bicarbonate and carbonic acid are present at 20:1, which makes the system most effective against added acid.

items.stem: The laboratory performed the calibration titration at 37 °C, the temperature of the analyser's electrodes, rather than at room temperature. Which statement best justifies this choice?

options.A: The ionic strength of a solution rises with temperature, and the apparent pKa′ of carbonic acid depends on the ionic strength.
options.B: Kw equals 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ only at 37 °C, so the electrodes can measure pH accurately only at that temperature.
options.C: Ka is an equilibrium constant and changes with temperature, so a pKa′ measured at 25 °C would not apply to blood at 37 °C.
options.D: The solubility coefficient of CO₂ does not depend on temperature, so temperature needs to be controlled only for the electrodes.

why_correct: Ka is the equilibrium constant of HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻. Like every equilibrium constant, its value is fixed only at a given temperature: changing the temperature re-establishes equilibrium with a different K (the forward and reverse rate constants respond differently to temperature). Concentration or pressure changes shift the position of an equilibrium but leave K unchanged; temperature is the one variable that changes K itself.

The analyser uses pKa′ to convert measured pH and PCO₂ into [HCO₃⁻] for blood at 37 °C, so the constant it needs is the one that holds at 37 °C in a plasma-like solution. Titrating at the same temperature (and at plasma ionic strength, 0.15 mol/L NaCl) measures the constant under the conditions in which it will be applied.
The passage's own data illustrate the principle: Kw, another equilibrium constant, is 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 37 °C but 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C.

why_wrong.A: Ionic strength does affect pKa′, which is why the titration used 0.15 mol/L NaCl, but ionic strength is set by the dissolved ions, not by temperature; the statement confuses two separate conditions.
why_wrong.B: Kw is 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C and 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 37 °C (passage); pH can be measured at any temperature with a thermostatted, calibrated electrode.
why_wrong.D: The solubility of a gas in water falls as temperature rises, so the 0.03 coefficient is itself a 37 °C value; the claim is false, and it also ignores the dependence of Ka on temperature.

error_types.A: true but irrelevant: ionic strength matters but is not a function of temperature
error_types.B: outside knowledge contradicting the passage: Kw at 37 °C is given as 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁴
error_types.D: reversed relationship: gas solubility does change with temperature

items.takeaway: Only temperature changes the value of an equilibrium constant such as Ka or Kw, so a constant must be measured, or looked up, at the temperature at which it will be used.
sources: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 13.3 Shifting Equilibria: Le Châtelier's Principle (2019): a change in temperature changes the value of the equilibrium constant, whereas changes in concentration or pressure do not.
Acid-Base Physiology (Brandis), 2.2 Buffering (anaesthesiamcq.com): the pKa of the bicarbonate system depends on temperature, [H⁺] and ionic strength (6.099 at 37 °C, pH 7.4).
OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 11.3 Solubility (2019): the solubility of gases in water decreases as temperature rises.

items.stem: From the uninhibited data in Table 1, the kinase's Km and Vmax are closest to:
why_correct: Vmax is the rate the enzyme approaches when the substrate saturates it. In Table 1 the rate rises from 109 nmol/min at 200 µmol/L to 119 at 2000 µmol/L, a tenfold increase in [S] for almost no gain, so the plateau is at about 120 nmol/min.
Km is the substrate concentration at which v₀ = Vmax/2 = 60 nmol/min. The table gives exactly 60 nmol/min at [S] = 20 µmol/L, so Km = 20 µmol/L.
Check with the Michaelis–Menten equation at 40 µmol/L: 120 × 40/(20 + 40) = 80 nmol/min, as tabulated; and at 2000 µmol/L: 120 × 2000/2020 ≈ 119.

why_wrong.A: 60 nmol/min is Vmax/2, the rate at Km, not the maximum; the rates in the table go well above 60.
why_wrong.B: 60 µmol/L is the apparent Km in the presence of the inhibitor (the passage states it), not the enzyme's own Km, which comes from the uninhibited column.
why_wrong.C: Km is not the highest substrate concentration tested, and 119 is a rate near saturation rather than a concentration; Km is defined by the half-maximal rate.

error_types.A: misread graph: the half-maximal rate taken as Vmax
error_types.B: misread graph: the inhibited value used for the uninhibited enzyme
error_types.C: wrong formula: Km confused with the largest [S] tested

items.takeaway: Read Vmax from the plateau at saturating substrate and Km as the substrate concentration that gives half of it.
sources: Biology LibreTexts, Biochemistry Free For All (Ahern, Rajagopal, Tan), 4.1 Basic Principles of Catalysis: Km is the substrate concentration that causes the enzyme to work at half of Vmax; Vmax is the maximum velocity.
OpenStax Biology 2e, 6.5 Enzymes (2018): the rate rises with substrate until the active sites are saturated.

items.stem: If the uninhibited data in Table 1 were plotted as 1/v₀ against 1/[S] (a Lineweaver–Burk plot), with v₀ in nmol/min and [S] in µmol/L, the intercepts on the vertical and horizontal axes would be:
why_correct: Taking reciprocals of the Michaelis–Menten equation gives 1/v₀ = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax, a straight line in 1/[S].

Setting 1/[S] = 0 gives the vertical intercept 1/Vmax = 1/120 min/nmol; setting 1/v₀ = 0 gives the horizontal intercept −1/Km = −1/20 L/µmol (that is, −0.05), on the negative side of the axis. The slope is Km/Vmax = 20/120 = 1/6.
Check with one data point: at [S] = 10 µmol/L, 1/[S] = 0.10 and 1/v₀ should be (1/6)(0.10) + 1/120 = 0.0167 + 0.0083 = 0.025 min/nmol, so v₀ = 40 nmol/min, as in Table 1.

why_wrong.A: The two intercepts have been swapped: 1/Vmax belongs on the vertical axis (the rate axis) and −1/Km on the horizontal (the substrate axis).
why_wrong.B: These are Vmax and Km themselves; a double-reciprocal plot gives their reciprocals, and the units (min/nmol, L/µmol) show it.
why_wrong.D: The horizontal intercept is −1/Km, to the left of the origin; a positive intercept would require a negative Km.

error_types.A: reversed relationship: the intercepts interchanged
error_types.B: wrong formula: reciprocals not taken
error_types.D: sign or unit error: the horizontal intercept is negative

items.takeaway: On a Lineweaver–Burk plot the vertical intercept is 1/Vmax, the horizontal intercept is −1/Km and the slope is Km/Vmax.
sources: Biology LibreTexts, Biochemistry Free For All (Ahern, Rajagopal, Tan), 4.1 Basic Principles of Catalysis: Km is the negative reciprocal of the x-intercept and Vmax the reciprocal of the y-intercept of a Lineweaver–Burk plot.

items.stem: The inhibitor's effect on Km and Vmax fits a competitive model, in which the apparent Km equals Km(1 + [I]/Ki). Using the Km from the uninhibited data, the apparent Km given in the passage and the inhibitor concentration used, Ki is closest to:
why_correct: Passage: with 20 µmol/L inhibitor the apparent Km was 60 µmol/L and Vmax was unchanged. From the uninhibited column of Table 1, Km = 20 µmol/L (the rate there, 60 nmol/min, is half of the 120 nmol/min plateau).
Competitive inhibition: Km,app = Km(1 + [I]/Ki). So 60 = 20 × (1 + 20/Ki), which gives 1 + 20/Ki = 3, 20/Ki = 2 and Ki = 10 µmol/L.

Shortcut: the apparent Km tripled, so [I]/Ki = 2 and Ki is half the inhibitor concentration. A Ki below the concentration tested means most of the free enzyme carries inhibitor at 20 µmol/L, yet Vmax is still reached at saturating substrate because the peptide displaces it (Table 1: 117 against 119 nmol/min at 2000 µmol/L).

why_wrong.B: 20 µmol/L is the inhibitor concentration itself; Ki would equal [I] only if the apparent Km had doubled (1 + [I]/Ki = 2), but it tripled.
why_wrong.C: 40 µmol/L is the difference between the apparent and true Km (60 − 20); the competitive relation is multiplicative, Km,app = Km(1 + [I]/Ki), not additive.
why_wrong.D: 60 µmol/L is the apparent Km read straight from the passage, not the inhibition constant; Ki describes the inhibitor–enzyme pair and is found from how far the apparent Km exceeds Km.

error_types.B: wrong formula: Ki set equal to [I] whatever the Km ratio
error_types.C: wrong formula: the Km difference taken as Ki
error_types.D: misread graph: the apparent Km reported as Ki

items.takeaway: For a competitive inhibitor, Km,app = Km(1 + [I]/Ki): the factor by which the apparent Km exceeds Km, minus one, equals [I]/Ki.
sources: Chemistry LibreTexts, Biochemistry Online (Jakubowski), Competitive Inhibition (CSU Chico CHEM 451, 8.4 Enzyme Inhibition): Kmapp = Km(1 + I/Kis), the Km term multiplied by 1 + I/Kis, while Vm does not change.

Biology LibreTexts, Biochemistry Free For All (Ahern, Rajagopal, Tan), 4.2 Control of Enzymatic Activity: competitive inhibition leaves Vmax unchanged and raises the apparent Km; it is overcome by raising the substrate concentration.

items.stem: The assay included MgCl₂ in excess of ATP. Mg²⁺ is required in the assay because it:

options.A: is consumed as a co-substrate, donating the electrons that reduce the γ-phosphate before it is transferred
options.B: binds the negatively charged phosphates of ATP, forming the Mg²⁺–ATP complex that the kinase recognises as its substrate
options.C: is covalently bonded to the kinase as a prosthetic group and carries the phosphate between ATP and the peptide
options.D: raises the pH of the buffer to the kinase's optimum

why_correct: Passage: in the cell ATP exists almost entirely as its complex with Mg²⁺. Inorganic ions such as Mg²⁺ are cofactors: non-protein helpers an enzyme needs for activity. For enzymes that use ATP, the true substrate is the metal–nucleotide complex, and the enzymes are essentially inactive without a divalent metal ion.

The triphosphate chain of ATP carries several negative charges. Mg²⁺ coordinates phosphate oxygens, neutralising part of that charge and holding the phosphates in a defined conformation that the active site can bind and from which the γ-phosphate can be transferred.
Because the Mg²⁺–ATP dissociation constant is about 0.1 mmol/L, adding MgCl₂ in excess of ATP (5 mmol/L against 1 mmol/L) ensures that essentially all the ATP is in the complexed, usable form.

why_wrong.A: Phosphoryl transfer is not a redox reaction and Mg²⁺ is not consumed; it is a cofactor, released unchanged after each turnover.
why_wrong.C: Mg²⁺ binds ATP and the enzyme noncovalently; a prosthetic group is a tightly bound organic cofactor such as heme, and the phosphate is transferred directly from ATP to the substrate hydroxyl.
why_wrong.D: Mg²⁺ is not a base and MgCl₂ does not raise pH; the buffer sets the pH at 7.5.

error_types.A: wrong formula: a redox role given to a Lewis-acid cofactor
error_types.C: out of scope: a prosthetic group is covalently or tightly bound and organic
error_types.D: true but irrelevant: pH is set by the buffer, not the salt

items.takeaway: Kinases use Mg²⁺–ATP, not free ATP: the Mg²⁺ cofactor neutralises and positions the phosphates so that the γ-phosphate can be transferred.
sources: OpenStax Biology 2e, 6.5 Enzymes (2018): cofactors are inorganic ions such as Fe²⁺ and Mg²⁺ that enzymes require for activity.

Berg, Tymoczko and Stryer, Biochemistry, 5th ed. (2002), section 9.4 (NMP kinases): enzymes using ATP are essentially inactive without divalent metal ions; the metal ion–nucleotide complex is the true substrate; the ATP–Mg²⁺ dissociation constant is about 0.1 mM.

items.stem: After dialysis, the inhibitor-treated enzyme showed 85% of the activity of untreated enzyme. Which conclusion is best supported, and what additional sample is most needed to interpret the remaining 15% loss?

options.A: Most of the inhibition is reversible, since dialysis restored most of the activity; enzyme dialysed without inhibitor is needed to show how much activity the dialysis itself removes.
options.B: The inhibitor is partly irreversible, because 15% of the enzyme must have been covalently modified; a sample with a higher inhibitor concentration is needed to measure the covalent fraction.
options.C: The inhibitor was not removed by dialysis, because activity did not return fully; enzyme assayed with inhibitor but without dialysis is needed.
options.D: The inhibitor is noncompetitive, because activity was measured at a single substrate concentration; a full substrate series after dialysis is needed to classify it.

why_correct: A reversible inhibitor binds noncovalently and dissociates; dialysis against inhibitor-free buffer removes the free inhibitor through the membrane, the bound inhibitor dissociates to restore equilibrium, and activity returns. An irreversible inhibitor is covalently attached and stays with the enzyme, so activity does not return. At 20 µmol/L substrate the rate rose from 30 nmol/min with inhibitor present (half of the uninhibited 60, Table 1) to 51 nmol/min after dialysis (85%), so most of the inhibition was reversible.

The 15% shortfall has two candidate causes: incomplete reversal (some inhibitor still bound or irreversibly attached) or damage to the enzyme during 12 hours of dialysis (denaturation, adsorption to the membrane, loss of a cofactor). The passage says no other samples were dialysed, so the experiment cannot tell them apart.

The missing control is enzyme carried through the identical dialysis without inhibitor. If it also loses about 15%, the inhibition was fully reversible; if it loses nothing, the 15% is a genuine residual inhibition. Treating a procedure's own effect as part of the result is the classic confound this control removes.

why_wrong.B: Attributing the 15% loss to covalent modification assumes the dialysis itself was harmless, which was never tested; and a higher inhibitor concentration would not separate reversible from irreversible loss.
why_wrong.C: The rate rose from half of the uninhibited value with inhibitor present to 85% after dialysis, so most of the inhibitor was clearly removed; the proposed sample is simply the inhibited measurement already in Table 1.
why_wrong.D: Inhibitor type is read from the change in Km and Vmax across a substrate series with inhibitor present (the passage reports competitive-type behaviour); a single post-dialysis rate says nothing about mechanism, and the question is about reversibility.

error_types.B: too extreme: a residual loss assigned to a mechanism without the control
error_types.C: outside knowledge contradicting the passage: activity rose substantially after dialysis
error_types.D: out of scope: inhibitor type is not what the dialysis tests

items.takeaway: Recovery of activity after dialysis shows reversible (noncovalent) inhibition, but only an enzyme-only sample dialysed in parallel can show whether any residual loss is inhibition or the cost of the procedure.
sources: Biology LibreTexts, Biochemistry Free For All (Ahern, Rajagopal, Tan), 4.2 Control of Enzymatic Activity: irreversible inhibitors become covalently bound to the enzyme; reversible inhibitors bind noncovalently.

Chemistry LibreTexts, The Basics of General, Organic, and Biological Chemistry (Ball et al.), 18.8 Enzyme Inhibition: a reversible inhibitor can dissociate from the enzyme; an irreversible inhibitor bonds covalently and the inhibition cannot be reversed.

items.stem: The afternoon patient's 250 MBq dose was to be drawn from the second vial. The time at which that vial's activity fell below 250 MBq was closest to:
why_correct: Table 1 confirms the half-life stated in the passage: the first vial halves every 110 min (800 → 400 → 200 → 100 MBq). The second vial, 1200 MBq at 08:00, follows the same steps: 600 MBq at 09:50, 300 MBq at 11:40, 150 MBq at 13:30 and 75 MBq at 15:20.
250 MBq lies between 300 MBq (11:40) and 150 MBq (13:30), so the activity crossed 250 MBq between those two times, and 12:10 is the only choice in that interval.

Estimate of where: 250/300 = 5/6 ≈ 0.83 and (½)^(1/4) ≈ 0.84, so the crossing came about a quarter of a half-life (about 28 min) after 11:40, near 12:08. By 15:20 only 1200/16 = 75 MBq remained, so the planned injection could not be drawn from this vial.

why_wrong.A: 11:05 is when the first vial (400 MBq at 09:50, 200 MBq at 11:40) passed 250 MBq; the afternoon dose was to come from the second vial, calibrated at 1200 MBq.
why_wrong.C: 13:30 is the first time in Table 1 at which the second vial's activity (150 MBq) is already below 250 MBq; the activity falls continuously and was still 300 MBq at 11:40, so the crossing came before 13:30.
why_wrong.D: 15:20 is the planned injection time; the passage reserves the vial for that patient, but by then four half-lives had passed and only 75 MBq remained.

error_types.A: misread graph: the first vial's activities used for the second vial
error_types.C: misread graph: the first tabulated time below the threshold taken as the crossing
error_types.D: true but irrelevant: the planned time, not the time the activity crossed 250 MBq

items.takeaway: Step the activity down by half at each half-life and bracket the target: 1200 MBq is 300 after two half-lives and 150 after three, so it passes 250 MBq a little after the second.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 31.5 Half-Life and Activity (2022): activity falls to half its value in each half-life; N = N₀e^(−λt).
NNDC NuDat (KAERI nuclide table) and TUNL Nuclear Data Evaluation, A = 18: fluorine-18 half-life 109.77 min.

items.stem: The decay constant of fluorine-18, and the fraction of a dose's activity that remains 55 minutes after calibration, are closest to:
why_correct: 55 min is half of one half-life, so the fraction remaining is (½)^(1/2) = 1/√2 ≈ 0.71. Equivalently e^(−λt) = e^(−0.693 × 0.5) = e^(−0.35) ≈ 0.71.
Shortcut: 2^(−0.5) = 1/1.414 = 0.707. Decay is exponential, so half of a half-life leaves about 71%, not 75%.

why_wrong.A: 9.1 × 10⁻³ min⁻¹ is 1/T½ without the factor ln 2, and a fraction of 0.50 would require a full half-life (110 min), not 55 min.
why_wrong.B: The fraction is right, but 9.1 × 10⁻³ min⁻¹ is 1/T½ without the factor ln 2; λ = ln 2/T½, not 1/T½.
why_wrong.C: The decay constant is right, but 0.75 treats decay as linear (half of the loss over half the time); exponential decay leaves 71% after half a half-life.

error_types.A: wrong formula: ln 2 omitted and 55 min treated as one half-life
error_types.B: wrong formula: ln 2 omitted from λ = ln 2/T½
error_types.C: wrong formula: linear interpolation of an exponential

items.takeaway: λ = 0.693/T½, and the fraction left after time t is (½)^(t/T½); half a half-life leaves 1/√2 ≈ 71%.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 31.5 Half-Life and Activity (2022): λ = ln 2/t½ ≈ 0.693/t½; N = N₀e^(−λt).

items.stem: Which statement correctly describes the nuclear change in the decay of fluorine-18 and the origin of the photons the scanner detects?

options.A: Fluorine-18 becomes neon-18 (Z rises by one, A unchanged); the emitted particle is a photon of 511 keV.
options.B: Fluorine-18 becomes oxygen-17 (Z and A both fall by one); the positron is detected directly by the ring.
options.C: Fluorine-18 becomes oxygen-18 (Z falls by one, A unchanged); the positron annihilates with an electron, producing two photons that move in opposite directions.
options.D: Fluorine-18 becomes oxygen-18 (Z falls by one, A unchanged); the excited oxygen-18 nucleus then emits two gamma rays in opposite directions.

why_correct: In positron (β⁺) emission a proton in the nucleus becomes a neutron, emitting a positron and a neutrino: Z falls by one and A is unchanged. ¹⁸₉F → ¹⁸₈O + e⁺ + ν. Both mass number (18 = 18 + 0) and charge (9 = 8 + 1) are conserved.

The positron is antimatter; after slowing in tissue it meets an electron and the pair annihilates, converting their rest mass (2 × 511 keV) into two photons. Momentum conservation requires the photons to leave in opposite directions, and energy conservation gives each one 511 keV. The scanner exploits this: two detectors on opposite sides must fire at the same moment.
Z determines the element, so lowering Z by one turns fluorine (9) into oxygen (8); the daughter oxygen-18 is stable.

why_wrong.A: Z rising by one is beta-minus decay (a neutron becoming a proton, emitting an electron); positron emission lowers Z, and the detected photons come from annihilation, not from the decay itself.
why_wrong.B: Positron emission does not change A (a proton becomes a neutron, so the nucleon count is constant); and the positron travels only about a millimetre before annihilating, so it never reaches the detectors.
why_wrong.D: The photons come from electron–positron annihilation outside the nucleus, not from a nuclear transition; fluorine-18 decays to the ground state of oxygen-18.

error_types.A: reversed relationship: β⁻ change in Z applied to β⁺ decay
error_types.B: wrong formula: A changed in a decay that conserves nucleon number
error_types.D: wrong formula: annihilation photons attributed to gamma decay

items.takeaway: Positron emission lowers Z by one with A unchanged; the positron then annihilates with an electron to give two 511 keV photons travelling in opposite directions.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 31.4 Nuclear Decay and Conservation Laws (2022): β⁺ decay, daughter has Z − 1 and the same A; annihilation converts the pair's mass into photons moving in opposite directions.
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 32.1 Diagnostics and Medical Imaging (2022): PET detects two 0.511 MeV photons that move directly away from one another.
TUNL Nuclear Data Evaluation, A = 18: fluorine-18 positron decay is entirely to the ground state of oxygen-18.

items.stem: The wavelength of each annihilation photon, and the region of the electromagnetic spectrum in which it lies, are:
why_correct: Each photon carries 511 keV, the rest energy of one electron (passage). E = hf = hc/λ, so λ = hc/E.

Picometre wavelengths and MeV-scale energies are the gamma-ray end of the spectrum; the hardest X-rays overlap this region, and the two are distinguished by origin (nuclear or annihilation photons are called gamma rays).

why_wrong.B: 4.9 × 10⁻¹² m corresponds to 255 keV, as if the 511 keV were shared between the two photons; each photon carries the full rest energy of one particle.
why_wrong.C: 2.4 × 10⁻⁹ m comes from 1240/511 with the energy read as 511 eV instead of 511 keV; the factor of 1000 moves the answer from gamma rays to soft X-rays.
why_wrong.D: 5.1 × 10⁻⁷ m (510 nm, green light) treats the number 511 as a wavelength in nanometres; visible photons carry only 2–3 eV, a hundred-thousandth of the energy here.

error_types.B: wrong formula: the energy halved between the photons
error_types.C: sign or unit error: keV read as eV
error_types.D: sign or unit error: an energy treated as a wavelength

items.takeaway: λ = hc/E with hc = 1240 eV·nm; a 511 keV photon has λ ≈ 2.4 pm, in the gamma-ray region.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 29.3 Photon Energies and the Electromagnetic Spectrum (2022): E = hf = hc/λ with hc = 1240 eV·nm; gamma rays have the highest photon energies.
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 24.3 The Electromagnetic Spectrum (2022): gamma rays and X-rays overlap in frequency and differ by source.
NIST CODATA 2022: electron mass energy equivalent 0.510 998 950 69 MeV; h = 6.626 070 15 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.

items.stem: A student derives an expression for the pressure inside an alveolus and checks it by dimensional analysis. In SI base units, a pressure is expressed as:
why_correct: Pressure is force per unit area: 1 Pa = 1 N/m². Force is mass times acceleration, so 1 N = 1 kg·m·s⁻².
Dividing by m²: 1 Pa = kg·m·s⁻² / m² = kg·m⁻¹·s⁻².
Check with another route: pressure is also energy per unit volume (the terms of Bernoulli's equation), J/m³ = kg·m²·s⁻²/m³ = kg·m⁻¹·s⁻², the same combination.

why_wrong.A: kg·m⁻³ is a density (mass per volume).
why_wrong.C: kg·m·s⁻² is the newton, a force; pressure is force divided by area.
why_wrong.D: kg·m²·s⁻² is the joule, an energy; pressure is energy per unit volume, so it has m⁻¹, not m².

error_types.A: wrong formula: density instead of pressure
error_types.C: wrong formula: force not divided by area
error_types.D: wrong formula: energy not divided by volume

items.takeaway: Pa = N/m² = kg·m⁻¹·s⁻²; the same units as energy per unit volume, which is why every term in Bernoulli's equation is a pressure.
sources: NIST Special Publication 811, Guide for the Use of the International System of Units, Table 3 (2008): newton N = m·kg·s⁻²; pascal Pa = N/m² = m⁻¹·kg·s⁻².
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 1.2 Physical Quantities and Units (2022): SI base units and derived units.

items.stem: Povidone-iodine antiseptic releases iodine. Which statement about iodine (I, atomic number 53, group 17) is correct?

options.A: It has one valence electron and forms I⁺ ions, like the alkali metals of group 1.
options.B: It has seven valence electrons and typically forms I⁺ ions by losing one.
options.C: It is a metalloid, and as an element it exists as single atoms rather than molecules.
options.D: It has seven valence electrons and typically gains one to form I⁻, isoelectronic with xenon.

why_correct: Elements in the same group share a valence configuration. Group 17, the halogens (F, Cl, Br, I), have ns²np⁵: seven valence electrons, one short of the noble-gas octet.

A halogen reaches the octet most easily by gaining one electron, forming a −1 halide ion; I⁻ is isoelectronic with xenon (Z = 54), the noble gas that follows iodine. As elements the halogens are diatomic (I₂), each atom sharing one electron pair to complete its octet.
The halogens are reactive nonmetals; their chemistry with metals is ionic (NaI, KI) and with nonmetals covalent.

why_wrong.A: One valence electron and +1 ions describe group 1 (the alkali metals); iodine is in group 17.
why_wrong.B: Seven valence electrons is right, but a halogen gains an electron to complete its octet rather than losing one; I⁺ is not the typical ion.
why_wrong.C: Iodine is a nonmetal (the metalloids are B, Si, Ge, As, Sb and Te), and like the other halogens it exists as diatomic I₂ molecules, each atom completing its octet by sharing one electron pair.

error_types.A: reversed relationship: group 1 behaviour assigned to group 17
error_types.B: reversed relationship: electron loss instead of gain
error_types.C: wrong formula: wrong class of element and wrong elemental form

items.takeaway: Halogens (group 17) have seven valence electrons, exist as diatomic molecules and form −1 ions isoelectronic with the next noble gas.
sources: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 2.5 The Periodic Table (2019): the halogens are group 17; fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine are nonmetals with similar properties.
OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 18.11 Occurrence, Preparation, and Properties of Halogens (2019): halogens form −1 halide ions and diatomic molecules.

items.stem: In one resonance structure of the nitrate ion, NO₃⁻, nitrogen is bonded to one oxygen by a double bond and to the other two by single bonds, and every atom has an octet. The formal charges on nitrogen, the double-bonded oxygen and each single-bonded oxygen are, respectively:
why_correct: Formal charge = valence electrons − nonbonding electrons − ½(bonding electrons).

Nitrogen (5 valence electrons) has four bonds (8 bonding electrons) and no lone pair: 5 − 0 − 4 = +1. The double-bonded oxygen (6 valence) has two lone pairs (4 electrons) and two bonds (4 electrons): 6 − 4 − 2 = 0. Each single-bonded oxygen has three lone pairs (6 electrons) and one bond (2 electrons): 6 − 6 − 1 = −1.
Check: the formal charges sum to +1 + 0 − 1 − 1 = −1, the charge of the ion. The three equivalent resonance structures differ only in which oxygen is double-bonded.

why_wrong.A: A nitrogen with four bonds and no lone pair carries +1; with 0 on nitrogen the charges would sum to −2, not the ion's −1.
why_wrong.B: The signs are assigned to the wrong oxygens: the oxygen with two bonds and two lone pairs is neutral, and each oxygen with one bond and three lone pairs is −1.
why_wrong.D: A charge of −⅓ on each oxygen describes the resonance hybrid, the average over the three structures; the question asks about one resonance structure, in which charges are whole numbers.

error_types.A: wrong formula: nitrogen's bonding electrons miscounted
error_types.B: reversed relationship: charges swapped between the two oxygen types
error_types.D: true but irrelevant: the hybrid's average charge, not a single structure's

items.takeaway: Formal charge = V − N − B/2; in each nitrate resonance structure N is +1, the double-bonded O is 0 and the single-bonded oxygens are −1, summing to −1.
sources: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 7.4 Formal Charges and Resonance (2019): formal charge = valence electrons − nonbonding electrons − ½ bonding electrons; the nitrate ion's three resonance forms.

items.stem: A patient takes a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug that inhibits cyclooxygenase. Synthesis of which lipid is reduced as a direct result?

options.A: Triacylglycerol, the storage lipid of adipose tissue
options.B: Phosphatidylcholine, a glycerophospholipid of the membrane bilayer
options.C: Prostaglandin E₂, a C₂₀ eicosanoid that acts as a local signal in inflammation
options.D: Cholesterol, the sterol that moderates membrane fluidity

why_correct: Prostaglandins are 20-carbon lipids built from arachidonic acid, a polyunsaturated fatty acid released from membrane phospholipids. The committed step, conversion of arachidonic acid to the cyclic endoperoxide PGH₂, is catalysed by cyclooxygenase (COX), and PGH₂ is then converted to prostaglandins such as PGE₂ and to thromboxanes.

Prostaglandins act locally, near where they are made, on inflammation, pain, fever, platelet aggregation, gastric secretion and smooth muscle. Inhibiting COX therefore lowers prostaglandin synthesis, which is how NSAIDs reduce inflammation and pain.
Of the four choices only the prostaglandin is a signalling lipid; the others are storage, structural and membrane components made by unrelated pathways.

why_wrong.A: Triacylglycerols are esters of glycerol with three fatty acids, made for energy storage by acyltransferases; COX is not involved.
why_wrong.B: Phosphatidylcholine is a structural membrane lipid; its synthesis does not use cyclooxygenase (though membrane phospholipids are the source of the arachidonic acid that COX acts on).
why_wrong.D: Cholesterol is made from acetyl-CoA through the mevalonate pathway (the target of statins, not NSAIDs).

error_types.A: out of scope: a storage lipid made by a different pathway
error_types.B: true but irrelevant: the phospholipid supplies the precursor but is not the COX product
error_types.D: out of scope: a different pathway and drug class

items.takeaway: Prostaglandins are local-acting eicosanoid signals made from arachidonic acid by cyclooxygenase; NSAIDs act by blocking that enzyme.
sources: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 27.4 Prostaglandins and Other Eicosanoids (2023): eicosanoid biosynthesis begins with conversion of arachidonic acid to PGH₂ by cyclooxygenase (COX); prostaglandins affect blood pressure, platelet aggregation, gastric secretion and inflammation.
OpenStax Organic Chemistry, Chapter 15 Chemistry Matters: Aspirin, NSAIDs, and COX-2 Inhibitors (2023): NSAIDs act by inhibiting cyclooxygenase.
OpenStax Biology 2e, 3.3 Lipids (2018): triacylglycerols, phospholipids and steroids.

items.stem: The initial rate of the reaction A + B → products was measured in three trials. Trial 1: [A] = 0.10 M, [B] = 0.10 M, rate = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ M/s. Trial 2: [A] = 0.20 M, [B] = 0.10 M, rate = 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ M/s. Trial 3: [A] = 0.20 M, [B] = 0.20 M, rate = 1.6 × 10⁻³ M/s. The rate law is:
why_correct: Compare trials in which only one concentration changes. Trials 1 and 2: [A] doubles at fixed [B] and the rate rises from 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ to 8.0 × 10⁻⁴, a factor of 4 = 2²; the reaction is second order in A.
Trials 2 and 3: [B] doubles at fixed [A] and the rate rises from 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ to 1.6 × 10⁻³, a factor of 2 = 2¹; first order in B.

So rate = k[A]²[B], overall third order. Check k from trial 1: k = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴/(0.10² × 0.10) = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴/1.0 × 10⁻³ = 0.20 M⁻²·s⁻¹; trial 3 then predicts 0.20 × 0.04 × 0.20 = 1.6 × 10⁻³ M/s, as measured. The orders are not the coefficients in the balanced equation; they come only from experiment.

why_wrong.A: First order in A would make the rate double, not quadruple, when [A] doubles between trials 1 and 2.
why_wrong.C: The orders are swapped: it is [A] whose doubling quadruples the rate and [B] whose doubling merely doubles it.
why_wrong.D: Second order in B would quadruple the rate between trials 2 and 3; it only doubled.

error_types.A: wrong formula: orders read from the balanced equation
error_types.C: reversed relationship: the two orders interchanged
error_types.D: misread graph: the factor between trials 2 and 3 taken as 4

items.takeaway: Find each order by doubling one concentration at a time: a doubled rate means first order, a quadrupled rate second order.
sources: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 12.3 Rate Laws (2019): the method of initial rates; rate laws are determined by experiment and not predicted by stoichiometry.

items.stem: A peptide hormone contains the residues valine, serine, aspartate and lysine. Which statement correctly classifies one of these side chains at pH 7.4?

options.A: Aspartate: basic, carrying a positive charge on its side chain
options.B: Lysine: acidic, carrying a negative charge on its side chain
options.C: Serine: nonpolar and hydrophobic, with no hydrogen-bonding group
options.D: Valine: nonpolar and hydrophobic, with a branched hydrocarbon side chain

why_correct: Valine's side chain is an isopropyl group, pure hydrocarbon: it cannot hydrogen-bond or ionise, so it is nonpolar and hydrophobic, and such residues tend to be buried in a protein's core. Like the other natural amino acids it has the L configuration (S by the sequence rules).

The other three residues are hydrophilic. Serine has a hydroxyl (polar, uncharged). Aspartate's side chain is a carboxylic acid with pKa about 4, so at pH 7.4 it is deprotonated, a carboxylate anion: acidic, negatively charged. Lysine's side chain is a primary amine with pKa about 10.5, protonated at pH 7.4: basic, positively charged.
Rule of thumb: a side-chain group is in its charged form when the pH is more than about two units from its pKa on the appropriate side.

why_wrong.A: Aspartate is acidic; at pH 7.4 its side-chain carboxyl has lost its proton and carries a negative charge.
why_wrong.B: Lysine is basic; its side-chain amine is protonated and positive at pH 7.4.
why_wrong.C: Serine's hydroxyl group is polar and hydrogen-bonds with water; serine is classified as polar, uncharged.

error_types.A: reversed relationship: an acidic residue called basic
error_types.B: reversed relationship: a basic residue called acidic
error_types.C: wrong formula: a polar hydroxyl side chain classed as nonpolar

items.takeaway: At pH 7.4, Asp and Glu are negative (acidic), Lys and Arg positive (basic), Ser and Thr polar but uncharged, and Val, Leu and Ile nonpolar and hydrophobic.
sources: OpenStax Biology 2e, 3.4 Proteins (2018): valine is nonpolar aliphatic; serine polar uncharged; lysine positively charged; aspartate negatively charged.
OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.1 Structures of Amino Acids (2023): side-chain pKa values (aspartic acid about 3.65, lysine about 10.53) and the L (S) configuration of natural amino acids.

items.stem: The axons rested at −70 mV and fired at −55 mV. When the voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open at threshold, the ion movement that follows is best described as:

options.A: Na⁺ entering the axon, driven by its concentration gradient but opposed by the membrane potential
options.B: Na⁺ leaving the axon, driven down its concentration gradient toward the extracellular fluid
options.C: Na⁺ entering the axon, carried by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump against its concentration gradient
options.D: Na⁺ entering the axon, driven by both its concentration gradient and the inside-negative potential

why_correct: Na⁺ is about ten times more concentrated outside the axon than inside, so its concentration gradient points inward.

At threshold the inside of the axon is still negative (−55 mV), so the electrical force on a positive ion also points inward. Both parts of the electrochemical gradient drive Na⁺ in through the open channels, and the rapid inward current produces the rising phase of the action potential.

Shortcut: at rest and at threshold both forces on Na⁺ point into the cell. Once the inside turns positive the electrical force opposes entry, and net entry stops only at the Na⁺ equilibrium potential, about +60 mV.

why_wrong.A: The membrane potential is inside-negative at threshold, so it attracts the cation inward; the electrical force opposes Na⁺ entry only once the inside has become positive, late in the rising phase.
why_wrong.B: Na⁺ is more concentrated outside the axon, so the concentration gradient drives it in, not out; it is K⁺ that leaves during repolarization.
why_wrong.C: Flux through an open channel is passive. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses ATP to move Na⁺ out of the cell (and K⁺ in), restoring the gradients between action potentials.

error_types.A: sign or unit error: the direction of the electrical force on a cation at a negative membrane potential
error_types.B: reversed relationship: direction of the Na⁺ concentration gradient
error_types.C: reversed relationship: the pump moves Na⁺ out, and channel flux is passive

items.takeaway: At threshold, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ flows in, pushed by both its concentration gradient and the inside-negative membrane potential.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 12.4 The Action Potential (2022): resting potential −70 mV, threshold about −55 mV; at threshold voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ rushes in, driven by a tenfold concentration gradient and by electrical attraction; K⁺ leaves later to repolarize.
OpenStax Biology 2e, 35.2 How Neurons Communicate (2018): the Na⁺/K⁺ pump moves three Na⁺ out and two K⁺ in using ATP.

items.stem: In Table 1, an internode of fibre 1 has one hundredth of the capacitance of the bare internode of fibre 4, although the two axons have the same diameter and internode length. The reduction arises because the 100 stacked bilayers:

options.A: behave as 100 capacitors in series, equivalent to one capacitor whose plate separation is 100 times that of a single bilayer
options.B: behave as 100 capacitors in parallel, so that each bilayer holds one hundredth of the charge a single bilayer would hold
options.C: lower the dielectric constant of the material between axoplasm and extracellular fluid to one hundredth of its value
options.D: reduce the area of membrane in contact with the axoplasm to one hundredth of that of the bare axon

why_correct: Each bilayer is a thin insulating layer between two conducting fluids, so a stack of n bilayers is n capacitors in series: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ + … = n/C₁, giving C = C₁/n. With n = 100, C falls to one hundredth.

The same result follows from the parallel-plate formula C = κε₀A/d: stacking 100 bilayers of the same material multiplies the separation d between the conducting fluids by 100 while the area and κ stay the same, so C falls by 100. Check: 314 pF/100 = 3.14 pF, the Table 1 value for fibre 1.
Consequence: for the same change in voltage the node's inward current has to deliver one hundredth of the charge (Q = CV) to the internode, which is why charging it, and conducting, is faster.

why_wrong.B: Capacitors in parallel add (C_p = C₁ + C₂ + …), which would make the sheath's capacitance 100 times larger, not smaller.
why_wrong.C: The dielectric constant is a property of the lipid, roughly the same for every bilayer; stacking layers changes the thickness of the insulator, not its κ.
why_wrong.D: The membrane area facing the axoplasm is πdL whether or not a sheath is present; the outer wraps if anything have a larger area. Capacitance falls because the separation between the conducting fluids grows.

error_types.B: reversed relationship: parallel and series combination of capacitors
error_types.C: wrong formula: κ attributed to the number of layers
error_types.D: wrong formula: A instead of d changed by the sheath

items.takeaway: Stacked membranes are capacitors in series: C ∝ A/d, so a sheath of n bilayers has 1/n of a single membrane's capacitance and needs 1/n of the charge to change its voltage.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 19.5 Capacitors and Dielectrics (2022): C = κε₀A/d for a parallel-plate capacitor.
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 19.6 Capacitors in Series and Parallel (2022): 1/C_s = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ + …; series capacitors are equivalent to one capacitor with a larger plate separation.
Stony Brook University, Cellular Neurophysiology, 4.6 Conduction of Action Potentials along Axons: myelination reduces the capacitance and increases the resistance of the internodal membrane.

items.stem: In the model, the axial resistance R of one 1.0 mm internode of fibre 1 (axon diameter 10 µm) is closest to:
why_correct: R = ρL/A with ρ = 1.0 Ω·m, L = 1.0 × 10⁻³ m and A = πr², where r = 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ m: A = π × 25 × 10⁻¹² m² ≈ 7.9 × 10⁻¹¹ m².
Check against Table 1: τ = RC = 1.3 × 10⁷ Ω × 3.14 × 10⁻¹² F ≈ 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ s = 40 µs, the listed value. Shortcut: 10⁻³/(8 × 10⁻¹¹) = 1.25 × 10⁷.

why_wrong.A: 1.3 MΩ is ten times too small, the result of writing 1 mm as 10⁻⁴ m or 25 µm² as 2.5 × 10⁻¹⁰ m²; keep the powers of ten with the units.
why_wrong.B: 3.2 MΩ comes from using the diameter in place of the radius, A = π(10 µm)² = 3.1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m², four times the true area.
why_wrong.D: 51 MΩ is the resistance of the 5 µm fibre (fibre 2), whose radius is 2.5 µm: halving the diameter quarters the area and quadruples R.

error_types.A: sign or unit error: a power of ten lost in the length or the area
error_types.B: wrong formula: diameter used as the radius
error_types.D: misread graph: the 5 µm fibre's diameter used

items.takeaway: Axial resistance R = ρL/A ∝ 1/d²: halving an axon's diameter quadruples the resistance of each unit length.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 20.3 Resistance and Resistivity (2022): R = ρL/A.

Tasaki and Matsumoto, On the Cable Theory of Nerve Conduction, Bulletin of Mathematical Biology 64:1069–1082 (2002): measured axis-cylinder resistance of a frog motor fibre 1.45 × 10⁸ Ω/cm, that is about 15 MΩ per millimetre, the same order as the model value.

items.stem: Suppose fibre 3 remyelinated until its sheath contained 40 bilayers along every internode, with no other change. Based on the model and on the relationship between τ and measured velocity in Table 1, its conduction velocity would be closest to:
why_correct: Read the table: across fibres 1–3 the product v × τ is constant (24 × 40 = 960, 12 × 80 = 960, 4.8 × 200 = 960 µm), so the measured velocity is inversely proportional to τ, as the model's v ≈ L/τ predicts (the measured values are 4% below 1.0 mm/τ).
C ∝ 1/n, so doubling the bilayers from 20 to 40 halves C from 15.7 pF to 7.85 pF; R is unchanged (same axon), so τ = RC halves from 200 µs to 100 µs.
v ≈ 960 µm/100 µs = 9.6 m/s, or L/τ = 1.0 mm/100 µs = 10 m/s. Shortcut: halving τ doubles v: 4.8 → 9.6 m/s.

why_wrong.A: 2.4 m/s halves the velocity when τ halves; velocity varies inversely with τ, not with it.
why_wrong.B: 4.8 m/s assumes the velocity is fixed by the axon diameter alone; Table 1 shows fibres 1 and 3, with the same diameter, differing fivefold because of the sheath.
why_wrong.D: 19 m/s applies the factor 2 twice, as if velocity scaled with the square of the number of bilayers; C, and so τ and v, change in simple proportion to n.

error_types.A: reversed relationship: velocity taken as proportional to τ
error_types.B: misread graph: the bilayer column ignored, velocity taken to depend on diameter alone
error_types.D: wrong formula: the bilayer ratio squared

items.takeaway: In the cable model the time to charge the next internode is τ = RC, and conduction velocity is inversely proportional to it; a thinner sheath raises C and slows conduction in proportion.
sources: Tasaki and Matsumoto, On the Cable Theory of Nerve Conduction, Bulletin of Mathematical Biology 64:1069–1082 (2002): in the internode ∂V/∂t = (1/(c_m r_i)) ∂²V/∂x², the time for the potential to reach a given level is proportional to x² c_m r_i, and the internodal conduction time is set by this spread.
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 21.6 DC Circuits Containing Resistors and Capacitors (2022): the time constant τ = RC of charging through a resistor.

items.stem: In the treated rats the sciatic nerve conduction velocity was 40% lower than in the vehicle group. Which additional step is most necessary before the slowing can be attributed to loss of myelin rather than to a change in the axons themselves?

options.A: Comparing the treated group with a group of untreated rats of the same age that received no injections at all
options.B: Recording the treated nerves again at a lower temperature to test whether the velocity falls still further
options.C: Raising the stimulus strength until the amplitude of the treated nerves' response matches the vehicle group's
options.D: Measuring axon diameters and sheath thickness in both groups and comparing velocities between fibres of equal axon diameter

why_correct: Table 1 shows two independent determinants of velocity: axon diameter (fibres 1 and 2, 10 µm and 5 µm) and sheath thickness (fibres 1 and 3). A 40% fall in a whole-nerve recording could come from thinner sheaths or from a loss or shrinkage of the large, fast axons, and the passage states that the treated axons were not examined.

Measuring both variables in both groups, and comparing velocity between treated and vehicle fibres of the same axon diameter, holds diameter constant so that any remaining difference can be attributed to the sheath. This is the comparison the passage's model demands.
Shortcut: to attribute an effect to one variable, measure the other candidate variable and hold it fixed.

why_wrong.A: An uninjected group would show whether the injection procedure itself matters; the vehicle group already serves that purpose. It says nothing about whether the slowing came from the sheath or from the axon.
why_wrong.B: Cooling slows conduction in every fibre, myelinated or not, so a further fall would not distinguish the two explanations.
why_wrong.C: A stronger stimulus recruits more fibres and changes the amplitude of the response, not the speed of the fastest fibres; it does not test what caused the slowing.

error_types.A: true but irrelevant: a control for the injection, not for the mechanism of slowing
error_types.B: out of scope: temperature affects all fibres alike
error_types.C: true but irrelevant: amplitude, not velocity

items.takeaway: Conduction velocity depends on both axon diameter and sheath thickness, so slowing is attributed to demyelination only after the axons are measured and velocities compared at matched diameter.
sources: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 12.4 The Action Potential (2022): both myelination and axon diameter influence conduction speed; wider axons conduct faster.
OpenStax Biology 2e, 35.1 Neurons and Glial Cells (2018): myelin, produced by Schwann cells and oligodendrocytes, insulates the axon and speeds transmission; demyelination slows or blocks conduction.

items.stem: Drug W is filtered into the urine. In urine of pH 5.0, the fraction of W present as its anion is closest to:
why_correct: Passage: log([A⁻]/[HA]) = pH − pKa. For W, pKa = 4.0 (Table 1), so at pH 5.0 the ratio is 10¹ = 10: ten anions for every neutral molecule.
Shortcut: one pH unit above the pKa, a weak acid is about 91% ionized; two units above, about 99%; at the pKa, 50%.

why_wrong.A: 9% is the fraction that remains un-ionized (1/11); the question asks for the anion.
why_wrong.B: 50% is the split only when the pH equals the pKa (4.0); the urine is one unit more basic than that.
why_wrong.D: 99% corresponds to a 100:1 ratio, two pH units above the pKa, the situation in the pH 6.0 intestinal fluid of Figure 1, not in urine of pH 5.0.

error_types.A: reversed relationship: un-ionized fraction reported instead of ionized
error_types.B: wrong formula: pH set equal to pKa
error_types.D: misread graph: the pH 6.0 value from Figure 1 used

items.takeaway: For a weak acid, [A⁻]/[HA] = 10^(pH − pKa): one unit above the pKa the acid is 10/11 (91%) ionized.
sources: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 14.6 Buffers (2019): the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]).
OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 14.3 Relative Strengths of Acids and Bases (2019): Ka, pKa and percent ionization of weak acids.

items.stem: The passage states that the ionized form of a drug crosses a lipid bilayer far more slowly than the un-ionized form. This is best explained by the fact that an ion in water:

options.A: is held by ion–dipole attractions to a shell of water that the bilayer's nonpolar interior cannot replace
options.B: is much larger than the neutral molecule and cannot fit between the hydrocarbon tails of the lipid bilayer
options.C: is repelled by the net positive charge that the phospholipid head groups give to the membrane's surface
options.D: can cross the membrane only when a transport protein specific for that ion is present in the bilayer

why_correct: A dissolved ion is hydrated: water's partial charges orient around it and bind to it by ion–dipole attractions, which release energy when the ion dissolves.

Entering the hydrocarbon interior of a bilayer means giving up those attractions with nothing of comparable strength to replace them, since the interior offers only dispersion forces. The energy cost makes the ion's passage extremely slow; a neutral molecule loses much less in leaving water and crosses readily.
Shortcut: the barrier is the charge, not the size; the un-ionized and ionized forms of a drug differ by one proton.

why_wrong.B: A drug anion and its neutral acid differ by a single proton and are almost the same size; size is not what distinguishes them.
why_wrong.C: Phospholipid head groups are zwitterionic or anionic, not net positive, and in any case repulsion by surface charge would not explain why cations and anions are both excluded. The barrier is the nonpolar interior.
why_wrong.D: Ions do cross bilayers without proteins, only very slowly; 'only' overstates the barrier and does not explain why the ionized form is slower.

error_types.B: wrong formula: size invoked where charge is the barrier
error_types.C: outside knowledge contradicting the passage: membrane surfaces are not net positive
error_types.D: too extreme: ions cross slowly without transporters

items.takeaway: Ions are hydrated by ion–dipole attractions; shedding that water to enter a nonpolar bilayer costs far too much energy, so only the un-ionized form of a drug diffuses across membranes at a useful rate.
sources: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 11.2 Electrolytes (2019): the electrostatic attraction between an ion and a molecule with a dipole is an ion–dipole attraction; water molecules surround and solvate dissolved ions.

OpenStax Biology 2e, 5.2 Passive Transport (2018): although small ions could fit through the membrane's spaces, their charge prevents them from crossing; nonpolar, lipid-soluble molecules pass through the fatty core.

items.stem: Which statement best explains why the sodium-salt tablet of W dissolved faster in fluid at pH 2.0, even though at equilibrium W is 99% un-ionized at that pH?

options.A: The salt releases W as its neutral acid, which crosses the gastric mucosa faster than the anion that the free-acid tablet releases into the fluid
options.B: The sodium ions neutralize the gastric fluid, raising its pH above 4.0, so that W remains mostly as its highly soluble anion in the bulk fluid
options.C: The sodium ions are co-transported with the drug anion into the mucosal cells, pulling further drug out of the dissolving tablet and into solution
options.D: The salt releases W as its anion, far more water-soluble than the neutral acid; protonation to the acid occurs only once the anion is in solution

why_correct: Dissolution and absorption are separate steps. A solid dissolves at a rate proportional to its solubility in the fluid at its surface; the ionic salt, whose anion is strongly hydrated, is far more soluble than the neutral, hydrogen-bonded acid, so the salt tablet releases drug much faster.

The anion that leaves the solid is then protonated by the bulk acid (pH 2.0 is two units below the pKa, so 99% ends up as HA), but by then the drug is already in solution. Whether any of the neutral acid then precipitates depends on its own solubility and the dose; in this test 85% of the dose was in solution at 10 minutes.
The passage confirms the two steps are separate: once dissolved, drug from either tablet is in the same equilibrium, which is why the total exposure was the same and only the time to peak differed.

why_wrong.A: The sodium salt releases the anion, not the acid, and the question concerns how fast the solid dissolves in the test fluid, not how fast drug crosses the mucosa.
why_wrong.B: Fluid at pH 2.0 contains 0.010 mol/L H⁺, about 9 mmol in 900 mL; a 1.0 mmol dose of the salt can consume at most 1 mmol of it, leaving the pH near 2.05. The bulk fluid stays far below the pKa.
