why_wrong.C: Co-transport is a process of living membranes; the dissolution test used a vessel of simulated gastric fluid with no cells, and the tablet dissolved faster there.

error_types.A: reversed relationship: salt and acid swapped, and dissolution confused with absorption
error_types.B: too extreme: a millimole of salt cannot neutralize the gastric fluid
error_types.C: out of scope: a transport mechanism invoked for a cell-free dissolution test

items.takeaway: A drug's salt dissolves faster because its ion is far more water-soluble than the neutral molecule; the pH of the fluid then sets the ionized:un-ionized ratio of what has dissolved, and that ratio governs absorption.
sources: Serajuddin, Salt formation to improve drug solubility, Advanced Drug Delivery Reviews 59:603–616 (2007): salt formation is the most common and effective way of raising the solubility and dissolution rate of acidic and basic drugs.

OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 11.2 Electrolytes and 11.1 The Dissolution Process (2019): ionic compounds dissolve and dissociate as hydrated ions; dissolution is favoured when solute–solvent attractions outweigh solute–solute attractions.
OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 14.6 Buffers (2019): the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation gives the ionized:un-ionized ratio at a given pH.

items.stem: The investigators measured each drug's partition coefficient at a pH at which the drug was more than 99% un-ionized. Which statement best justifies this part of the design?

options.A: The ionized form partitions into octanol more strongly than the neutral form, so a partly ionized sample would overstate the drug's affinity for the bilayer
options.B: The neutral molecule's partitioning reflects only its own interactions with octanol and with water, so the value can be compared between drugs whatever their pKa values
options.C: The un-ionized fraction at the chosen pH equals the fraction of an oral dose that is absorbed, so the value measured there predicts the plasma level directly
options.D: Weak acids and weak bases are both fully ionized near pH 7, so a partition coefficient can be measured only far from neutral pH

why_correct: A partition coefficient compares how well a molecule's intermolecular interactions are satisfied in each solvent: dispersion and dipole contacts with octanol against hydrogen bonding and, for an ion, strong ion–dipole hydration in water.

Measured on the neutral species, log P is a property of the molecule alone. Measured on a partly ionized sample, the apparent coefficient (log D) falls with the ionized fraction and so depends on the buffer's pH and on the drug's pKa, which would confound the comparison across four drugs with different pKa values.
The design separates the two factors the passage then combines: how lipophilic the neutral molecule is (log P) and how much of the drug is neutral at a given pH (Henderson–Hasselbalch).

why_wrong.A: The ion is the form held in water by hydration; it partitions into octanol far less than the neutral form, so a partly ionized sample would understate, not overstate, lipophilicity.
why_wrong.C: A partition coefficient is an equilibrium ratio of concentrations in two solvents, not a fraction absorbed; absorption also depends on the ionized fraction at the site, the surface area and the time available.
why_wrong.D: At pH 7 a weak acid of pKa 7.0 (drug X) is only half ionized and a base of pKa 5.0 (drug Z) is almost entirely neutral; 'fully' and 'only' are both wrong.

error_types.A: reversed relationship: which form prefers octanol
error_types.C: wrong formula: a partition coefficient treated as a fraction absorbed
error_types.D: too extreme: 'fully ionized' and 'only' contradict Table 1

items.takeaway: log P is the octanol–water partition coefficient of the neutral molecule, set by its intermolecular interactions with each solvent; the pH-dependent value (log D) also depends on the ionized fraction and pKa.
sources: ACD/Labs, LogP vs LogD application note: log P is the partition coefficient of the un-ionized species and is independent of pH; log D includes the ionized species and varies with pH.
OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 10.1 Intermolecular Forces and 11.3 Solubility (2019): dispersion, dipole–dipole and hydrogen-bonding interactions decide how a solute distributes between solvents.
OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 11.2 Electrolytes (2019): ion–dipole attractions hold dissolved ions in water.

items.stem: Based on Figure 1 and Table 1, which drug would be expected to be absorbed most readily from the stomach?
why_correct: Read the chart at pH 2.0: W and X are essentially all un-ionized (99.0% and 100.0%), while the two bases are almost entirely protonated (Y 0.0%, Z 0.1%). Only the acids have a neutral form available to cross the gastric epithelium.

Then read Table 1: W has log P 2.5, inside the range the investigators considered favourable, whereas X has log P −1.0, meaning its neutral molecule favours water over octanol ten to one and partitions poorly into the bilayer. W is both neutral and lipophilic, so it is absorbed most readily.

Two checks are needed because the bar chart alone cannot separate W from X; the ionized fraction and the lipophilicity of the neutral form are independent requirements. Most drugs, acids included, are absorbed mainly in the small intestine because of its far larger surface; the question concerns the stomach only.

why_wrong.B: X is un-ionized in the stomach, but its log P of −1.0 means the neutral molecule hardly enters the lipid phase; the chart alone is not enough.
why_wrong.C: Y has a favourable log P, but at pH 2.0 a base of pKa 9.0 is protonated to one part in ten million; there is almost no neutral form to cross the membrane.
why_wrong.D: Z reaches 90.9% un-ionized only in the intestine (pH 6.0); in the stomach it is 0.1% un-ionized, the wrong bar for this question.

error_types.B: true but irrelevant: un-ionized but too hydrophilic to partition
error_types.C: reversed relationship: a weak base is ionized in acid
error_types.D: misread graph: the intestinal bar read for the stomach

items.takeaway: Absorption from a compartment needs both a large un-ionized fraction at its pH and a neutral form lipophilic enough to enter the membrane; a weak acid with a moderate log P meets both in the stomach.
sources: Hogben, Schanker, Tocco and Brodie, Absorption of drugs from the stomach II. The human, J Pharmacol Exp Ther 120:540–545 (1957), summarized in Deranged Physiology, Factors which determine the lipid solubility of drugs: weak acids are un-ionized and lipid-soluble in acid; the pH-partition principle.
ACD/Labs, LogP vs LogD application note: a negative log P marks a compound that prefers water to octanol.
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 23.4 The Stomach (2022): gastric pH 1.5–3.5; the stomach absorbs little apart from some substances such as aspirin and alcohol.

items.stem: From Table 1, the fold purification and the yield achieved after step 3, relative to the cleared lysate, are closest to:
why_correct: Specific activity = total activity / total protein. Step 1: 2,000 U / 500 mg = 4.0 U/mg. Step 3: 1,200 U / 4.0 mg = 300 U/mg.
Fold purification = 300 / 4.0 = 75. Yield = activity recovered / activity started with = 1,200 / 2,000 = 60%.

why_wrong.A: 60 and 75 are the right numbers in the wrong places: 60% is the yield and 75 the fold purification.
why_wrong.C: 75% is the yield of step 3 relative to step 2 (1,200/1,600); the question asks for the yield relative to the lysate.
why_wrong.D: 125 is the ratio of total protein (500 mg / 4.0 mg); fold purification is the ratio of specific activities, which also accounts for the activity lost.

error_types.A: reversed relationship: fold and yield swapped
error_types.C: wrong formula: step yield instead of overall yield
error_types.D: wrong formula: protein ratio instead of specific-activity ratio

items.takeaway: Specific activity is activity per milligram of protein; fold purification is its ratio to the starting material, and yield is the fraction of the starting activity recovered.
sources: Colorado State University, Preparing a Summary Purification Table (handout): specific activity = activity/protein; fold purification compares each step's specific activity with the starting lysate; yield is the activity recovered.
Biology LibreTexts, Biochemistry Free For All (Ahern, Rajagopal, Tan), 8.2 Fractionation and Chromatography Techniques: specific activity rises as a protein is purified.

items.stem: The enzyme was eluted from the Ni²⁺ column with 250 mmol/L imidazole because imidazole:

options.A: reduces the Ni²⁺ to metallic nickel, which no longer coordinates the histidine side chains of the tag
options.B: denatures the tagged protein, so that its histidine side chains can no longer reach the nickel ions
options.C: lowers the pH of the buffer, so that the histidine side chains become protonated and lose their lone pairs
options.D: is the ring of the histidine side chain and competes with the tag's histidines for the coordination sites on Ni²⁺

why_correct: The His tag binds because the imidazole ring of each histidine donates a nitrogen lone pair to an empty coordination site on the immobilized Ni²⁺.

Free imidazole is that same ring. At 250 mmol/L it vastly outnumbers the tag's six histidines, occupies the coordination sites and displaces the protein, which then washes off; the 20 mmol/L wash removes proteins whose few scattered histidines bind more weakly.
Shortcut: affinity columns are eluted with free ligand or a ligand look-alike that competes for the same binding site.

why_wrong.A: No redox chemistry is involved; imidazole is a Lewis base, not a reducing agent, and the column is reused with its Ni²⁺ intact.
why_wrong.B: Imidazole at these concentrations is not a denaturant; the enzyme emerges active, as the 1,600 U recovered at step 2 shows.
why_wrong.C: Imidazole is a weak base, not an acid, so adding it does not lower the pH. Protonating the histidines by lowering the pH is a different elution method, not what imidazole does.

error_types.A: out of scope: a redox reaction that does not occur
error_types.B: outside knowledge contradicting the passage: the eluted enzyme is active
error_types.C: wrong formula: low-pH elution attributed to a basic additive

items.takeaway: Imidazole elutes His-tagged proteins by competing with the histidine imidazole rings for the coordination sites on the immobilized Ni²⁺.
sources: Biology LibreTexts, Biochemistry Free For All (Ahern, Rajagopal, Tan), 8.2 Fractionation and Chromatography Techniques: histidine side chains bind nickel or cobalt ions; His-tagged proteins are eluted by adding imidazole.
Bio-Rad, His-tag purification guide: imidazole competes with the His tag for binding to the metal-charged resin; low imidazole in the wash removes weakly bound contaminants.

items.stem: On the SDS-PAGE gels described in the passage, the distance each protein migrated depended chiefly on its:

options.B: net charge in the native state

why_correct: SDS is an anionic detergent that unfolds proteins into rod-like shapes and coats them with negative charge roughly in proportion to their length, so every protein has about the same charge-to-mass ratio.

With charge and shape made uniform, the gel's sieving is the only thing left to separate them: smaller proteins thread through the pores faster and travel farther. Heating with DTT also breaks disulfide bonds so that each chain runs alone.
That is why the 50 kDa band reports the mass of the polypeptide chain, not of the assembled enzyme.

why_wrong.A: The isoelectric point governs isoelectric focusing, in which proteins stop where the pH equals their pI; SDS masks native charge.
why_wrong.B: Native charge matters in a native gel; SDS swamps it with a uniform negative charge.
why_wrong.D: SDS unfolds every protein into a similar rod, so native shape no longer differs between them.

error_types.A: wrong formula: the separating principle of isoelectric focusing
error_types.B: wrong formula: the separating principle of native PAGE
error_types.D: outside knowledge contradicting the passage: SDS removes shape differences

items.takeaway: SDS-PAGE separates polypeptides by mass because SDS unfolds them and gives them a uniform charge-to-mass ratio; smaller chains run farther.
sources: Biology LibreTexts, Biochemistry Free For All (Ahern, Rajagopal, Tan), 8.3 Electrophoresis: SDS denatures proteins to rod-like shapes and makes their charge proportional to mass; they move at velocities inversely related to size; mercaptoethanol or DTT breaks disulfide bonds; native gels separate by charge as well as mass.

items.stem: Gel filtration placed the enzyme at about 100 kDa, whereas SDS-PAGE, with or without DTT, showed a single band at 50 kDa. These results are best explained by an enzyme that is:

options.A: a dimer of two identical 50 kDa chains held together by noncovalent interactions
options.B: a dimer of two identical 50 kDa chains linked by an interchain disulfide bond
options.C: a single 100 kDa chain that SDS cleaves into two 50 kDa halves
options.D: a 50 kDa monomer, two of which are bridged by a Ni²⁺ ion shared between their His tags

why_correct: Gel filtration measures the size of the native, folded assembly: about 100 kDa. SDS unfolds proteins and breaks noncovalent contacts, and the chain it reveals is 50 kDa, the mass predicted from the sequence; so the native enzyme is two such chains, a quaternary structure.

The band is the same without DTT, so no disulfide holds the chains together; the association is through noncovalent interactions (hydrophobic contacts, hydrogen bonds, salt bridges), which SDS disrupts and gel filtration preserves.
Shortcut: native mass ÷ SDS-PAGE mass = number of subunits, if the SDS band survives omission of the reducing agent.

why_wrong.B: A disulfide-linked dimer would still run as 100 kDa in the lane without DTT, because SDS does not break covalent bonds; the passage says the band was 50 kDa with and without DTT.
why_wrong.C: SDS denatures proteins but does not hydrolyse peptide bonds, and the sequence predicts a 50 kDa chain, not 100 kDa.
why_wrong.D: The dimer was seen on a gel-filtration column run in nickel-free buffer and again after EDTA, which chelates any stray Ni²⁺, so a metal bridge cannot be what holds it together.

error_types.B: outside knowledge contradicting the passage: the non-reduced lane rules out a disulfide
error_types.C: wrong formula: denaturation confused with hydrolysis
error_types.D: outside knowledge contradicting the passage: the dimer persisted without nickel and with EDTA

items.takeaway: A native mass that is a multiple of the SDS-PAGE band mass, unchanged by reducing agent, indicates subunits held together noncovalently: quaternary structure.
sources: OpenStax Biology 2e, 3.4 Proteins (2018): quaternary structure is the association of two or more polypeptide subunits through weak interactions and sometimes disulfide bonds; denaturation disrupts folding without breaking peptide bonds.

Biology LibreTexts, Biochemistry Free For All (Ahern, Rajagopal, Tan), 8.3 Electrophoresis: SDS unfolds and coats proteins; reducing agents break disulfide bonds; 8.2: in gel filtration larger molecules elute first.

items.stem: After step 4 the specific activity fell although little protein was lost. Which experiment most directly tests the hypothesis that EDTA removed a metal ion the enzyme requires, as opposed to the enzyme having been denatured during the overnight dialysis?

options.A: Running the step 4 enzyme on SDS-PAGE beside the step 3 enzyme, with and without DTT, and comparing the positions of the bands
options.B: Continuing the dialysis of the step 4 enzyme against the EDTA buffer for a further 48 hours and measuring whether its activity falls further
options.C: Measuring the absorbance of the step 4 sample at 280 nm to confirm the protein concentration that the Bradford assay reported
options.D: Dialysing a portion of the step 4 enzyme briefly against EDTA-free buffer, adding a little ZnCl₂ to half of it, and comparing the halves' activities

why_correct: The two hypotheses predict different responses to added metal. If EDTA stripped a catalytic Zn²⁺ from an otherwise intact enzyme, supplying Zn²⁺ should restore the activity; a denatured enzyme would not recover.

The EDTA is removed first so that a small (micromolar) amount of zinc is free to bind, rather than being chelated or having to be added at the millimolar levels that themselves inhibit many enzymes. The half with no added zinc, handled identically, controls for the extra dialysis and for any change over time, so the comparison isolates the effect of the metal.

Shortcut: to test 'X was removed', put X back under conditions where it can act, keep everything else the same, and see whether function returns. Reversal by the specific ion is the classic evidence for a metal cofactor.

why_wrong.A: A bound Zn²⁺ ion adds about 65 Da to a 50 kDa chain, invisible on a gel, and SDS unfolds every protein anyway, so the gel cannot show whether the enzyme had already lost its fold or its metal.
why_wrong.B: Both hypotheses predict that a longer dialysis could lower the activity further, so a further fall would not tell them apart.
why_wrong.C: The question is why activity per milligram fell, not whether the milligrams were counted correctly; confirming the protein value with a second assay addresses neither hypothesis.

error_types.A: true but irrelevant: SDS-PAGE reports neither bound metal nor folding
error_types.B: out of scope: an outcome both hypotheses predict
error_types.C: true but irrelevant: checks the denominator, not the cause

items.takeaway: Loss of activity after a chelator is attributed to a metal cofactor when adding the metal back restores activity; denaturation is not reversed by added ions.
sources: OpenStax Biology 2e, 6.5 Enzymes (2018): cofactors are inorganic ions such as Fe²⁺, Mg²⁺ and Zn²⁺ that some enzymes require; DNA polymerase needs a bound zinc ion; heat and extreme pH denature enzymes.

Lindskog and Malmström, J Biol Chem 237:1129 (1962): chelators remove the single zinc from carbonic anhydrase, which the enzyme needs for activity; Udom and Brady, Biochem J 187:329–335 (1980): zinc salts or zinc-thionein restore activity to zinc apoenzymes (apo-thermolysin and apo-aldolase fully, apo-carbonic anhydrase partly).

items.stem: In loop 1 the echoes from the umbilical artery returned at a frequency above 3.00 MHz. This occurred because the red cells moving toward the probe:

options.A: returned sound that travelled faster through the moving blood, so that more cycles reached the probe each second
options.B: met wavefronts more often than a stationary reflector would, but re-emitted them with the spacing unchanged, so the shift arose once
options.C: met wavefronts more often than a stationary reflector would, then re-emitted them with a shortened spacing, so the frequency was raised twice
options.D: returned echoes of lower frequency, which the scanner reports as a positive shift by convention for arterial flow

why_correct: Passage: a cell moving toward the probe 'first meets wavefronts more often than a stationary reflector would' (moving observer, frequency raised by a factor (c + v)/c) 'and then re-emits the sound as a moving source' (wavelength shortened, frequency raised again by c/(c − v)).

For v much smaller than c each step raises the frequency by about f₀v/c, so the echo returns at about f₀(1 + 2v/c): higher than transmitted, with twice the shift a single moving source would give. That factor 2 is the one in Equation 1.
Approach raises frequency; recession lowers it. The vein, flowing away, gave negative shifts in Table 1, consistent with this.

why_wrong.A: The speed of sound is set by the medium, not by the motion of the reflector; the Doppler effect changes frequency and wavelength, not propagation speed.
why_wrong.B: The cells act both as receiver and as re-emitter; leaving out the second shift halves the effect and contradicts the factor 2 in Equation 1.
why_wrong.D: Echoes from cells moving toward the probe are higher, not lower, in frequency, and the passage defines the sign of Δf by the direction of flow, not by vessel type.

error_types.A: wrong formula: the Doppler shift attributed to a change in wave speed
error_types.B: wrong formula: the second (moving-source) shift omitted
error_types.D: reversed relationship: the sign of the shift for approach

items.takeaway: Blood moving toward the probe returns echoes at a higher frequency, and the shift is doubled because the cells act first as moving receivers and then as moving sources.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 17.7 Ultrasound (2022): in Doppler ultrasound of blood there is a double shift, one as the blood receives the sound and one as it re-emits it (Example 17.8 with 1,540 m/s).
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 17.4 Doppler Effect and Sonic Booms (2022): the observed frequency rises for approach and falls for recession.

items.stem: The wavelength of the 3.00 MHz beam in soft tissue is closest to:
why_correct: Shortcut: 1,500/3 = 500, so λ ≈ 500 × 10⁻⁶ m = 0.5 mm; the exact figure is slightly larger.
Detail smaller than about a wavelength cannot be resolved, which is why half a millimetre is the order of the finest detail a 3 MHz scan can show.

why_wrong.A: 0.11 mm uses the speed of sound in air (about 330 m/s); the beam travels through tissue, where sound is nearly five times faster.
why_wrong.C: 1.9 mm comes from inverting the ratio, f/v = 1.9 × 10³ m⁻¹, and misreading the unit; wavelength is speed divided by frequency.
why_wrong.D: 5.1 mm is ten times too large: 1,540/3 × 10⁶ is 5.1 × 10⁻⁴ m, not 5.1 × 10⁻³ m.

error_types.A: wrong formula: the speed of sound in air used for tissue
error_types.C: wrong formula: frequency divided by speed
error_types.D: sign or unit error: a power of ten

items.takeaway: λ = v/f: at 1,540 m/s a 3 MHz ultrasound beam has a wavelength of about 0.5 mm, which sets the scale of the detail it can resolve.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 17.2 Speed of Sound, Frequency, and Wavelength (2022): v = fλ; frequency is fixed by the source, wavelength by the medium.
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 17.7 Ultrasound (2022): details smaller than the wavelength are hard to detect; 1,540 m/s used for tissue.

items.stem: A 3 MHz probe was chosen for the fetal examination rather than the 10 MHz probe used for superficial structures. Compared with the 10 MHz beam, the 3 MHz beam:

options.A: travels faster through tissue, so echoes from deep structures return before they have been absorbed
options.B: carries more energy in each cycle, so it reflects more strongly from interfaces deep in the body
options.C: resolves finer detail, because resolution improves as the wavelength becomes longer
options.D: is attenuated less, so it reaches deeper structures, at the cost of coarser resolution from its longer wavelength

why_correct: Passage: 'higher frequencies are attenuated more strongly over the same path'. Absorption in tissue rises with frequency, so a 10 MHz beam loses its energy within a few centimetres while a 3 MHz beam can reach a fetus through the maternal abdomen.
The price is resolution: detail smaller than about a wavelength cannot be resolved, and at 3 MHz the wavelength is about 0.5 mm against about 0.15 mm at 10 MHz.
The probe itself is a piezoelectric crystal that converts voltage to vibration and returning pressure to voltage, so one crystal both sends the pulse and receives the echo.

why_wrong.A: The speed of sound in a medium does not depend on frequency; both beams travel at about 1,540 m/s in tissue.
why_wrong.B: Reflection at an interface depends on the change in acoustic impedance, not on the frequency; the energy a beam carries is set by its intensity, and the lower frequency is chosen because it is absorbed less, not because it reflects more.
why_wrong.C: Resolution improves as the wavelength becomes shorter, so the 3 MHz beam resolves coarser, not finer, detail.

error_types.A: wrong formula: wave speed made frequency-dependent
error_types.B: wrong formula: reflection attributed to frequency
error_types.C: reversed relationship: resolution and wavelength

items.takeaway: Higher ultrasound frequencies give finer resolution (shorter wavelength) but are absorbed more strongly and penetrate less; deep structures are imaged with lower frequencies.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 17.7 Ultrasound (2022): higher-frequency ultrasound allows greater detail but does not penetrate as well, because high frequencies are strongly absorbed; the transducer is a piezoelectric crystal that both transmits and receives.
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 17.2 Speed of Sound, Frequency, and Wavelength (2022): the speed of sound is a property of the medium.

items.stem: Using Equation 1 and Table 1, the peak systolic blood speed in the umbilical artery is closest to:
why_correct: Rearrange Equation 1: v = Δf c / (2 f₀ cos θ). In loop 1, θ = 0° and cos θ = 1, with Δf = 2,000 Hz, f₀ = 3.00 × 10⁶ Hz and c = 1,540 m/s.

Shortcut: Δf/f₀ = 2,000/3,000,000 = 2/3 × 10⁻³, and v = (Δf/f₀)(c/2) ≈ 0.67 × 10⁻³ × 770 ≈ 0.51 m/s. Check with loop 2: Δf = 1,000 Hz and cos 60° = 0.5 give the same speed, as they must for the same vessel.

why_wrong.A: 0.26 m/s results from using the loop 2 shift (1,000 Hz) without dividing by cos 60° = 0.5; the angle halves the shift, not the speed.
why_wrong.C: 1.0 m/s leaves out the factor 2 in Equation 1, treating the cells as a moving source only.
why_wrong.D: 2.1 m/s multiplies by 2 instead of dividing: v = Δf c/(2 f₀), since the double shift makes Δf twice as large for a given speed.

error_types.A: wrong formula: cos θ omitted for the 60° loop
error_types.C: wrong formula: the factor 2 for the double shift omitted
error_types.D: sign or unit error: the factor 2 applied on the wrong side

items.takeaway: v = Δf c / (2 f₀ cos θ): a 2 kHz shift at 3 MHz along the flow corresponds to about 0.5 m/s, and the same speed gives half the shift at 60°.
sources: British Medical Ultrasound Society, Concepts of Doppler (teaching notes): Δf = 2 f₀ v cos θ / c; the factor 2 accounts for the wave travelling to the moving cells and back; angles above 60° give large velocity errors.
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 17.7 Ultrasound (2022): Example 17.8, a 2.50 MHz beam and blood at 20.0 cm/s with 1,540 m/s give a 649 Hz beat frequency (about 2 f₀ v / c).

Spurway, Logan, Pak and Nielsen, Australasian Journal of Ultrasound in Medicine 20:155–162 (2017): umbilical vein peak velocity about 18 cm/s at 36 weeks, consistent with the 0.15 m/s implied by the vein's shift.

items.stem: An ambulance travelling at 20 m/s approaches an obstruction. The driver's reaction time is 1.0 s, during which the speed does not change; the brakes then slow the vehicle uniformly at 5.0 m/s² until it stops. The total distance travelled from the moment the obstruction is seen is closest to:
why_correct: Reaction phase (constant speed): d₁ = vt = 20 m/s × 1.0 s = 20 m.
Braking phase (constant deceleration): v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀) with v = 0, v₀ = 20 m/s and a = −5.0 m/s², so d₂ = v₀²/(2|a|) = 400/10 = 40 m.
Total: 20 m + 40 m = 60 m. Check the braking phase another way: t = v₀/|a| = 4.0 s and average speed 10 m/s give 40 m.

why_wrong.A: 40 m is the braking distance alone; the vehicle covers a further 20 m before the brakes are applied.
why_wrong.C: 80 m treats the 4.0 s of braking as if the speed stayed at 20 m/s; during uniform deceleration the average speed is half the initial speed.
why_wrong.D: 100 m adds the 20 m reaction distance to that same overestimate of 80 m.

error_types.A: true but irrelevant: braking distance without the reaction distance
error_types.C: wrong formula: distance = v₀t during deceleration
error_types.D: wrong formula: the 80 m error plus the reaction distance

items.takeaway: Stopping distance = reaction distance (v₀t) + braking distance (v₀²/2a); doubling the speed quadruples the braking part.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 2.5 Motion Equations for Constant Acceleration in One Dimension (2022): v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀); Example 2.12 adds the distance covered during a driver's reaction time to the braking distance.

items.stem: Bicarbonate ion acts as a base in reaction 1 and as an acid in reaction 2: (1) HCO₃⁻ + H₃O⁺ ⇌ H₂CO₃ + H₂O; (2) HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻ ⇌ CO₃²⁻ + H₂O. The conjugate acid of HCO₃⁻ and the conjugate base of HCO₃⁻ are, respectively:
why_correct: A conjugate acid is the base plus one proton; a conjugate base is the acid minus one proton. Adding H⁺ to HCO₃⁻ gives H₂CO₃ (reaction 1); removing H⁺ from HCO₃⁻ gives CO₃²⁻ (reaction 2).
A species that can both donate and accept a proton, such as HCO₃⁻, is amphiprotic; its conjugate acid and conjugate base differ from it by one proton in opposite directions.
Shortcut: conjugate pairs differ by exactly one H⁺ and one unit of charge: H₂CO₃ / HCO₃⁻ and HCO₃⁻ / CO₃²⁻.

why_wrong.B: CO₃²⁻ has one proton fewer than bicarbonate, so it is the conjugate base, and H₂CO₃ has one more, so it is the conjugate acid; the pair is reversed.
why_wrong.C: H₃O⁺ and OH⁻ are the acid and base that react with bicarbonate; a species' conjugates are formed from that species itself, not from its reaction partner.
why_wrong.D: Water is the conjugate base of H₃O⁺ in reaction 1 and the conjugate acid of OH⁻ in reaction 2; it is not conjugate to bicarbonate in either.

error_types.B: reversed relationship: conjugate acid and base swapped
error_types.C: wrong formula: reaction partners taken as conjugates
error_types.D: wrong formula: water's conjugates assigned to bicarbonate

items.takeaway: An amphiprotic species such as HCO₃⁻ has a conjugate acid one proton richer (H₂CO₃) and a conjugate base one proton poorer (CO₃²⁻).
sources: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 14.1 Brønsted-Lowry Acids and Bases (2019): conjugate acid and conjugate base defined; bicarbonate is amphiprotic, HCO₃⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CO₃²⁻ + H₃O⁺ and HCO₃⁻ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ + OH⁻.

items.stem: α-D-Glucopyranose and β-D-glucopyranose are anomers. How do the two differ, and how are they related in aqueous solution?

options.A: They differ in configuration at every stereocentre, as enantiomers do, and cannot interconvert without breaking bonds
options.B: They differ in configuration only at C4, as glucose and galactose do, and cannot interconvert without an enzyme
options.C: They differ in configuration only at C5, the carbon that defines the D series, and interconvert through the open-chain form
options.D: They differ in configuration only at C1, the hemiacetal carbon formed on ring closure, and interconvert through the open-chain form

why_correct: When glucose's C5 hydroxyl adds to the C1 aldehyde, C1 becomes a new stereocentre, the anomeric carbon. The two possible configurations there are the α and β anomers; every other stereocentre is the same in both.

In water the hemiacetal opens and recloses reversibly, so each pure anomer slowly converts into an equilibrium mixture (about one third α and two thirds β), observed as a changing optical rotation: mutarotation. No enzyme or bond-breaking beyond the reversible ring opening is required.
Shortcut: anomers are epimers at the anomeric (hemiacetal or hemiketal) carbon, and only that carbon can flip through the open chain.

why_wrong.A: Enantiomers are mirror images differing at every stereocentre; the anomers share the configuration of C2–C5 and differ only at C1.
why_wrong.B: Glucose and galactose are C4 epimers; the anomers differ at C1, and they interconvert without any enzyme.
why_wrong.C: C5 is the carbon whose configuration assigns the D or L series; it is unchanged by ring closure, and the anomers differ at C1.

error_types.A: wrong formula: enantiomers confused with anomers
error_types.B: wrong formula: C4 epimers confused with anomers
error_types.C: wrong formula: the D/L stereocentre confused with the anomeric carbon

items.takeaway: Anomers differ only at the anomeric carbon (C1 of an aldose) created by ring closure, and they interconvert in water through the open-chain form (mutarotation).
sources: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 25.5 Cyclic Structures of Monosaccharides: Anomers (2023): cyclization makes C1 a new chirality centre, the anomeric centre; α and β anomers; pure anomers interconvert in water by reversible ring opening to the aldehyde (mutarotation), reaching a 37:63 equilibrium mixture.

items.stem: Partial hydrogenation of a vegetable oil adds H₂ across a C=C bond of an unsaturated fatty acid chain: R–CH=CH–R′ + H₂ → R–CH₂–CH₂–R′. Using average bond energies of 611 kJ/mol (C=C), 345 kJ/mol (C–C), 415 kJ/mol (C–H) and 436 kJ/mol (H–H), the enthalpy change per mole of C=C hydrogenated is closest to:
why_correct: ΔH ≈ Σ(bond energies of bonds broken) − Σ(bond energies of bonds formed). Broken: one C=C (611) and one H–H (436), total 1,047 kJ/mol. Formed: one C–C (345) and two C–H (2 × 415 = 830), total 1,175 kJ/mol.
ΔH ≈ 1,047 − 1,175 = −128 kJ/mol: exothermic, as hydrogenations are (measured heats of hydrogenation run from −136 kJ/mol for ethylene to about −115 to −125 kJ/mol for substituted alkenes).

Shortcut: the C–H bonds already on the alkene carbons appear on both sides and cancel; only the π bond and H–H are broken, and only a C–C σ bond and two new C–H bonds are made. Bond-energy sums are estimates because the tabulated values are averages.

why_wrong.A: −564 kJ/mol forgets that the H–H bond must be broken: 611 − 1,175.
why_wrong.C: +128 kJ/mol subtracts in the wrong order (formed − broken); breaking bonds costs energy and forming them releases it, so the sign here is a sign error.
why_wrong.D: +287 kJ/mol counts only one new C–H bond (1,047 − 760); hydrogenation adds two hydrogens, one to each carbon.

error_types.A: wrong formula: a broken bond omitted
error_types.C: sign or unit error: formed minus broken
error_types.D: wrong formula: one of the two new C–H bonds omitted

items.takeaway: ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed); hydrogenating one C=C breaks C=C and H–H (1,047 kJ) and forms C–C and two C–H (1,175 kJ), about −130 kJ/mol.
sources: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 7.5 Strengths of Ionic and Covalent Bonds (2019): Table 7.2 average bond energies H–H 436, C–H 415, C–C 345, C=C 611 kJ/mol; ΔH = ΣD(bonds broken) − ΣD(bonds formed), a rough estimate because the values are averages.

OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 7.6 Stability of Alkenes (2023): Table 7.2 heats of hydrogenation, ethylene −136, propene −125, cis-2-butene −119, trans-2-butene −115 kJ/mol; 8.6 Reduction of Alkenes: Hydrogenation: vegetable oils are hydrogenated on a large scale to make the saturated fats in margarine.

items.stem: A cylinder of medical gas is filled to a high pressure and stored outdoors in winter. Under which conditions does a real gas deviate most from PV = nRT, and why?

options.A: Low pressure and high temperature, because the molecules then collide with one another so often that their motion is no longer random
options.B: Low pressure and low temperature, because the molecules then spread so far apart that they rarely strike the walls of the container
options.C: High pressure and low temperature, because the molecules' own volume then matters and their attractions are not overcome by thermal motion
options.D: High pressure and high temperature, because the molecules then move so fast that the gas becomes easier to compress than the ideal law predicts

why_correct: The ideal gas law assumes molecules of negligible volume with no forces between them. At high pressure the molecules are crowded, so their own volume is an appreciable part of the total and the gas is harder to compress than predicted; at low temperature the molecules move slowly, so their mutual attractions pull them together and lower the pressure below the ideal value.
The van der Waals equation corrects for both: b for the excluded volume and a for the attractions. The compressibility factor Z = PV/nRT departs furthest from 1 at high pressure and low temperature.
Shortcut: gases behave ideally when they are dilute and hot (low P, high T), which is the opposite of a cold, full cylinder.

why_wrong.A: Low pressure and high temperature are the conditions under which real gases come closest to ideal behaviour; frequent collisions do not make motion non-random.
why_wrong.B: At low pressure the molecules are far apart, which makes the ideal law work better, not worse; the wall collisions that create pressure never cease.
why_wrong.D: High temperature overwhelms the attractions and brings the gas closer to ideal behaviour; a crowded gas is harder, not easier, to compress because of the molecules' own volume.

error_types.A: reversed relationship: the ideal regime named as the non-ideal one
error_types.B: wrong formula: the wrong half of the conditions, with a false mechanism
error_types.D: reversed relationship: temperature and compressibility

items.takeaway: Real gases deviate most from PV = nRT at high pressure (molecular volume matters) and low temperature (attractions matter); they are most ideal when dilute and hot.
sources: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 9.6 Non-Ideal Gas Behavior (2019): the ideal gas law fails at high pressure because the molecules' own volume becomes appreciable and attractions are no longer insignificant, and works best at low pressure and high temperature; the compressibility factor Z and the van der Waals equation.

items.stem: A patient who drank rubbing alcohol (propan-2-ol, isopropanol) has a high blood level of the product formed when alcohol dehydrogenase oxidizes the carbon that carries the hydroxyl group. That product is:
why_correct: Propan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol: the carbon bearing the OH is bonded to two other carbons and one hydrogen. Oxidation removes that hydrogen and the O–H hydrogen, converting C–OH into C=O.

A secondary alcohol therefore gives a ketone, here propanone, better known as acetone, CH₃COCH₃. Alcohol dehydrogenase does this with NAD⁺ as the hydride acceptor, just as it converts ethanol to acetaldehyde.

Clinically, isopropanol poisoning is recognized by ketosis (acetone in the blood and breath) without the metabolic acidosis seen with methanol or ethylene glycol, because acetone is not oxidized further to an acid.

why_wrong.B: Propanal is the aldehyde from oxidizing the primary alcohol propan-1-ol; propan-2-ol's hydroxyl carbon has no second hydrogen to give an aldehyde and is not at the chain end.
why_wrong.C: A carboxylic acid arises only from further oxidation of an aldehyde, which needs a primary alcohol; a ketone's carbonyl carbon has no hydrogen left to remove without breaking a C–C bond.
why_wrong.D: Propene is the product of dehydration (elimination of water), not of oxidation; the H and the OH leave together, so the average oxidation state of the carbons is unchanged.

error_types.B: wrong formula: the primary-alcohol product
error_types.C: too extreme: oxidation carried past what a secondary alcohol allows
error_types.D: wrong formula: elimination confused with oxidation

items.takeaway: Oxidizing a secondary alcohol gives a ketone; a primary alcohol gives an aldehyde and then an acid; isopropanol is metabolized to acetone.
sources: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 17.7 Oxidation of Alcohols (2023): primary alcohols are oxidized to aldehydes or carboxylic acids, secondary alcohols to ketones, tertiary alcohols normally not at all; biological oxidations use NAD⁺.
StatPearls, Isopropanol Toxicity (NCBI Bookshelf NBK493181): isopropanol is converted to acetone in the liver by alcohol dehydrogenase; the result is ketosis without metabolic acidosis.

items.stem: Using Table 1 and the heat of combustion of benzoic acid given in the passage, the gross energy of the bar is closest to:
why_correct: Passage: "the heat released is q = CΔT, where C is the heat capacity of the assembly." The same assembly was used for both runs, so C is the same and, for equal 1.000 g masses, q(bar)/q(benzoic acid) = ΔT(bar)/ΔT(benzoic acid).

Two-step check: C = 26.4 kJ / 2.40 K = 11.0 kJ/K, then q = 11.0 kJ/K × 2.00 K = 22.0 kJ. The sample was dried, so the 48 g of dry matter in a 50 g bar (Table 2) hold about 1,060 kJ, roughly 250 kcal (1 kcal = 4.184 kJ).

why_wrong.A: 11.0 is the heat capacity of the assembly in kJ/K, not an energy per gram of sample.
why_wrong.C: 31.7 kJ/g inverts the ratio of the temperature rises (2.40/2.00); the bar raised the temperature less than benzoic acid did, so it released less energy per gram.
why_wrong.D: 52.8 kJ/g multiplies 26.4 kJ by the bar's 2.00 K rise without dividing by the 2.40 K rise of the calibration run.

error_types.A: sign or unit error: a heat capacity (kJ/K) reported as an energy per gram
error_types.C: reversed relationship: ratio of temperature rises inverted
error_types.D: wrong formula: q = (26.4 kJ) × ΔT instead of C × ΔT with C from the calibration

items.takeaway: In a calibrated bomb calorimeter q = CΔT; with the same assembly and equal masses, the energies of two samples are in the ratio of their temperature rises.
sources: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 5.2 Calorimetry (2019): bomb calorimeters are calibrated by burning a known mass of benzoic acid, and the energy of a sample is calculated from the temperature rise and the calorimeter's heat capacity.
NIST Standard Reference Material 39j certificate: benzoic acid heat of combustion 26,434 J/g.

items.stem: In exercising muscle, glucose can be converted anaerobically to lactic acid: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 C₃H₆O₃. Using the standard enthalpies of combustion given in the passage, ΔH° for this conversion, per mole of glucose, is closest to:
why_correct: Hess's law: glucose and two lactic acids burn to the same products, 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O. Write glucose → 2 lactic acid as (glucose + 6 O₂ → 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O) minus 2 × (lactic acid + 3 O₂ → 3 CO₂ + 3 H₂O).

Sense check: lactic acid still holds almost all of glucose's combustion energy (2 × 1,360 = 2,720 of 2,800 kJ), so the anaerobic step releases only about 3% of it; the rest is released when lactate is later oxidized completely.

why_wrong.A: −4,160 kJ/mol adds the two combustion enthalpies (−2,800 − 1,360); Hess's law subtracts the products' combustion enthalpies from the reactants'.
why_wrong.B: −1,440 kJ/mol subtracts the combustion enthalpy of one mole of lactic acid; the equation forms two moles.
why_wrong.D: +80 kJ/mol has the right magnitude but the wrong sign: the reactants' combustion enthalpy (−2,800) is more negative than the products' (−2,720), so the conversion is exothermic.

error_types.A: wrong formula: combustion enthalpies added instead of reactants minus products
error_types.B: wrong formula: stoichiometric coefficient of 2 dropped
error_types.D: sign or unit error: products and reactants interchanged

items.takeaway: For a reaction whose reactants and products all burn to the same products, ΔH°rxn = Σ ΔcH°(reactants) − Σ ΔcH°(products), each weighted by its coefficient.
sources: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 5.3 Enthalpy (2019): Hess's law (the enthalpy change of a process equals the sum of the enthalpy changes of its steps, because enthalpy is a state function) and the standard enthalpy of combustion.

NIST Chemistry WebBook, condensed-phase thermochemistry: α-D-glucose ΔcH°(solid) = −2,805.0 ± 1.3 kJ/mol; lactic acid ΔcH°(solid) = −1,362.8 kJ/mol (Meyerhof 1922). With the unrounded values the result is −79.4 kJ/mol.

items.stem: Taking the reacting contents of the sealed bomb as the system, which statement about the combustion measurement is correct?

options.A: Because the volume is fixed, no pressure–volume work is done, and the heat that flows out equals the decrease in the system's internal energy.
options.B: Because the bomb sits in water at atmospheric pressure, the heat measured equals the system's enthalpy change rather than its internal energy change.
options.C: Because the sample releases a large amount of energy, the heat q for the combustion is a large positive quantity in the first law.
options.D: Because faster combustion loses less heat to the surroundings, the internal energy change depends on how quickly the sample burns.

why_correct: First law: ΔU = q + w, with q the heat entering the system and w the work done on it. In a rigid bomb ΔV = 0, so w = −PΔV = 0 and ΔU = q.
The reaction releases heat, so q is negative for the system, and the heat that warms the water and bomb, which the passage calls q = CΔT, equals −ΔU of the contents.
Passage: "the heat it releases equals the decrease in the internal energy of its contents." Internal energy is a state function, so this ΔU is the same however fast the sample burns.

why_wrong.B: The water outside the bomb is at constant pressure, but the system is the bomb's contents, whose volume cannot change; constant-volume heat equals ΔU, and ΔH differs from it by Δ(PV), small for foods but not zero.
why_wrong.C: Heat leaves the reacting system, so by the convention ΔU = q + w the system's q is negative; the surroundings' q is positive.
why_wrong.D: Internal energy is a state function: ΔU depends only on the initial and final states of the contents, not on the rate or path of the reaction.

error_types.B: wrong formula: constant-pressure relation q = ΔH applied to a constant-volume system
error_types.C: sign or unit error: heat released by the system given a positive sign
error_types.D: wrong formula: a state function treated as path dependent

items.takeaway: At constant volume w = 0 and q = ΔU; at constant pressure q = ΔH. Heat released by the system is negative, and state functions such as U and H do not depend on the path.
sources: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 5.3 Enthalpy (2019): ΔU = q + w with q positive for heat flowing into the system and w positive for work done on it; U and H are state functions; at constant pressure q = ΔH, whereas a bomb calorimeter's constant-volume heat is not equal to ΔH.
OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 5.2 Calorimetry (2019): bomb calorimeters operate at constant volume.

items.stem: The gross energy measured in the bomb exceeded the Atwater estimate from Table 2. The investigators wished to measure directly the energy that a person actually obtains from the bar. Which protocol most directly measures this quantity?

options.A: Burn the bar in a constant-pressure (coffee-cup) calorimeter rather than in the bomb, so that the heat measured is the enthalpy change, as it is in the body.
options.B: Measure volunteers' resting oxygen consumption for one hour after they eat the bar, and convert the volume of oxygen used to energy at about 20 kJ per litre.
options.C: Measure the rise in volunteers' core temperature during the hours after they eat the bar, and multiply it by the heat capacity of the body.
options.D: Feed volunteers a known mass of the bar as their only food, collect all faeces and urine, burn these in the bomb, and subtract their energy from the bar's gross energy.

why_correct: Passage: metabolizable energy is "the gross energy less the energy lost in faeces and urine." The direct measurement is therefore a balance: energy in (bomb value of the food eaten) minus energy out in excreta (bomb values of faeces and urine).

This is how the Atwater factors were derived: the energy of unabsorbed food appears in the faeces, and the energy of incompletely oxidized protein appears in the urine as urea and other nitrogen compounds.
Design points: the bar must be the only food so that the excreta can be attributed to it, and collection must be complete over the whole transit time.

why_wrong.A: The constant-volume and constant-pressure values differ by Δ(PV), well under 1% for foods (passage); the gap between the bomb and the Atwater estimate comes from losses in excreta, not from the pressure–volume term.
why_wrong.B: Indirect calorimetry gives the energy the body expends during that hour, drawn from all its fuels, mostly stored ones; it does not measure how much of the bar's energy was absorbed, which is used or stored over days.
why_wrong.C: Core temperature is held nearly constant by thermoregulation, and the heat produced is lost to the surroundings; the body is not an insulated calorimeter, so its temperature does not record energy absorbed.

error_types.A: true but irrelevant: ΔH and ΔU differ, but not enough to explain the gap
error_types.B: true but irrelevant: energy expenditure measured in place of energy absorbed from the food
error_types.C: wrong formula: the body treated as an insulated calorimeter with q = CΔT

items.takeaway: Metabolizable energy = gross energy of the food − energy of faeces − energy of urine, each measured by bomb calorimetry; that balance, not a different calorimeter, is the direct measurement.
sources: Merrill and Watt, Energy Value of Foods: Basis and Derivation, USDA Agriculture Handbook 74 (1955, revised 1973), Part II: available energy of a food is its heat of combustion less that of the urinary and faecal residues; protein's heat of combustion of 5.65 kcal/g is reduced by 1.25 kcal/g for unoxidized urinary compounds.

FAO Food and Nutrition Paper 77, Food energy: methods of analysis and conversion factors (2003), chapter 3: metabolizable energy as gross energy less faecal, urinary (and gaseous and surface) losses; the Atwater general factors and the 8 kJ/g fibre factor.

items.stem: Based on Figure 1 and the heater power stated in the passage, the heat capacity of the calorimeter assembly is closest to:
why_correct: Energy delivered = power × time. The heater ran from t = 60 s to t = 360 s, 300 s, at 110 W: E = 110 J/s × 300 s = 33,000 J = 33.0 kJ.
From Figure 1 the temperature rose from 25.00 °C to 28.00 °C, ΔT = 3.00 K (a kelvin and a degree Celsius are the same size for a difference).

C = E/ΔT = 33.0 kJ / 3.00 K = 11.0 kJ/K. Cross-check with Table 1: 26.4 kJ / 2.40 K = 11.0 kJ/K. The flat segments before and after heating show that heat loss to the room was negligible over the run.

why_wrong.A: 0.037 kJ/K divides the power (110 W) by ΔT without multiplying by the 300 s the heater ran; it has units of W/K, a rate, not a heat capacity.
why_wrong.C: 13 kJ/K uses 360 s, the clock time when the heater was switched off, instead of the 300 s it was on (it started at 60 s): 110 × 360 / 3.00 = 13.2 kJ/K.
why_wrong.D: 33 kJ is the energy delivered; a heat capacity divides this by the temperature rise, which was 3.00 K, not 1 K.

error_types.A: wrong formula: power divided by ΔT, time omitted
error_types.C: misread graph: heater-off time used as the heating duration
error_types.D: sign or unit error: energy reported in place of energy per kelvin

items.takeaway: Electrical calibration: C = Pt/ΔT, with the heating time read from when the heater was on, not from the clock, and ΔT read between the two plateaus.
sources: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 5.1 Energy Basics (2019): heat capacity C = q/ΔT in J/°C (equivalently J/K); the watt as a joule per second.
OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 5.2 Calorimetry (2019): a bomb calorimeter's heat capacity is determined by calibration before the sample is burned.

items.stem: In Figure 1 each peptide appears mainly as a single peak. Which statement correctly describes how these ions are formed and what the horizontal axis reports?

options.A: The laser ejects an electron from each peptide, leaving a radical cation that fragments extensively; the axis reports the mass of each fragment in daltons, with no charge involved.
options.B: Each peptide gains a proton from the matrix, giving an [M + H]⁺ ion; the axis reports mass in daltons, so a doubly protonated peptide appears two units higher than a singly protonated one.
options.C: Each peptide gains a proton from the matrix, giving an [M + H]⁺ ion; the axis reports mass divided by charge number, so a doubly protonated peptide appears near half this value.
options.D: Each peptide loses a proton to the basic matrix, giving an [M − H]⁻ ion one unit lighter than the neutral peptide; the axis reports mass divided by charge number.

why_correct: Passage: "the matrix transfers a proton to most sample molecules, giving [M + H]⁺ ions." Protonation adds one hydrogen (about 1.007 Da) and one positive charge; MALDI is a soft method, so the intact peptide is seen rather than fragments.

The axis is m/z, mass divided by charge number. For z = 1 the peak sits at M + 1.007; a doubly protonated peptide has mass M + 2.015 and z = 2, so it appears at (M + 2.015)/2, close to half the singly charged value.
This is why Figure 1 can be read as peptide masses: every main peak is singly charged.

why_wrong.A: Electron ejection to a radical cation with extensive fragmentation describes electron-impact ionization of small volatile molecules; the passage's laser-matrix method protonates intact peptides.
why_wrong.B: A second proton adds one more unit of mass but also a second charge, and the axis is m/z, not mass, so the doubly charged ion appears near half the m/z value, not two units higher.
why_wrong.D: The matrix is an acid that donates protons, and the passage states that positive [M + H]⁺ ions are formed; deprotonation to [M − H]⁻ describes negative-ion mode, not this experiment.

error_types.A: outside knowledge contradicting the passage: electron-impact ionization substituted for proton transfer from the matrix
error_types.B: wrong formula: the axis treated as mass rather than mass-to-charge ratio
error_types.D: reversed relationship: proton loss instead of proton gain

items.takeaway: MALDI gives intact [M + H]⁺ ions; the spectrum's axis is m/z, so a doubly charged ion appears at about half the m/z of the singly charged ion of the same molecule.
sources: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 12.4 Mass Spectrometry in Biological Chemistry: Time-of-Flight (TOF) Instruments (2023): in MALDI the matrix absorbs the laser energy and protonates the sample; electrospray and MALDI are soft methods that give M + Hₙⁿ⁺ ions with little fragmentation.

OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 12.1 Mass Spectrometry of Small Molecules: Magnetic-Sector Instruments (2023): electron-impact ionization produces a cation radical that fragments; the mass spectrum plots intensity against m/z.

items.stem: Singly charged ions of m/z 900 reached the detector 30.5 µs after the laser pulse. Under the same conditions, the singly charged T5 ions (m/z 1,626) would arrive after approximately:
why_correct: Passage: every singly charged ion acquires the same kinetic energy eV, so ½mv² = eV gives v = √(2eV/m), and t = L/v = L√(m/2eV). With L and V fixed, t ∝ √m: heavier ions are slower and arrive later.

Check from first principles: at 20 kV an ion of 900 Da has v = √(2 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2 × 10⁴ / (900 × 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷)) ≈ 6.5 × 10⁴ m/s, so a 2.0 m tube is crossed in 2.0/6.5 × 10⁴ ≈ 3.1 × 10⁻⁵ s = 31 µs, consistent with the passage.

why_wrong.A: 17 µs scales the time as 1/m (30.5 × 900/1,626); heavier ions take longer, not less time, and the dependence is on the square root.
why_wrong.B: 23 µs scales the time as 1/√m (30.5 × 3/4), the inverse of the correct dependence: a heavier ion at the same kinetic energy is slower.
why_wrong.D: 55 µs scales the time directly with m (30.5 × 1,626/900); because kinetic energy depends on v², the speed, and hence the time, depends on the square root of the mass.

error_types.A: reversed relationship: time taken as inversely proportional to mass
error_types.B: reversed relationship: time taken as inversely proportional to the square root of mass
error_types.D: wrong formula: time taken as proportional to mass instead of its square root

items.takeaway: In a time-of-flight analyser all ions of the same charge share the same kinetic energy, so v ∝ 1/√m and the flight time t ∝ √(m/z): lighter ions arrive first.
sources: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 12.4 Mass Spectrometry in Biological Chemistry: Time-of-Flight (TOF) Instruments (2023): each ion in the packet is given the same energy; lighter molecules move faster and heavier ones slower, v = √(2E/m).
NIST CODATA 2022: elementary charge 1.602 176 634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; atomic mass constant 1.660 539 068 92 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

items.stem: The investigators' main purpose in digesting a second sample of the protein with chymotrypsin was to:

options.A: obtain peptides with different end points, so that the extra 79.97 Da could be assigned to one part of T3 independently of the fragmentation data.
options.B: remove the phosphate group from T3, because chymotrypsin hydrolyses phosphate esters as well as peptide bonds.
options.C: cleave T3 after its lysine into smaller pieces, which fly faster down the tube and are therefore detected with greater sensitivity.
options.D: confirm that the protein contains lysine and arginine, the residues after which trypsin cleaves, by showing that the two digests differ.

why_correct: Passage: chymotrypsin "cleaves on the carboxyl side of phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan." Within the T3 region (Ala-Tyr-Ser-Leu-Gln-Asp-Val-Phe-Lys) it cuts after Tyr-2 and after Phe-8, so Tyr-2 and Ser-3, the two candidate sites, end up in different chymotryptic peptides.

If the peptide ending at Tyr-2 has its predicted mass and the peptide beginning at Ser-3 is 79.97 Da heavier, the modification is on Ser-3, not Tyr-2. This is a second, independent line of evidence, with different peptide boundaries, that must agree with the y-ion ladder.

Using two proteases of different specificity is the general strategy for ordering and cross-checking peptide fragments, because each enzyme alone gives pieces whose relation to one another is ambiguous.

why_wrong.B: Chymotrypsin is a protease; it hydrolyses peptide bonds after aromatic residues and does not remove phosphate. Removing the phosphate would be the job of a phosphatase, a different control.
why_wrong.C: Trypsin, not chymotrypsin, cleaves after lysine, and T3 already ends at its lysine; faster flight has nothing to do with the purpose of a second digest.
why_wrong.D: The trypsin digest already produced peptides ending in lysine or arginine; confirming trypsin's specificity was not in question and would not locate the modification.

error_types.B: outside knowledge contradicting the passage: a protease treated as a phosphatase
error_types.C: outside knowledge contradicting the passage: chymotrypsin given trypsin's specificity
error_types.D: true but irrelevant: trypsin's specificity was never the question

items.takeaway: A second protease with different specificity gives peptides with different boundaries, so an unexpected mass can be assigned to a region, and overlapping fragments can be ordered.
sources: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.6 Peptide Sequencing: The Edman Degradation (2023): trypsin cleaves only on the carboxyl side of arginine and lysine; chymotrypsin only on the carboxyl side of phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan; fragments are fitted together by their overlaps.
Unimod entry 21 (Phospho): HPO₃, monoisotopic mass shift 79.966331 Da, on Ser, Thr or Tyr.

items.stem: In Table 2 the difference between consecutive y ions equals the mass of one residue of T3. The residue between fragments y7 and y6 is best identified as:
why_correct: y7 − y6 = 916.4 − 749.4 = 167.0 Da. Fragment y7 holds residues 3–9 and y6 holds 4–9, so this is residue 3, predicted to be serine (87.03); 167.0 matches no unmodified residue in Table 1 (the nearest are Tyr 163.06 and Trp 186.08), so residue 3 is modified.
Passage: phosphorylation adds HPO₃, 79.97 Da. 167.0 − 80.0 = 87.0 = serine, so residue 3 is phosphoserine, which also accounts for the 79.97 Da excess of the whole peptide.

Check the alternative, phosphorylation of Tyr-2: y8 − y7 = 1,079.5 − 916.4 = 163.1 = unmodified tyrosine, so the phosphate is not there. The rest of the ladder reads y6 − y5 = 113.1 = Leu and y5 − y4 = 128.0 = Gln, as the sequence predicts.

why_wrong.A: Unmodified serine would give a step of 87.0 Da; the observed 167.0 is 80 Da more. Choosing serine amounts to placing the phosphate elsewhere, on Tyr-2, but the y8 − y7 step of 163.1 shows tyrosine unmodified.
why_wrong.C: Phosphothreonine would weigh 101.05 + 79.97 = 181.0 Da; the observed step is 167.0, and the sequence has no threonine at position 3.
why_wrong.D: Phosphotyrosine would weigh 163.06 + 79.97 = 243.0 Da, which is not a step in the ladder; the tyrosine step (y8 − y7 = 163.1) shows Tyr-2 unmodified.

error_types.A: misread graph: the 167.0 Da step read as serine's 87.0, placing the 80 Da elsewhere
error_types.C: wrong formula: 80 Da added to threonine rather than to the residue that gives 167
error_types.D: wrong formula: 80 Da added to tyrosine rather than subtracted from the observed 167

items.takeaway: Consecutive y (or b) ions differ by one residue mass; a step that matches no residue but equals a residue plus 80.0 Da marks a phosphorylated Ser, Thr or Tyr.
sources: University of Washington Proteomics Resource, residue mass table (Unimod elemental masses): Ser 87.032028, Thr 101.047679, Tyr 163.063329, Leu 113.084064, Gln 128.058578.
Unimod entry 21 (Phospho): HPO₃, monoisotopic mass 79.966331 Da, sites S, T, Y.

OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.6 Peptide Sequencing: The Edman Degradation (2023): most peptide sequencing is now done by mass spectrometry with electrospray or MALDI sources and time-of-flight analysers.

items.stem: In Figure 1 the peak one unit above the monoisotopic peak of T2 has 44% of its intensity. Treating this peak as due to carbon-13 alone, as the investigators did, the number of carbon atoms in T2 is closest to:
why_correct: Each carbon atom has a 1.1% chance of being ¹³C (passage). In a molecule with n carbons the chance that exactly one of them is ¹³C is about n × 0.011 when that product is well below 1, so the M+1 peak has about n × 1.1% of the monoisotopic peak's intensity.

Mental math: 1.1% per carbon means 11% per 10 carbons, so 44% corresponds to 40 carbons. The explanation of the method also shows its limit: ¹⁵N (0.37%), ²H and ¹⁷O add to M+1 too, so the true carbon count is a little below this estimate.

why_wrong.A: 4 treats the abundance as 11% rather than 1.1% (0.44/0.11); it is a factor-of-ten slip in converting the percentage.
why_wrong.B: 22 halves the result as though T2 were doubly charged; the isotope ratio does not depend on the ion's charge, and the passage's peaks are singly charged.
why_wrong.D: 44 treats the carbon-13 abundance as exactly 1%; with the passage's 1.1% the count is 40.

error_types.A: sign or unit error: percentage misconverted by a factor of ten
error_types.B: wrong formula: the charge state applied to an isotope ratio
error_types.D: wrong formula: 1.1% abundance rounded to 1%

items.takeaway: The M+1 peak of an organic molecule is about n × 1.1% of the M peak, where n is the number of carbons, so n ≈ (M+1 intensity, %) / 1.1.
sources: IUPAC CIAAW, Carbon: isotopic abundances (2009): ¹³C amount fraction interval 0.0096–0.0116, so 1.1% is a representative value.
OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 12.2 Interpreting Mass Spectra (2023): the M+1 peak arises from molecules containing a ¹³C atom, with natural abundance about 1.1%.

items.stem: For Patient C, the spectacle lens that corrects distance vision must have a focal length and power of:
why_correct: Passage: "a distance lens must form a virtual image of a distant object at the patient's far point." For C the far point is 50 cm (Table 1), so with dₒ → ∞ the image must be at dᵢ = −0.50 m (virtual, on the object's side).
1/f = 1/dₒ + 1/dᵢ = 0 + 1/(−0.50 m) = −2.0 m⁻¹, so f = −0.50 m = −50 cm and P = 1/f = −2.0 D: a diverging lens, as myopia requires.
Rule: a distance lens for a myope has a focal length equal to minus the far point, so its power is −1/(far point in metres).

why_wrong.B: −0.02 D divides 1 by 50 with the focal length left in centimetres; power in diopters requires f in metres (1/0.50 m = 2.0 m⁻¹).
why_wrong.C: +2.0 D has the right magnitude but is a converging lens; it would make rays from a distant object converge before they reach the eye, worsening the overconvergence of a myopic eye.
why_wrong.D: +4.0 D is 1/0.25 m, the power associated with the 25 cm reading distance, not with C's far point; it is a converging lens, the opposite of what distance correction for myopia needs.

error_types.B: sign or unit error: centimetres used in P = 1/f
error_types.C: sign or unit error: sign of the virtual image distance dropped
error_types.D: wrong formula: the reading distance used in place of the far point

items.takeaway: Lens power P = 1/f with f in metres; a myope's distance lens is diverging with f = −(far point), so a 50 cm far point needs −2.0 D.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 26.2 Vision Correction (2022): the correction for nearsightedness is a diverging spectacle lens that forms an image no farther than the far point; a virtual image on the same side as the object has a negative image distance; P = 1/dₒ + 1/dᵢ with distances in metres gives diopters (Example 26.3).
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 25.6 Image Formation by Lenses (2022): the thin-lens equation and P = 1/f; a diverging lens has negative f and negative power.

items.stem: The reading lens prescribed for Patient B should have a power closest to:
why_correct: Passage: "A reading lens must form a virtual image of the page, held at 25 cm, at the patient's near point." For B the near point is 100 cm (Table 1): dₒ = +0.25 m, dᵢ = −1.00 m (virtual).

Why it works: B's eye can focus anything at 100 cm or beyond with its remaining accommodation (amplitude 1.0 D); the lens makes the page at 25 cm look as though it were at 100 cm. Compare A: 4.0 − 2.0 = +2.0 D for a 50 cm near point.

why_wrong.A: +1.0 D is 1/1.00 m alone, the term for the image at the near point; it omits the object term 1/0.25 m.
why_wrong.C: +4.0 D is 1/0.25 m alone, the power that would focus the page at infinity, as if B had no accommodation left; B can still focus at 100 cm, which reduces the lens needed by 1.0 D.
why_wrong.D: +5.0 D adds 4.0 and 1.0, treating the image distance as positive; the image is virtual and on the same side as the page, so its term is negative.

error_types.A: wrong formula: object term omitted
error_types.C: wrong formula: image term omitted
error_types.D: sign or unit error: virtual image distance taken as positive

items.takeaway: Reading-lens power = 1/(reading distance) − 1/(near point), both in metres; a near point of 100 cm and a 25 cm page need 4 − 1 = +3 D.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 26.2 Vision Correction (2022): Example 26.4, a person with a near point of 100 cm reading at 25 cm needs a converging lens of about +3.2 D when the 1.5 cm lens–eye separation is included (+3.0 D when it is neglected, as the passage does).
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 26.1 Physics of the Eye (2022): presbyopia is corrected with converging lenses of about 1.0 to 3.5 D.

items.stem: Most of the eye's refracting power comes from the front surface of the cornea rather than from the lens, even though the lens has the higher refractive index. By Snell's law, this is because:

options.A: the cornea is thicker than the lens, so light travels a longer path inside it and is deviated more.
options.B: the cornea's front surface is flatter than the surfaces of the lens, and a flatter surface bends light through a larger angle.
options.C: the lens lies behind the pupil, where the beam is narrowest, so fewer rays reach it and less bending is needed.
options.D: the air–cornea boundary has the largest change in refractive index in the eye, whereas the lens is bathed in fluids of nearly its own index.

why_correct: Snell's law, n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, bends a ray only where n changes, and the bending grows with the ratio n₂/n₁. Passage indices: air 1.00 → cornea 1.38 is a step of 0.38; aqueous humour 1.34 → lens 1.41 is a step of only 0.07.

So the first surface of the cornea does most of the work (about two-thirds of the eye's roughly 50 D), and the lens, surrounded by aqueous and vitreous humour of index 1.34, adds the rest and provides the adjustable part through accommodation.
This is also why the eye cannot focus under water: with water (1.33) in place of air, the index step at the cornea almost vanishes.

why_wrong.A: Refraction happens at the boundary, not along the path; the thickness of a medium does not change the angle through which a ray is bent at its surface.
why_wrong.B: Curvature matters in the opposite direction: for a given index step, a more curved surface has a shorter focal length and more power. The cornea's advantage is its index step, not flatness.
why_wrong.C: The width of the beam has no bearing on the angle through which each ray is refracted; Snell's law applies to every ray at the surface it crosses.

error_types.A: wrong formula: deviation attributed to path length rather than to the index change at a boundary
error_types.B: reversed relationship: flatter surface claimed to bend light more
error_types.C: true but irrelevant: beam width does not set refraction

items.takeaway: Refraction depends on the change in refractive index at a boundary; the air–cornea step (1.00 to 1.38) dwarfs the fluid–lens step (1.34 to 1.41), so the cornea supplies about two-thirds of the eye's power.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 26.1 Physics of the Eye (2022): Table 26.1 refractive indices (cornea 1.38, aqueous humour 1.34, lens 1.41, vitreous humour 1.34); the cornea provides about two-thirds of the eye's power because the speed of light changes considerably from air into the cornea.
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 25.3 The Law of Refraction (2022): Snell's law and the dependence of bending on the two indices.

items.stem: Based on Table 1, which patients cannot read a page at the clinic's 25 cm reading distance with the unaided eye, and therefore need a converging (positive-power) lens to do so?
why_correct: The unaided eye can focus only between its near point and its far point. A page at 25 cm is readable unaided only if the near point is at 25 cm or less.

Table 1: A's near point is 50 cm and B's is 100 cm, both beyond 25 cm, so each needs a converging lens that makes the page appear at their near point (+2.0 D and +3.0 D). C's near point is 25 cm, so C reads the page unaided, as the passage reports.

C's problem is the opposite one: a far point of 50 cm, corrected for distance with a diverging lens of −2.0 D. (Wearing that lens, C's near point would move out to 50 cm, which is why myopes often take their glasses off to read.)

why_wrong.A: B's near point (100 cm) is even farther from the page than A's; B needs the stronger reading lens of the two.
why_wrong.C: C's near point of 25 cm already reaches the page, so C needs no converging lens for reading with the unaided eye; a myope whose near point is still close reads without spectacles.
why_wrong.D: C needs a diverging lens, for distance; the patients who cannot see the page are A and B, whose near points lie beyond it.

error_types.A: misread graph: Patient B's 100 cm near point overlooked
error_types.C: misread graph: a near point of 25 cm treated as beyond the 25 cm page
error_types.D: reversed relationship: myopia (short far point) taken to need a converging lens

items.takeaway: A reading (converging) lens is needed when the near point lies beyond the reading distance; a short far point calls for a diverging distance lens instead.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 26.2 Vision Correction (2022): hyperopia and presbyopia are corrected with converging lenses forming an image at or beyond the near point; myopia with diverging lenses forming an image no farther than the far point.
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 26.1 Physics of the Eye (2022): the near point as the shortest distance at which a sharp focus can be obtained, which increases with age.

items.stem: Using Table 1, the standard potential at pH 7 for the re-oxidation of FADH₂ by ferricyanide, FADH₂ + 2 Fe(CN)₆³⁻ → FAD + 2 Fe(CN)₆⁴⁻ + 2 H⁺, and the direction in which the reaction proceeds under standard conditions, are:

options.A: −0.58 V; it does not proceed as written

why_correct: Ferricyanide is reduced (cathode half-reaction, E°′ = +0.36 V) and FADH₂ is oxidized, the reverse of FAD + 2 H⁺ + 2 e⁻ → FADH₂ (E°′ = −0.22 V). E°′cell = E°′(cathode) − E°′(anode) = 0.36 − (−0.22) = +0.58 V.
The ferricyanide half-reaction is doubled to balance the two electrons, but a potential is energy per unit charge and is not multiplied by the coefficient.

A positive cell potential means ΔG°′ = −nFE°′ = −2 × 96,485 C/mol × 0.58 V ≈ −1.1 × 10⁵ J/mol = −112 kJ/mol, so the reaction proceeds as written; this is what makes ferricyanide a usable substitute for oxygen (O₂/H₂O₂ gives 0.30 − (−0.22) = +0.52 V).

why_wrong.A: −0.58 V subtracts cathode from anode; the species with the more positive reduction potential, ferricyanide, is the one reduced, so the cell potential is positive.
why_wrong.B: +0.14 V computes 0.36 − 0.22, dropping the minus sign of the FAD potential; subtracting −0.22 adds 0.22.
why_wrong.D: +0.94 V doubles the ferricyanide potential (2 × 0.36 + 0.22) to match its coefficient of 2; potentials are intensive and are never scaled by stoichiometric coefficients.

error_types.A: sign or unit error: anode and cathode potentials interchanged
error_types.B: sign or unit error: negative reduction potential subtracted as if positive
error_types.D: wrong formula: a reduction potential multiplied by its stoichiometric coefficient

items.takeaway: E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode) using reduction potentials as tabulated, never scaled by coefficients; a positive E°cell means ΔG° = −nFE° is negative and the reaction is spontaneous.
sources: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 17.3 Electrode and Cell Potentials (2019): E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode; potentials are not multiplied when half-reactions are scaled.
OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 17.4 Potential, Free Energy, and Equilibrium (2019): ΔG° = −nFE°cell with F = 96,485 C/mol.

Jakubowski, Biochemistry Online (CSB/SJU), Oxidative Phosphorylation: Dehydrogenases, standard reduction potential table at pH 7: FAD/FADH₂ (free) −0.22 V; O₂/H₂O₂ +0.30 V. Chemistry LibreTexts, P1: Standard Reduction Potentials by Element: Fe(CN)₆³⁻/Fe(CN)₆⁴⁻ +0.356 V.

items.stem: In an open-circuit measurement on one strip, the ferrocyanide:ferricyanide ratio rose from 1:100 in the fresh strip to 1:1 after a glucose sample had reacted completely. Over this change the electrode potential:
why_correct: Passage: E = E°′ − (0.0592 V) log([Fe(CN)₆⁴⁻]/[Fe(CN)₆³⁻]), a one-electron couple (n = 1).
Fresh strip: ratio 1/100, log(0.01) = −2, so E = E°′ − 0.0592 × (−2) = E°′ + 0.118 V. After reaction: ratio 1, log 1 = 0, so E = E°′. The potential fell by 0.118 V, about 0.12 V.

Sense check: converting ferricyanide to ferrocyanide makes the couple more reduced, so its potential drops; each tenfold change in the ratio shifts a one-electron couple by 59 mV, and here the ratio changed a hundredfold, 2 × 59 mV.

why_wrong.A: 0.06 V is one tenfold step, or the result of wrongly using n = 2 (0.0592/2 per decade over two decades); the ferricyanide/ferrocyanide couple transfers one electron and the ratio changed by two decades.
why_wrong.C: 0.24 V would need a 10⁴-fold change in the ratio (four decades at 59 mV each); the change here was from 10⁻² to 10⁰, two decades.
why_wrong.D: The potential falls, not rises: more of the reduced form (ferrocyanide) makes Q larger and E = E°′ − 0.0592 log Q smaller.

error_types.A: wrong formula: n = 2 used for a one-electron couple
error_types.C: misread graph: two decades of ratio change counted as four
error_types.D: reversed relationship: sign of the Nernst shift inverted

items.takeaway: At 25 °C a one-electron couple's potential changes by 59 mV for each tenfold change in [reduced]/[oxidized]; more reduced form means a lower potential.
sources: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 17.4 Potential, Free Energy, and Equilibrium (2019): the Nernst equation E = E° − (0.0592 V/n) log Q at 25 °C, and its application to concentration cells (Example 17.8).
Chemistry LibreTexts, P1: Standard Reduction Potentials by Element: Fe(CN)₆³⁻ + e⁻ → Fe(CN)₆⁴⁻, +0.356 V (a one-electron couple).

items.stem: For the calibration sample, the average current of 10 µA over the 5.0 s measurement corresponds to the oxidation of how many moles of glucose? (Faraday constant F = 96,485 C/mol)
why_correct: Moles of electrons: n = Q/F = 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ C / 9.65 × 10⁴ C/mol ≈ 5.2 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol. Mental math: 5.0/9.65 ≈ 0.52 and 10⁻⁵/10⁴ = 10⁻⁹, so 0.52 × 10⁻⁹.

Passage: "each glucose molecule therefore delivers two electrons to the electrode," so moles of glucose = 5.2 × 10⁻¹⁰ / 2 = 2.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol. Scale check: 1 µL of blood at 5 mmol/L holds 5 × 10⁻⁹ mol of glucose, so about 5% of it was oxidized during the measurement.

why_wrong.B: 5.2 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol is the number of moles of electrons; each glucose supplies two of them.
why_wrong.C: 1.0 × 10⁻⁹ mol multiplies the moles of electrons by 2 instead of dividing by 2.
why_wrong.D: 2.6 × 10⁻⁴ mol treats the current as 10 A rather than 10 µA, a factor of 10⁶; that much glucose (about 47 mg) could not be in a 1 µL drop of blood.

error_types.B: wrong formula: two electrons per glucose not applied
error_types.C: reversed relationship: multiplied by 2 instead of divided
error_types.D: sign or unit error: microamperes read as amperes

items.takeaway: Moles of analyte = It/(zF): charge is current × time, divide by Faraday's constant for moles of electrons, then by the electrons transferred per molecule.
sources: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 17.7 Electrolysis (2019): Q = It, and the moles of electrons n = Q/F with F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻ (Example 17.9).
NIST CODATA 2022: Faraday constant 96,485.332 12 C/mol.

items.stem: In the first half-step of the enzyme's catalytic cycle described in the passage, which statement is correct?

options.A: Glucose is reduced at C1, and the enzyme's FAD is oxidized to supply the electrons that glucose gains.
options.B: Glucose is oxidized at C1, and a molecule of NAD⁺ bound to the enzyme accepts the electrons as a hydride ion.
options.C: Oxygen is reduced to water at the active site, and the energy released is used to phosphorylate glucose.
options.D: Glucose is oxidized at C1, and the enzyme's FAD accepts the two electrons, becoming FADH₂.

why_correct: Passage: "glucose + GOx·FAD → gluconolactone + GOx·FADH₂." C1 of glucose, a hemiacetal carbon bonded to one oxygen with one hydrogen, becomes the carbonyl carbon of a lactone (a cyclic ester) bonded to two oxygens: it has lost a hydrogen and gained a bond to oxygen, so glucose is oxidized.

Electrons lost by glucose must be gained by something: the flavin (FAD) is the acceptor, taking two electrons (and two protons) to become FADH₂. Glucose oxidase is a flavoprotein, so its redox carrier is FAD, not NAD⁺.
Oxygen appears only in the second half-step, where it re-oxidizes FADH₂ and is reduced to hydrogen peroxide, not to water.

why_wrong.A: The direction is reversed: glucose loses electrons (its C1 goes from hemiacetal to ester oxidation level) and FAD gains them.
why_wrong.B: Glucose oxidase is a flavoprotein; its bound cofactor is FAD. NAD⁺ is the hydride acceptor of soluble dehydrogenases, and the passage names FAD throughout.
why_wrong.C: Oxygen is consumed in the second half-step and is reduced to H₂O₂, not water; nothing in the cycle phosphorylates glucose, which hexokinase does elsewhere using ATP.

error_types.A: reversed relationship: oxidation and reduction interchanged
error_types.B: outside knowledge contradicting the passage: NAD⁺ substituted for the enzyme's FAD
error_types.C: outside knowledge contradicting the passage: O₂ reduced to water and glucose phosphorylated

items.takeaway: An oxidase oxidizes its substrate and reduces its bound flavin (FAD → FADH₂); the flavin is then re-oxidized by O₂, which becomes H₂O₂.
sources: ExPASy ENZYME, EC 1.1.3.4 glucose oxidase: β-D-glucose + O₂ = D-glucono-1,5-lactone + H₂O₂.
