Lowry, McAteer, El Atrash, Duff and O'Neill, Analytical Chemistry 66:1754–1761 (1994): β-D-glucose + GOx/FAD → D-glucono-δ-lactone + GOx/FADH₂; GOx/FADH₂ + O₂ → GOx/FAD + H₂O₂, with FAD the oxidized form of the prosthetic group.
OpenStax Biology 2e, 7.1 Energy in Living Systems (2018): oxidation as loss of electrons; NAD⁺ and FAD as electron carriers, FAD remaining bound to its enzyme.

items.stem: To test whether dissolved oxygen in a sample lowers the strip's current reading, which comparison is most appropriate?

options.A: Glucose standards at 5 and 10 mmol/L, both in air-equilibrated buffer, to check that the current doubles when the glucose doubles.
options.B: Venous and arterial blood drawn from the same volunteer at the same time, measured on strips from the same lot.
options.C: The same glucose standard measured with the working electrode held at +0.3 V and then at +0.6 V against the reference.
options.D: The same glucose standard in air-equilibrated buffer and in buffer deoxygenated with nitrogen, with everything else held identical.

why_correct: Passage: "Dissolved oxygen can still compete with ferricyanide for the reduced enzyme, diverting electrons into hydrogen peroxide, which is not oxidized at +0.3 V." The hypothesis is that oxygen lowers the current, so oxygen must be the only variable that changes.

Measuring one glucose standard with and without dissolved oxygen (air-equilibrated versus nitrogen-purged buffer), with the same strip lot, temperature and timing, isolates the oxygen effect; a lower current in the air-equilibrated sample would confirm interference, and its size tells whether the excess ferricyanide suppresses it enough.
A buffer standard, rather than blood, removes the other variables that differ between blood samples.

why_wrong.A: Comparing two glucose concentrations in the same oxygenated buffer tests linearity of the response; oxygen is the same in both, so it says nothing about oxygen interference.
why_wrong.B: Venous and arterial blood differ in oxygen, but also in glucose (tissues extract it), carbon dioxide and pH, so a difference in reading could not be attributed to oxygen; the comparison is confounded.
why_wrong.C: Changing the applied potential tests which species are oxidized at the electrode (at +0.6 V, hydrogen peroxide and interferents such as ascorbate); it does not vary the oxygen available to compete for FADH₂.

error_types.A: true but irrelevant: linearity tested, oxygen unchanged
error_types.B: true but irrelevant: oxygen differs, but so do glucose, CO₂ and pH, so the comparison is confounded
error_types.C: out of scope: electrode potential, not sample oxygen, is varied

items.takeaway: To test a suspected interferent, measure the same standard with and without it and hold every other condition fixed; paired biological samples that differ in several ways cannot isolate one cause.
sources: Lowry, McAteer, El Atrash, Duff and O'Neill, Analytical Chemistry 66:1754–1761 (1994): first-generation glucose electrodes were affected by the ambient oxygen concentration of the sample; mediated electrodes are relatively insensitive to changes in oxygen tension, depending on the mediator's kinetic interaction with the reduced enzyme.

Eggins, Chemical Sensors and Biosensors (Wiley 2002), chapter 5: the ambient oxygen level had to be controlled in first-generation sensors; a mediator should not react with oxygen; hydrogen peroxide is oxidized at about +0.65 V, where ascorbic acid interferes.

items.stem: In a crystal of sodium chloride the centres of neighbouring Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are about 0.30 nm apart. Treating each ion as a point charge of magnitude e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and taking k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C², the magnitude of the electrostatic force between the two ions is closest to:
why_correct: Coulomb's law: F = k|q₁q₂|/r² with q₁ = q₂ = e and r = 0.30 nm = 3.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m.
Shortcut: the 9.0 in k cancels the 9.0 in r², leaving F = 2.56 × 10⁻³⁸ × 10⁹ / 10⁻²⁰ = 2.56 × 10⁻⁹ N. The force is attractive (opposite charges) and acts along the line joining the ions.

why_wrong.A: 2.6 × 10⁻²⁷ N uses r = 0.30 m instead of 0.30 nm, a factor of (10⁹)² = 10¹⁸ in the denominator.
why_wrong.B: 7.7 × 10⁻¹⁹ N divides by r rather than r² (2.3 × 10⁻²⁸ / 3.0 × 10⁻¹⁰); Coulomb's law is an inverse-square law.
why_wrong.D: 5.1 × 10⁻⁹ N doubles the correct value, as if the product of the charges were 2e²; each ion carries one elementary charge, so the product is e².

error_types.A: sign or unit error: nanometres entered as metres
error_types.B: wrong formula: 1/r instead of 1/r²
error_types.D: wrong formula: charge product doubled

items.takeaway: F = kq₁q₂/r² with r in metres; between two single charges 0.3 nm apart the force is a few nanonewtons, enormous on an atomic scale.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 18.3 Coulomb's Law (2022): F = k|q₁q₂|/r², k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C², the force acting along the line joining the charges (Example 18.1 computes the electron–proton force in hydrogen).

OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 10.6 Lattice Structures in Crystalline Solids (2019): in NaCl the ions touch along the cell edge, with ionic radii Na⁺ 102 pm and Cl⁻ 181 pm, so neighbouring centres are about 283 pm (0.28 nm) apart; the item rounds this to 0.30 nm.
NIST CODATA 2022: elementary charge 1.602 176 634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

items.stem: Pauling electronegativities: H 2.1, C 2.5, N 3.0, O 3.5, S 2.5. Of the following bonds found in proteins, which is the most polar?
why_correct: Bond polarity grows with the difference in electronegativity between the bonded atoms. The differences are: C–H 2.5 − 2.1 = 0.4; N–H 3.0 − 2.1 = 0.9; O–H 3.5 − 2.1 = 1.4; S–H 2.5 − 2.1 = 0.4.

O–H has the largest difference, so it is the most polar: the shared pair sits closest to oxygen, giving a large δ⁻ on O and δ⁺ on H. This is why hydroxyl groups (serine, threonine, tyrosine) and water are strong hydrogen-bond donors.
Rule of thumb from the same scale: differences below about 0.4 are nearly nonpolar, 0.4 to 1.8 polar covalent, above 1.8 largely ionic.

why_wrong.A: C–H, difference 0.4, is nearly nonpolar, which is why hydrocarbon side chains are hydrophobic.
why_wrong.B: N–H, difference 0.9, is polar and hydrogen-bonds (backbone amides, lysine, arginine), but less strongly than O–H.
why_wrong.D: S–H, difference 0.4, is about as nonpolar as C–H, because sulfur's electronegativity is close to carbon's; thiols are poor hydrogen-bond donors despite sulfur's size.

error_types.A: reversed relationship: the smallest electronegativity difference chosen as most polar
error_types.B: true but irrelevant: N–H is polar, but its 0.9 difference is smaller than O–H's 1.4
error_types.D: wrong formula: polarity attributed to the heavier atom rather than to the electronegativity difference

items.takeaway: Rank bond polarity by electronegativity difference: O–H (1.4) > N–H (0.9) > C–H ≈ S–H (0.4), which is why O–H and N–H are hydrogen-bond donors and C–H and S–H are not.
sources: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 2.1 Polar Covalent Bonds and Electronegativity (2023): electronegativities H 2.1, C 2.5, N 3.0, O 3.5; C–H bonds are relatively nonpolar; a difference under 0.5 is nonpolar covalent, 0.5 to 2 polar covalent.

OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 7.2 Covalent Bonding (2019): electronegativity differences C–H 0.4, S–H 0.4, N–H 0.9, O–H 1.4; bonds with a difference below about 0.4 are nearly nonpolar, 0.4 to 1.8 polar covalent.

items.stem: A nucleoside analogue used as an antiviral drug is inactive as given and is converted by cellular kinases, in three steps, into the corresponding nucleotide triphosphate. In the active form, the phosphate groups are attached to the:

options.A: 5′-carbon of the sugar, through a phosphate ester to its hydroxyl group
options.B: 3′-carbon of the sugar, the position through which nucleotides are joined in a chain
options.C: N9 nitrogen of the purine base, displacing the sugar from the base
options.D: 1′-carbon of the sugar, in place of the nitrogenous base

why_correct: A nucleoside is a sugar (ribose or 2′-deoxyribose) joined at C1′ to a base; a nucleotide is a nucleoside with one to three phosphates on the 5′-hydroxyl, forming a phosphate ester at C5′. Kinases add phosphate there, giving the mono-, di- and then triphosphate.
The antiviral triphosphate mimics a natural nucleoside 5′-triphosphate (such as dGTP) so that a polymerase can take it up; that is why the 5′ position is the one phosphorylated.

Mnemonic: in a nucleic acid chain the 5′-phosphate of one nucleotide links to the 3′-hydroxyl of the previous one (a phosphodiester), so the free building block carries its phosphates at 5′ and keeps 3′-OH free.

why_wrong.B: The 3′-hydroxyl is where the next nucleotide's 5′-phosphate attaches during chain growth; a free nucleotide (and the active drug) carries its phosphates at the 5′ position, leaving 3′-OH available.
why_wrong.C: N9 of a purine (N1 of a pyrimidine) is the atom bonded to C1′ of the sugar through the N-glycosidic bond; phosphate is never attached to the base in a nucleotide.
why_wrong.D: C1′, the anomeric carbon, carries the base; replacing the base with phosphate would destroy the base pairing on which the drug's action depends.

error_types.B: true but irrelevant: the 3′ position is a chain-linking site, not where a nucleotide's own phosphates sit
error_types.C: wrong formula: the N-glycosidic bond site mistaken for the phosphate site
error_types.D: wrong formula: the anomeric carbon, which carries the base, mistaken for the phosphate site

items.takeaway: Nucleoside = sugar + base (C1′ to N9 or N1); nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate(s) on the 5′-hydroxyl; chains link 5′-phosphate to 3′-hydroxyl.
sources: OpenStax Biology 2e, 3.5 Nucleic Acids (2018): a nucleotide is a pentose sugar, a nitrogenous base attached at the 1′ position and a phosphate attached at the 5′ position; phosphodiester linkages join the 5′-phosphate of one sugar to the 3′-hydroxyl of the next.

OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 28.1 Nucleotides and Nucleic Acids (2023): a nucleoside is an aldopentose linked through its anomeric carbon to a purine or pyrimidine base; a nucleotide is a nucleoside bonded to a phosphate group; chains have a free 3′-hydroxyl at one end and a phosphate at C5′ at the other.

items.stem: A small volatile compound collected from the breath of a patient in diabetic ketoacidosis gives an infrared spectrum with a strong, sharp absorption at 1,715 cm⁻¹, C–H stretches just below 3,000 cm⁻¹, and no broad absorption anywhere between 2,500 and 3,600 cm⁻¹. The compound most likely contains:
why_correct: A strong, sharp band near 1,715 cm⁻¹ is a C=O stretch; 1,715 is the value for a saturated ketone (aldehydes about 1,730, esters about 1,735, acids about 1,710).

The absence of any broad band between 2,500 and 3,600 cm⁻¹ rules out O–H and N–H: an alcohol's O–H is a broad band at about 3,200 to 3,650 cm⁻¹, and a carboxylic acid's is broader still, from about 2,500 to 3,300 cm⁻¹, overlapping the C–H region.
C–H stretches just below 3,000 cm⁻¹ are sp³ C–H. Together: a saturated ketone, consistent with acetone, the ketone body exhaled in ketoacidosis that gives the breath its sweet smell.

why_wrong.A: A carboxylic acid has a C=O near 1,710 cm⁻¹ but also a very broad O–H band spanning roughly 2,500 to 3,300 cm⁻¹; the stem reports only sharp C–H stretches in that region and no broad absorption anywhere from 2,500 to 3,600 cm⁻¹.
why_wrong.B: An alcohol shows a broad O–H band at about 3,200 to 3,650 cm⁻¹ and no C=O; this spectrum has the reverse.
why_wrong.C: A C≡C stretch appears at about 2,100 to 2,260 cm⁻¹, weak and sharp; nothing there is reported, and 1,715 cm⁻¹ is far from the triple-bond region.

error_types.A: misread graph: the broad acid O–H band, which is absent, overlooked
error_types.B: misread graph: C=O band ignored and an absent O–H band assumed
error_types.C: wrong formula: C=O band misassigned to the C≡C region

items.takeaway: A sharp C=O near 1,715 cm⁻¹ with no broad O–H band (alcohol 3,200–3,650, acid 2,500–3,300 cm⁻¹) points to a ketone.
sources: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 12.8 Infrared Spectra of Some Common Functional Groups (2023): ketone C=O 1,715 cm⁻¹ (saturated), aldehyde 1,730, ester 1,735; alcohol O–H 3,400–3,650 cm⁻¹; alkane C–H 2,850–2,960; alkyne C≡C 2,100–2,260.
OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 12.7 Interpreting Infrared Spectra (2023): the broad carboxylic acid O–H absorption from about 2,500 to 3,100 cm⁻¹ and the diagnostic C=O region.
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 24.3 Lipid Metabolism (2022): in uncontrolled diabetes ketone bodies accumulate and acetone is removed by exhalation, giving the breath a sweet smell.

items.stem: On the phase diagram of carbon dioxide the triple point is at −56.6 °C and 5.1 atm, and the critical point at 31 °C and 73 atm. A block of dry ice (solid CO₂) is left in an open container at 1 atm and warms from −100 °C to room temperature, 20 °C. Which statement describes what happens?

options.A: It melts at −56.6 °C, and the liquid then boils before the temperature reaches 20 °C.
options.B: It sublimes directly to gas, because at 1 atm no liquid phase of CO₂ exists at any temperature.
options.C: It melts to a liquid that remains stable up to 20 °C, because 20 °C is below the critical temperature.
options.D: It becomes a supercritical fluid as soon as its temperature passes the triple point.

why_correct: Liquid CO₂ exists only above the triple-point pressure, 5.1 atm: below it the solid–gas line is the only boundary, so a horizontal path at 1 atm from −100 °C to 20 °C crosses from solid straight into gas.
That crossing is sublimation, which for CO₂ at 1 atm occurs at about −78 °C; the block shrinks and the 'smoke' seen is water vapour condensed by the cold gas.
Compare water, whose triple-point pressure is 0.006 atm: at 1 atm the path crosses the solid–liquid line, so ice melts.

why_wrong.A: Melting at the triple-point temperature happens only at the triple-point pressure (5.1 atm) or above; at 1 atm the path lies below the triple point and never meets the solid–liquid line.
why_wrong.C: A liquid needs a pressure above 5.1 atm; being below the critical temperature is necessary for a liquid but not sufficient. The critical point only marks where liquid and gas cease to be distinct.
why_wrong.D: A supercritical fluid requires both T > 31 °C and P > 73 atm; at 1 atm and 20 °C the CO₂ is an ordinary gas, and the triple point has nothing to do with the supercritical region.

error_types.A: misread graph: the triple-point temperature treated as a melting point at any pressure
error_types.C: wrong formula: the critical temperature treated as the condition for a liquid
error_types.D: too extreme: supercritical conditions claimed far below the critical pressure

items.takeaway: Below the triple-point pressure a solid sublimes rather than melts; CO₂'s triple point is 5.1 atm, so dry ice at 1 atm goes straight to gas, while water's 0.006 atm triple point lets ice melt.
sources: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 10.4 Phase Diagrams (2019): solid carbon dioxide does not melt at 1 atm but sublimes; the triple point and critical point of CO₂ (critical point about 31 °C and 73 atm); a supercritical fluid exists above the critical temperature and pressure.
Engineering LibreTexts, Introduction to Engineering Thermodynamics (Yan), Appendix F: triple point of carbon dioxide 216.55 K (−56.60 °C), 517 kPa (5.10 atm).
Chemeurope, Carbon dioxide (data page): critical point 304.18 K (31.03 °C), 7.38 MPa (72.8 atm).

items.stem: In a hypothetical biosynthetic pathway, A is converted to the end product E in four enzyme-catalysed steps, A → B → C → D → E, and E regulates the pathway by inhibiting one of the enzymes. The most effective arrangement for the cell is for E to inhibit:

options.A: enzyme 1 (A → B), binding at a regulatory site distinct from the active site, so that no intermediates accumulate when E is abundant.
options.B: enzyme 4 (D → E), competing with D for the active site, so that only the final step is slowed when E is abundant.
options.C: enzyme 1 (A → B), competing with A for the active site, because the end product E closely resembles the first substrate A.
options.D: all four enzymes equally, so that the concentrations of B, C and D stay constant whatever the level of E.

why_correct: Feedback inhibition: the end product of a pathway inhibits an enzyme early in that pathway, usually the first committed step. Blocking enzyme 1 stops the flow of A into the pathway, so no B, C or D is made and no ATP or carbon is wasted on intermediates that would not be used.

E is several reactions removed from A and does not resemble it, so E cannot compete at A's active site; it binds a separate regulatory (allosteric) site and shifts the enzyme to a less active conformation. Feedback inhibition operates by allosterism.
Examples: isoleucine inhibits threonine deaminase, the first enzyme of its synthesis; CTP inhibits aspartate transcarbamoylase; cholesterol inhibits HMG-CoA reductase.

why_wrong.B: Blocking the last step lets B, C and D pile up, wasting the material and ATP spent making them; an inhibitor at the final step controls nothing upstream.
why_wrong.C: The end product of a multistep pathway generally differs in structure from the first substrate, so it cannot act as a competitive inhibitor at that active site; end-product control is allosteric.
why_wrong.D: Inhibiting every enzyme equally would still let intermediates form and would waste the resources used to build them; one well-placed allosteric block at the entry to the pathway is sufficient and economical.

error_types.B: reversed relationship: the exit of the pathway blocked instead of its entry
error_types.C: wrong formula: the end product treated as a structural analogue of the first substrate
error_types.D: too extreme: every enzyme inhibited

items.takeaway: Feedback inhibition is allosteric and acts on an early (committed) step, so an abundant end product shuts the whole pathway off without accumulating intermediates.
sources: OpenStax Biology 2e, 6.5 Enzymes (2018): feedback inhibition uses a reaction product to regulate its own further production, binding an allosteric site on an upstream enzyme (isoleucine and threonine deaminase, Figure 6.21).

Biology LibreTexts, Biochemistry Free For All (Ahern, Rajagopal, Tan), 4.2 Control of Enzymatic Activity: inhibiting an early enzyme in a pathway stops the flow of materials and the ATP needed to process them; feedback inhibition always operates by allosterism; HMG-CoA reductase and cholesterol, ATCase and CTP.

glance.summary: This section tests biology and biochemistry as the foundation of medicine: the molecules of life and how cells use them, how genetic information is stored, expressed, and inherited, how cells divide and specialize, and how the organ systems keep the body stable. Most questions follow a passage describing an experiment, so reading data and judging study design matter as much as recall.
glance.math: Light arithmetic: ratios and percentages for genetics (Punnett squares, Hardy–Weinberg), simple probability, reading graphs and tables, and the occasional logarithm or exponential (pH, growth curves). No calculator.
glance.scores_note: Scores in this app are percent correct. They are not MCAT scaled scores (118–132), which only AAMC's equating can produce.

concepts.name: Biomolecules and the processes of life
concepts.summary: Foundational Concept 1 (AAMC): the molecules that make cells work. Proteins and enzymes, the path from gene to protein, inheritance and variation, and the pathways that harvest energy from fuel.

categories.name: Proteins and amino acids
categories.summary: From amino acids to working proteins: the chemistry of the building blocks, the four levels of structure and what holds them, non-enzyme jobs, and enzymes with their kinetics and control.

topics.name: Amino acids: configuration, dipolar ions, classification, and reactions
know: Every proteinogenic amino acid has an α-carbon bonded to an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen, and a side chain. All but glycine are chiral, and the ones in proteins have the L configuration (S by the sequence rules, except cysteine). At physiological pH the carboxyl is deprotonated and the amino group protonated, making the molecule a zwitterion with no net charge.

Classify by side chain: hydrophobic (Gly, Ala, Val, Leu, Ile, Met, Pro, Phe, Trp), polar and hydrophilic (Ser, Thr, Cys, Tyr, Asn, Gln), acidic (Asp, Glu), and basic (Lys, Arg, His). Hydrophobic residues cluster in protein cores and membrane-spanning segments; charged ones face water or form salt bridges. Histidine's side chain (pKa about 6) can gain or lose a proton near physiological pH, which makes it a common catalytic residue.

Reactions: two cysteine thiols oxidize to a disulfide, cystine, a covalent cross-link within or between chains that is reduced back by agents such as β-mercaptoethanol. Amino acids join through peptide bonds (amide bonds between one carboxyl and the next amino group, formed by condensation) into polypeptides; hydrolysis by acid, base, or proteases reverses it.
confusions: Zwitterion means net charge zero, not uncharged. Proline's side chain loops back onto its own nitrogen, which is why it kinks helices.

refs.label: OpenStax Biology 2e, 3.4 Proteins
OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.1 Structures of Amino Acids
OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.4 Peptides and Proteins

topics.name: Protein structure: primary to quaternary, stability, folding, and separation
know: Primary structure is the amino acid sequence, fixed by covalent peptide bonds. Secondary structure is local backbone folding held by backbone hydrogen bonds: the α-helix and the β-sheet (parallel or antiparallel). Tertiary structure is the full three-dimensional fold of one chain, driven by hydrophobic interactions (nonpolar side chains buried away from water), hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions, van der Waals contacts, and disulfide bonds; proline breaks helices and cystine cross-links stabilize the fold. Quaternary structure is the assembly of several chains, as in hemoglobin.

Conformational stability: the folded state is only marginally more stable than the unfolded one. The hydrophobic effect is driven by entropy: water molecules ordered in a solvation layer around exposed nonpolar groups are freed when those groups are buried. Denaturation (heat, extreme pH, urea, detergents, reducing agents) unfolds the protein and usually destroys function without breaking peptide bonds; some proteins refold spontaneously, showing the sequence specifies the fold, and chaperones assist folding in the cell.

Separation uses charge and size. The isoelectric point (pI) is the pH at which the protein's net charge is zero; below it the protein is positive, above it negative. Electrophoresis moves charged proteins through a gel: SDS–PAGE coats them with negative charge and separates by size alone, native gels separate by size and charge, and isoelectric focusing moves each protein to its pI along a pH gradient.
equations: \mathrm{pI} \approx \dfrac{\mathrm{p}K_{a1} + \mathrm{p}K_{a2}}{2}\ \ \text{(the two } \mathrm{p}K_a\text{ values bracketing the neutral form)}
confusions: Secondary-structure hydrogen bonds involve the backbone C=O and N–H, not the side chains; side chains drive tertiary structure.

OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.9 Protein Structure
OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.2 Amino Acids and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation: Isoelectric Points
Biology LibreTexts, Biochemistry Free For All (Ahern, Rajagopal, Tan), 8.3 Electrophoresis

topics.name: Nonenzymatic protein function: binding, immune system, and motors
know: Binding proteins hold ligands reversibly and specifically: hemoglobin binds oxygen cooperatively, giving a sigmoidal curve, and myoglobin stores it with a hyperbolic curve; transport proteins such as transferrin and albumin carry iron and fatty acids in blood; receptors bind hormones and transmitters. Affinity is described by the dissociation constant Kd, lower meaning tighter.

Immune proteins: antibodies (immunoglobulins) are Y-shaped molecules of two heavy and two light chains whose variable regions form two identical antigen-binding sites; binding neutralizes pathogens, marks them for phagocytosis, and activates complement. Each B-cell clone makes one specificity, and the vast repertoire comes from gene rearrangement.

Motor proteins turn ATP hydrolysis into movement along cytoskeletal tracks: myosin on actin (muscle contraction, cytokinesis), kinesin toward the plus end of microtubules and dynein toward the minus end (vesicle transport, cilia and flagella, chromosome movement). Structural proteins (collagen, keratin, actin, tubulin) provide shape and strength.
confusions: Kinesin and dynein travel opposite directions on the same microtubule; dynein also powers the beating of cilia by sliding microtubule doublets.

OpenStax Biology 2e, 42.3 Antibodies
OpenStax Biology 2e, 4.5 The Cytoskeleton

topics.name: Enzyme structure and function: catalysis, specificity, active site, induced fit, cofactors
know: Enzymes are biological catalysts, almost all proteins, that speed reactions by lowering the activation energy; they do not change the equilibrium or the ΔG, and they are not consumed. They are classified by reaction type: oxidoreductases, transferases (including kinases), hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases, and translocases.

The substrate binds at the active site, a pocket whose shape and chemistry match the substrate (specificity). The lock-and-key picture captures the fit; the induced-fit model adds that binding reshapes both enzyme and substrate toward the transition state. Catalysis works by orienting substrates, straining bonds, providing acidic or basic groups, and forming transient covalent intermediates.

Many enzymes need cofactors: inorganic ions (Mg²⁺, Zn²⁺, Fe²⁺) or organic coenzymes, most derived from water-soluble vitamins (NAD⁺ from niacin, FAD from riboflavin, coenzyme A from pantothenic acid, pyridoxal phosphate from B6, thiamine pyrophosphate from B1). Local conditions matter: each enzyme has an optimal temperature and pH; heat beyond the optimum and extreme pH denature it, and salt and solvent affect activity.
confusions: An enzyme speeds the forward and reverse reactions equally; it changes how fast equilibrium is reached, not where it lies.

refs.label: OpenStax Biology 2e, 6.5 Enzymes
OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.10 Enzymes and Coenzymes
IUBMB, EC 7 Translocases (seventh enzyme class, 2018)

topics.name: Control of enzyme activity: kinetics, inhibition, and regulatory enzymes
know: Michaelis–Menten kinetics: the initial rate rises with substrate and saturates at Vmax; Km is the substrate concentration giving half of Vmax and reflects affinity (lower Km, tighter binding). Vmax = kcat[E], so doubling the enzyme doubles Vmax but leaves Km unchanged. A Lineweaver–Burk plot of 1/v against 1/[S] gives a line with y-intercept 1/Vmax and x-intercept −1/Km. Cooperative enzymes with several subunits give a sigmoidal curve instead of a hyperbola.

Inhibition: competitive inhibitors bind the active site, raise the apparent Km, leave Vmax unchanged, and are overcome by more substrate; noncompetitive inhibitors bind elsewhere whether or not substrate is bound, lower Vmax, and leave Km unchanged; uncompetitive inhibitors bind only the enzyme–substrate complex and lower both Vmax and Km; mixed inhibitors alter both in other ratios. Irreversible inhibitors bond covalently.

Regulation: feedback inhibition by a pathway's end product acts on an early, committed step. Allosteric enzymes have regulatory sites separate from the active site; effectors shift them between low-activity and high-activity conformations. Covalent modification, most often phosphorylation by kinases and dephosphorylation by phosphatases, switches enzymes on or off reversibly. Zymogens (proenzymes such as pepsinogen, trypsinogen, and the clotting factors) are activated irreversibly by proteolytic cleavage where and when they are needed.
confusions: Only competitive inhibition is overcome by raising substrate. Km is a concentration, not a rate.

categories.name: Gene to protein
categories.summary: The flow of information: DNA structure, how it is copied and repaired, the genetic code, transcription and translation, how chromosomes are packed, how genes are switched on and off in prokaryotes and eukaryotes, and the tools of recombinant DNA.

topics.name: Nucleic acid structure and function
know: A nucleotide is a pentose sugar (ribose or 2′-deoxyribose) with a nitrogenous base at C1′ and one to three phosphates at C5′; a nucleoside lacks the phosphate. Purines (adenine, guanine) have two rings, pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine, uracil) one. Phosphodiester bonds between the 3′-OH of one sugar and the 5′-phosphate of the next build a sugar–phosphate backbone with the bases as side groups, so every strand has a 5′ → 3′ direction.

The Watson–Crick model: DNA is two antiparallel strands in a right-handed double helix, held by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases (A with T by two bonds, G with C by three) and by stacking of the flat bases, with the backbone outside and major and minor grooves along the surface. Because each strand specifies the other, DNA can be copied faithfully and carries heritable information from generation to generation.

Heating or alkali separates the strands (denaturation, melting); the melting temperature rises with GC content and length. Cooling lets complementary strands reanneal, and hybridization of a labelled probe to its complement is the basis of blots, microarrays, and PCR primers. RNA is usually single-stranded with internal base pairing, uses ribose and uracil, and is less stable than DNA.
confusions: The strands are antiparallel: the 5′ end of one lies beside the 3′ end of the other, so complementary sequences are written in opposite directions.

refs.label: OpenStax Biology 2e, 3.5 Nucleic Acids
OpenStax Biology 2e, 14.2 DNA Structure and Sequencing
OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 28.2 Base Pairing in DNA

topics.name: DNA replication
know: Replication is semiconservative: each new double helix keeps one parental strand and gains one new strand, as Meselson and Stahl showed. It begins at origins of replication, a single origin on the circular bacterial chromosome and many along each linear eukaryotic chromosome, and proceeds in both directions from each origin.

Enzymes: helicase unwinds the helix, single-strand binding proteins keep the strands apart, topoisomerase relieves the twisting ahead of the fork, primase lays down a short RNA primer, and DNA polymerase extends it, adding nucleotides only to a free 3′-OH, so synthesis is 5′ → 3′. The leading strand is made continuously toward the fork; the lagging strand is made in Okazaki fragments away from it, whose primers are replaced with DNA and whose nicks are sealed by DNA ligase. Polymerase proofreads with a 3′ → 5′ exonuclease.

Linear chromosomes lose a little from each 5′ end at every round because the last primer cannot be replaced. Telomeres, repetitive non-coding ends, absorb the loss, and telomerase, an enzyme with its own RNA template, extends them in germ cells, stem cells, and most cancers; telomere shortening in ordinary cells limits their divisions.
confusions: Both new strands grow 5′ → 3′; only the direction relative to the fork differs. The lagging strand is not made backward, it is made in pieces.

topics.name: DNA repair
know: During replication, polymerase proofreading removes a mispaired base at once with its 3′ → 5′ exonuclease; errors that slip through are caught by mismatch repair, which recognizes the distortion, identifies the new strand (in bacteria by its lack of methylation), cuts out the stretch, and resynthesizes it.

Damage from chemicals, radiation, and spontaneous reactions is handled by base excision repair (a glycosylase removes a single damaged base, then the gap is filled) and nucleotide excision repair (a stretch containing a bulky lesion such as a UV-induced thymine dimer is cut out and replaced). Double-strand breaks are rejoined by non-homologous end joining (error-prone) or repaired accurately by homologous recombination using the sister chromatid.

Failures of repair cause disease: xeroderma pigmentosum (defective nucleotide excision repair, extreme sun sensitivity and skin cancer), Lynch syndrome (mismatch repair defects, colorectal cancer), and BRCA1/2 mutations (homologous recombination, breast and ovarian cancer). Unrepaired damage that is copied becomes a permanent mutation.
confusions: Proofreading happens during synthesis; mismatch repair happens afterward on the new strand; excision repair handles damage, not copying errors.

topics.name: The genetic code and messenger RNA
know: The central dogma: information flows from DNA to RNA (transcription) to protein (translation); retroviruses add RNA → DNA by reverse transcription. The code is read in triplets: 64 codons of three nucleotides specify 20 amino acids plus stop. It is unambiguous (each codon means one amino acid), degenerate (most amino acids have several codons, differing mainly at the third position), non-overlapping, read without punctuation from a fixed start, and nearly universal.

AUG is the initiation codon and encodes methionine; UAA, UAG, and UGA are termination (stop) codons with no tRNA. Each tRNA's anticodon pairs antiparallel with the codon; wobble pairing at the third position lets one tRNA read several synonymous codons.

Mutations are named by effect: a missense mutation changes one amino acid, a nonsense mutation creates a premature stop, a silent mutation changes the codon but not the amino acid, and an insertion or deletion not divisible by three shifts the reading frame. mRNA is the working copy: in eukaryotes it carries a 5′ cap, a 3′ poly-A tail, and untranslated regions flanking the coding sequence.
confusions: Degenerate means redundant (several codons per amino acid), not ambiguous. The start codon sets the reading frame; everything downstream is read in threes from there.

topics.name: Transcription and RNA processing
know: RNA polymerase binds a promoter upstream of the gene (with sigma factor in bacteria, with transcription factors at the TATA box in eukaryotes), unwinds the DNA, and synthesizes RNA 5′ → 3′ complementary to the template strand (so the RNA matches the coding strand, with U for T). It needs no primer. Elongation continues until a terminator; in bacteria a hairpin or rho factor ends it, and in eukaryotes cleavage after the polyadenylation signal does. Eukaryotes use three polymerases: I for rRNA, II for mRNA, III for tRNA and small RNAs.

Kinds of RNA: mRNA carries the message; tRNA, a cloverleaf with an anticodon and an amino acid attached at its 3′ end by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase, is the adaptor; rRNA forms the ribosome's structure and catalytic core. Prokaryotic transcription and translation happen together in the cytoplasm; eukaryotic pre-mRNA is processed in the nucleus first.

Processing: a 7-methylguanosine cap is added to the 5′ end, a poly-A tail to the 3′ end (both protect the message and aid export and translation), and introns are removed by the spliceosome, a complex of small nuclear RNAs and proteins (snRNPs) that joins the exons; some RNAs splice themselves (ribozymes), showing RNA can catalyse. Alternative splicing lets one gene make several proteins, and exons often correspond to protein domains, which may have made it easier for new genes to arise by shuffling domains.
confusions: The template strand is read 3′ → 5′; the RNA produced has the sequence of the other (coding) strand. Introns are removed from RNA; the gene keeps them.

topics.name: Translation and post-translational modification
know: The ribosome has a small subunit that reads the mRNA and a large subunit whose rRNA catalyses peptide bond formation (a ribozyme), with three tRNA sites: A (aminoacyl, incoming), P (peptidyl, growing chain), and E (exit). Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S (30S + 50S), eukaryotic 80S (40S + 60S), which is why some antibiotics hit bacterial ribosomes selectively.

Initiation: the small subunit binds the mRNA (at the Shine–Dalgarno sequence in bacteria, by scanning from the cap in eukaryotes), the initiator tRNA (formyl-methionine in bacteria, methionine in eukaryotes) sits at AUG in the P site, and initiation factors bring in the large subunit using GTP. Elongation: a charged tRNA enters the A site, the chain is transferred onto it, and the ribosome shifts one codon (elongation factors, GTP). Termination: a stop codon in the A site is recognized by release factors, which free the polypeptide. Many ribosomes read one mRNA at once (a polysome).

After synthesis, proteins fold (often with chaperones) and may be modified: cleavage of signal peptides and propeptides, disulfide formation, glycosylation in the ER and Golgi, phosphorylation, acetylation, methylation, lipid attachment, and ubiquitination for degradation. A signal sequence directs ribosomes to the rough ER so that secreted and membrane proteins enter the secretory pathway.
confusions: The amino acid is attached to the tRNA's 3′ end by a specific synthetase; the ribosome does not check the amino acid, only the codon–anticodon match.

topics.name: Eukaryotic chromosome organization
know: Eukaryotic DNA is packaged with histone proteins: about 147 base pairs wrap around an octamer of histones to form a nucleosome, nucleosomes coil into a 30 nm fibre, and further looping condenses the chromatin into the chromosomes seen at mitosis. Supercoiling, the twisting of the helix on itself, compacts DNA and is managed by topoisomerases; bacterial chromosomes are negatively supercoiled.

Euchromatin is loosely packed, accessible, and transcribed; heterochromatin is tightly packed and largely silent, as in centromeres, telomeres, and the inactive X chromosome. Chemical marks on histones (acetylation opens chromatin, some methylations close it) and on DNA (methylation silences) switch regions between the two states.

Much of the genome is repetitive DNA (transposons, satellite repeats, gene families) rather than single-copy genes. Centromeres are the constricted regions where kinetochores assemble to attach spindle fibres; telomeres cap the ends, protect them from being treated as breaks, and shorten with each division unless telomerase restores them.
confusions: Histone acetylation generally activates transcription; DNA methylation generally represses it.

topics.name: Control of gene expression in prokaryotes: operons
know: Bacteria group related genes into operons transcribed as one mRNA from a shared promoter, with an operator between promoter and genes where a repressor can bind (Jacob and Monod's model). Control is mostly at the start of transcription.

Repression: the lac operon's repressor sits on the operator and blocks RNA polymerase until lactose (as allolactose) binds and releases it (an inducible operon). The trp operon's repressor binds the operator only when tryptophan, the end product, is attached to it, so the pathway shuts off when the product is plentiful (a repressible operon); attenuation adds fine control.

Positive control: the lac operon is fully active only when glucose is scarce, because low glucose raises cAMP, and cAMP bound to the catabolite activator protein (CAP) helps polymerase bind the weak promoter. So lac is strongly expressed only when lactose is present and glucose is absent; with both sugars present it runs at a low level.
confusions: The repressor is made constitutively by a separate gene (lacI); the operator is a DNA site, not a protein.

topics.name: Control of gene expression in eukaryotes
know: Eukaryotes regulate at every step. Transcription: RNA polymerase II needs general transcription factors at the promoter, and specific transcription factors bind enhancers and silencers, often far from the gene, looping DNA to activate or repress; combinations of factors give each cell type its pattern. Chromatin structure sets access: histone acetylation and DNA demethylation open genes, histone deacetylation and DNA methylation close them (epigenetic marks that can be inherited through cell division). Noncoding RNAs act too: microRNAs and small interfering RNAs pair with mRNAs to block translation or trigger degradation, and long noncoding RNAs such as Xist silence whole chromosomes.

Post-transcriptional control: alternative splicing of exons gives different proteins from one gene; capping, polyadenylation, nuclear export, and mRNA stability (controlled by 3′ untranslated region sequences and RNA-binding proteins) set how much protein a message yields. Translation is regulated by initiation factors; proteins are regulated after synthesis by modification and ubiquitin-tagged degradation. Gene amplification (extra copies) and gene duplication over evolution increase output and allow new functions.

Cancer is a failure of these controls. Oncogenes are mutated or overexpressed versions of genes that drive growth (growth factors, receptors, Ras, Myc); one activated copy suffices. Tumour suppressor genes (p53, Rb, BRCA1) normally restrain division or repair DNA; both copies must be lost. p53 halts the cycle or triggers apoptosis after DNA damage, and it is mutated in over half of human cancers.
confusions: Oncogenes act dominantly (gain of function); tumour suppressors act recessively at the cell level (loss of both copies, often one inherited mutation plus one somatic hit).

topics.name: Recombinant DNA and biotechnology
know: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific palindromic sites, leaving sticky or blunt ends; DNA ligase joins fragments with matching ends. Gene cloning inserts a fragment into a vector (a plasmid with an origin, a selectable marker such as antibiotic resistance, and a multiple cloning site) and transforms it into bacteria, which copy it; expression vectors add a promoter so the cloned gene is transcribed and translated. A genomic library holds fragments of a whole genome; a cDNA library holds reverse-transcribed mRNA, so it contains only expressed, intron-free sequences.

The polymerase chain reaction amplifies a target with two primers, a heat-stable polymerase, and cycles of denaturation, annealing, and extension, doubling the copies each cycle. Gel electrophoresis separates DNA by size (smaller fragments run farther); a Southern blot transfers DNA from a gel and probes it by hybridization (Northern for RNA, Western for protein with antibodies). Sanger sequencing reads chain-terminating fragments; next-generation methods sequence millions of fragments in parallel.

Gene expression is analysed with reverse-transcription PCR, microarrays, and RNA sequencing; gene function with knockouts, RNA interference, reporter genes, and CRISPR–Cas9 editing. Stem cells (embryonic, adult, induced pluripotent) can be guided into tissues. Applications: recombinant drugs such as insulin, vaccines, gene therapy (delivering a working gene, often by viral vector), forensic DNA profiling, genetically modified crops, and bioremediation. Safety and ethics: containment, off-target edits, germline editing, consent, privacy of genetic information, and equitable access.
confusions: cDNA lacks introns because it is copied from mature mRNA, which is why it is used to express human genes in bacteria, which cannot splice.

categories.name: Heredity and genetic diversity
categories.summary: How traits pass between generations and how variation arises: the evidence that DNA is the genetic material, Mendel's rules and their exceptions, meiosis, linkage and mutation, the analytic tools of genetics, and evolution.

topics.name: Evidence that DNA is the genetic material
know: Griffith (1928) found that a harmless strain of pneumococcus could be transformed into a deadly one by something in heat-killed deadly bacteria. Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty (1944) showed the transforming substance was DNA: destroying proteins or RNA left it active, destroying DNA abolished it.

Hershey and Chase (1952) labelled bacteriophage protein with radioactive sulfur and DNA with radioactive phosphorus; only the phosphorus entered the infected bacteria and appeared in new phage, so DNA, not protein, carried the instructions.

Chargaff's rules (A = T and G = C in every species) and Franklin and Wilkins's X-ray diffraction images gave Watson and Crick the data for the double helix (1953), whose complementary strands explained how genetic information could be copied.
confusions: Transformation here means uptake of DNA from the environment, not the cancer-biology sense of the word.

refs.label: OpenStax Biology 2e, 14.1 Historical Basis of Modern Understanding

topics.name: Mendelian concepts
know: A gene is a heritable unit at a fixed locus on a chromosome; alleles are its alternative versions, and a population may carry many (multiple alleles, as for ABO blood type). An individual with two identical alleles is homozygous, with two different ones heterozygous; the genotype is the allele combination, the phenotype the observable trait. The wild type is the common form in nature.

Mendel's laws: segregation (the two alleles separate into different gametes, so each gamete carries one) and independent assortment (genes on different chromosomes are inherited independently). With complete dominance the heterozygote looks like the dominant homozygote, so a monohybrid cross of heterozygotes gives a 3:1 phenotype ratio and a dihybrid cross 9:3:3:1. A recessive trait appears only in homozygotes and can skip generations.

Exceptions: incomplete dominance (the heterozygote is intermediate, pink snapdragons), codominance (both alleles show, AB blood), penetrance (the fraction of carriers who show the trait at all) and expressivity (how strongly it shows), leakage (gene flow between species through fertile hybrids), and hybrid viability (crosses between species may give sterile or inviable offspring). A gene pool is all the alleles in a population.
confusions: Dominant does not mean common or better: Huntington disease is dominant and rare. Incomplete dominance blends the phenotype; codominance shows both.

topics.name: Meiosis, linkage, recombination, sex-linked traits, and other factors affecting genetic variability
know: Meiosis makes haploid gametes from a diploid cell in two divisions after one round of DNA replication. In prophase I homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis) along the synaptonemal complex, forming a tetrad of four chromatids, and non-sister chromatids exchange segments (crossing over) at chiasmata; in metaphase I the pairs line up and assort independently; meiosis I separates homologues (reductional) and meiosis II separates sister chromatids like mitosis. Compared with mitosis, meiosis halves the chromosome number, involves pairing and crossing over, and produces four genetically different cells.

Genes on the same chromosome are linked and tend to be inherited together; a single crossover between them produces recombinant gametes, and the recombination frequency (up to 50%) grows with the distance between them, which is the basis of gene mapping. A double crossover between two loci restores the parental combination and so is undercounted. Variation also comes from independent assortment (2ⁿ combinations) and random fertilization.

Sex is determined by the X and Y chromosomes in humans (XY male; the SRY gene on the small, gene-poor Y triggers male development). X-linked recessive traits such as haemophilia and red–green colour blindness appear mostly in males, who have one X; carrier mothers pass them to half their sons. Mitochondrial (cytoplasmic) genes are inherited from the mother only.
confusions: Sister chromatids are identical copies; homologues are the maternal and paternal versions. Crossing over is between homologues' non-sister chromatids.

topics.name: Mutation and genetic drift
know: A mutation is a heritable change in DNA sequence, arising spontaneously from replication errors or induced by mutagens (radiation, chemicals, some viruses); many mutagens are also carcinogens, and nearly all carcinogens are mutagenic, because cancer begins with mutations in growth-control genes. Types: base substitution (point mutations, which may be silent, missense, or nonsense), insertion and deletion (frameshifts if not multiples of three), inversion, translocation between chromosomes, and mispairing of repeats. Errors in transcription or translation affect only that RNA or protein and are not inherited.

Most mutations are neutral or harmful; a few are advantageous and are the raw material of evolution. Inborn errors of metabolism are inherited enzyme defects (phenylketonuria, galactosemia, lysosomal storage diseases) that block a pathway so a substrate accumulates or a product is missing.

Genetic drift is random change in allele frequencies from sampling in small populations; it can fix or lose alleles regardless of fitness. It is strong after a bottleneck (a crash in numbers) or a founder event (a few individuals start a new population), which explains the high frequency of some disorders in isolated groups.
confusions: A mutation in a somatic cell can cause cancer but is not passed to offspring; only germline mutations are inherited.

topics.name: Analytic methods: Hardy–Weinberg, test crosses, gene mapping, and biometry
know: The Hardy–Weinberg principle: in a large, randomly mating population with no mutation, migration, or selection, allele frequencies do not change and genotype frequencies are p², 2pq, and q². It is the null model: a departure shows that some evolutionary force is acting. Given the frequency of a recessive phenotype (q²), you can find q, p, and the carrier frequency 2pq.

A test cross mates an individual of unknown genotype with a homozygous recessive; the offspring ratio reveals whether it was homozygous or heterozygous (a backcross mates a hybrid with a parent). Generations are labelled P (parental), F1 (first filial), and F2.

Gene mapping uses crossover frequencies: one percent recombination between two loci is one map unit (centimorgan), and distances add for nearby loci. Biometry applies statistics to inheritance: the chi-square test compares observed with expected ratios, the product rule multiplies probabilities of independent events, the sum rule adds mutually exclusive ones, and pedigrees track traits through families to infer the mode of inheritance.
confusions: q² is the frequency of the recessive phenotype, not of the recessive allele; take the square root first.

topics.name: Evolution: natural selection, speciation, and evolutionary time
know: Natural selection: individuals vary in heritable traits, more are born than survive, and those whose traits suit the environment leave more offspring, so the traits spread. Fitness is reproductive success relative to others, measured as the share of the next generation's gene pool, not strength or longevity. Selection acts by differential reproduction and can be directional, stabilizing, or disruptive; sexual selection acts on mating success. Group selection (traits favoured for the good of the group) is a weak force compared with selection on individuals and kin.

Speciation is the splitting of one species into two when gene flow stops: allopatric (geographic separation) or sympatric (within one area, for instance by polyploidy or habitat choice), followed by reproductive isolation. Related ideas: polymorphism (several forms coexisting), adaptation and specialization to a niche, inbreeding (mating among relatives, which raises homozygosity and exposes recessive defects), outbreeding (which restores heterozygosity), and bottlenecks (which cut variation and let drift act).

Evolutionary time can be read from the genome: mutations accumulate at a roughly steady rate, so sequence differences between species act as a molecular clock once the rate is calibrated against independently dated events such as fossils.
confusions: Evolution happens to populations over generations, not to individuals; an individual's acquired traits are not inherited.

categories.summary: How cells get and spend energy: the thermodynamics and ATP, the sugars themselves, glycolysis and its neighbours, the citric acid cycle, fat and protein metabolism, oxidative phosphorylation, and the hormones that coordinate it all.

topics.name: Principles of bioenergetics: free energy, ATP, and biological redox
know: A reaction proceeds in the direction that lowers free energy: ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q, and at equilibrium ΔG = 0 so ΔG° = −RT ln Keq (biochemists use ΔG°′ at pH 7). Spontaneous means ΔG < 0, not fast. Exothermic reactions release heat (ΔH < 0); endothermic absorb it, and either can be spontaneous depending on entropy and temperature (ΔG = ΔH − TΔS). Concentration matters through Q: by Le Châtelier's principle a cell can push a reaction with positive ΔG°′ forward by keeping reactants high and removing products, as glycolysis does.

ATP hydrolysis to ADP and Pi has ΔG°′ ≈ −30.5 kJ/mol (about −7.3 kcal/mol) and about −50 to −60 kJ/mol at cellular concentrations, because the products relieve charge repulsion, gain resonance stabilization, and are better solvated. Cells couple it to unfavourable reactions by phosphoryl group transfer, phosphorylating a substrate or protein, rather than by releasing heat; the ΔG°′ values of coupled reactions add, and compounds such as phosphoenolpyruvate and creatine phosphate have higher transfer potential than ATP.

Biological oxidation–reduction moves electrons in half-reactions ranked by standard reduction potential E°′; electrons flow from the more negative couple to the more positive, releasing ΔG°′ = −nFΔE°′. Soluble carriers NAD⁺ (accepts a hydride, two electrons and one proton) and NADP⁺ shuttle electrons between enzymes; flavoproteins carry FAD or FMN bound to the enzyme and can take electrons one or two at a time.
equations: \Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT\ln Q,\qquad \Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K_{eq}
confusions: ATP's phosphoanhydride bonds are not unusually strong; the energy comes from the products being more stable than ATP. ΔG°′ is fixed; ΔG depends on concentrations.

topics.name: Carbohydrates: structure, configuration, anomers, and glycosidic bonds
know: Monosaccharides are aldoses or ketoses with three to seven carbons (triose, pentose, hexose); glucose, galactose, and mannose are aldohexoses, fructose a ketohexose, ribose an aldopentose. In a Fischer projection the configuration of the stereocentre farthest from the carbonyl sets D or L; almost all natural sugars are D. Epimers differ at one stereocentre (glucose and galactose at C4, glucose and mannose at C2).

In water a hydroxyl adds to the sugar's own carbonyl to form a cyclic hemiacetal: a six-membered pyranose for glucose (the chair with all substituents equatorial in β-D-glucose) or a five-membered furanose for fructose and ribose. Ring closure creates the anomeric carbon: α has the new OH on the opposite side from the CH₂OH (down in a Haworth projection), β on the same side (up). Anomers interconvert through the open form (mutarotation), and the open aldehyde makes glucose a reducing sugar.

A glycosidic bond is an acetal between an anomeric carbon and another hydroxyl; it is hydrolysed by acid or by specific enzymes, not by base. Disaccharides: maltose (glucose α-1,4 glucose), lactose (galactose β-1,4 glucose), sucrose (glucose α-1 to fructose β-2, so both anomeric carbons are tied up and it is non-reducing). Polysaccharides: starch (amylose α-1,4; amylopectin with α-1,6 branches), glycogen (like amylopectin but more branched, in liver and muscle), cellulose (β-1,4, indigestible by humans), and chitin.
confusions: α/β describe the anomeric carbon; D/L describe the stereocentre farthest from the carbonyl. Lactase cuts a β bond, so lactose is digestible even though cellulose is not.

topics.name: Glycolysis, fermentation, gluconeogenesis, and the pentose phosphate pathway
know: Glycolysis, in the cytosol of every cell, converts one glucose to two pyruvate with a net gain of 2 ATP (4 made by substrate-level phosphorylation, 2 spent) and 2 NADH. The investment phase traps glucose (hexokinase; glucokinase in liver), isomerizes it, and commits it at phosphofructokinase-1, the rate-limiting step; the payoff phase splits fructose 1,6-bisphosphate (aldolase) into two triose phosphates that are oxidized (NADH) and yield ATP at phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase. Feeder pathways bring in other sugars: glycogen and starch are broken to glucose 1-phosphate or glucose, fructose and galactose enter after conversion.

Without oxygen, NADH must be reoxidized so glycolysis can continue: fermentation reduces pyruvate to lactate (muscle, red blood cells) or to ethanol and CO₂ (yeast), with no further ATP. With oxygen, pyruvate enters mitochondria for the citric acid cycle and respiration yields about 30–32 ATP per glucose in total (counting 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 per FADH₂; older texts, including OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology, count 3 and 2 and quote 36–38).

Gluconeogenesis, mainly in liver (and kidney), makes glucose from lactate, glycerol, and glucogenic amino acids by reversing glycolysis except at its three irreversible steps, which are bypassed by pyruvate carboxylase and PEP carboxykinase, fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase, and glucose 6-phosphatase; it costs about 6 ATP equivalents per glucose. The pentose phosphate pathway (cytosol) oxidizes glucose 6-phosphate, with glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase rate-limiting, to make NADPH for biosynthesis and antioxidant defence and ribose 5-phosphate for nucleotides; its non-oxidative phase interconverts sugar phosphates and returns carbons to glycolysis.
confusions: Fermentation makes no extra ATP; its job is to regenerate NAD⁺. Muscle lacks glucose 6-phosphatase, so its glycogen feeds only itself, while liver glycogen feeds the blood.

topics.name: Principles of metabolic regulation: glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, and glycogen
know: Metabolism runs at a dynamic steady state: concentrations of intermediates stay roughly constant while flux through a pathway changes. Control sits at irreversible, committed steps, which are regulated allosterically (within seconds), by covalent modification such as phosphorylation (minutes), and by hormones changing enzyme amounts (hours). Opposed pathways are reciprocally regulated so that both do not run at once (a futile cycle).

Glycolysis versus gluconeogenesis: phosphofructokinase-1 is activated by AMP and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate and inhibited by ATP and citrate, while fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase is inhibited by AMP and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate; pyruvate kinase is inhibited by ATP and alanine and, in liver, by glucagon-driven phosphorylation; hexokinase is inhibited by its product glucose 6-phosphate. Insulin raises fructose 2,6-bisphosphate and favours glycolysis; glucagon lowers it and favours gluconeogenesis.

Glycogen: glycogen synthase builds α-1,4 chains from UDP-glucose and a branching enzyme adds α-1,6 branches; glycogen phosphorylase removes glucose 1-phosphate from the ends and a debranching enzyme handles the branches. Phosphorylation (triggered by glucagon in liver and epinephrine in muscle through cAMP and protein kinase A) activates phosphorylase and inactivates synthase; insulin does the reverse through dephosphorylation. Allosteric signals add local control: AMP activates muscle phosphorylase, glucose 6-phosphate activates synthase, and glucose inhibits liver phosphorylase. Metabolic control analysis quantifies how much each enzyme controls flux; control is usually shared rather than held by one 'rate-limiting' enzyme.
confusions: Epinephrine mobilizes muscle glycogen for the muscle's own use; glucagon acts on liver (muscle lacks glucagon receptors) to raise blood glucose.

topics.name: Acetyl-CoA production and the citric acid cycle
know: Pyruvate enters the mitochondrial matrix and the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex oxidizes it to acetyl-CoA, CO₂, and NADH (using thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD, and NAD⁺); the complex is inhibited by its products acetyl-CoA and NADH and by ATP, and by phosphorylation when energy is plentiful. Acetyl-CoA also arrives from fatty acid oxidation and ketogenic amino acids.

The cycle: acetyl-CoA condenses with oxaloacetate to citrate (citrate synthase), which is isomerized to isocitrate and oxidatively decarboxylated twice (isocitrate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase) to succinyl-CoA; substrate-level phosphorylation gives GTP (or ATP) as succinate forms, then succinate dehydrogenase (complex II, FAD) gives fumarate, hydration gives malate, and malate dehydrogenase regenerates oxaloacetate. Per acetyl-CoA: 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP, 2 CO₂; the two carbons lost are not those that just entered.

Regulation: citrate synthase, isocitrate dehydrogenase, and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase are slowed by NADH and ATP and (for isocitrate dehydrogenase) sped by ADP; the cycle needs NAD⁺ regenerated by the electron transport chain, so it stops without oxygen. Per glucose, respiration yields about 30–32 ATP: 2 from glycolysis, 2 from the cycle, and the rest from oxidative phosphorylation of 10 NADH (about 2.5 ATP each) and 2 FADH₂ (about 1.5 each). Intermediates also feed biosynthesis (amino acids, heme, fatty acids via citrate), and anaplerotic reactions such as pyruvate carboxylase refill them.
confusions: The cycle uses no oxygen directly, yet it is aerobic because NAD⁺ and FAD are regenerated only by the chain that ends at oxygen.

topics.name: Metabolism of fatty acids and proteins
know: Fatty acids are long hydrocarbon chains with a carboxyl end, mostly even-numbered (16–18 carbons), saturated or with cis double bonds. Dietary fat is emulsified by bile salts and hydrolysed by pancreatic lipase in the small intestine, reassembled into triacylglycerols in the intestinal cells, and shipped in chylomicrons through lymph and blood; lipoprotein lipase on capillary walls releases fatty acids to tissues. In fasting, hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue (activated by glucagon and epinephrine, inhibited by insulin) frees fatty acids, which travel bound to albumin.

Oxidation: fatty acids are activated to acyl-CoA in the cytosol, carried into the mitochondrial matrix by the carnitine shuttle, and shortened by β-oxidation, each round removing two carbons as acetyl-CoA and yielding one FADH₂ and one NADH; palmitate (16 C) gives 8 acetyl-CoA in 7 rounds, about 106 ATP net. Unsaturated fatty acids need an isomerase and a reductase for their double bonds; odd-chain acids end in propionyl-CoA, which enters the cycle as succinyl-CoA. When acetyl-CoA exceeds the cycle's capacity (fasting, uncontrolled diabetes), the liver makes ketone bodies (acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate, acetone) that the brain and muscle can burn.

Anabolism: fatty acid synthesis runs in the cytosol from acetyl-CoA exported as citrate, with acetyl-CoA carboxylase (rate-limiting; activated by citrate and insulin, inhibited by glucagon and palmitoyl-CoA) making malonyl-CoA and fatty acid synthase adding two carbons per cycle using NADPH; the product is then esterified to glycerol. Lipids and polysaccharides are built without a template, by enzymes that add units in a defined order rather than by copying a sequence. Protein metabolism: amino acids are transaminated (pyridoxal phosphate) to keto acids, the nitrogen is removed by deamination of glutamate and disposed of as urea in the liver, and the carbon skeletons are glucogenic (enter as pyruvate or cycle intermediates), ketogenic (acetyl-CoA; leucine and lysine), or both.
confusions: β-oxidation and fatty acid synthesis are not reversals of each other: different enzymes, compartments (matrix versus cytosol), carriers (CoA versus acyl carrier protein), and cofactors (NAD⁺/FAD versus NADPH).

topics.name: Oxidative phosphorylation: the electron transport chain, chemiosmosis, and mitochondria
know: The electron transport chain in the inner mitochondrial membrane passes electrons from NADH (complex I) and FADH₂ (complex II and other flavoproteins) to ubiquinone, then through complex III, cytochrome c, and complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) to oxygen, forming water. Complexes I, III, and IV pump protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space; complex II does not, which is why FADH₂ yields less ATP. Carriers: NADH and NADPH (soluble, two-electron), flavoproteins (FMN/FAD), iron–sulfur centres and cytochromes (heme iron, one electron at a time), and lipid-soluble ubiquinone.

Chemiosmosis: the proton gradient plus the membrane potential form a proton-motive force; protons flow back through ATP synthase (F₀ channel, F₁ catalytic head) and turn its rotor to make ATP from ADP and Pi, which is exported in exchange for ADP. Cytosolic NADH from glycolysis enters by the malate–aspartate shuttle (as NADH) or the glycerol phosphate shuttle (as FADH₂). Uncouplers such as 2,4-dinitrophenol and the natural protein thermogenin let protons leak back, releasing the energy as heat instead of ATP; cyanide and carbon monoxide block complex IV, oligomycin blocks ATP synthase.

Regulation is by demand: the rate is set by ADP availability (respiratory control), so a resting cell with high ATP and low ADP slows the chain, which backs up NADH and slows the cycle too. Mitochondria have their own circular DNA and ribosomes and divide independently (evidence of endosymbiotic origin). Electrons that leak to oxygen form superoxide and other reactive oxygen species, which are detoxified by superoxide dismutase, catalase, and glutathione; oxidative stress damages lipids, proteins, and DNA. Mitochondria also launch apoptosis: when the outer membrane is permeabilized, cytochrome c leaks into the cytosol and activates caspases.
confusions: The chain itself makes no ATP; it builds the proton gradient, and ATP synthase spends it. Oxygen is consumed at complex IV, not at the synthase.

topics.name: Hormonal regulation and integration of metabolism
know: Hormones coordinate metabolism across tissues. Insulin (from pancreatic β cells after a meal) is a peptide hormone acting through a receptor tyrosine kinase: it drives glucose uptake into muscle and fat (GLUT4), glycogen and fat synthesis, and protein synthesis, and it suppresses gluconeogenesis and lipolysis. Glucagon (α cells, in fasting) acts through a G protein-coupled receptor and cAMP to raise blood glucose by glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis in liver and to release fatty acids from fat. Epinephrine adds the stress response (muscle glycogenolysis, lipolysis); cortisol raises gluconeogenesis and protein breakdown over hours; thyroid hormone sets the basal metabolic rate.

Tissue-specific metabolism: the liver buffers blood glucose (glycogen, gluconeogenesis, glucose 6-phosphatase), makes ketone bodies, and synthesizes lipoproteins and urea; skeletal muscle stores glycogen for its own use and burns fatty acids and ketones, releasing lactate and alanine; adipose tissue stores and releases fat; the brain depends on glucose and, after days of fasting, on ketone bodies; red blood cells use glycolysis only. Fed state: insulin stores fuel. Fasting: glucagon mobilizes glycogen, then gluconeogenesis and fat; after several days ketones spare protein.

Body mass reflects energy balance over time. Leptin from adipose tissue signals fat stores to the hypothalamus and lowers intake; ghrelin from the stomach raises it; insulin and gut peptides modulate both. Obesity (body mass index of 30 or more) usually involves leptin resistance and a defended set point rather than leptin deficiency, and it raises the risk of insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease.
confusions: Insulin and glucagon act on the same liver enzymes in opposite directions through phosphorylation state; muscle responds to epinephrine, not glucagon.

concepts.name: Assemblies of molecules, cells, and organs
concepts.summary: Foundational Concept 2 (AAMC): cells as organized assemblies. Membranes, organelles, and tissues; prokaryotes and viruses; and how cells divide, differentiate, and specialize.

categories.name: Assemblies of molecules, cells, and tissues
categories.summary: The cell as a structure: the plasma membrane and how things cross it, the organelles of eukaryotic cells, the cytoskeleton, and how cells join into epithelial and connective tissue.

topics.name: Plasma membrane: composition, fluid mosaic model, and membrane dynamics
know: The plasma membrane contains the cell and controls what enters and leaves. It is a bilayer of amphipathic lipids: phospholipids (glycerophospholipids with a phosphate head group, and sphingolipids) with their polar heads facing water and tails inward; cholesterol, a steroid, wedged between them; and glycolipids on the outer face. Waxes are not membrane components but related esters that waterproof surfaces.

The fluid mosaic model: proteins float in and on the lipid bilayer. Integral proteins span it (channels, carriers, receptors, pumps) with hydrophobic α-helices; peripheral proteins sit on either surface; carbohydrates attached to lipids and proteins form the glycocalyx used in recognition. The two leaflets differ in composition (asymmetry).

Membrane dynamics: lipids diffuse rapidly sideways but rarely flip between leaflets; fluidity rises with temperature and with unsaturated (kinked) fatty acids and falls with saturated ones, while cholesterol moderates it in both directions (stiffening a warm membrane, keeping a cold one from freezing). Membranes grow, fuse, and bud, which underlies vesicle traffic, endocytosis, and exocytosis.
confusions: Cholesterol makes membranes less fluid when warm and more fluid when cold; it is a buffer of fluidity, not simply a stiffener.

topics.name: Solute transport across membranes, membrane potential, receptors, and vesicle traffic
know: Thermodynamics: a solute moves spontaneously down its electrochemical gradient (concentration and, for ions, charge); moving it up the gradient costs energy. Osmosis is the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane toward the side with more solute; osmotic pressure is a colligative property (it depends on the number of dissolved particles, π = iMRT), so cells shrink in hypertonic and swell or burst in hypotonic solutions. Passive transport needs no energy: simple diffusion of small nonpolar molecules through the bilayer, and facilitated diffusion through channels (ion-selective pores, some gated) and carriers (which bind and flip, saturable, as GLUT transporters do for glucose).

Active transport uses energy to move solutes against their gradients: primary active transport spends ATP directly (the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pumps 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per ATP, keeping Na⁺ low and K⁺ high inside and helping set the membrane potential); secondary active transport couples a solute to the downhill flow of Na⁺ or H⁺ (symport of glucose with Na⁺ in the gut, antiport of Ca²⁺ against Na⁺). The resting membrane potential (about −70 mV in neurons, inside negative) arises mainly from K⁺ leaking out through open channels and from the pump; the Nernst equation gives each ion's equilibrium potential.

Membrane receptors bind extracellular ligands and change cell behaviour (ion-channel receptors, G protein-coupled receptors, receptor kinases). Bulk transport moves material in vesicles: endocytosis (phagocytosis of particles, pinocytosis of fluid, and receptor-mediated endocytosis of specific ligands such as LDL through clathrin-coated pits) and exocytosis (secretion by fusion of vesicles with the membrane), both requiring ATP.
confusions: Facilitated diffusion is passive even though it uses a protein; the test is whether the solute moves down its gradient. Tonicity depends on non-penetrating solutes only.

topics.name: Intercellular junctions: gap junctions, tight junctions, and desmosomes
know: Tight junctions seal neighbouring epithelial cells together near their apical surface so that nothing passes between them; they force solutes to cross through the cells (gut lining, blood–brain barrier, bladder) and keep apical and basolateral membrane proteins apart.

Desmosomes are rivet-like anchors: cadherin proteins link to intermediate filaments (keratin) inside each cell, giving mechanical strength to tissues under stress such as skin and heart muscle; hemidesmosomes anchor cells to the basement membrane.

Gap junctions are channels made of connexin proteins that join the cytoplasm of adjacent cells, letting ions and small molecules pass directly; they synchronize cardiac and smooth muscle and couple cells electrically and metabolically. Plant cells use plasmodesmata for the same purpose.
confusions: Tight junctions block passage between cells; gap junctions permit passage between cells; desmosomes only hold cells together.

topics.name: Membrane-bound organelles and the defining features of eukaryotic cells
know: Eukaryotic cells are defined by a membrane-bound nucleus, internal membrane-bound organelles that compartmentalize functions, and division by mitosis. The nucleus holds the chromosomes, separating transcription from translation; the nucleolus inside it assembles ribosomal subunits; the double-membraned nuclear envelope is pierced by nuclear pores that regulate traffic of RNA and proteins.

Mitochondria make most of the cell's ATP: a smooth outer membrane, an inner membrane folded into cristae that carries the electron transport chain and ATP synthase, and a matrix with the citric acid cycle enzymes; they have their own circular DNA and ribosomes and replicate by division. Lysosomes are acidic vesicles of hydrolytic enzymes that digest worn organelles and material taken in by endocytosis. Peroxisomes break down fatty acids and detoxify compounds, producing and then destroying hydrogen peroxide with catalase.

The endoplasmic reticulum is a network of membranes continuous with the nuclear envelope: the rough ER, studded with ribosomes, folds and modifies secreted and membrane proteins; the smooth ER makes lipids and steroids, detoxifies drugs, and stores calcium. The Golgi apparatus receives vesicles from the ER, modifies proteins (glycosylation), sorts them, and packages them into vesicles for secretion, the membrane, or lysosomes. Together these form the endomembrane system.
confusions: Mitochondria and the nucleus have double membranes; the ER is a single membrane folded into sheets and tubes (its lumen is one continuous space).

topics.name: The cytoskeleton: microfilaments, microtubules, intermediate filaments, cilia, flagella, and centrioles
know: The cytoskeleton supports the cell, holds organelles in place, and powers movement. Microfilaments are thin, flexible polymers of actin: they form the cell cortex, drive cell crawling and the contractile ring that pinches a dividing cell in two (cleavage), and with myosin produce contraction in muscle and elsewhere.

Microtubules are hollow tubes of α- and β-tubulin dimers with a dynamic plus end; they resist compression, form the tracks for kinesin and dynein transport and the mitotic spindle, and are nucleated at the microtubule-organizing centre (centrosome), which in animal cells contains a pair of centrioles (nine triplets of microtubules). Cilia and flagella are microtubule bundles in a 9 + 2 arrangement bent by dynein; cilia line the airways and oviducts, and a flagellum propels sperm. Drugs that disrupt microtubules (colchicine, taxanes, vinca alkaloids) stop mitosis.
Intermediate filaments (keratins, lamins, neurofilaments, vimentin) are rope-like and permanent; they give tensile strength, anchor desmosomes, and form the nuclear lamina.
confusions: Bacterial flagella are rotating protein filaments driven by a proton gradient; eukaryotic flagella are microtubule-based and bend. They share only the name.

topics.name: Tissues formed from eukaryotic cells: epithelial and connective tissue
know: Epithelial tissue covers surfaces and lines cavities and glands. Its cells are tightly packed, polarized (an apical surface facing the lumen or outside, a basal surface attached to a basement membrane), avascular, and quickly renewed. It is classified by layers (simple: one layer; stratified: several; pseudostratified) and by shape (squamous, cuboidal, columnar): simple squamous for exchange (alveoli, capillaries), simple columnar for absorption and secretion (gut), stratified squamous for protection (skin, oesophagus), transitional for stretch (bladder). Glands are epithelial: exocrine glands secrete through ducts, endocrine glands into blood.

Connective tissue binds, supports, and protects; it has few cells in a lot of extracellular matrix, which the cells secrete: ground substance plus fibres (collagen for strength, elastin for recoil, reticular fibres for scaffolding). Cell types include fibroblasts (make the matrix), adipocytes (fat), chondrocytes (cartilage), osteocytes (bone), and the blood cells; macrophages and mast cells patrol it.

Types: loose connective tissue (areolar, adipose, reticular), dense connective tissue (tendons, ligaments, dermis), cartilage (hyaline, elastic, fibrocartilage), bone, and blood (a connective tissue whose matrix is plasma). Muscle and nervous tissue are the other two primary tissue types.
confusions: Epithelium has no blood vessels of its own and is fed by diffusion from the connective tissue beneath; most connective tissue is well supplied, though cartilage has no vessels and tendons and ligaments few.

categories.name: Prokaryotes and viruses
categories.summary: Life without a nucleus, and the particles that borrow cells: cell theory, the structure, growth, and genetics of bacteria and archaea, and the structure and life cycles of viruses.

topics.name: Cell theory: history and impact
know: Hooke named cells from cork in 1665; Leeuwenhoek saw living microbes with his lenses; Schleiden (plants) and Schwann (animals) concluded in the 1830s that all organisms are made of cells; Virchow added in the 1850s that every cell comes from a pre-existing cell, which, with Pasteur's experiments against spontaneous generation, completed the theory.

Modern cell theory: all living things are made of one or more cells; the cell is the basic unit of structure and function; and cells arise only from division of existing cells. Later additions: cells carry hereditary information in DNA, have similar chemistry and metabolism, and energy flow occurs within them.

Impact: it unified biology across plants, animals, and microbes, made disease a problem of cells (cellular pathology, germ theory), and underlies modern cell biology, histology, and cancer biology. Viruses, which are not cells and cannot reproduce alone, sit outside the theory.
confusions: Cell theory says cells come from cells; it does not explain the origin of the first cell, which is a separate question.
