topics.name: Classification and structure of prokaryotic cells
know: Prokaryotes form two domains. Bacteria have peptidoglycan cell walls and ester-linked membrane lipids; Archaea have different walls (no peptidoglycan), ether-linked lipids, and transcription machinery closer to eukaryotes, and many live in extreme environments. Both lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, keep their circular chromosome in a nucleoid, use 70S ribosomes, and divide by binary fission rather than mitosis.

Bacteria are classified by shape: cocci (spheres, in pairs, chains, or clusters), bacilli (rods), and spirilla or spirochetes (spirals). The cell wall of peptidoglycan protects against osmotic lysis; Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan layer that retains the crystal violet stain, Gram-negative bacteria have a thin layer plus an outer membrane with lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin). Capsules, pili (attachment and conjugation), and endospores (dormant, heat-resistant forms) are found in some species.

Flagella are rigid helical filaments of flagellin rotated by a motor in the membrane that is powered by the proton-motive force, not ATP; reversing the motor changes swimming from a straight run to a tumble.
confusions: Prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles but not structure: they have a cytoskeleton, a nucleoid, and sometimes internal membranes for photosynthesis.

topics.name: Growth and physiology of prokaryotic cells
know: Bacteria reproduce by binary fission: the chromosome replicates from its single origin, the copies move apart, and the cell pinches in two, giving exponential growth (the population doubles each generation time, as short as 20 minutes). A batch culture passes through lag, exponential (log), stationary (nutrients exhausted, waste accumulates), and death phases.

Oxygen relationships: obligate aerobes need it, obligate anaerobes are killed by it, facultative anaerobes use it when available and ferment otherwise, and aerotolerant and microaerophilic organisms sit between. Lifestyles range from free-living to symbiotic (mutualists in the gut make vitamin K and digest fibre) and parasitic (pathogens). Chemotaxis: bacteria swim toward attractants and away from repellents by biasing the run-and-tumble pattern, lengthening runs when conditions improve.

Bacteria adapt genetically fast because of large populations, short generations, and horizontal gene transfer. Antibiotic resistance arises by mutation (altered targets, pumps that expel the drug, enzymes such as β-lactamase that destroy it) and spreads on plasmids; selection by antibiotic use enriches resistant strains.
confusions: Exponential growth is a phase, not a permanent state; in stationary phase division and death balance.

topics.name: Genetics of prokaryotic cells: plasmids, transformation, conjugation, and transposons
know: Besides the chromosome, bacteria carry plasmids, small circular DNA molecules that replicate independently and often carry genes for antibiotic resistance, toxins, or conjugation. Genes move between cells by three routes of horizontal transfer, and recombination then incorporates the new DNA into the chromosome.

Transformation: a competent cell takes up naked DNA from its surroundings (Griffith's pneumococci; used in the lab to insert plasmids). Conjugation: a donor carrying the F (fertility) plasmid builds a pilus to a recipient and transfers a copy of the plasmid, or, if F is integrated into the chromosome (an Hfr strain), part of the chromosome. Transduction: a bacteriophage carries bacterial DNA from one cell to another.

Transposons are mobile DNA segments that cut or copy themselves into new positions using a transposase, often carrying resistance genes between plasmids and chromosomes; they also exist in eukaryotic genomes, where they make up a large share of the DNA.
confusions: Conjugation is not sexual reproduction: no new cell is formed, and transfer is one-way from donor to recipient.

topics.name: Virus structure
know: A virus is a genome (DNA or RNA, single- or double-stranded, linear or circular) packed in a protein coat, the capsid, built from repeating capsomere subunits in helical or icosahedral form; some viruses add an envelope taken from the host membrane studded with viral glycoproteins used for attachment. Viruses have no ribosomes, no metabolism, and no organelles, so they cannot reproduce outside a host cell.

Size: most are about 20–250 nm (a few giant viruses are larger), far smaller than bacteria (roughly 0.5–5 µm) and eukaryotic cells (10–100 µm), so they pass through filters that trap bacteria and are seen only by electron microscopy.

A typical bacteriophage has an icosahedral head holding double-stranded DNA, a tail sheath that contracts to inject the genome, and tail fibres that recognize receptors on the bacterial surface. Classification uses genome type and replication strategy (the Baltimore classes), capsid shape, and the presence of an envelope.
confusions: Enveloped viruses are more fragile (soap and drying destroy the envelope) but better at hiding from immunity; naked viruses survive longer on surfaces.

topics.name: Viral life cycles, transduction, retroviruses, prions, and viroids
know: Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites that replicate only inside a specific host cell. The general cycle: attachment to a receptor on the host surface (which sets the host range), penetration (phage injection; animal viruses by endocytosis or envelope fusion), uncoating, replication of the genome and synthesis of viral proteins using the host's ribosomes, enzymes, and energy, self-assembly of new particles, and release by lysis (naked viruses) or budding (enveloped viruses, which take their envelope on the way out).

Phages follow a lytic cycle (replicate and burst the cell) or a lysogenic cycle (integrate as a prophage and replicate passively with the host until induced). Transduction: a phage accidentally packages host DNA and delivers it to the next cell, either random fragments (generalized) or genes next to the prophage site (specialized). Animal viruses can also persist as latent (herpes) or chronic infections.

Retroviruses such as HIV carry RNA and reverse transcriptase, which copies the RNA into DNA; integrase inserts that DNA into the host genome as a provirus, where it is transcribed into new genomes and mRNAs; HIV infects CD4 T cells and its reverse transcriptase is error-prone, driving rapid evolution. Subviral agents: viroids are small naked circular RNAs that infect plants without coding proteins; prions are misfolded proteins that convert normal copies to the misfolded form, causing transmissible spongiform encephalopathies such as Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease, and they contain no nucleic acid.
confusions: Reverse transcription violates the usual DNA → RNA direction but not the central dogma's core claim; it is why antiretroviral drugs can target an enzyme human cells lack.

categories.name: Cell division, differentiation, specialization
categories.summary: Making new cells and new kinds of cells: mitosis and the cell cycle, the signals for growth and death, gametes and reproduction, early embryonic development, and the mechanisms that specialize cells.

topics.name: Mitosis and the cell cycle
know: The cell cycle: G₁ (growth), S (DNA replication, giving each chromosome two sister chromatids joined at the centromere), G₂ (preparation), and M (mitosis plus cytokinesis); G₀ is a resting state outside the cycle in which many differentiated cells (neurons, mature muscle) stay permanently (growth arrest). Interphase is G₁ + S + G₂.

Mitosis: prophase (chromosomes condense, the spindle forms between the two centrosomes, each with a pair of centrioles and radiating asters), prometaphase (the nuclear envelope breaks down and spindle microtubules attach to the kinetochores at each centromere), metaphase (chromosomes line up on the equator), anaphase (sister chromatids separate and are pulled to opposite poles as kinetochore microtubules shorten and motor proteins act, while the poles move apart), telophase (chromosomes decondense and nuclear envelopes re-form), then cytokinesis by an actin–myosin contractile ring in animals or a cell plate in plants.

Control: checkpoints at G₁/S (cell size, nutrients, DNA damage; the restriction point past which the cycle is committed), G₂/M (replication complete, damage repaired), and the spindle checkpoint in metaphase (all kinetochores attached). Cyclins rise and fall and activate cyclin-dependent kinases that drive each transition; p53 halts the cycle after DNA damage and triggers apoptosis if repair fails, and Rb blocks entry to S phase until phosphorylated. Cancer cells lose these controls, divide without limit, ignore damage, and evade apoptosis.
confusions: Chromosome number is counted by centromeres: after S phase a human cell has 46 chromosomes with 92 chromatids; after anaphase each pole briefly has 46 single-chromatid chromosomes.

topics.name: Biosignaling: oncogenes and apoptosis
know: Growth signals reach the nucleus through pathways such as growth factor → receptor tyrosine kinase → Ras → MAP kinase cascade → transcription factors that start the cycle. Proto-oncogenes encode these components; a mutation that keeps one permanently on (constitutively active Ras, amplified Myc, overexpressed receptors) makes it an oncogene, and one such allele is enough to drive growth. Tumour suppressors such as p53 and Rb act as brakes and must lose both copies.

Apoptosis is programmed cell death: the cell shrinks, its DNA is cut into fragments, the membrane blebs, and the remains are packaged for phagocytes without inflammation, unlike necrosis, in which the cell swells and bursts. It is executed by caspases, proteases activated in a cascade.

Two routes: the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway, triggered by DNA damage, stress, or loss of survival signals, in which Bcl-2 family proteins control release of cytochrome c from mitochondria, which assembles the apoptosome and activates caspase-9; and the extrinsic pathway, in which death ligands (Fas ligand, TNF) bind surface receptors and activate caspase-8. Apoptosis sculpts the embryo (removing webbing between digits), deletes self-reactive lymphocytes, and removes damaged cells; its failure contributes to cancer, and its excess to neurodegeneration.
confusions: Apoptosis is tidy and silent; necrosis spills contents and inflames. A cell with mutant p53 may survive DNA damage it should have died from.

topics.name: Gametogenesis, ovum and sperm, and the reproductive sequence
know: Gametogenesis is meiosis plus maturation. Spermatogenesis, in the seminiferous tubules from puberty on, continuously turns spermatogonia into sperm, each primary spermatocyte yielding four haploid sperm (one cycle takes about 64 days), supported by Sertoli cells and driven by testosterone from Leydig cells. Oogenesis begins before birth: oogonia enter meiosis I and arrest in prophase I as primary oocytes; from puberty, one completes meiosis I each cycle to give a secondary oocyte (arrested in metaphase II) and a polar body, and meiosis II finishes only if a sperm enters, giving one ovum and more polar bodies.

Sperm are small, mobile, and numerous: a head with condensed DNA and an acrosome of enzymes, a midpiece packed with mitochondria, and a flagellum. The ovum is large and immobile, with cytoplasm, organelles, and stored nutrients. Each gamete contributes one haploid set of nuclear DNA; the ovum also supplies nearly all the cytoplasm, the mitochondria (hence maternal inheritance of mitochondrial DNA), and the first developmental signals, while the sperm supplies the centriole.

Reproductive sequence: fertilization in the ampulla of the uterine tube within about a day of ovulation; the zygote divides as it travels and implants in the endometrium about six to seven days later; the embryo develops the placenta and organs over the first eight weeks and grows as a fetus until birth (parturition) at about 38 weeks after fertilization, driven by oxytocin and prostaglandins; lactation follows under prolactin and oxytocin.
confusions: A woman is born with all her primary oocytes; a man makes new sperm throughout life. The egg released at ovulation has not finished meiosis.

topics.name: Embryogenesis: fertilization, cleavage, blastula, gastrulation, germ layers, and neurulation
know: Fertilization: the sperm penetrates the corona radiata, the acrosome reaction digests a path through the zona pellucida, membranes fuse, and the egg blocks further sperm (the fast electrical block and the slower cortical reaction that hardens the zona); the egg completes meiosis II and the pronuclei combine. Cleavage follows: rapid mitotic divisions without growth produce ever smaller cells, a solid morula, and then a hollow blastula (in mammals a blastocyst with an outer trophoblast that becomes the placenta and an inner cell mass that becomes the embryo).

Gastrulation is the first cell movements: cells migrate inward (in mammals through the primitive streak) to form three germ layers. Ectoderm gives the epidermis, hair, nails, lens, and the whole nervous system; mesoderm gives muscle, bone, cartilage, dermis, blood and vessels, heart, kidneys, and gonads; endoderm gives the lining of the gut and respiratory tract and the liver, pancreas, thyroid, and bladder lining.

Neurulation: the notochord (mesoderm) induces the overlying ectoderm to thicken into the neural plate, fold, and close into the neural tube, which becomes the brain and spinal cord; failure to close causes spina bifida or anencephaly, and folate reduces the risk. Neural crest cells break away from the tube's margins and migrate to form the peripheral nervous system, melanocytes, the adrenal medulla, and parts of the face. Development depends on environment–gene interaction: teratogens (alcohol, thalidomide, rubella, some drugs) disrupt it most during organ formation in weeks 3–8.
confusions: The nervous system is ectoderm, not mesoderm, even though it lies deep; the adrenal cortex is mesoderm while the adrenal medulla is neural crest.

topics.name: Mechanisms of development: specialization, communication, stem cells, regeneration, and aging
know: All cells of an embryo carry the same genome; they become different by expressing different genes. Determination commits a cell to a fate before any visible change; differentiation then produces the specialized structure and proteins of a tissue type (muscle, neuron, epithelium). Both are driven by gene regulation: transcription factors switched on by position and signals, with master regulators such as the Hox genes setting the body plan along the head-to-tail axis.

Cells communicate during development by induction: one tissue secretes signalling molecules (morphogens such as Sonic hedgehog or Wnt) whose concentration gradient tells neighbouring cells what to become; cell–cell contact and adhesion molecules guide cell migration, as when neural crest cells travel to their targets. Programmed cell death removes cells that are no longer needed (interdigital webbing, excess neurons).

Stem cells divide to renew themselves and to produce differentiated cells. Totipotent cells (the zygote and early blastomeres) can form everything including placenta; pluripotent cells (inner cell mass, embryonic stem cells, and induced pluripotent stem cells reprogrammed from adult cells) can form any body tissue; multipotent adult stem cells (hematopoietic, intestinal) replace cells of one lineage. Regeneration varies across species: planarians regrow whole bodies and salamanders regrow limbs, while humans regenerate liver and blood but not neurons or limbs. Senescence is the loss of division capacity with age, linked to telomere shortening (the Hayflick limit), accumulated DNA damage, and oxidative stress; aging reflects these cellular changes plus declining repair.
confusions: Differentiation usually does not change the DNA sequence; the differences are in expression. The exceptions, such as antibody gene rearrangement in lymphocytes, are rare.

concepts.name: Organ systems and homeostasis
concepts.summary: Foundational Concept 3 (AAMC): the body as an integrated whole. The nervous and endocrine systems that coordinate it and the organ systems that carry out its functions.

categories.name: Nervous and endocrine systems
categories.summary: The two coordinating systems: how the nervous system is organized and how neurons signal, the receptors and ion channels that carry signals into cells, the steroid and terpene lipids, and the glands, hormones, and feedback loops of the endocrine system.

topics.name: Nervous system: organization, reflexes, autonomic control, and integration with the endocrine system
know: The nervous system controls and integrates the other systems and lets the body adapt to the outside world. The central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) processes information; the peripheral nervous system carries it in through sensory (afferent) neurons and out through motor (efferent) neurons to effectors (muscles, glands). The motor division splits into the somatic system (skeletal muscle, voluntary) and the autonomic system (smooth and cardiac muscle, glands, involuntary).

The sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions act antagonistically on most organs: sympathetic activity (noradrenaline at the target, adrenaline from the adrenal medulla) prepares for action, raising heart rate and blood pressure, dilating airways and pupils, and slowing digestion; parasympathetic activity (acetylcholine, largely via the vagus nerve) slows the heart and promotes digestion and other rest functions. Most organs receive both and the balance sets their state.

A reflex is an automatic response through a reflex arc: receptor → sensory neuron → (interneuron in the spinal cord) → motor neuron → effector, a negative feedback loop that acts before the brain is involved; supraspinal circuits in the brainstem and cortex modulate, suppress, or build on spinal reflexes. The nervous and endocrine systems are coupled through the hypothalamus, which turns neural signals into hormone release and is itself regulated by feedback from circulating hormones.
confusions: Autonomic does not mean unregulated: the hypothalamus and brainstem set autonomic tone continuously.

topics.name: The nerve cell: structure, resting and action potentials, synapses, summation, and glia
know: A neuron has a cell body (nucleus and organelles), dendrites that receive input, and an axon that carries action potentials to terminals. Myelin, made by Schwann cells in the periphery and oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system, insulates the axon, and the signal jumps between the gaps, the nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction), which makes conduction much faster. Other glia: astrocytes (support, blood–brain barrier, ion balance), microglia (immune defence), ependymal cells (cerebrospinal fluid).

The resting potential (about −70 mV, inside negative) results from the Na⁺/K⁺ pump (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in) and from K⁺ leaking out down its gradient. An action potential is all-or-none: if a stimulus depolarizes the membrane to threshold (about −55 mV), voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ rushes in (depolarization to about +30 mV), they inactivate, voltage-gated K⁺ channels open and K⁺ flows out (repolarization, then a brief hyperpolarization), and the pump restores the gradients. The refractory period keeps it travelling one way; stimulus strength is coded by firing frequency, not amplitude.

At a chemical synapse the action potential opens Ca²⁺ channels, vesicles release neurotransmitter, and it binds receptors on the postsynaptic cell to produce an excitatory (depolarizing) or inhibitory (hyperpolarizing) postsynaptic potential; it is then removed by reuptake or degradation (acetylcholinesterase). Graded potentials add by spatial summation (many synapses at once) and temporal summation (rapid repeats at one synapse); the neuron fires if the sum at the axon hillock reaches threshold. Electrical synapses use gap junctions for fast, direct coupling.
confusions: The pump does not cause the action potential; it maintains the gradients the channels use. Hyperpolarization makes a neuron harder to fire; inhibition is not 'no signal'.

topics.name: Biosignaling: gated ion channels, receptor enzymes, G protein-coupled receptors, and the Nernst equation
know: Gated ion channels open in response to a signal and let a specific ion flow down its gradient. Voltage-gated channels (Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺) respond to membrane potential and generate action potentials; ligand-gated channels (the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, GABA-A, glutamate receptors) open when a transmitter binds and produce fast postsynaptic potentials; mechanically gated channels respond to stretch or pressure in sensory cells.

Receptor enzymes have a ligand-binding domain outside and a catalytic domain inside; receptor tyrosine kinases (insulin, growth factor receptors) dimerize on binding, phosphorylate each other, and recruit signalling proteins (Ras, PI3 kinase). G protein-coupled receptors are seven-pass membrane proteins that, on binding a ligand, activate a trimeric G protein by exchanging GDP for GTP; the α subunit then regulates effectors such as adenylyl cyclase (cAMP → protein kinase A) or phospholipase C (IP₃ releases Ca²⁺, diacylglycerol activates protein kinase C), amplifying the signal through second messengers. Epinephrine, glucagon, and most neurotransmitter and hormone receptors use this route.

The electrochemistry behind membrane potentials is that of a concentration cell: the same ion at different concentrations on two sides of a membrane gives a potential, with the Nernst equation giving the equilibrium potential at which diffusion and electrical forces balance. For K⁺ it is about −90 mV and for Na⁺ about +60 mV in a typical cell; the resting potential sits near the K⁺ value because the membrane is most permeable to K⁺, and opening Na⁺ channels drives it toward the Na⁺ value. Electrons do not flow across the membrane; ions carry the current.
confusions: A ligand-gated channel changes the membrane potential in milliseconds; a G protein-coupled receptor acts over seconds through second messengers; a receptor kinase changes gene expression over minutes to hours.

topics.name: Lipids as signals: steroids, terpenes, and terpenoids
know: Steroids share a core of four fused rings, three six-membered and one five-membered. Cholesterol is the parent: it modulates membrane fluidity and is converted in the adrenal cortex and gonads to the steroid hormones (cortisol and aldosterone, testosterone, estradiol, progesterone), in the liver to bile acids, and in the skin, with sunlight, to vitamin D. Being lipid-soluble, steroid hormones travel on carrier proteins, cross membranes, and act on intracellular receptors that regulate transcription.

Terpenes are built from five-carbon isoprene units joined head to tail: monoterpenes (10 C, menthol, limonene), sesquiterpenes (15 C), diterpenes (20 C, including vitamin A's retinol, which the body makes by splitting the tetraterpene β-carotene), triterpenes (30 C, squalene, the precursor of cholesterol), and the polyprenyl tail of ubiquinone. Terpenoids are terpenes with added oxygen functions.

Isoprene units come from the mevalonate pathway (acetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA → mevalonate → isopentenyl pyrophosphate); HMG-CoA reductase is the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis and the target of statins.
confusions: Cholesterol is not a fat (no glycerol or ester) and is essential; the problem is its transport in LDL, not the molecule itself.

topics.name: Endocrine system: glands, hormones, and neuroendocrine links
know: The endocrine system provides specific chemical control at the level of cells, tissues, and organs. An endocrine gland releases its product, a hormone, into the blood (an exocrine gland secretes into a duct); a hormone is a signalling molecule carried by blood to distant target cells that have receptors for it. Hormones are peptides and proteins (insulin, glucagon, growth hormone, pituitary hormones), amino acid derivatives (thyroid hormones, catecholamines, melatonin), or steroids (cortisol, aldosterone, sex hormones).

Major glands and products: the hypothalamus (releasing and inhibiting hormones to the anterior pituitary; oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone, stored and released by the posterior pituitary); the anterior pituitary (growth hormone, prolactin, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH); the thyroid (T₃ and T₄ for metabolic rate; calcitonin lowers blood calcium); the parathyroids (parathyroid hormone raises calcium); the adrenal cortex (cortisol, aldosterone, androgens) and medulla (adrenaline, noradrenaline); the pancreatic islets (insulin, glucagon); the gonads (testosterone; estrogen and progesterone); the pineal gland (melatonin); and the thymus, kidney (erythropoietin, renin), heart, gut, and adipose tissue (leptin) as secondary endocrine organs.

Neuroendocrinology: the hypothalamus is the interface, turning neural input into hormone output through the hypothalamic–pituitary portal vessels and the neurosecretory cells of the posterior pituitary; the adrenal medulla is modified sympathetic nervous tissue. Tropic hormones from the pituitary control other glands in axes (hypothalamus → pituitary → thyroid, adrenal cortex, gonads).
confusions: The posterior pituitary stores hormones made in the hypothalamus; the anterior pituitary makes its own, under hypothalamic releasing hormones.

topics.name: Endocrine system: mechanisms of hormone action, transport, specificity, second messengers, and feedback
know: Hormones act only on cells with matching receptors, which is what gives them specificity despite travelling everywhere in the blood. Water-soluble hormones (peptides, catecholamines) cannot cross membranes: they bind surface receptors and act through second messengers (cAMP, IP₃ and Ca²⁺, cGMP) that activate kinases and change enzyme activity within seconds to minutes; the cascade amplifies one hormone molecule into many product molecules. Lipid-soluble hormones (steroids, thyroid hormone) travel bound to plasma proteins, diffuse into cells, bind intracellular receptors, and alter transcription over hours.

Transport: hormones reach targets only through the blood supply, so delivery depends on circulation and on carrier proteins that extend a steroid's half-life; peptide hormones are cleared in minutes. The response of a target depends on receptor number (up- and down-regulation) and on the presence of other hormones (permissive, synergistic, and antagonistic effects, as with insulin and glucagon).

Control is by feedback: in negative feedback the hormone or its effect suppresses further release (thyroid hormone inhibits TSH and TRH; cortisol inhibits ACTH and CRH; calcium inhibits parathyroid hormone), stabilizing the level; in rarer positive feedback the effect amplifies release until an endpoint (oxytocin in labour, the LH surge before ovulation). The nervous system sets many loops through the hypothalamus and can override them under stress.
confusions: Second messengers are inside the cell; the hormone (first messenger) stays outside. A hormone's effect differs between tissues because the receptors and the downstream machinery differ.

categories.name: Main organ systems
categories.summary: The body's working systems and how they fit together: respiratory, circulatory, lymphatic, immune, digestive, excretory, reproductive, muscular, skeletal, and skin.

topics.name: Respiratory system
know: Functions: gas exchange (O₂ in, CO₂ out), pH control through CO₂, thermoregulation and water loss through evaporation from the airways (panting in animals), and protection by filtering particles with nasal hairs and the mucus–cilia escalator that sweeps trapped material up to be swallowed. Air passes through the nose and pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, and bronchioles to the alveoli, tiny thin-walled sacs wrapped in capillaries whose enormous total surface area allows exchange.

Breathing: inhalation is active, the diaphragm contracts and flattens and the external intercostals lift the ribs, enlarging the chest so that intrapulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric and air flows in; quiet exhalation is passive elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall. Surface tension in the fluid lining the alveoli would collapse them, and the pleural fluid keeps the lungs coupled to the chest; surfactant lowers the surface tension, which is why premature infants lacking it struggle to breathe.

Alveolar exchange is by diffusion down partial-pressure gradients: alveolar P_O₂ (about 100 mmHg) exceeds venous blood's (about 40), and venous P_CO₂ (about 45) exceeds alveolar (about 40); Henry's law relates the amount of each gas dissolving to its partial pressure. Breathing is regulated by the medulla and pons, driven chiefly by central chemoreceptors sensing the pH change that CO₂ produces in cerebrospinal fluid and, less, by peripheral chemoreceptors sensing low O₂; hyperventilation blows off CO₂ and raises pH (respiratory alkalosis), hypoventilation does the reverse.
confusions: The main drive to breathe is CO₂ (through pH), not low oxygen; oxygen becomes the driver only when it is very low.

topics.name: Circulatory system: heart, vessels, blood, gas transport, and clotting
know: The circulatory system carries oxygen, nutrients, hormones, ions, and fluid, removes wastes, moves heat (dilating skin vessels sheds it, constricting them conserves it), and defends the body. The four-chambered heart keeps two circuits separate: the right side pumps deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary circulation to the lungs; the left side pumps oxygenated blood through the systemic circulation. Valves (tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral, aortic) keep flow one way; the sinoatrial node sets the rhythm. Blood pressure is reported as systolic (contraction) over diastolic (relaxation), about 120/80 mmHg.

Arteries are thick-walled and elastic and carry blood away from the heart under high pressure; arterioles have muscular walls whose constriction is the main source of peripheral resistance and controls where blood goes; capillaries are one endothelial cell thick, the site where gases, nutrients, wastes, and heat exchange by diffusion and where fluid filters out and is partly reabsorbed; venules and veins are thin-walled, low-pressure, high-volume reservoirs with valves and the help of skeletal muscle to return blood. Endothelial cells line every vessel and release factors that control vessel tone and clotting.

Blood is plasma (water, proteins such as albumin and clotting factors, electrolytes, nutrients, hormones) plus cells: red cells made in bone marrow under erythropoietin and destroyed after about 120 days in the spleen and liver, white cells, and platelets. Plasma volume is regulated by the kidneys through antidiuretic hormone and aldosterone. Clotting: platelets plug a damaged vessel and a cascade of plasma factors ends in thrombin converting fibrinogen to fibrin, which meshes the clot; vitamin K and calcium are needed. Oxygen travels bound to hemoglobin in red cells (hematocrit is the red-cell fraction, about 45%); hemoglobin's sigmoidal binding curve shifts right (lower affinity, more unloading) with higher CO₂, lower pH, higher temperature, and 2,3-BPG. CO₂ is carried mostly as bicarbonate (via carbonic anhydrase in red cells), some bound to hemoglobin, and a little dissolved; the heart and vessels are regulated by autonomic nerves and by hormones such as adrenaline, angiotensin II, and antidiuretic hormone.
confusions: Arteries carry blood away from the heart regardless of oxygen content: the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood. The Bohr shift helps active tissue: acid and CO₂ make hemoglobin release oxygen.

topics.name: Lymphatic system
know: The lymphatic system is a one-way network of blind-ended lymphatic capillaries, collecting vessels with valves, lymph nodes, and the thoracic and right lymphatic ducts that empty into the veins near the heart. Lymph is the fluid it carries, moved by skeletal muscle contraction and breathing rather than a pump.

Functions: it returns to the blood the fluid and protein that filter out of capillaries each day (about three litres), keeping tissue fluid balanced (blocked lymphatics cause swelling, lymphedema); it absorbs dietary fats as chylomicrons through the lacteals of the intestinal villi and delivers them to the blood; and it is part of the immune system: lymph nodes filter lymph and house lymphocytes and macrophages, and lymphoid organs (bone marrow, thymus, spleen, tonsils) produce and mature lymphocytes.
Because lymph flows through nodes before returning to the blood, infection and cancer cells spread along it, which is why nodes swell in infection and are examined for metastasis.
confusions: Lymph is not a separate fluid; it is interstitial fluid once it has entered a lymphatic vessel.

topics.name: Immune system: innate and adaptive immunity
know: Innate (nonspecific) immunity is present from birth and responds the same way to any invader: barriers (skin, mucus, stomach acid), phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages, dendritic cells) that engulf microbes, natural killer cells that kill infected and tumour cells, complement proteins, inflammation, fever, and interferons. Adaptive (specific) immunity is learned, targets a particular antigen, and remembers it: B lymphocytes (from bone marrow) make antibodies (humoral immunity); T lymphocytes (matured in the thymus) include helper T cells that coordinate the response and cytotoxic T cells that kill infected cells (cell-mediated immunity).

Tissues: bone marrow (where all blood cells arise and B cells mature), thymus (T-cell maturation and deletion of self-reactive clones), spleen (filters blood, mounts responses to blood-borne antigens, recycles red cells), and lymph nodes (filter lymph, where antigen-presenting cells meet lymphocytes). An antigen is any molecule recognized by a receptor; an antibody is a Y-shaped immunoglobulin whose two variable arms bind one antigen with high specificity. Antigen presentation: cells display peptide fragments on major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules; MHC class I on all nucleated cells shows internal peptides to cytotoxic T cells, MHC class II on antigen-presenting cells shows ingested material to helper T cells.

Clonal selection: each lymphocyte carries one receptor specificity; the antigen selects the matching clone, which proliferates into effector cells (plasma cells secrete antibody) and long-lived memory cells that make the second response faster and stronger (the basis of vaccination). Antibodies neutralize, agglutinate, opsonize for phagocytosis, and activate complement. Tolerance to self is learned by deleting or silencing self-reactive clones; when it fails, autoimmune diseases (type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus) result; MHC differences also cause transplant rejection.
confusions: Helper T cells do not kill; they direct. Cytotoxic T cells kill infected body cells; antibodies act on pathogens outside cells.

topics.name: Digestive system
know: Ingestion: saliva lubricates food and begins starch digestion with amylase; the tongue and pharynx form a bolus that the oesophagus moves to the stomach by peristalsis, waves of smooth-muscle contraction that drive the whole tract. The stomach stores and churns food into chyme; its gastric juice has hydrochloric acid (pH about 2) from parietal cells, which kills microbes and unfolds proteins, pepsinogen from chief cells, activated to pepsin to begin protein digestion, and mucus and bicarbonate from the lining that protect the stomach from digesting itself; it has a fundus, body, and antrum ending at the pyloric sphincter.

The liver sits above the gut and receives nutrient-rich blood from it through the hepatic portal vein; it makes bile, regulates blood glucose (storing glycogen, releasing glucose, making it from other molecules), synthesizes plasma proteins, and detoxifies drugs and ammonia (to urea). Bile, stored and concentrated in the gall bladder and released into the duodenum, contains bile salts that emulsify fats so lipase can work and bile pigments for excretion. The pancreas secretes digestive enzymes (amylase, lipase, trypsin and chymotrypsin as inactive zymogens, nucleases) and bicarbonate through the pancreatic duct into the duodenum, where the bicarbonate neutralizes stomach acid.

The small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum) finishes digestion with pancreatic and brush-border enzymes and absorbs nearly all nutrients and most water through villi and microvilli, which hugely expand its surface; sugars and amino acids enter the blood, fats the lymph. The large intestine (caecum, colon, rectum) absorbs water and electrolytes and houses bacteria that ferment fibre and make vitamin K; feces are stored in the rectum and expelled through the anal sphincters. Control: hormones (gastrin stimulates acid secretion; secretin triggers pancreatic bicarbonate; cholecystokinin triggers enzyme release and gall-bladder contraction and slows the stomach), and the enteric nervous system, a local network that coordinates motility and secretion with parasympathetic stimulation and sympathetic inhibition.
confusions: Most absorption happens in the small intestine, not the stomach (which absorbs little besides alcohol and some drugs). Bile emulsifies fat; it contains no enzymes.

topics.name: Excretory system: the kidney and urine formation
know: The kidneys keep the internal environment stable: they regulate blood pressure and volume (through sodium and water handling and the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system), osmolarity (osmoregulation), acid–base balance (excreting H⁺ and regenerating bicarbonate), and they remove soluble nitrogenous waste as urea along with drugs and excess ions. Each kidney has an outer cortex and inner medulla; urine collects in the renal pelvis and passes down the ureter to the bladder, where it is stored until the sphincters relax and it leaves through the urethra.

The nephron is the working unit (about a million per kidney): blood is filtered in the glomerulus, a capillary tuft inside Bowman's capsule, by pressure, so water and small solutes but not cells or proteins enter the tubule. The proximal tubule reabsorbs most of the filtrate, essentially all glucose and amino acids, most sodium, bicarbonate, and water, and secretes H⁺, drugs, and organic acids. The loop of Henle, dipping into the medulla, creates a concentration gradient as a counter-current multiplier: the descending limb lets water out, the ascending limb pumps salt out and is impermeable to water, so the medullary interstitium becomes very salty. The distal tubule fine-tunes sodium, potassium, calcium, and pH under aldosterone and parathyroid hormone; the collecting duct, running back through the salty medulla, reabsorbs water when antidiuretic hormone inserts aquaporins, concentrating the urine.

Urine formation is therefore filtration, reabsorption, and secretion; the glomerular filtration rate (about 125 mL/min, 180 L/day, nearly all reabsorbed) is held steady by autoregulation. Osmoregulation adjusts final urine from dilute (no ADH) to concentrated (high ADH); aldosterone raises sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. The bladder's smooth muscle contracts under parasympathetic control, the internal sphincter is involuntary and the external sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary control.
confusions: ADH controls water reabsorption, aldosterone controls sodium; water follows sodium in the proximal tubule but needs ADH in the collecting duct. Glucose appears in urine only when filtered load exceeds the transporters' capacity (as in diabetes).

topics.name: Reproductive system: structures and hormonal control
know: Male: the testes (gonads) make sperm in the seminiferous tubules and testosterone in Leydig cells; sperm mature in the epididymis, travel through the vas deferens, and mix with fluid from the seminal vesicles, prostate, and bulbourethral glands to form semen, which leaves through the urethra of the penis. Female: the ovaries (gonads) release an oocyte each cycle into the uterine (fallopian) tube, where fertilization occurs; the uterus with its endometrial lining supports the embryo, the cervix opens into the vagina, and the external genitalia include the labia and clitoris. The female gonads are internal and the gametes are produced cyclically rather than continuously.

Hormonal control: gonadotropin-releasing hormone from the hypothalamus drives FSH and LH from the anterior pituitary. In males, LH stimulates testosterone and FSH with testosterone sustains spermatogenesis; testosterone drives male development, secondary sex characteristics, and libido, with negative feedback (and inhibin on FSH). In females, FSH grows follicles that secrete estrogen; rising estrogen triggers an LH surge that causes ovulation at mid-cycle (about day 14 of 28); the ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum, secreting progesterone and estrogen that thicken the endometrium; if no pregnancy occurs, the corpus luteum degenerates, hormone levels fall, and the lining is shed (menstruation). Estrogen directs female sexual development.

In pregnancy, human chorionic gonadotropin from the embryo maintains the corpus luteum until the placenta takes over progesterone and estrogen production; parturition is driven by positive feedback of oxytocin with prostaglandins; lactation depends on prolactin for milk production and oxytocin for let-down, both released through neural reflexes from suckling. Puberty, the cycle, and sexual behaviour are integrated with the nervous system through the hypothalamus.
confusions: The LH surge causes ovulation; progesterone dominates the second half of the cycle. Menstruation is caused by the fall in progesterone, not its rise.

topics.name: Muscle system and the muscle cell: types, sarcomere, contraction, control, and fatigue
know: Muscle supports and moves the body, helps return venous blood (the skeletal-muscle pump), and generates heat (shivering). Three types: skeletal (striated, multinucleate, voluntary, attached to bone), cardiac (striated, branched cells joined by intercalated discs with gap junctions, involuntary, self-exciting), and smooth (unstriated spindle cells, involuntary, in vessels and hollow organs). Skeletal fibres are slow-twitch (red: many mitochondria and myoglobin, oxidative, fatigue-resistant) or fast-twitch (white: glycolytic, powerful, fatigue quickly); cardiac and smooth muscle contract more slowly than skeletal.

A skeletal fibre is packed with myofibrils made of repeating sarcomeres: thick myosin filaments in the A band, thin actin filaments anchored at Z lines in the I band, the H zone where only myosin lies, and the M line at the centre. Sliding filament model: myosin heads bind actin, pull (power stroke, releasing ADP and Pi), release when ATP binds, and re-cock as ATP is hydrolysed, so the filaments slide and the sarcomere shortens while the filaments keep their length. Tropomyosin covers the myosin-binding sites on actin until calcium binds troponin and moves it aside.

Control: a motor neuron releases acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction (motor end plate), the fibre's action potential runs along the membrane and into the T-tubules, which trigger the sarcoplasmic reticulum to release Ca²⁺; contraction ends when Ca²⁺ is pumped back. A motor neuron and its fibres form a motor unit, and force is graded by recruiting units and raising firing rate. Cardiac contraction is triggered by Ca²⁺ entering from outside plus release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and is modulated, not initiated, by sympathetic (faster, stronger) and parasympathetic (slower) nerves; smooth muscle is involuntary and autonomic. Oxygen debt: during hard work muscle uses creatine phosphate and anaerobic glycolysis, accumulating lactate; the extra oxygen consumed afterward restores creatine phosphate and clears lactate, and fatigue is now thought to reflect ion shifts, phosphate build-up, and depleted glycogen more than lactate itself (older texts blame lactic acid).
confusions: ATP is needed to release myosin from actin, which is why rigor mortis sets in when ATP runs out. The H zone and I band shorten during contraction; the A band does not.

topics.name: Skeletal system: bone, cartilage, joints, and endocrine control
know: The skeleton gives rigidity and support, protects organs (skull, rib cage), anchors muscles for movement, stores calcium and phosphate, and houses the marrow that makes blood. Vertebrates have an endoskeleton of living bone that grows with the body, unlike the external exoskeleton of arthropods that must be moulted. Bones are classified as long (limbs; a shaft of compact bone around a marrow cavity with spongy bone at the ends), short, flat, and irregular.

Bone is a connective tissue whose matrix is collagen fibres hardened by calcium phosphate crystals (hydroxyapatite): collagen resists tension, mineral resists compression. Cells: osteoblasts build matrix, osteocytes maintain it from within their lacunae, and osteoclasts dissolve it; bone is continually remodelled, and it heals and strengthens in response to load. Cartilage (chondrocytes in a firm, flexible, avascular matrix) covers joint surfaces, forms the nose, ears, and intervertebral discs, and is the template for most bones in development (endochondral ossification). Ligaments join bone to bone; tendons join muscle to bone.

Joints: fibrous (skull sutures, immovable), cartilaginous (between vertebrae, slightly movable), and synovial (hinge, ball-and-socket, pivot, and others, freely movable, with a fluid-filled capsule). Endocrine control of bone and calcium: parathyroid hormone raises blood calcium by stimulating osteoclasts, kidney reabsorption, and vitamin D activation; calcitonin lowers it; vitamin D promotes intestinal absorption; growth hormone and thyroid hormone drive growth, and estrogen and testosterone close the growth plates at puberty and protect bone mass, which is why bone loss accelerates after menopause.
confusions: Osteoblasts build and osteoclasts clear; parathyroid hormone's net effect is to raise blood calcium by taking it from bone.

topics.name: Skin system
know: Skin has two layers resting on a fatty hypodermis: the epidermis, a stratified squamous epithelium whose keratinocytes are born at the base and die as they move up into a tough, water-resistant layer of keratin, with melanocytes making pigment and Langerhans cells for immunity; the dermis, connective tissue with blood vessels, nerves, hair follicles, and glands; beneath them the hypodermis, a fat layer that insulates and cushions, is strictly not part of the skin. The keratin and lipids of the outer epidermis make the skin nearly impermeable to water, which prevents dehydration (and so supports osmoregulation).

Thermoregulation: sweat glands in the dermis secrete watery sweat whose evaporation cools; arterioles in the dermis dilate to shed heat and constrict to keep it; the fat layer insulates; and erector muscles raise hairs (goosebumps), which traps air in furred animals. These responses are run by the hypothalamus through sympathetic nerves and are modified by hormones (adrenaline, thyroid hormone).

Protection: the keratinized surface, nails, calluses, and hair resist abrasion, and the intact epidermis, its acidic surface, and its immune cells block microbes; melanin absorbs ultraviolet light. Skin also makes vitamin D under sunlight and carries receptors for touch, pressure, temperature, and pain.
confusions: Sweat cools only when it evaporates; in humid air it drips off without cooling. Vasodilation of skin vessels is a heat-loss response, not a warming one.

skills.name: Knowledge of Scientific Concepts and Principles
skills.what: Do you know the concept and can you recognize it in a new setting? These questions test recall and understanding of structures, pathways, and relationships: which enzyme, which organelle, which hormone, which germ layer.
skills.example: A question might describe a cell that cannot produce ATP by oxidative phosphorylation and ask which structure is most likely defective, expecting you to recognize the inner mitochondrial membrane.

skills.name: Scientific Reasoning and Problem-solving
skills.what: Can you use the concept to work something out? These questions ask you to predict the effect of a mutation, a drug, or a hormone change, trace a pathway forward or backward, or apply a genetic rule to a pedigree.
skills.example: Given that a drug blocks the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, a question might ask what happens to the resting membrane potential over time, expecting you to reason that it decays toward zero as the gradients run down.

skills.name: Reasoning about the Design and Execution of Research
skills.what: Do you understand how the experiment in the passage was done and what it can show? These questions ask about controls, variables, the purpose of a step, sources of error, and whether a conclusion follows.
skills.example: After a passage describing a knockout-mouse experiment, a question might ask why the researchers included wild-type littermates, expecting you to identify them as the control that shares genetic background and environment.

skills.name: Data-based and Statistical Reasoning
skills.what: Can you read the data and judge what it supports? These questions ask you to interpret a gel, a growth curve, a kinetics plot, or a table, find a trend, and decide whether a difference is meaningful.
skills.example: Given a Lineweaver–Burk plot with and without an inhibitor, a question might ask which type of inhibition the data show, expecting you to compare the intercepts.

research_methods.name: Study designs in biology
know: Controlled experiments manipulate one variable at a time with everything else held constant; in biology the comparison is often a wild-type or vehicle-treated control, a sham surgery, or an untreated culture. Genetic tools (knockouts, knockdowns, overexpression, rescue by adding the gene back) test whether a gene is necessary and sufficient for a phenotype.

Observational and epidemiological designs (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional) show association, not cause; model organisms (E. coli, yeast, flies, worms, zebrafish, mice) trade relevance for control, and results may not transfer to humans.

research_methods.name: Variables and controls
know: Independent variable: what the researcher changes. Dependent variable: what is measured. Controlled variables: held constant. A confounding variable changes with the treatment and could explain the result. A negative control should show no effect (buffer alone, a scrambled sequence); a positive control proves the assay can detect an effect (a known activator).
Blinding and randomization apply to animals and samples as much as to people: cages, plates, and the order of measurement should be randomized and the scorer blinded.

research_methods.name: Measurement: reliability, validity, and error
know: Reliability is reproducibility (replicates agree); validity is whether the assay measures what it claims (an antibody that cross-reacts gives a reliable but invalid signal). Random error scatters measurements and shrinks with replication; systematic error shifts them all one way (a miscalibrated pipette) and does not.

Biological replicates (different animals or cultures) capture biological variation; technical replicates (the same sample measured again) capture only measurement noise, and treating them as independent inflates significance.

research_methods.name: Sampling and bias
know: Random sampling makes a sample representative; convenience samples (one strain, one sex, one age) limit generalization. Survivorship and selection bias arise when the cells, animals, or patients that remain in a study differ from those that dropped out.
Sample size sets precision: small groups give wide confidence intervals and miss real effects (low power) or produce chance 'significant' results.

research_methods.name: Correlation and causation
know: A correlation between two measurements (gene expression and tumour size, say) does not show which causes the other or whether a third factor drives both; a manipulation with a proper control is needed for cause.
A dose–response relationship, consistency across models, temporal order (cause before effect), and a known mechanism strengthen a causal argument.

research_methods.name: Descriptive statistics
know: Mean, median, and mode locate the centre; standard deviation describes spread; the standard error of the mean (SD ÷ √n) describes how precisely the mean is known and shrinks with sample size. In a normal distribution about 68% of values lie within one SD and about 95% within two.
Skewed data (cell counts, viral loads) are often log-transformed or summarized by the median.

research_methods.name: Reading figures
know: Check the axes and units, whether a scale is linear or logarithmic (bacterial growth and dilutions are usually log), what the bars show (mean or median), and what the error bars are (SD, SEM, or confidence interval). On a gel, size runs from large at the top to small at the bottom, and band intensity tracks amount.
Survival curves, dose–response curves, and kinetics plots each have standard shapes; a shift to the right on a dose–response curve means less potency, a lower plateau means less efficacy.

research_methods.name: Significance and uncertainty
know: A p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme as the one observed if there were really no effect; p < 0.05 is the usual threshold for statistical significance. A 95% confidence interval that excludes zero (or a ratio of 1) is significant at that level. Type I error is a false positive, Type II a false negative; power rises with sample size and effect size.
Significance is not importance: report the effect size. Multiple comparisons inflate false positives unless corrected.

research_methods.name: Research ethics
know: Human studies need informed consent, institutional review board approval, confidentiality, and a favourable balance of benefit to risk; vulnerable groups get extra protection. Animal studies need justification, the fewest animals that give a valid answer, minimization of pain and distress, and oversight by an animal care committee.
Data must be reported as obtained, with conflicts of interest declared; genetic and biobank data raise privacy and consent issues for relatives as well as participants.

math_toolkit.name: Genetics arithmetic
know: Punnett squares give offspring ratios; for two independent genes multiply the single-gene probabilities (product rule) and add probabilities of mutually exclusive outcomes (sum rule). Hardy–Weinberg: if the recessive phenotype frequency is q², take the square root for q, then p = 1 − q and carriers are 2pq.
Recombination frequency in percent equals map distance in centimorgans for nearby genes; it cannot exceed 50%.
math_toolkit.example: If 1 in 2,500 newborns has a recessive disease, q² = 0.0004, q = 0.02, p ≈ 0.98, and the carrier frequency 2pq ≈ 0.039, about 1 in 25.

math_toolkit.name: Exponential growth and dilution
know: A doubling population follows N = N₀ × 2ⁿ after n generations; the number of generations in time t is t divided by the generation time. Serial dilutions multiply: three 1:10 dilutions give 1:1000, so a count of 50 colonies from 0.1 mL of the final dilution means 50 × 1000 × 10 = 5 × 10⁵ cells per mL of the original.
On a semi-log plot exponential growth is a straight line; the slope gives the growth rate.
math_toolkit.example: A culture with a 30-minute doubling time grows 2⁸ = 256-fold in four hours.

math_toolkit.name: Ratios, percentages, and rates
know: Percent change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100. Rates (filtration, flow, reaction velocity) are amounts per time; compare them by ratio. Relative values on a graph (fold change) are read against the control set to 1.
Keep units: µg to mg divides by 1,000; mL to L divides by 1,000; a 2 mM solution is 2 mmol per litre.
math_toolkit.example: If the control enzyme rate is 20 µmol/min and the treated rate is 15 µmol/min, activity fell 25%, to 0.75 of control.

math_toolkit.name: Logs and pH
know: pH = −log[H⁺]; each pH unit is a tenfold change in [H⁺]. log 2 ≈ 0.3, log 3 ≈ 0.48, log 5 ≈ 0.7. For [H⁺] = a × 10⁻ⁿ, pH = n − log a. Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([base]/[acid]), so at pH = pKa the two forms are equal, and one unit away the ratio is 10:1.
Half-lives: after n half-lives, 1/2ⁿ remains; 10% remaining is a little more than three half-lives.
math_toolkit.example: At pH 7.4 with a pKa of 6.1, log(ratio) = 1.3, so bicarbonate to carbonic acid is about 20:1.

math_toolkit.name: Reading a kinetics or binding plot
know: On a Michaelis–Menten curve, Vmax is the plateau and Km is the [S] at half of it. On a Lineweaver–Burk plot the y-intercept is 1/Vmax and the x-intercept is −1/Km; a competitive inhibitor shares the y-intercept, a noncompetitive one shares the x-intercept.
A sigmoidal binding curve means cooperativity; a right shift means lower affinity (higher P₅₀ or Kd).
math_toolkit.example: If Vmax is 100 units and the rate at 2 mM substrate is 50 units, Km is 2 mM; at 6 mM the rate is 100 × 6/(2 + 6) = 75 units.

cars.attribution: Organized according to the AAMC's What's on the MCAT Exam? outline. Descriptions are our own. See the official outline for the authoritative list.

glance.summary: CARS is a reading section with no content to memorize: nine passages (AAMC's published structure) of about 500–600 words from the humanities and social sciences, each followed by five to seven questions that ask what the passage says, how its argument is built, and what follows if its ideas are pushed somewhere new. The passage and the question stem supply all you need; the section assumes no prior coursework, and outside knowledge can mislead.
glance.scores_note: Scores in this app are percent correct. They are not MCAT scaled scores (118–132), which only AAMC's equating can produce.

cars.no_outside_knowledge: There is no content outline for CARS. You are not expected to know anything about the passage's subject, and an answer that depends on something the passage did not say is wrong even when the fact is true. Treat each passage as a closed world.

passage_types.name: Humanities
passage_types.what: Writing that argues about ideas, works, and values. The author often has a stance and a voice; the tone may be reflective, playful, or combative, and a common shape is claim, example, qualification. Read for the author's opinion and how far it is pressed.

passage_types.name: Social sciences
passage_types.what: Writing that explains or interprets how people and societies behave, often with evidence, studies, or historical accounts. The tone tends toward reporting: a question, evidence or findings, competing explanations, and a conclusion, often in that order. Read for what is claimed, what supports it, and where the author hedges.

skill_areas.name: Foundations of Comprehension
skill_areas.what: Understanding what the passage says: its main idea, the role a sentence or paragraph plays, what a word or phrase means where it is used, and what the author implies without stating. The scope is local: a sentence and its neighbours, or the passage's overall point.
asks: The main idea or central thesis of the passage.
What a word, phrase, or image means in its context (a familiar word used in an unusual sense).
Why the author included a particular example, sentence, or paragraph.
What the author implies by a tone, a comparison, or a transition.
skill_areas.example: A passage about a composer calls one symphony 'an argument in sound'; a question asks what the phrase most nearly means as used, and the answer must come from how the surrounding sentences describe the work, not from any general sense of 'argument'.

skill_areas.name: Reasoning Within the Text
skill_areas.what: Putting distant parts of the passage together: inferring the author's purpose, position, assumptions, or bias from the whole, and judging how well the argument is built, whether the evidence supports the claim, whether a generalization is justified, whether a cited source is credible, and whether two parts of the passage conflict. Your own opinion of the author's conclusion is beside the point.
asks: What the author's attitude toward a subject is, judged from the whole passage.
Which assumption the argument depends on.
Which claim the passage supports best, or least.
Where the passage is inconsistent, or which of its claims rests on the least evidence.
skill_areas.example: An author praises a reform in two paragraphs and in a third notes the data behind it came from the reformers themselves; a question asks what this detail suggests about the author's confidence, and the answer draws on the passage's own hedging rather than on the reader's view of the reform.

skill_areas.name: Reasoning Beyond the Text
skill_areas.what: Taking the passage somewhere it did not go: applying its ideas to a new situation, picking the option whose parts relate to each other the way two things in the passage do, or deciding how a new fact introduced by the question would affect the author's argument (support it, weaken it, require a change). Only the passage and the new information count.
asks: How the author would most likely respond to a new case or claim.
Which of several situations is most analogous to one described in the passage.
Whether a new finding strengthens, weakens, or is irrelevant to the argument.
Which added statement would change the author's conclusion least, or most.
skill_areas.example: A passage argues that a craft tradition survived because it adapted its tools without changing its goals; a question describes a dance school that changed its goals to keep its tools and asks what the author would predict, and the answer applies the passage's own principle to the new case.

wrong_answer_patterns.name: Too extreme
wrong_answer_patterns.what: Uses absolute words (always, never, only, all, proves) where the passage was measured. Authors in CARS passages often qualify their claims; an option stronger than the passage is wrong even when it points the right way.
wrong_answer_patterns.spot: Compare the option's strength with the author's own language; look for 'some', 'often', 'may' in the passage.

wrong_answer_patterns.name: Out of scope
wrong_answer_patterns.what: Brings in a topic, group, or time period the passage never addresses, or answers a broader question than the one asked.
wrong_answer_patterns.spot: Ask whether the passage gives any basis for the option; if you would need to assume something about a subject it never mentions, drop it.

wrong_answer_patterns.name: Outside knowledge
wrong_answer_patterns.what: States something true in the world (or that you believe) but not supported by, or contrary to, the passage. The question is about the passage's argument, not reality.
wrong_answer_patterns.spot: If an option feels right because you know the topic, check that the passage actually says it.

wrong_answer_patterns.name: True but irrelevant
wrong_answer_patterns.what: Restates something the passage does say, but it does not answer the question asked (a detail offered as a main idea, a cause offered as a consequence).
wrong_answer_patterns.spot: Re-read the question stem; confirm the option addresses that precise task, not just the passage.

wrong_answer_patterns.name: Reversed relationship
wrong_answer_patterns.what: Swaps cause and effect, or attributes to the author a view the author reports in order to reject it.
wrong_answer_patterns.spot: Track who holds each view in the passage and which direction each relationship runs.

wrong_answer_patterns.name: Half right
wrong_answer_patterns.what: Two clauses joined together, one supported and one not; the unsupported half makes the whole option wrong.
wrong_answer_patterns.spot: Check every clause separately, especially after 'and' or 'because'.

wrong_answer_patterns.name: Distorted detail
wrong_answer_patterns.what: Takes real words from the passage and bends their meaning slightly (a different degree, a different subject, a different time).
wrong_answer_patterns.spot: An option that echoes the passage's wording deserves as much scrutiny as any other; verify the meaning, not the words.

approaches.name: Read for the argument, not the facts
approaches.what: On a first pass, aim to be able to state in a sentence what the author is claiming and how they feel about it. Track the structure: where a claim is made, where an example supports it, where a concession or counterargument appears, and whether the ending resolves, qualifies, or calls for more. Details can be found again; the shape of the argument is much harder to reconstruct on the fly.

approaches.name: Mark the signals
approaches.what: Words such as 'however', 'although', 'for example', 'therefore', and 'some argue' tell you what a sentence is doing. Noting them (mentally or with the highlighter) can make 'why did the author include this' and 'what does the author believe' questions quicker to answer.

approaches.name: Predict before you look
approaches.what: After reading a question, form your own short answer from the passage before reading the options. Then eliminate options that contradict your prediction, are too extreme, or go beyond the passage. Many people find this blunts the pull of well-written wrong answers.

approaches.name: Go back to the text when a question points to a place
approaches.what: For questions about a specific claim, paragraph, or word, re-read that part and its neighbours. A paragraph number in the question is a pointer worth using. Answering from memory of a passage read five minutes ago is a common source of errors.

approaches.name: Hold outside knowledge at arm's length
approaches.what: If you know the subject, use that only to read faster, never to pick an answer. Ask of every option: could someone who knew nothing about this topic justify it from the passage alone?

approaches.name: Manage the clock as a choice, not a crisis
approaches.what: Nine passages in 90 minutes is about ten minutes each. Some people do passages in order; some skim all nine first and start with the most comfortable; some skip a hard passage and return. Try each approach in practice and keep the one that gives you the best score, not the one that feels fastest. Many find it better to mark a question and move on than to stall on it.

approaches.name: Review by category
approaches.what: When you miss a question, name the pattern (too extreme, out of scope, outside knowledge, misread the question) and the skill area. Patterns repeat; naming them shows you what to practise.

chem_phys.attribution: Organized according to the AAMC's What's on the MCAT Exam? outline. Descriptions are our own. See the official outline for the authoritative list.

glance.summary: This section asks you to apply general chemistry, physics, organic chemistry, and biochemistry to how the body works: tissues and organs treated as mechanical, electrical, and chemical systems. Most questions hang off a passage describing an experiment, a device, or a physiological situation, and they reward reasoning from the data more than recall.
glance.math: Arithmetic without a calculator: scientific notation, ratios and percentages, exponents and logarithms (pH, decibels), unit conversion, estimation, basic trigonometry and vectors, and solving simple simultaneous equations. No calculus.
glance.scores_note: Scores in this app are percent correct. They are not MCAT scaled scores (118–132), which only AAMC's equating can produce.

concepts.name: Physical processes in living systems
concepts.summary: Foundational Concept 4 (AAMC): the physical principles that living systems obey. Motion and forces, fluids and gases, electricity and circuits, light and sound, and atomic structure, each applied to the body.

categories.name: Motion, forces, work, energy, equilibrium
categories.summary: Classical mechanics as it shows up in living systems: describing motion, the forces behind it, the energy bookkeeping, and when things balance.

topics.name: Units, dimensions, and vectors
know: SI base units you will use: metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol). Everything else is built from them, and checking that both sides of an equation carry the same units catches most algebra mistakes.
A scalar has size only (mass, speed, energy); a vector has size and direction (displacement, velocity, acceleration, force). Vectors add head-to-tail, or by adding x- and y-components separately.
Resolve a vector of magnitude A at angle θ from the x-axis into A cos θ and A sin θ; recover its magnitude with the Pythagorean theorem.
equations: A_x = A\cos\theta,\quad A_y = A\sin\theta,\quad |\vec A| = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}
confusions: Two vectors of equal magnitude in opposite directions add to zero; two equal vectors at right angles add to √2 times the magnitude, not twice it.

refs.label: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 1.2 Physical Quantities and Units
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 3.3 Vector Addition and Subtraction: Analytical Methods

topics.name: Speed, velocity, and acceleration
know: Average velocity is displacement over time (a vector); average speed is distance over time (a scalar). Instantaneous velocity is the slope of a position–time graph; acceleration is the slope of a velocity–time graph, and the area under a velocity–time graph is displacement.

With constant acceleration, four equations cover every problem (the subscript 0 marks the starting value). Free fall near Earth's surface is the special case a = g ≈ 9.8 m/s² downward, with air resistance ignored.
Projectile motion separates into constant horizontal velocity and vertically accelerated motion that share the same time.
equations: x = x_0 + v_0 t + \tfrac12 a t^2
confusions: An object thrown upward has zero velocity at its peak but its acceleration is still g. Velocity and acceleration can point in opposite directions (slowing down).

refs.label: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 2.3 Time, Velocity, and Speed
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 2.5 Motion Equations for Constant Acceleration
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 3.4 Projectile Motion
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 2.8 Graphical Analysis of One-Dimensional Motion

topics.name: Newton's laws of motion
know: First law: with no net force, velocity stays constant (inertia; mass measures it). Second law: net force equals mass times acceleration, applied separately along each axis. Third law: forces come in pairs of equal magnitude and opposite direction acting on two different bodies, so they never cancel on one body.

Weight is the gravitational force mg, which is not the same thing as mass. The normal force is whatever perpendicular contact force the surface must supply, not automatically mg (on an incline it is mg cos θ).
Free-body diagrams: draw only the forces acting on the chosen body, then sum components along convenient axes.
confusions: Motion does not require a net force; a change in motion does. Tension in a massless rope is the same at both ends.

refs.label: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 4.2 Newton's First Law of Motion: Inertia
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 4.3 Newton's Second Law of Motion
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 4.4 Newton's Third Law of Motion
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 4.5 Normal, Tension, and Other Examples of Forces

topics.name: Friction
know: Static friction adjusts to prevent sliding, up to a maximum of μs·N; kinetic friction has the fixed value μk·N once sliding starts, and μk is usually smaller than μs.

Friction opposes relative sliding between the surfaces, so it can point in the direction an object moves (it is what pushes a walking foot forward). It depends on the normal force, not on the contact area.
On an incline the normal force is N = mg cos θ, so an object starts to slide when tan θ exceeds μs.
confusions: Use μs·N only at the point of impending motion. Below that, static friction equals whatever is needed to balance the other forces.

refs.label: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 5.1 Friction

topics.name: Center of mass
know: The center of mass is the mass-weighted average position of a system. Gravity acts as if applied there, and an object balances when it is supported under it.
For point masses, each coordinate is Σ mᵢxᵢ / Σ mᵢ. Uniform symmetric objects have it at their geometric centre, which can lie outside the material (a ring, a boomerang).
Stability: an object tips when the vertical line through its center of mass falls outside its base of support, so a lower center of mass and a wider base both increase stability.
confusions: The center of mass of a system moves as if all external forces acted on it there, whatever the parts do internally.

topics.name: Equilibrium and torque
know: Equilibrium needs both the net force and the net torque to be zero. Torque is force times lever arm (the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the force's line of action), τ = rF sin θ, where θ is the angle between r and the force, with counterclockwise usually taken as positive.
You may choose any pivot. Picking it where an unknown force acts removes that force from the torque equation.
Most joints act as third-class levers (effort between fulcrum and load), so muscles exert forces much larger than the load they lift, over a shorter distance.
confusions: A force whose line of action passes through the pivot produces no torque, however large it is.

OpenStax College Physics 2e, 9.2 The Second Condition for Equilibrium

topics.name: Work, the work–energy theorem, and mechanical advantage
know: Work is the component of force along the displacement times the distance, W = Fd cos θ, in joules (N·m). A force perpendicular to the motion (normal force, centripetal force) does no work; work is negative when the force opposes the displacement, as friction does.
Work–energy theorem: the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy.
Simple machines (levers, ramps, pulleys) trade force for distance. Mechanical advantage is output force over input force, but output work can never exceed input work; efficiency is W_out / W_in.

A conservative force's work depends only on the endpoints (gravity, ideal springs), so it can be stored as potential energy. Friction is nonconservative: its work depends on the path and is lost as heat.
confusions: Carrying a bag horizontally at constant speed does zero work on it in the physics sense (force up, displacement sideways), however tiring it feels.

topics.name: Kinetic and potential energy, conservation, and power
know: Kinetic energy is ½mv². Gravitational potential energy is mgh relative to a chosen reference height; spring potential energy is ½kx² for a stretch or compression x of a spring with constant k.
When only conservative forces do work, KE + PE stays constant. With friction or other nonconservative forces, the total changes by the work they do: KE₁ + PE₁ + W_nc = KE₂ + PE₂.
Power is the rate of doing work or transferring energy, in watts (J/s): P = W/t, or P = Fv for a force along a constant velocity. 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
confusions: Doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy (and the stopping distance at a fixed braking force) while only doubling momentum.

topics.name: Periodic motion and waves
know: Period T is the time per cycle; frequency f = 1/T in hertz. Amplitude is the maximum displacement from equilibrium. Phase says where in its cycle an oscillation is: two oscillators in phase move together, 180° out of phase move oppositely.

Simple harmonic motion happens when the restoring force is proportional to displacement (Hooke's law, F = −kx). Mass on a spring: T = 2π√(m/k), independent of amplitude. Simple pendulum: T = 2π√(L/g), independent of mass (for small swings).

Transverse waves (a string, light) oscillate perpendicular to the direction of travel; longitudinal waves (sound) oscillate along it. For any wave v = fλ: the medium sets the speed, the source sets the frequency, and the wavelength adjusts.
confusions: A stiffer spring (bigger k) means a shorter period; a heavier mass means a longer one. A pendulum's period does not depend on the bob's mass.
