categories.name: Fluids and gas exchange
categories.summary: How liquids and gases behave at rest and in motion, and how that physics runs the circulation and the lungs.

topics.name: Density, specific gravity, and buoyancy
know: Density ρ = m/V. Water is 1.00 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³. Specific gravity is density relative to water, so it has no units: an SG of 1.05 means 1.05 g/cm³.

Archimedes' principle: the buoyant force equals the weight of fluid displaced, F_b = ρ_fluid·V_submerged·g. A floating object has a submerged fraction equal to ρ_object/ρ_fluid; it sinks if it is denser than the fluid.
Apparent weight in a fluid = true weight − buoyant force, which is how specific gravity is measured by weighing something in air and then in water.
confusions: The buoyant force depends on the displaced volume and the fluid's density, not on the object's density or its depth (for an incompressible fluid).

refs.label: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 11.2 Density
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 11.7 Archimedes' Principle

topics.name: Hydrostatic pressure and Pascal's law
know: Pressure is force per area (Pa = N/m²); 1 atm = 101.3 kPa = 760 mmHg = 760 torr. In a fluid at rest, pressure rises with depth, P = P₀ + ρgh, and depends only on depth and density, not on the container's shape.
Gauge pressure is pressure above atmospheric (P_absolute = P_gauge + P_atm). Blood pressures and tyre pressures are gauge pressures.

Pascal's law: squeeze an enclosed fluid anywhere and the same extra pressure appears everywhere inside it, with nothing lost on the way. A hydraulic lift therefore multiplies force in the ratio of piston areas, F₂/F₁ = A₂/A₁, while the large piston moves a proportionally shorter distance (work is conserved).
confusions: ρgh needs SI units: for water, each 10 m of depth adds about 98 kPa, roughly 1 atm. A 760 mm column of mercury balances 1 atm because mercury is 13.6 times denser than water.

refs.label: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 11.4 Variation of Pressure with Depth in a Fluid
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 11.5 Pascal's Principle
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 11.6 Gauge Pressure, Absolute Pressure, and Pressure Measurement

topics.name: Viscosity and Poiseuille flow
know: Viscosity η (Pa·s) is a fluid's internal resistance to flow; an ideal fluid has none. Laminar flow moves in smooth layers, fastest at the centre of a tube and zero at the walls.

Poiseuille's law for laminar flow through a tube of radius r and length L: Q = πr⁴ΔP/(8ηL). Flow is extremely sensitive to radius (halving r cuts flow 16-fold at the same pressure difference), which is why small changes in vessel diameter control blood flow so effectively.
Resistance R = 8ηL/(πr⁴) gives ΔP = QR, the fluid analogue of Ohm's law. Resistances add in series and as reciprocals in parallel.
confusions: Poiseuille's law applies only to laminar flow of a viscous fluid, while Bernoulli's equation assumes no viscosity. Don't apply both to the same pressure drop.

refs.label: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 12.4 Viscosity and Laminar Flow; Poiseuille's Law

topics.name: Continuity, Bernoulli's equation, and the Venturi effect
know: Continuity for an incompressible fluid: the volume flow rate Q = Av is the same at every cross-section, so fluid speeds up where the pipe narrows.

Bernoulli's equation (steady, incompressible, nonviscous flow along a streamline): P + ½ρv² + ρgh is constant. At equal heights, faster flow means lower pressure (the Venturi effect). A pitot tube measures flow speed from the difference between stagnation pressure and static pressure.
Each term is an energy per unit volume: pressure work, kinetic energy, and gravitational potential energy.
equations: P_1 + \tfrac12\rho v_1^2 + \rho g h_1 = P_2 + \tfrac12\rho v_2^2 + \rho g h_2
confusions: In a narrowing, pressure drops even though the fluid is being 'squeezed'; the pressure gradient is what accelerates it. Continuity applies to the total cross-sectional area of a branching network, so blood slows in the capillaries, whose combined area is huge.

refs.label: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 12.1 Flow Rate and Its Relation to Velocity

topics.name: Turbulence and surface tension
know: Flow turns turbulent (chaotic eddies, more resistance, noise) above a critical speed. The Reynolds number N_R = 2ρvr/η predicts it: laminar below about 2000, turbulent above about 3000 in a tube. Turbulence produces the Korotkoff sounds heard when a blood-pressure cuff is released and the murmurs of narrowed valves.

Surface tension γ (N/m) comes from cohesion between liquid molecules; it pulls drops into spheres and lets small insects stand on water. Surfactants lower it; lung surfactant lowers it more and more as an alveolus shrinks, which is what keeps small alveoli from emptying into larger ones.

The pressure inside a droplet or bubble exceeds the pressure outside by an amount that grows as the radius shrinks (2γ/r for a single surface such as a droplet or alveolus; twice that for a soap bubble with two surfaces). Capillary action, adhesion to the wall plus surface tension, raises a wetting liquid in a narrow tube.
confusions: Higher viscosity makes turbulence less likely; higher speed, density, and tube radius make it more likely.

Physics LibreTexts, Classical Mechanics (Tatum), 20.2.1 Excess Pressure Inside Drops and Bubbles

topics.name: Pressure and flow in the circulatory system
know: Blood pressure is reported as systolic/diastolic gauge pressure in mmHg, about 120/80 in a healthy adult's arteries; mean arterial pressure is roughly diastolic plus one-third of the pulse pressure. Pressure falls around the circuit: highest in the aorta, dropping most across the arterioles (the main site of resistance), low in the capillaries, and only a few mmHg in the great veins entering the heart.

Flow = ΔP/R, with cardiac output about 5 L/min at rest. Arterioles regulate regional flow with smooth muscle because resistance goes as 1/r⁴. Capillaries have the largest total cross-sectional area, so blood moves slowest there, which allows exchange.

Veins are thin-walled, compliant reservoirs holding most of the blood volume; one-way valves and the skeletal-muscle pump return blood against gravity. Elastic arteries stretch during systole and recoil during diastole, smoothing the pulsatile flow.
confusions: Blood is fastest in the aorta and slowest in a capillary, yet the capillaries together carry the same total flow (continuity across total area). Gravity adds ρgh: standing, the arterial pressure in the feet is well above that at heart level.

topics.name: Absolute temperature, pressure, and molar volume
know: Gas laws need absolute temperature: K = °C + 273.15. Zero kelvin is where an ideal gas's pressure or volume would extrapolate to zero, and average molecular kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature.

Pressure units: 1 atm = 760 mmHg = 760 torr = 101.325 kPa = 1.01325 bar. A mercury barometer balances atmospheric pressure against the weight of a mercury column (P = ρgh); a manometer reads a pressure difference the same way.
At STP (0 °C and 1 atm) one mole of an ideal gas occupies 22.4 L; this follows from PV = nRT and is the conversion between gas volume and moles in stoichiometry.
confusions: Temperature ratios only make sense in kelvin: warming from 20 °C to 40 °C is 293 K to 313 K, a 7% rise, not a doubling. IUPAC now defines STP at 1 bar (molar volume 22.7 L); MCAT-style problems use 1 atm and 22.4 L.

OpenStax College Physics 2e, 13.1 Temperature

topics.name: The ideal gas law and the simple gas laws
know: PV = nRT, with R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K) or 8.314 J/(mol·K). An ideal gas has point particles with no intermolecular forces; real gases approach this at low pressure and high temperature.

Hold two variables fixed and the law reduces to the named laws: Boyle (PV constant at fixed n and T), Charles (V/T constant at fixed n and P), Gay-Lussac (P/T constant), Avogadro (V/n constant at fixed T and P). The combined form P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ handles any change at fixed n.
Gas density is ρ = PM/(RT): higher at high pressure, low temperature, and high molar mass M.
confusions: Match R to your units: 0.0821 with litres and atmospheres, 8.314 with cubic metres and pascals (joules).

refs.label: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 9.2 Relating Pressure, Volume, Amount, and Temperature: The Ideal Gas Law
OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 9.3 Stoichiometry of Gaseous Substances, Mixtures, and Reactions

topics.name: Kinetic molecular theory and heat capacities of gases
know: Kinetic molecular theory pictures a gas as many tiny particles in constant random motion with elastic collisions, negligible volume, and no attractions. Pressure comes from collisions with the walls, and the average translational kinetic energy per molecule is (3/2)k_B·T, the same for every gas at a given temperature.
At the same temperature lighter molecules move faster: the root-mean-square speed is √(3RT/M). Rates of effusion and diffusion therefore scale as 1/√M (Graham's law).

Heat capacity at constant volume (C_V) is smaller than at constant pressure (C_P) because at constant pressure part of the heat goes into expansion work; for an ideal gas C_P − C_V = R per mole. A monatomic ideal gas has C_V = (3/2)R and C_P = (5/2)R; diatomic gases near room temperature have C_V ≈ (5/2)R because rotation also stores energy.
equations: C_P - C_V = R\ \text{(per mole, ideal gas)}
confusions: Molecules in a mixture share the same average kinetic energy but not the same average speed; the heavier ones are slower.

refs.label: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 9.5 The Kinetic-Molecular Theory
OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 9.4 Effusion and Diffusion of Gases
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 13.4 Kinetic Theory
OpenStax University Physics Volume 2, 3.5 Heat Capacities of an Ideal Gas

topics.name: Real gases and the van der Waals equation
know: Real gases deviate from PV = nRT at high pressure (molecules take up volume, so the gas is harder to compress than predicted) and at low temperature (attractions pull molecules together, lowering the pressure). The compressibility factor Z = PV/(nRT) is exactly 1 for an ideal gas.

The van der Waals equation corrects both effects: b is the excluded volume per mole and a measures the strength of attraction. a grows with the strength of the attractions (polar molecules, and large, easily polarized ones); b grows with molecular size.
Deviations are smallest for small, nonpolar molecules (He, H₂) and under high temperature and low pressure.
confusions: The a term makes the measured pressure lower than ideal (attractions); the b term makes the measured volume larger than ideal (finite size). Which one dominates depends on the conditions.

refs.label: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 9.6 Non-Ideal Gas Behavior

topics.name: Partial pressure, mole fraction, and Dalton's law
know: In a mixture of ideal gases each gas exerts the pressure it would exert alone. Dalton's law: the total pressure is the sum of the partial pressures, and each partial pressure is the gas's mole fraction times the total, P_A = X_A·P_total.

Air at 760 mmHg is about 21% O₂, so inspired P_O₂ is about 160 mmHg; after humidification in the airways (water vapour 47 mmHg at 37 °C) it is lower. A gas collected over water likewise includes water's vapour pressure.
Henry's law: the concentration of a gas dissolved in a liquid is proportional to its partial pressure above the liquid, C = k_H·P, the basis of blood-gas transport and decompression sickness.
confusions: Mole fraction, not mass fraction, sets partial pressure. Dissolved gas is described by the partial pressure it is in equilibrium with, which is why blood gases are reported in mmHg.

categories.name: Electrochemistry and circuits
categories.summary: Charges at rest and in motion: fields, potentials, circuits, magnetism, electrochemical cells, and the nerve cell as a biological wire.

topics.name: Charge, conductors, insulators, and Coulomb's law
know: Charge comes in units of e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and is conserved: it moves between objects but is never created or destroyed. Like charges repel, opposite charges attract.

Conductors (metals, electrolyte solutions) let charge move freely; insulators hold it in place. A conductor can be charged by contact or by induction (grounding it while a charged object is nearby). A neutral insulator is attracted to a charged object because its molecules polarize.
Coulomb's law: F = kq₁q₂/r² with k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². The force acts along the line joining the charges, obeys Newton's third law, and falls off as the inverse square of the distance.
confusions: Doubling the separation cuts the force to a quarter. In a conductor at rest, excess charge sits on the surface and the field inside is zero.

topics.name: Electric field, potential, and electrostatic energy
know: The electric field is the force per unit positive test charge, E = F/q (N/C = V/m). A point charge gives E = kQ/r², pointing away from positive charge and toward negative; fields from several charges add as vectors. Field lines start on positive charges, end on negative ones, never cross, and are densest where the field is strongest.

Electric potential V is potential energy per unit charge (1 V = 1 J/C): V = kQ/r for a point charge, a scalar, so potentials from several charges simply add. Potential difference drives charge: ΔPE = qΔV, and in a uniform field E = ΔV/d.

The electrostatic energy of two point charges is U = kq₁q₂/r, positive for like charges. One electron-volt is the energy an elementary charge gains across 1 V: 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to field lines, and moving along one takes no work.
confusions: Field falls as 1/r² but potential as 1/r. A positive charge accelerates toward lower potential; a negative charge toward higher. The potential can be nonzero where the field is zero (the midpoint between two equal positive charges).

topics.name: Current, electromotive force, and voltage
know: Current is the rate of charge flow, I = ΔQ/Δt, in amperes (1 A = 1 C/s). Conventional current points the way positive charge would move, opposite to the electron flow that actually carries current in metals; in solutions both cations and anions carry it.

Electromotive force (emf, ε) is the potential difference a source provides per unit charge when no current flows. A real battery has internal resistance r, so its terminal voltage V = ε − Ir drops as it delivers more current.
Direct current flows one way; alternating current reverses periodically (60 Hz household supply). Electrical power P = IV = I²R = V²/R, in watts.
confusions: A battery's emf is fixed by its chemistry; its terminal voltage sags under load. Current is the same at every point of a single series loop; it is not used up.

topics.name: Resistance, Ohm's law, resistivity, and resistor networks
know: Ohm's law, V = IR, holds for ohmic conductors; R is in ohms. Resistance depends on material and geometry, R = ρL/A: longer and thinner means more resistance, and a metal's resistivity ρ rises with temperature.

Series: the same current flows through each resistor, voltages add, and R_series = R₁ + R₂ + …, larger than any one of them. Parallel: each resistor sees the same voltage, currents add, and 1/R_parallel = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …, smaller than the smallest; two equal resistors in parallel give half of one.
Kirchhoff's rules: the current entering a junction equals the current leaving (charge conservation), and the voltage changes around any closed loop sum to zero (energy conservation).
confusions: Adding a resistor in parallel lowers the total resistance and raises the total current; adding one in series does the opposite. Resistivity is a property of the material; resistance belongs to the specific piece.

topics.name: Capacitors and dielectrics
know: A capacitor stores separated charge: C = Q/V, in farads (1 F = 1 C/V). A parallel-plate capacitor has C = κε₀A/d, where ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m and κ is the dielectric constant (1 for vacuum). The field between the plates is uniform, E = V/d. Inserting a dielectric raises the capacitance because its polarization partly cancels the field between the plates.
Stored energy U = ½QV = ½CV² = Q²/(2C). Capacitors combine opposite to resistors: in parallel they add (C_p = C₁ + C₂); in series the reciprocals add.

With the battery still connected, V is fixed and a dielectric increases Q; with the battery disconnected, Q is fixed and the dielectric lowers V. In an RC circuit the capacitor charges and discharges exponentially with time constant τ = RC.
confusions: Capacitors in series all carry the same charge; capacitors in parallel share the same voltage. A dielectric increases capacitance; moving the plates apart decreases it.

topics.name: Conductivity and electrical meters
know: Metallic conduction is carried by mobile electrons through a lattice of fixed positive ions and gets worse as temperature rises (more lattice vibration). Electrolytic conduction in solutions is carried by ions, so it increases with ion concentration, ion charge and mobility, and temperature; pure water barely conducts, while strong-electrolyte solutions conduct well.
Conductivity σ is the reciprocal of resistivity. A conductance measurement distinguishes strong electrolytes (fully dissociated, high conductance) from weak ones and from nonelectrolytes.

An ammeter measures current, so it is wired in series and has very low resistance (to leave the current unchanged). A voltmeter measures potential difference, so it is wired in parallel across the element and has very high resistance (to draw almost no current).
confusions: A voltmeter wired in series stops the circuit; an ammeter wired in parallel shorts it. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance, an ideal voltmeter infinite resistance.

topics.name: Magnetic fields and the Lorentz force
know: Magnetic field strength B is measured in tesla (1 T = 1 N/(A·m)). Field lines leave a magnet's north pole, enter its south pole, and form closed loops. Moving charges and currents produce magnetic fields: a long straight wire makes circular field lines of magnitude B = μ₀I/(2πr), with μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A.

A charge moving through a magnetic field feels F = qvB sin θ, perpendicular to both v and B (right-hand rule for a positive charge; reverse it for a negative one). Because the force is always perpendicular to the velocity it does no work: it changes direction, not speed, so a charge moving perpendicular to B circles with radius r = mv/(qB).

A wire of length L carrying current I feels F = ILB sin θ. The full Lorentz force on a charge is F = qE + qv × B; a velocity selector balances the electric and magnetic forces so only one speed passes straight through.
confusions: A stationary charge feels no magnetic force, and neither does one moving parallel to B. Magnetic forces never change a particle's kinetic energy.

topics.name: Electrolytic cells and Faraday's law
know: An electrolytic cell uses an external power source to force a nonspontaneous redox reaction (ΔG > 0, E_cell < 0): electrolysis of water or molten NaCl, electroplating, recharging a battery. The electrolyte is an ion-containing liquid that carries current between the electrodes.

In every electrochemical cell, oxidation happens at the anode and reduction at the cathode, and electrons travel through the external wire from anode to cathode. In an electrolytic cell the power source makes the anode positive and the cathode negative, the reverse of a galvanic cell.

Faraday's law of electrolysis: the moles of product equal the charge passed divided by z·F, where z is the number of electrons per ion and F = 96,485 C per mole of electrons. Charge is current times time, Q = It.
equations: \text{mol of product} = \dfrac{It}{zF},\qquad z = \text{electrons per ion},\quad F = 96{,}485\ \mathrm{C/mol\ e^-}
confusions: Anode and cathode are defined by the reaction (oxidation versus reduction), not by sign: the anode is negative in a galvanic cell but positive in an electrolytic cell. In both, cations migrate toward the cathode and anions toward the anode.

refs.label: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 17.7 Electrolysis

topics.name: Galvanic cells, reduction potentials, and cell potential
know: A galvanic (voltaic) cell turns a spontaneous redox reaction into current: two half-cells joined by a wire and a salt bridge, which keeps each half-cell electrically neutral as ions flow. Electrons leave the anode (oxidation, the negative terminal) and enter the cathode (reduction, the positive terminal).

Standard reduction potentials E° are measured against the standard hydrogen electrode (0.00 V) at 1 M, 1 bar (about 1 atm), and 25 °C. The more positive E°, the more readily the species is reduced, so it is the stronger oxidizing agent. E°_cell = E°_cathode − E°_anode, using both values as written (reduction) and never multiplying by stoichiometric coefficients.

A positive E°_cell means a spontaneous reaction: ΔG° = −nFE°, and combining with ΔG° = −RT ln K (R the gas constant, T in kelvin) links E° to the equilibrium constant. Cell notation lists anode | anode solution || cathode solution | cathode.
confusions: Reversing a half-reaction flips the sign of E°, but scaling it does not change E°, because potential is energy per unit charge. Electrons flow in the wire; ions flow in the salt bridge, anions toward the anode and cations toward the cathode.

refs.label: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 17.2 Galvanic Cells
OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 17.3 Electrode and Cell Potentials
OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 17.4 Potential, Free Energy, and Equilibrium

topics.name: The Nernst equation, concentration cells, and batteries
know: The Nernst equation gives the cell potential under nonstandard conditions: E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q; at 25 °C this is E° − (0.0592 V/n) log Q. The potential falls toward zero as the reaction approaches equilibrium (Q → K).

A concentration cell has identical electrodes in solutions of different concentration, so E° = 0 and its small voltage comes only from the concentration difference; the cell runs in the direction that evens out the concentrations. The same equation gives each ion's equilibrium potential across a cell membrane; the K⁺ value lies close to the resting potential.

Batteries: the lead–acid (lead-storage) battery uses Pb and PbO₂ electrodes in sulfuric acid, gives about 2 V per cell, and is rechargeable (recharging runs it as an electrolytic cell). Nickel–cadmium cells (Cd anode, nickel oxyhydroxide cathode, alkaline electrolyte) are rechargeable at about 1.2 V. A battery's emf is set by its chemistry; its size sets how much charge it can deliver.
confusions: A concentration cell stops when the two concentrations are equal, not when one side is empty. A higher ion concentration on the cathode side raises E.

topics.name: The nerve cell as an electrical conductor
know: A neuron keeps a resting membrane potential of about −70 mV (inside negative) through the Na⁺/K⁺ pump and K⁺ leak channels. Electrically, the membrane is a capacitor and its ion channels are variable resistors.

An action potential is an all-or-none wave of depolarization: at threshold, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ rushes in; then K⁺ channels open and K⁺ leaves to repolarize the membrane. It travels one way because the channels just behind it are refractory.

Myelin, laid down by Schwann cells in peripheral nerves and oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system, insulates the axon: it raises membrane resistance and lowers capacitance, so the signal jumps between the bare nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction). Myelinated and wider axons conduct faster; demyelination slows or blocks conduction.
confusions: The action potential has a fixed amplitude; stimulus strength is coded in firing frequency. Myelin speeds conduction by letting the signal skip, not by making ions move faster.

categories.name: Light and sound
categories.summary: Waves that carry information: sound and ultrasound, light and the electromagnetic spectrum, spectroscopy that reveals molecular structure, and the optics of lenses, mirrors, and the eye.

topics.name: Sound: production, speed, intensity, and decibels
know: Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave made by a vibrating source, and it needs a medium. Its speed depends on the medium's stiffness and density: fastest in solids, slower in liquids, slowest in gases (about 343 m/s in air at 20 °C, about 1500 m/s in water), and it rises with temperature in air.

Pitch is perceived frequency (humans hear roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz). Loudness tracks intensity I = P/A in W/m², which falls as 1/r² from a point source. Sound level in decibels is β = 10 log(I/I₀) with I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m² (the threshold of hearing): every 10 dB is a tenfold change in intensity, 3 dB roughly a doubling, 20 dB a hundredfold.
Attenuation: intensity drops with distance both by spreading out and by absorption in the medium, and higher frequencies are absorbed more.
confusions: Decibels add logarithmically: two equal sources are 3 dB louder than one, not double the decibel number. Frequency does not change when sound enters a new medium; wavelength and speed do.

topics.name: The Doppler effect
know: When a source and an observer move relative to each other, the observed frequency shifts: higher as they approach, lower as they separate. f_obs = f_s (v ± v_obs)/(v ∓ v_src), where v is the speed of sound; use the upper signs for motion toward each other.

Only the relative motion along the line joining them matters. A moving source changes the wavelength in the medium, while a moving observer changes how quickly wavefronts are met, so the two cases give slightly different numbers at the same speed.

Doppler ultrasound measures blood flow speed from the frequency shift of echoes off moving red cells; the shift is roughly doubled because the cells act first as moving receivers and then as moving sources. The same physics explains the red shift of receding galaxies and the sonic boom when a source outruns its own sound.
confusions: The shift depends on velocity, not distance: a source passing at constant speed sounds higher, then lower, sweeping through its true pitch as it goes by, because only the velocity component along the line to the listener counts. For speeds much smaller than v, Δf/f ≈ v_relative/v.

topics.name: Resonance in pipes and strings, ultrasound, and shock waves
know: Standing waves form when reflected waves interfere with incoming ones, and a system resonates when driven at one of its natural frequencies. A string fixed at both ends, or a pipe open at both ends, supports wavelengths λ_n = 2L/n (every harmonic, f_n = nv/2L). A pipe closed at one end has a node at the closed end and supports only odd harmonics, λ_n = 4L/n with n = 1, 3, 5, …
A string's fundamental rises with tension and falls with length and with mass per unit length, since v = √(T/μ). A pipe's depends on the speed of sound in the gas inside it.

Ultrasound (above 20 kHz) images tissue by timing echoes from boundaries where the acoustic impedance (ρv) changes; higher frequency gives finer resolution but shallower penetration. Shock waves: an object moving faster than sound piles its wavefronts into a cone (sonic boom), and focused shock waves are used to break kidney stones (lithotripsy).
confusions: A closed pipe has no even harmonics, and its fundamental is an octave below an open pipe of the same length. Displacement nodes in a sound wave are pressure antinodes.

topics.name: Interference, diffraction, thin films, and X-ray diffraction
know: Waves superpose: in phase they reinforce (constructive interference), half a wavelength out of phase they cancel (destructive). Young's double slit gives bright fringes where the path difference d sin θ = mλ and dark ones where it is (m + ½)λ; fringes spread farther apart for longer wavelengths and for closer slits.

A diffraction grating (many slits) obeys the same d sin θ = mλ but gives sharp, bright maxima, which is how spectrometers separate wavelengths. A single slit of width a has dark fringes at a sin θ = mλ, so narrower slits spread light more. Diffraction limits resolution, which is why shorter wavelengths (electrons, X-rays) resolve finer detail.

Thin films: light reflected from the top and bottom surfaces interferes. A reflection from a higher-index medium flips the phase by half a wavelength, and the wavelength inside the film is λ/n. X-ray diffraction: crystal planes a distance d apart reflect constructively when mλ = 2d sin θ (Bragg's law, with θ measured from the crystal planes rather than from the normal), the method that revealed the structure of DNA.
confusions: For a single slit the formula locates dark fringes; for a double slit the same form locates bright ones. Red light makes wider fringes than blue.

topics.name: Electromagnetic radiation, the spectrum, colour, and polarization
know: An electromagnetic wave is a pair of oscillating electric and magnetic fields, perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel. It needs no medium and moves at c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum (slower in matter, v = c/n). Accelerating charges produce it.

Photon energy is E = hf = hc/λ with h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s. From low to high frequency: radio, microwave, infrared, visible (about 700 nm red to 400 nm violet), ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays. Energy per photon rises with frequency, which is why ultraviolet and beyond can break bonds and ionize.

Perceived colour depends on wavelength, and an object looks the colour it reflects or transmits, not the one it absorbs. Linear polarization: the electric field oscillates in one plane; a polarizing filter passes that component, two crossed filters pass nothing, and reflected glare is partly polarized. Circular polarization: the field direction rotates as the wave advances.
equations: I = I_0\cos^2\theta\ \text{(Malus's law, ideal linear polarizer)}
confusions: Shorter wavelength means higher frequency and higher photon energy. Brightness is about the number of photons; colour and photon energy are about frequency.

topics.name: Infrared spectroscopy
know: Infrared light excites molecular vibrations (stretches and bends) at frequencies set by bond stiffness and the masses of the atoms; a vibration absorbs only if it changes the molecule's dipole moment. Spectra are plotted in wavenumbers (cm⁻¹), larger meaning higher energy.

Landmark absorptions: O–H of an alcohol broad at about 3400–3650 cm⁻¹, and very broad from about 2500 to 3100 for a carboxylic acid; N–H at 3300–3500 (sharper); C–H just below 3000 for sp³ carbon and just above for sp²; C≡C and C≡N at 2100–2260; C=O strong and sharp near 1700 (esters about 1735, aldehydes about 1730, ketones about 1715, acids about 1710, amides about 1690; conjugation lowers any of these by roughly 20–30 cm⁻¹ and ring strain raises them); C=C about 1650. Below about 1500 cm⁻¹ is the fingerprint region, unique to each compound but hard to assign.
Use IR to confirm that a functional group is present or gone: when an alcohol is oxidized to a ketone, the broad O–H disappears and a sharp C=O appears.
confusions: Symmetric diatomics such as O₂ and N₂ show no IR stretch because their dipole does not change. The C=O peak near 1700 cm⁻¹ is the most diagnostic single absorption; its exact position reports conjugation and ring strain.

topics.name: Visible and ultraviolet spectroscopy
know: Ultraviolet and visible light promote electrons to higher molecular orbitals: π → π* transitions in C=C and conjugated systems, and n → π* transitions from lone pairs on O or N. Each added conjugated double bond narrows the HOMO–LUMO gap and shifts the absorption to longer wavelength; with enough conjugation (β-carotene's eleven double bonds) the absorption reaches the visible and the compound is coloured.

A substance shows the complement of the colour it absorbs: absorbing blue-violet (around 450 nm) looks yellow-orange, absorbing green looks red or purple. Transition-metal complexes are coloured by d-orbital transitions. Acid–base indicators change colour because their protonated and deprotonated forms absorb at different wavelengths.
Beer–Lambert law: absorbance A = εlc is proportional to concentration (ε is the molar absorptivity, l the path length), the basis of spectrophotometric assays and calibration curves.
confusions: Absorbance is logarithmic: A = 1 means 10% of the light is transmitted, A = 2 means 1%. More conjugation means a longer wavelength absorbed (lower energy), not shorter.

topics.name: Proton NMR spectroscopy
know: Nuclei with spin (¹H, ¹³C) behave like tiny magnets. In a strong field they align with or against it, and radio-frequency energy flips them at a resonance frequency that depends on the local electronic environment. Electron density shields a proton; electronegative atoms, π systems, and carbonyls deshield it and move its signal downfield, to a higher chemical shift in ppm relative to tetramethylsilane at 0.

Read four things from a ¹H spectrum: the number of signals equals the number of chemically nonequivalent sets of protons; the chemical shift places each set (alkyl about 0.9–1.5 ppm, next to a carbonyl or alkene 2–2.5, next to N about 2.2–3, next to O about 3.3–4.5, vinyl 4.5–6.5, aromatic 6.5–8, aldehyde 9–10, carboxylic acid 10–12); the integration gives the relative number of protons; and spin–spin splitting divides a signal into n + 1 peaks for n equivalent protons on adjacent carbons, with intensities from Pascal's triangle.
Protons on O or N usually appear as broad singlets and exchange with D₂O. Equivalent protons do not split one another. ¹³C NMR gives one signal per unique carbon.
equations: \text{number of peaks} = n + 1\ \text{(} n \text{ equivalent neighbouring protons)}
confusions: A triplet means two neighbouring protons, not three. Symmetry reduces the count of signals: acetone's six protons give one singlet.

topics.name: Reflection, refraction, dispersion, and total internal reflection
know: Light travels in straight lines through a uniform medium. Reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal. Refraction: light bends when it enters a medium where its speed differs. The index of refraction n = c/v is at least 1 (water 1.33, glass about 1.5), and Snell's law is n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂: entering a slower (higher-n) medium bends the ray toward the normal, leaving it bends the ray away.

Dispersion: n varies slightly with wavelength (higher for violet than red in glass), so a prism or raindrop spreads white light into a spectrum with violet bent most. Chromatic aberration in lenses comes from the same effect.

Total internal reflection: going from higher to lower n, the refracted ray reaches 90° at the critical angle, sin θ_c = n₂/n₁, and beyond it all the light reflects. This traps light inside optical fibres and endoscopes.
confusions: Frequency is unchanged across a boundary; speed and wavelength both drop in the higher-n medium (λ = λ₀/n). Total internal reflection happens only when going from high n to low n.

topics.name: Spherical mirrors
know: A concave (converging) mirror brings parallel rays to a real focal point in front of it at f = R/2; a convex (diverging) mirror spreads them as if from a virtual focus behind it, so its f is negative. The centre of curvature lies at distance R.

Mirror equation: 1/d_o + 1/d_i = 1/f, with magnification m = −d_i/d_o. Sign convention: d_i is positive for a real image in front of the mirror (inverted) and negative for a virtual image behind it (upright); |m| > 1 means enlarged.

Concave-mirror cases: an object beyond C gives a smaller, inverted, real image between f and C; an object between f and C gives a larger, inverted, real image beyond C; an object inside f gives an enlarged, upright, virtual image (a makeup mirror). A convex mirror always gives a smaller, upright, virtual image with a wide field of view (a car's side mirror). A plane mirror is the R → ∞ case: virtual, upright, same size, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
confusions: Real images are inverted and can be projected on a screen; virtual images are upright and cannot. A negative magnification means inverted, not reduced.

refs.label: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 25.7 Image Formation by Mirrors

topics.name: Thin lenses, lens power, combinations, and aberration
know: A converging (convex) lens has positive f and brings parallel rays to a real focus on the far side; a diverging (concave) lens has negative f and forms only reduced, upright, virtual images. The thin-lens equation matches the mirror equation, 1/d_o + 1/d_i = 1/f with m = −d_i/d_o, except that a real image (d_i > 0) forms on the side opposite the object.

Lens power P = 1/f in diopters when f is in metres: a +2 D lens has f = 0.5 m, and a −4 D lens is diverging. Powers of thin lenses in contact add. For lenses in series, the image of the first lens is the object of the next, and the total magnification is the product of the individual ones.

Aberrations: spherical aberration blurs because rays through the lens edge focus closer than central rays (reduced by using only the central part of the lens); chromatic aberration blurs colours because n depends on wavelength (corrected with compound lenses).
equations: P_{total} = P_1 + P_2\ \text{(thin lenses in contact)}
confusions: A converging lens gives a virtual, enlarged image only when the object sits inside the focal length (a magnifying glass). Shorter focal length means greater power.

refs.label: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 25.6 Image Formation by Lenses
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 26.6 Aberrations

topics.name: The eye and optical instruments
know: The eye is a converging system. The cornea does most of the refracting (the air–cornea boundary has the biggest index change), and the flexible lens adds adjustable power through accommodation by the ciliary muscle, forming a real, inverted image on the retina that the brain re-inverts. A relaxed eye focused at infinity has a total power of about 50 D.

Nearsightedness (myopia): distant objects focus in front of the retina because the eye is too long or too strong; it is corrected with a diverging (negative) lens. Farsightedness (hyperopia): near objects would focus behind the retina; corrected with a converging (positive) lens. Presbyopia is the loss of accommodation with age; astigmatism is uneven curvature, corrected with a cylindrical lens.

A magnifying glass is a single converging lens with the object inside f. A compound microscope uses a short-focal-length objective to make a real, enlarged image and an eyepiece to magnify it further. A refracting telescope pairs a long-focal-length objective with a short-focal-length eyepiece, giving angular magnification of magnitude f_o/f_e with an inverted image.
equations: P_{eye} = \dfrac{1}{d_o} + \dfrac{1}{d_i}\ \ (d_i \approx 0.02\ \mathrm{m}\text{, fixed; distances in metres give diopters)}
confusions: Myopia needs a minus lens and hyperopia a plus lens; a prescription of −2.5 D is a diverging lens with f = −0.4 m. The retinal image is real and inverted.

categories.name: Atoms, nuclear decay, electronic structure
categories.summary: The atom from the inside out: nuclei and radioactivity, how electrons are arranged, why the periodic table has the shape it does, and the mole-based bookkeeping of chemical change.

topics.name: The nucleus, isotopes, and binding energy
know: Atomic number Z counts protons and defines the element; mass number A is protons plus neutrons. Isotopes share Z but differ in neutron number. The atomic weight on the periodic table is the natural-abundance-weighted average of the isotope masses in unified atomic mass units (u).

The strong nuclear force binds nucleons but acts only over very short range, so heavier nuclei need extra neutrons to outweigh proton–proton repulsion, and every nucleus with more than 83 protons is radioactive.

Binding energy is the energy released when nucleons assemble, or needed to pull them apart, and equals the mass defect times c² (E = Δmc²). Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56, so fusing light nuclei and splitting heavy ones both release energy.
confusions: Atomic weight is an average: chlorine's 35.45 belongs to no single atom. Mass number is a count and has no units.

topics.name: Radioactive decay and half-life
know: Alpha decay emits a helium nucleus (⁴₂He): Z falls by 2 and A by 4; alpha particles are stopped by paper or skin. Beta-minus decay turns a neutron into a proton and emits an electron (⁰₋₁e) and an antineutrino: Z rises by 1, A is unchanged. Positron (beta-plus) emission turns a proton into a neutron, so Z falls by 1 (the basis of PET imaging); electron capture has the same net effect. Gamma emission is a photon from an excited nucleus with no change in Z or A.

Decay is first-order: N = N₀e^(−λt), with half-life T½ = ln 2/λ ≈ 0.693/λ. After n half-lives N = N₀/2ⁿ. Activity (decays per second, in becquerels; 1 Ci = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq) equals λN and falls with the same half-life.
A semi-log plot of N or activity against time is a straight line with slope −λ, which is how half-lives are read from data. Balance nuclear equations by conserving total A and total Z on both sides.
confusions: After three half-lives one-eighth remains, not zero and not one-third. Beta particles come from the nucleus; they are not orbital electrons.

topics.name: Mass spectrometry
know: A mass spectrometer ionizes a sample, accelerates the ions through a voltage, and sorts them by mass-to-charge ratio (m/z), classically by bending them in a magnetic field (r = mv/(qB), so heavier ions curve less) or by timing their flight down a tube. The output is a plot of signal against m/z.

Uses: measuring isotope masses and abundances (the source of the periodic table's atomic weights), identifying compounds from the molecular ion peak (M⁺) and its fragment pattern, and analysing proteins by electrospray or MALDI time-of-flight instruments.
Isotope patterns are diagnostic: a compound with one chlorine shows M and M+2 peaks in a 3:1 ratio, one bromine gives about 1:1.
confusions: The x-axis is m/z, not mass: a doubly charged ion appears at half its mass.

topics.name: Quantum numbers, orbitals, and electron configurations
know: Each electron is described by four quantum numbers: n (shell; sets size and energy: 1, 2, 3, …), l (subshell shape: 0 = s, 1 = p, 2 = d, 3 = f, up to n − 1), mₗ (orientation, from −l to +l, giving 1, 3, 5, or 7 orbitals per subshell), and mₛ (spin, +½ or −½). An orbital holds at most two electrons, and they must have opposite spins (Pauli exclusion principle), so a shell holds 2n² electrons.

Fill from the lowest energy up (1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p 5s 4d …), placing one electron in each orbital of a subshell before pairing (Hund's rule). Write configurations as 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ or [Ne] 3s² 3p¹. The ground state is the lowest-energy arrangement; anything else is an excited state. Cations lose electrons from the highest n first, so Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶, not 4s² 3d⁴.

Effective nuclear charge Z_eff is the net positive charge an electron feels after inner electrons shield it; it rises across a period and pulls the valence electrons in. Atoms or ions with unpaired electrons are paramagnetic (drawn into a magnetic field); with every electron paired they are diamagnetic (weakly repelled).
equations: Z_{eff} \approx Z - S\ \ (S = \text{shielding by inner electrons})
confusions: Chromium and copper are the common exceptions ([Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵ and [Ar] 4s¹ 3d¹⁰). The 4s subshell fills before 3d but empties first when a transition metal ionizes.

topics.name: Line spectra, the Bohr atom, the photoelectric effect, and uncertainty
know: Atoms absorb and emit light only at specific wavelengths (line spectra) because electron energies are quantized: a photon is absorbed when its energy equals a gap, E_photon = E_high − E_low, and emitted when the electron drops back. Each element's lines are a fingerprint, the basis of atomic absorption and emission spectroscopy.

Bohr's model of hydrogen puts the electron in orbits with energies E_n = −13.6 eV/n². The ground state is n = 1, and the energy rises toward 0 as n → ∞ (ionization). Transitions ending at n = 2 form the Balmer series, whose first four lines (from n = 3 to 6) are visible and the rest ultraviolet; those ending at n = 1 form the ultraviolet Lyman series. The model fails for atoms with more than one electron, though its energy levels are right for hydrogen-like ions.

Photoelectric effect: light ejects electrons from a metal only above a threshold frequency, and the fastest electrons have KE = hf − φ, where φ is the metal's work function; brighter light ejects more electrons, not faster ones. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle: position and momentum cannot both be known exactly (Δx·Δp ≥ ħ/2), so electrons occupy probability clouds (orbitals) rather than paths.
confusions: A larger energy gap means a shorter wavelength: n = 2 → 1 is far more energetic than 3 → 2. Light below the threshold frequency ejects nothing however intense it is.

topics.name: The periodic table: groups and families
know: Elements in a column (group) share a valence electron configuration and therefore share chemistry. Alkali metals (group 1, ns¹) are soft, very reactive metals that form +1 ions and react violently with water. Alkaline earth metals (group 2, ns²) form +2 ions and are less reactive. Halogens (group 17, ns² np⁵) are reactive nonmetals that gain one electron to form −1 halides and exist as diatomic molecules. Noble gases (group 18, filled shells) are nearly inert.

Transition metals (the d-block) show multiple oxidation states, form coloured complexes, and are often paramagnetic. Representative (main-group) elements are the s- and p-blocks. The oxygen group (group 16, the chalcogens) typically forms −2 ions or two covalent bonds.

Metals (left and centre) lose electrons, conduct heat and electricity, and form basic oxides; nonmetals (upper right) gain or share electrons and form acidic oxides; the metalloids along the staircase (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te) sit between and act as semiconductors. Hydrogen is a nonmetal despite sitting above group 1.
confusions: Reactivity runs opposite ways: alkali metals become more reactive down the group (the outer electron is easier to lose), halogens become less reactive down the group (an extra electron is harder to gain).

topics.name: Periodic trends
know: Valence electrons are the outermost-shell electrons (for main-group elements, the last digit of the group number) and set bonding behaviour. Across a period Z_eff rises and atoms shrink; down a group new shells are added and atoms grow. Cations are smaller than their parent atoms and anions larger; in an isoelectronic series the species with more protons is smaller.

First ionization energy (to remove the outermost electron from a gaseous atom) rises across a period and falls down a group, with small dips just after a filled subshell (Be → B) and a half-filled one (N → O). The second ionization energy is always larger than the first and jumps sharply once a noble-gas core is reached (Na⁺ → Na²⁺).

Electron affinity (the energy change when a gaseous atom gains an electron) is most favourable for the halogens; noble gases and group 2 have little or none. Electronegativity, an atom's pull on shared electrons, increases across a period and up a group, peaking at fluorine (about 4.0 on the Pauling scale); the difference between bonded atoms predicts bond polarity.
confusions: Ionization energy and atomic radius run in opposite directions. Electron affinity is irregular; do not assume it climbs smoothly to the right.

topics.name: Moles, molar mass, formulas, and percent composition
know: One mole is 6.022 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's number), and the molar mass in g/mol equals the formula mass in u read from the periodic table. Divide mass by molar mass to get moles, multiply moles by N_A to get particles, and (for a gas at STP, 0 °C and 1 atm) multiply moles by 22.4 to get litres.

The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; the molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of it, found by comparing the molar mass with the empirical formula mass. From percent composition: assume 100 g, convert each element to moles, divide by the smallest, and clear fractions.

Percent mass of an element is its mass in one mole of the compound divided by the molar mass, times 100. Density ρ = m/V links volume to mass (g/mL for liquids and solids, g/L for gases). Metric prefixes: kilo 10³, centi 10⁻², milli 10⁻³, micro 10⁻⁶, nano 10⁻⁹.
equations: \%\,\text{mass of X} = \dfrac{\text{mass of X in one mole}}{\text{molar mass}}\times 100
confusions: Glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) and formaldehyde (CH₂O) share an empirical formula; only the molar mass tells them apart. Molecular weight (u) and molar mass (g/mol) are the same number.

topics.name: Oxidation numbers, redox agents, and disproportionation
know: Oxidation numbers are electron bookkeeping. Rules (when two conflict, the earlier one wins): a free element is 0; a monatomic ion equals its charge; fluorine is −1; group 1 is +1 and group 2 is +2; hydrogen is +1 (−1 in metal hydrides); oxygen is −2 (−1 in peroxides); the numbers sum to the charge on the species.

Oxidation is a rise in oxidation number (loss of electrons), reduction a fall (gain). The oxidizing agent is the species that gets reduced; the reducing agent is the one that gets oxidized. Common oxidizing agents: O₂, the halogens, MnO₄⁻, Cr₂O₇²⁻, H₂O₂. Common reducing agents: alkali metals, H₂, LiAlH₄, NaBH₄.
In a disproportionation one species is both oxidized and reduced, as when hydrogen peroxide decomposes: oxygen at −1 goes to 0 in O₂ and to −2 in water.
confusions: Agents are named for what they do to the other reactant, so the oxidizing agent itself gains electrons.

topics.name: Chemical equations, balancing, limiting reactants, and yield
know: A balanced equation has the same number of each atom, and the same total charge, on both sides, with state symbols (s, l, g, aq). Coefficients give mole ratios; subscripts are never changed. Balance one element at a time, leaving H and O for last, then clear any fractions.

Balance redox equations by half-reactions: split into oxidation and reduction, balance atoms other than O and H, then O with H₂O, H with H⁺, and charge with electrons; scale so the electrons cancel and add. In basic solution, add OH⁻ to both sides to neutralize the H⁺.

The limiting reactant runs out first and sets the theoretical yield: convert each reactant to moles, divide by its coefficient, and the smallest result limits. Percent yield is actual over theoretical times 100.
confusions: The limiting reactant is not necessarily the one with the smaller mass or even fewer moles; it is the one with the smallest moles-per-coefficient ratio.

concepts.name: Chemical processes in living systems
concepts.summary: Foundational Concept 5 (AAMC): the chemistry that makes living systems possible. Solutions and acids, the bonds and shapes of molecules, how mixtures are separated, the biological molecules themselves, and the energy and rate rules that govern their reactions.

categories.name: Water and solutions
categories.summary: Acids, bases, and buffers; the ions that live in water; what dissolves and what precipitates; and how titrations measure all of it.

topics.name: Brønsted–Lowry acids and bases, Kw, and pH
know: Brønsted–Lowry: an acid donates a proton and a base accepts one. Every acid has a conjugate base (the acid minus H⁺), and the stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base. Water is amphoteric and self-ionizes: Kw = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C, so pure water has [H⁺] = 10⁻⁷ M and pH 7, and pH + pOH = 14.

pH = −log[H⁺], so one pH unit is a tenfold change in [H⁺]. Strong acids (HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, H₂SO₄, HClO₄) and strong bases (group 1 hydroxides and the heavier group 2 hydroxides) dissociate completely, so [H⁺] or [OH⁻] equals the nominal concentration. Weak acids (acetic acid, HF, carbonic acid, ammonium) and weak bases (ammonia, amines) ionize only partly.
Mental pH: for [H⁺] = a × 10⁻ⁿ, pH = n − log a, so 3 × 10⁻⁴ M gives pH ≈ 3.5. Kw rises with temperature, so neutral water at 37 °C is slightly below pH 7 yet still neutral.
confusions: Strength (degree of ionization) is not concentration: a dilute strong acid can have a higher pH than a concentrated weak acid. More acidic hydrogens do not make an acid stronger.

topics.name: Weak acids and bases: Ka, Kb, pKa, and salt hydrolysis
know: A weak acid HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻ has Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA]; pKa = −log Ka, and a smaller pKa means a stronger acid. Kb and pKb are defined the same way for a base. For a conjugate pair Ka × Kb = Kw, so pKa + pKb = 14.

For a weak acid alone in water with Ka much smaller than its concentration C, [H⁺] ≈ √(Ka·C). Adding a salt of its conjugate base pushes the equilibrium back (the common-ion effect) and turns the solution into a buffer. Percent ionization rises on dilution even though [H⁺] falls.

Salts hydrolyse: a strong-acid/strong-base salt (NaCl) is neutral; a weak-acid/strong-base salt (sodium acetate) is basic because the anion accepts protons; a strong-acid/weak-base salt (NH₄Cl) is acidic; small, highly charged metal cations (Al³⁺, Fe³⁺) are acidic too.
confusions: pKa belongs to the acid; pH belongs to the solution. They are equal only when the acid is exactly half-neutralized.

topics.name: Buffers and the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation
know: A buffer is a weak acid with its conjugate base (or a weak base with its conjugate acid) in comparable amounts: added H⁺ is taken up by the base and added OH⁻ by the acid, so the pH barely moves. Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]). A buffer works best when pH ≈ pKa (ratio near 1), holds within about one pH unit either side, and its capacity grows with the total concentration.

Common systems: the CO₂/bicarbonate system in blood (apparent pKa 6.1 when dissolved CO₂ is counted as the acid, 6.4 for H₂CO₃ itself; it holds pH 7.4 far from its pKa because it is open: the lungs adjust CO₂ and the kidneys adjust HCO₃⁻), phosphate (H₂PO₄⁻/HPO₄²⁻, pKa about 7.2) inside cells, acetate in the lab, and protein side chains such as histidine (pKa near 6).
On a titration curve the buffer region is the flat stretch around the half-equivalence point, where pH = pKa; the curve climbs steeply at the equivalence point.
confusions: Diluting a buffer leaves its pH nearly unchanged (the ratio is the same) but lowers its capacity. A strong acid and its salt do not buffer.

topics.name: Common ions, hydration, and hydronium
know: Know the common ions by name, formula, and charge. Cations: Na⁺, K⁺, NH₄⁺, Ag⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, Zn²⁺, Cu²⁺, Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺, Al³⁺. Anions: the halides, hydroxide OH⁻, nitrate NO₃⁻, nitrite NO₂⁻, acetate CH₃COO⁻, bicarbonate HCO₃⁻, carbonate CO₃²⁻, sulfate SO₄²⁻, sulfite SO₃²⁻, phosphate PO₄³⁻ and its protonated forms, perchlorate ClO₄⁻, chlorate ClO₃⁻, hypochlorite ClO⁻, permanganate MnO₄⁻, dichromate Cr₂O₇²⁻, cyanide CN⁻, peroxide O₂²⁻.

In water, ions are hydrated: water's partially negative oxygens surround cations and its partially positive hydrogens surround anions. The hydration energy released helps pay for breaking the crystal lattice, which decides whether a salt dissolves. A proton in water is the hydronium ion H₃O⁺, usually written H⁺ for short.

Naming patterns: -ate has one more oxygen than -ite; per-…-ate has one more than -ate and hypo-…-ite one fewer than -ite; adding H⁺ to a polyatomic anion gives the hydrogen (bi-) form (HCO₃⁻, HSO₄⁻, H₂PO₄⁻).
confusions: Nitrate is NO₃⁻ and nitrite NO₂⁻; sulfate SO₄²⁻ and sulfite SO₃²⁻. Ammonium NH₄⁺ is a cation; ammonia NH₃ is neutral.

topics.name: Concentration units, Ksp, the common-ion effect, complex ions, and pH
know: Concentration units: molarity M = moles of solute per litre of solution; molality m = moles per kilogram of solvent (independent of temperature); mole fraction; mass percent; parts per million (about mg/L in dilute aqueous solution). Dilution: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂.

A sparingly soluble salt MₐXᵦ(s) ⇌ aM + bX has Ksp = [M]ᵃ[X]ᵇ. With molar solubility s, [M] = as and [X] = bs, so Ksp = s² for an AB salt and 4s³ for AB₂. A precipitate forms when the ion product Q exceeds Ksp. Compare solubilities directly from Ksp only for salts of the same formula type.

Common-ion effect: an ion already in solution lowers a salt's solubility (used for selective precipitation in qualitative analysis). Forming a complex ion such as Ag(NH₃)₂⁺ (formation constant Kf) pulls the metal into solution and raises solubility. Lowering the pH dissolves salts whose anion is a weak base (carbonates, hydroxides, phosphates, fluorides) by protonating it, but does not affect salts of strong-acid anions such as chloride.
confusions: Solubility (how much dissolves) and Ksp (a product of concentrations) are related but not interchangeable. The common-ion effect lowers solubility without changing Ksp.

topics.name: Titrations, indicators, and titration curves
know: In a titration, a solution of known concentration (the titrant) is added to a measured volume of analyte until the reaction is complete. At the equivalence point the moles of acid and base match (for a 1:1 pair, MₐVₐ = MᵦVᵦ). The endpoint is where the indicator changes colour, so pick an indicator whose pKa lies near the equivalence-point pH.

Curve shapes: strong acid with strong base reaches equivalence at pH 7 with a long, steep jump, so almost any indicator works. Weak acid with strong base starts higher, has a buffer region where pH = pKa at the half-equivalence point, and reaches equivalence above 7 because the conjugate base is basic; use phenolphthalein. Weak base with strong acid mirrors this with equivalence below 7; use methyl red (or bromocresol green). A polyprotic acid shows one jump per proton when successive pKa values are at least about 3 units apart; otherwise the steps merge (sulfuric acid's second proton).
Redox titrations use an oxidizing titrant such as permanganate (self-indicating, purple to colourless) or iodine with starch; match moles of electrons rather than moles of protons.
equations: M_a V_a = M_b V_b\ \text{(1:1 stoichiometry at equivalence)}
confusions: The equivalence point (stoichiometric) and the endpoint (colour change) are different things that a well-chosen indicator brings close together. Equivalence is at pH 7 only for a strong acid–strong base titration.

categories.name: Molecules and intermolecular interactions
categories.summary: How atoms bond and what shape the result takes; the three-dimensional identity of molecules (isomers and chirality); and the weak forces between molecules that set the properties of liquids.

topics.name: Lewis structures, formal charge, resonance, and Lewis acids and bases
know: A Lewis structure shows valence electrons as bonds and lone pairs: count the valence electrons (adjusting for charge), join the atoms with single bonds, complete octets on the outer atoms, give any leftovers to the central atom, and form multiple bonds if the central atom still lacks an octet. Hydrogen holds two electrons; atoms from period 3 on (P, S) can exceed eight; B and Be can have fewer; odd-electron species (NO, NO₂) are radicals.

Formal charge = valence electrons − nonbonding electrons − ½(bonding electrons). The best structure minimizes formal charges and puts any negative charge on the most electronegative atom. Resonance structures differ only in where electrons are drawn; the real molecule is a single weighted blend (the hybrid) with delocalized electrons spread over several atoms, as in carbonate, nitrate, benzene, and carboxylate ions.

A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair (BF₃, AlCl₃, metal cations, H⁺); a Lewis base donates one (NH₃, water, hydroxide, any lone pair). Every Brønsted base is a Lewis base, but the Lewis definition also covers reactions with no proton transfer, such as a metal ion binding ligands.
confusions: Resonance is not a rapid flipping between structures; the molecule has one structure that none of the drawings captures alone. Formal charge is a bookkeeping device, not a real charge.

topics.name: Bond polarity, partial ionic character, and dipole moments
know: A bond between atoms of different electronegativity is polar covalent: the shared pair sits closer to the more electronegative atom, leaving partial charges δ⁺ and δ⁻. The bigger the difference, the more ionic character; a difference above roughly 1.8 is usually treated as ionic, below about 0.4 as nonpolar.

A bond dipole has a size (dipole moment μ = charge × separation, in debye) and a direction toward the negative end. A molecule's dipole is the vector sum of its bond dipoles, so symmetric shapes (linear CO₂, tetrahedral CCl₄, trigonal planar BF₃) are nonpolar despite polar bonds, while water, ammonia, and chloroform are polar.
Polarity sets intermolecular forces, boiling points, solubility (like dissolves like), and how a molecule interacts with proteins and membranes.
confusions: Polar bonds do not guarantee a polar molecule; check the geometry. A lone pair on the central atom usually breaks the symmetry.

topics.name: VSEPR shapes, hybridization, σ and π bonds, and structural formulas
know: VSEPR: the electron groups around a central atom (bonds of any order and lone pairs) spread as far apart as possible. Two groups: linear, 180°. Three: trigonal planar, 120°. Four: tetrahedral, 109.5°. Five: trigonal bipyramidal. Six: octahedral. Lone pairs take up room but are not part of the named molecular shape, giving bent (water, about 104.5°), trigonal pyramidal (ammonia, about 107°), seesaw, T-shaped, and square planar molecules, and they squeeze the bond angles a little.

Hybridization follows the electron-group count: sp (two groups, linear), sp² (three, trigonal planar), sp³ (four, tetrahedral). A σ bond is head-on overlap along the bond axis; a π bond is side-by-side overlap of unhybridized p orbitals above and below it. Every bond has one σ bond; a double bond is σ + π and a triple bond σ + 2π. More s character (sp > sp² > sp³) means shorter, stronger bonds and a more electronegative atom.

Drawing structures: carbon makes 4 bonds; nitrogen 3 plus a lone pair; oxygen 2 plus two lone pairs; hydrogen and the halogens 1; phosphorus usually 3 or 5; sulfur 2, 4, or 6; silicon 4 like carbon. Skeletal (line) structures leave out carbons and their hydrogens. Delocalization: p orbitals on neighbouring sp² atoms overlap into an extended π system (conjugation), lowering the energy, which is why benzene's six bonds are all the same length.
confusions: Shape names describe where the atoms are: water is bent, not tetrahedral, though its electron-group geometry is tetrahedral. An atom with a lone pair next to a π system (the nitrogen of an amide) is sp² so that the lone pair can delocalize.

topics.name: Multiple bonds: length, strength, and rigidity
know: Bond order (single 1, double 2, triple 3) tracks strength and length: more bonds between the same two atoms give a shorter, stronger bond with a higher bond dissociation energy (average bond energies roughly C–C 350, C=C 610, C≡C 835 kJ/mol; lengths about 154, 134, and 120 pm).

A π bond prevents rotation: the two ends of a double bond cannot turn without breaking the π overlap, which is why alkenes have cis–trans (E/Z) isomers and why the peptide bond is planar and rigid. Single bonds rotate freely, giving conformers.

The second (π) bond is weaker than the first (σ), so a double bond is worth less than two single bonds; that is why addition across C=C is favourable. In resonance hybrids such as benzene the bond order is fractional (1.5) and the lengths are intermediate.
confusions: Shorter means stronger for bonds between the same pair of atoms; comparing different atom pairs needs care (C–F is short and very strong, I–I long and weak).

topics.name: Isomers: structural, stereo, and conformational
know: Isomers share a molecular formula. Constitutional (structural) isomers differ in connectivity (butane and 2-methylpropane; ethanol and dimethyl ether). Stereoisomers share connectivity but differ in 3-D arrangement and come in two kinds: enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images; diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images, including the cis–trans (geometric) isomers of alkenes and rings and compounds with several stereocentres that differ at some but not all of them. Conformational isomers (conformers) interconvert by rotation about single bonds (staggered and eclipsed, chair and boat) and are the same compound.

A molecule with n stereocentres has at most 2ⁿ stereoisomers; a meso compound (with an internal mirror plane) is achiral despite having stereocentres and reduces the count. Enantiomers share every physical property except the direction they rotate plane-polarized light and the way they interact with other chiral molecules such as enzymes and receptors. Diastereomers have different physical properties (melting point, boiling point, solubility) and can be separated by ordinary means.
Cyclohexane chairs: each substituent is axial or equatorial, a ring flip swaps them, and bulky groups prefer equatorial positions to avoid 1,3-diaxial strain.
confusions: Cis–trans isomers are diastereomers, not enantiomers. Inverting every stereocentre gives the enantiomer; inverting only some gives a diastereomer.

topics.name: Chirality, optical activity, and R/S, D/L, and E/Z configuration
know: A carbon bearing four different groups is a stereocentre. A molecule is chiral if it cannot be superimposed on its mirror image; the quick test is the absence of an internal mirror plane. Chiral compounds are optically active: a solution rotates plane-polarized light clockwise (+, dextrorotatory) or counterclockwise (−, levorotatory). Specific rotation [α] = α/(l × c), with the path length in decimetres and the concentration in g/mL; a racemic mixture (equal amounts of both enantiomers) shows no net rotation.

Absolute configuration (R/S, Cahn–Ingold–Prelog): rank the four substituents by atomic number at the first point of difference (a multiple bond counts as duplicated atoms), point the lowest-priority group away from you, and trace 1 → 2 → 3: clockwise is R, counterclockwise is S. If the lowest-priority group points toward you, reverse the answer. In a Fischer projection the horizontal bonds come toward you, so with the lowest group on a vertical bond read the answer directly, and on a horizontal bond reverse it.

Relative configuration compares two centres or two molecules (same or opposite handedness) without naming each. D/L for sugars and amino acids is a relative system referenced to glyceraldehyde. E/Z for alkenes: rank the two groups on each carbon; higher priorities on the same side is Z (zusammen), on opposite sides E (entgegen). R/S and D/L say nothing about the sign of rotation, which must be measured.
confusions: (R) does not mean (+); the sign of rotation is experimental. Swapping any two substituents on a stereocentre inverts its configuration. Enantiomers have equal and opposite specific rotations.

topics.name: Intermolecular forces: hydrogen bonding, dipole forces, and dispersion
know: Intermolecular forces are far weaker than covalent bonds but decide melting and boiling points, viscosity, surface tension, vapour pressure, and solubility. London dispersion forces (instantaneous dipole–induced dipole) act between all molecules and grow with size (more electrons are more polarizable) and surface area, which is why larger alkanes and I₂ are liquids or solids. Dipole–dipole forces act between polar molecules; ion–dipole forces hold ions in water.

Hydrogen bonding is an especially strong dipole interaction between a hydrogen bonded to N, O, or F and a lone pair on another N, O, or F. It explains water's high boiling point and why ice floats, the DNA double helix, α-helices and β-sheets, and why alcohols boil far above ethers of the same mass.

Typical ranking: ionic > ion–dipole > hydrogen bonding > dipole–dipole > dispersion, though for large molecules dispersion wins in total. Stronger intermolecular forces mean a higher boiling point, higher viscosity, and lower vapour pressure.
confusions: Hydrogen bonds are attractions between molecules, not covalent bonds within one. Unbranched chains boil higher than their branched isomers because they pack better and have more dispersion contact.

categories.name: Separation and purification
categories.summary: The lab methods that pull one compound out of a mixture: extraction, distillation, chromatography, the protein-purification toolkit, and resolving enantiomers.

topics.name: Extraction, distillation, and recrystallization
know: Liquid–liquid extraction partitions a compound between two immiscible solvents (water and an organic solvent such as ether) according to where it is more soluble, and acid–base chemistry does the sorting: wash the organic layer with aqueous base to pull an acid into the water as its salt (bicarbonate takes carboxylic acids; hydroxide takes phenols as well), or with aqueous acid to pull an amine in as its ammonium salt; then neutralize the aqueous layer to recover the compound. Several small extractions remove more than one large one. The denser layer is on the bottom, usually the aqueous one unless the organic solvent is chlorinated.

Distillation separates liquids by boiling point. Simple distillation works when the boiling points are far apart (lab manuals quote minimum gaps from about 25 °C up to 100 °C) or when the impurity is nonvolatile; fractional distillation adds a packed column that provides repeated vaporization–condensation cycles for closer boiling points; vacuum distillation lowers the boiling points of high-boiling or heat-sensitive compounds. An azeotrope boils at a fixed composition that distillation cannot change (ethanol–water at about 95.6% ethanol by mass), so ordinary distillation cannot give pure ethanol.

Recrystallization purifies a solid with a solvent that dissolves it hot but not cold, leaving impurities behind in the mother liquor. A sharp melting point at the literature value signals purity; impurities depress the melting point and widen the range.
confusions: A bicarbonate wash removes carboxylic acids but not most phenols (too weakly acidic); hydroxide removes both. Distillation separates by volatility, not by polarity.

topics.name: Chromatography: TLC, paper, column, gas, and HPLC
know: Every chromatography separates a mixture between a stationary phase and a mobile phase that moves past it; components that cling more to the stationary phase move more slowly. On a polar stationary phase (silica, alumina, paper) polar compounds move slowly and nonpolar ones quickly, and a more polar eluent speeds everything up. Reverse-phase HPLC uses a nonpolar (C18) stationary phase with a polar mobile phase, so the order flips.

Thin-layer chromatography (TLC): spots on a silica plate climb with the solvent; the retention factor R_f = distance moved by the spot / distance moved by the solvent front (between 0 and 1) is smaller for more polar compounds. TLC is the standard way to follow a reaction. Paper chromatography works the same way on cellulose. Column chromatography scales the idea up for purification, collecting fractions as they elute.

Gas chromatography vaporizes the sample into an inert carrier gas flowing through a coated column; components separate by volatility and affinity for the coating, with lower-boiling compounds eluting first, and the outlet is often a mass spectrometer (GC–MS). High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) pumps liquid at high pressure through a column of very fine particles for high-resolution separation of nonvolatile compounds, including drugs and peptides.
equations: R_f = \dfrac{\text{distance travelled by the spot}}{\text{distance travelled by the solvent front}}
confusions: A high R_f means a weakly retained (on silica, less polar) compound. Keep the phases straight: in TLC the plate is stationary and the solvent mobile.

topics.name: Protein purification and electrophoresis
know: Proteins are separated by size, charge, and binding. Size-exclusion (gel-filtration) chromatography: porous beads delay small proteins, so large ones elute first. Ion-exchange chromatography: a charged resin binds proteins of opposite charge (an anion exchanger binds proteins that are negative, i.e. at a pH above their pI); a salt gradient or pH change releases them, most strongly charged last. Affinity chromatography: a ligand on the beads (an antibody, a substrate analogue, nickel for His-tagged proteins) binds the target specifically; everything else washes through and the target is eluted with free ligand or a pH shift. Salting out with ammonium sulfate precipitates proteins by differences in solubility.

Electrophoresis moves charged molecules through a gel in an electric field. SDS–PAGE coats proteins with negative charge in proportion to their mass and unfolds them, so they separate by size alone, smaller proteins travelling farther; adding a reducing agent (β-mercaptoethanol or DTT) also breaks disulfide bonds. Native PAGE keeps the folded shape and separates by size and charge together. Isoelectric focusing runs proteins along a pH gradient until each stops where the pH equals its pI and it carries no net charge; a 2-D gel combines isoelectric focusing with SDS–PAGE. Agarose gels separate DNA fragments by length.

Quantitation and purity: absorbance at 280 nm (aromatic side chains) or a dye-binding assay such as Bradford gives protein concentration; specific activity (activity per milligram of protein) rises with each purification step while total yield falls; a single band on SDS–PAGE indicates purity. A Western blot identifies one protein with an antibody after transfer from the gel to a membrane.
confusions: In size-exclusion chromatography the largest proteins come out first; in SDS–PAGE the smallest run farthest. A protein is negatively charged above its pI and positively charged below it.

topics.name: Racemic mixtures and the resolution of enantiomers
know: A racemic mixture (equal amounts of two enantiomers) is optically inactive and forms whenever a reaction creates a stereocentre from achiral reactants with no chiral influence present. Enantiomers cannot be separated by ordinary distillation, crystallization, or chromatography because their physical properties are identical.

Resolution turns them into diastereomers, which do differ: react a racemic acid with a single enantiomer of a chiral base (or a racemic amine with a single-enantiomer chiral acid such as tartaric acid) to form diastereomeric salts, separate those by crystallization, then release each enantiomer with acid or base. Alternatives are chiral chromatography (a chiral stationary phase holds the two enantiomers differently) and enzymes, which act on only one enantiomer (kinetic resolution).

Enantiomeric excess, ee = (major − minor)/(major + minor) × 100%. The optical purity, the observed specific rotation divided by that of the pure enantiomer, times 100%, is in practice equal to the ee.
confusions: The resolving agent must itself be a single enantiomer; a racemic one gives a racemic set of diastereomers that cannot be separated.

categories.summary: The organic chemistry that living things are made of: nucleic acids, amino acids and proteins, lipids, sugars, and the carbonyl, alcohol, and acid chemistry that links them together.

topics.name: Nucleotides and nucleic acids
know: A nucleotide is a five-carbon sugar (ribose in RNA, 2′-deoxyribose in DNA) joined at C1′ to a nitrogenous base and at C5′ to one to three phosphates; without the phosphate it is a nucleoside. Purines (adenine, guanine) have two fused rings; pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine in DNA, uracil in RNA) have one. The backbone is sugar–phosphate, linked by phosphodiester bonds from the 3′-OH of one sugar to the 5′-phosphate of the next, so every strand has a direction (5′ → 3′) and is negatively charged at physiological pH.

DNA is two antiparallel strands wound into a right-handed double helix (the Watson–Crick B form), held by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases (A pairs with T through two, G with C through three) and, even more, by stacking of the flat bases. Chargaff's rule follows: A = T and G = C. GC-rich DNA melts (denatures) at a higher temperature, and separated strands reanneal on cooling, the basis of hybridization and PCR. RNA is usually single-stranded but folds back on itself into hairpins and more complex shapes (the tRNA cloverleaf, ribozymes); its 2′-OH makes it easier to hydrolyse than DNA.
Nucleotides also carry energy (ATP, GTP), form coenzymes (NAD⁺, FAD, coenzyme A), and act as second messengers (cAMP, cGMP).
confusions: Nucleoside = sugar + base; a nucleotide adds phosphate. Thymine is DNA-only and uracil RNA-only. The two strands are antiparallel: one runs 5′ → 3′ while its partner runs 3′ → 5′.

topics.name: Amino acids: structure, classification, and synthesis
know: The 20 proteinogenic amino acids share an α-carbon carrying an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen, and a variable side chain (R). All but glycine are chiral, and the natural ones have the L configuration (S by the sequence rules, except cysteine, whose sulfur makes it R). At physiological pH they are zwitterions (dipolar ions): the carboxyl is deprotonated (pKa about 2) and the amino group protonated (pKa about 9–10), so the net charge is zero even though both groups are charged.

Classify by side chain: nonpolar/hydrophobic (Gly, Ala, Val, Leu, Ile, Met, Pro, Phe, Trp); polar, uncharged/hydrophilic (Ser, Thr, Cys, Tyr, Asn, Gln); acidic (Asp, Glu, side-chain pKa about 4); basic (Lys, pKa about 10.5; Arg, about 12.5; His, about 6, the only side chain that buffers near physiological pH). Hydrophobic residues bury themselves in protein cores; charged and polar ones face the water.

Laboratory syntheses give racemic products. Strecker synthesis: an aldehyde reacts with ammonia and cyanide to give an α-aminonitrile, which acid hydrolysis converts to the α-amino acid. Gabriel (phthalimidomalonate) synthesis: potassium phthalimide displaces bromide from diethyl bromomalonate; the malonate α-carbon is then deprotonated and alkylated with the side-chain halide; hydrolysis of the imide and esters followed by decarboxylation releases the racemic amino acid. OpenStax teaches the closely related amidomalonate route, in which diethyl acetamidomalonate is alkylated and then hydrolysed.
confusions: Zwitterion means net charge zero, not uncharged. 'Acidic' and 'basic' amino acids are named for their side chains; every amino acid has one acidic and one basic group on the α-carbon.
