topics.name: Peptides and proteins: the peptide bond, hydrolysis, structure levels, and pI
know: A peptide bond is an amide between one amino acid's carboxyl group and the next one's amino group, formed by condensation (loss of water) on the ribosome. Resonance gives it partial double-bond character, so it is planar and rigid and almost always trans; rotation happens only at the φ and ψ bonds on either side. Peptides are written and numbered from the N-terminus to the C-terminus.

Hydrolysing peptide bonds takes strong acid or base with heat, or enzymes: trypsin cuts after Lys or Arg, chymotrypsin after Phe, Trp, or Tyr, and cyanogen bromide after Met. Two cysteine side chains can be oxidized to a disulfide (cystine), a covalent cross-link that stabilizes extracellular proteins and is broken by reducing agents.

Primary structure is the sequence. Secondary structure is local backbone folding held by backbone hydrogen bonds: the right-handed α-helix (3.6 residues per turn, each C=O bonded to the N–H four residues ahead) and β-sheets (parallel or antiparallel strands); proline and glycine tend to break helices. Tertiary structure is the full three-dimensional fold driven by side-chain interactions. The isoelectric point pI is the pH at which the net charge is zero: for a neutral side chain it is the average of the two α pKa values; for an acidic residue average the two lowest pKa values, for a basic residue the two highest.
equations: \mathrm{pI} \approx \dfrac{\mathrm{p}K_{a1} + \mathrm{p}K_{a2}}{2}\ \ \text{(the two } \mathrm{p}K_a \text{ values that bracket the neutral form)}
confusions: Below its pI a protein is positively charged; above it, negative. α-helix hydrogen bonds run along the backbone, not between side chains.

topics.name: Three-dimensional protein structure, stability, and folding
know: Tertiary structure is held by many weak interactions: the hydrophobic effect (nonpolar side chains cluster inside, away from water), hydrogen bonds, ionic salt bridges between charged side chains, van der Waals contacts, and sometimes covalent disulfide bonds. The hydrophobic effect is driven by entropy: water molecules that would be ordered in a solvation layer around exposed nonpolar groups are set free when those groups are buried, so the water's entropy rises even though the chain becomes more ordered.
Quaternary structure is the assembly of two or more folded chains (subunits) into one protein, as in hemoglobin (α₂β₂) and many enzymes; it makes cooperativity and allosteric regulation possible.

Denaturation unfolds a protein (losing secondary, tertiary, and quaternary structure but not its sequence) through heat, extreme pH, urea or guanidinium, detergents such as SDS, organic solvents, or heavy metals, and usually destroys function. Some proteins refold when the stress is removed: Anfinsen's ribonuclease experiment showed that the sequence alone can specify the fold. Chaperones assist folding in the crowded cell, and misfolded aggregates underlie prion and amyloid diseases.
confusions: Denaturation does not break peptide bonds; only hydrolysis does. A folded protein is only marginally more stable than its unfolded state, by tens of kJ/mol.

topics.name: Nonenzymatic protein function: binding, immune, and motor proteins
know: Binding proteins carry or store ligands reversibly: hemoglobin binds O₂ cooperatively (a sigmoidal curve) while myoglobin stores it (a hyperbolic curve); transferrin carries iron, albumin carries fatty acids and drugs; membrane receptors and transporters bind signals and substrates. Binding strength is described by the dissociation constant Kd: the lower the Kd, the tighter the binding.

Immune system: antibodies (immunoglobulins) are Y-shaped proteins of two heavy and two light chains joined by disulfides. The variable regions at the two tips form identical antigen-binding sites, while the constant region recruits complement and immune cells. Each B-cell clone makes antibodies of one specificity; binding can neutralize a pathogen, tag it for phagocytosis, or trigger complement.

Motor proteins convert ATP hydrolysis into movement: myosin walks along actin filaments (muscle contraction, cytokinesis); kinesin carries cargo toward the plus end of microtubules and dynein toward the minus end (vesicle transport, and the bending of cilia and flagella). Each has an ATP-binding head and a tail that holds cargo or another filament. Structural proteins (collagen, keratin, actin, tubulin) give shape and strength.
confusions: Myoglobin's oxygen affinity is higher than hemoglobin's at low partial pressures, which is why it can take oxygen from the blood. Kinesin and dynein travel in opposite directions along the same microtubule.

topics.name: Lipids: storage, structural, and signalling lipids
know: Storage: triacylglycerols are glycerol esterified with three fatty acids; they are nonpolar, hold the most energy per gram of any fuel (about 9 kcal/g), and are stored in adipose tissue. Fatty acids are long hydrocarbon chains ending in a carboxyl: saturated chains pack tightly (solid fats), while cis double bonds kink unsaturated chains and lower melting points (oils). Saponification, hydrolysis of a triacylglycerol with hot base, gives glycerol plus fatty acid salts (soap), which form micelles with polar heads outward and tails inward.

Structural: glycerophospholipids (phosphatides) have glycerol with two fatty acids and a phosphate that carries a polar head group (choline, ethanolamine, serine, inositol); sphingolipids are built on sphingosine instead (sphingomyelin in myelin; cerebrosides and gangliosides carry sugars). Both are amphipathic and form the lipid bilayer. Waxes are esters of a long-chain fatty acid with a long-chain alcohol, used for waterproofing.

Signals and cofactors: the fat-soluble vitamins A (retinal in vision), D (calcium and phosphate balance), E (antioxidant), and K (blood clotting). Steroids share four fused rings (three six-membered and one five-membered); cholesterol moderates membrane fluidity and is the precursor of steroid hormones (cortisol, aldosterone, estrogens, testosterone) and bile acids. Prostaglandins are 20-carbon eicosanoids made from arachidonic acid by cyclooxygenases; they act locally on inflammation, platelet aggregation, blood pressure, and smooth muscle such as the uterus, which is why NSAIDs that block COX reduce them.
confusions: Cholesterol has no glycerol backbone and is not a fat; it makes membranes less fluid when warm but more fluid when cold. Trans fats pack like saturated fats despite being unsaturated.

topics.name: Carbohydrates: monosaccharides, rings, anomers, and polysaccharides
know: Monosaccharides are polyhydroxy aldehydes (aldoses) or ketones (ketoses), named by carbon count (triose, pentose, hexose): glucose, galactose, and mannose are aldohexoses, fructose is a ketohexose, ribose an aldopentose. In a Fischer projection the stereocentre farthest from the carbonyl sets D (OH on the right) or L; almost all natural sugars are D. Epimers differ at exactly one stereocentre (glucose and galactose at C4, glucose and mannose at C2).

In water one of a sugar's own hydroxyls adds to its carbonyl to make a cyclic hemiacetal: glucose's C5-OH gives a six-membered pyranose, while fructose's C5-OH (on its C2 ketone) or ribose's C4-OH gives a five-membered furanose. Ring closure creates a new stereocentre, the anomeric carbon (C1 of an aldose): in a Haworth projection the α anomer has the anomeric OH down (trans to the CH₂OH) and the β anomer has it up (and equatorial in the chair). Anomers interconvert through the open-chain form (mutarotation). Only the open aldehyde form reduces Tollens' or Benedict's reagent, so any sugar with a free anomeric carbon is a reducing sugar. In base, keto–enol tautomerism through an enediol interconverts glucose, fructose, and mannose.

A glycosidic bond is an acetal between an anomeric carbon and another hydroxyl; it is stable to base but hydrolysed by acid or by specific enzymes. Disaccharides: maltose (glucose α-1,4 glucose), lactose (galactose β-1,4 glucose), sucrose (glucose α-1,2 fructose, both anomeric carbons tied up, so non-reducing). Polysaccharides: starch (amylose, linear α-1,4; amylopectin with α-1,6 branches), glycogen (α-1,4 with more frequent α-1,6 branches; animal storage), and cellulose (linear β-1,4 chains hydrogen-bonded into fibres that humans cannot digest).
confusions: α and β describe the anomeric carbon; D and L describe the stereocentre farthest from the carbonyl. Humans digest α-glycosidic links (starch) but not cellulose's β-1,4 links, although lactase does cut lactose's β-1,4 bond.

topics.name: Aldehydes and ketones: properties, nucleophilic addition, and oxidation
know: Aldehydes (RCHO, suffix -al) and ketones (RCOR′, suffix -one) have a polar, planar sp² carbonyl: the carbon is electrophilic and the oxygen accepts hydrogen bonds, so they boil above alkanes but below alcohols and the small ones dissolve in water. Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones (less steric hindrance and only one electron-donating alkyl group).

Nucleophilic addition: a nucleophile attacks the carbonyl carbon, the oxygen becomes an alkoxide, and protonation gives an alcohol. Water gives a hydrate (gem-diol); one alcohol gives a hemiacetal and a second alcohol, with acid, an acetal (the chemistry of sugar rings and glycosidic bonds; acetals also serve as protecting groups because they survive base and nucleophiles but open in aqueous acid). A primary amine gives an imine (C=N, a Schiff base) and a secondary amine an enamine, both through a carbinolamine that loses water, fastest near pH 4–5. Hydride reagents (NaBH₄ for aldehydes and ketones; LiAlH₄ also reduces esters and acids) give alcohols; Grignard reagents give alcohols with a new C–C bond; HCN gives a cyanohydrin.

Oxidation: aldehydes oxidize readily to carboxylic acids (chromic acid or KMnO₄, or the mild Tollens' Ag⁺ and Benedict's Cu²⁺ reagents, which double as tests). Ketones resist oxidation because the carbonyl carbon has no hydrogen.
confusions: A hemiacetal has an OH and an OR on the same carbon; an acetal has two OR groups. Imine formation needs a primary amine; a secondary amine has no second N–H to lose and gives an enamine instead.

topics.name: Enols, enolates, aldol chemistry, and kinetic versus thermodynamic enolates
know: Hydrogens on the carbon next to a carbonyl (α-hydrogens) are weakly acidic (pKa about 19–20 for a ketone, about 9–11 for a 1,3-dicarbonyl) because the conjugate base is a resonance-stabilized enolate with the negative charge shared by oxygen. Base removes an α-H to give the enolate; acid catalyses formation of the enol. Keto and enol forms are tautomers (constitutional isomers that interconvert by moving a proton and a double bond), and the keto form is almost always favoured unless the enol is conjugated or internally hydrogen-bonded.

Consequences: a stereocentre at the α-carbon racemizes through the planar enol or enolate; α-halogenation and alkylation go through the enolate. The aldol reaction joins two carbonyl compounds: an enolate adds to another carbonyl carbon to give a β-hydroxy carbonyl, which dehydrates on heating to a conjugated α,β-unsaturated carbonyl; the retro-aldol reaction runs backward (aldolase in glycolysis does both). Enolates also drive Claisen condensations of esters and Michael additions.

Kinetic versus thermodynamic enolate: a strong, bulky base (LDA) at low temperature removes the more accessible, less hindered α-H fastest, giving the kinetic enolate (less substituted double bond); a weaker base at higher temperature lets the system equilibrate to the more substituted, more stable thermodynamic enolate. Electron-withdrawing substituents make α-hydrogens more acidic; steric hindrance slows both enolate formation and addition.
confusions: Only α-hydrogens are enolizable; an aldehyde's C–H on the carbonyl carbon is not acidic. Aldol products keep both carbonyl carbons; β-hydroxy means the OH sits two carbons from the carbonyl.

topics.name: Alcohols: acidity, oxidation, substitution, protection, and sulfonate esters
know: Alcohols (R–OH, suffix -ol) are primary, secondary, or tertiary according to the carbon that carries the OH. Hydrogen bonding gives them high boiling points and, for small ones, water solubility. They are weak acids (pKa about 16–18; phenols about 10, far more acidic because the phenoxide is resonance-stabilized); electron-withdrawing groups raise acidity and alkyl groups lower it. Their conjugate bases, alkoxides, are strong bases.

Oxidation: primary alcohols go to aldehydes with a mild reagent (PCC) and on to carboxylic acids with strong oxidants (CrO₃/H₂SO₄, KMnO₄); secondary alcohols give ketones; tertiary alcohols cannot be oxidized without breaking a C–C bond. The reverse, carbonyl reduction with NaBH₄ or LiAlH₄, regenerates the alcohol.

Hydroxide is a poor leaving group, so substitution needs activation: protonation (SN1 for tertiary and secondary alcohols with HX; SN2 for primary), conversion to a mesylate (MsCl) or tosylate (TsCl), which leaves the stereocentre untouched and installs an excellent leaving group for SN2 with inversion, or reagents such as SOCl₂ and PBr₃. Protection: an alcohol can be masked as a silyl ether (TBDMS, removed with fluoride) or an acetal so that it survives a Grignard or hydride step, then unmasked.
confusions: Making a mesylate or tosylate does not touch the C–O bond, so the stereocentre keeps its configuration; the SN2 displacement that follows inverts it. PCC stops at the aldehyde; aqueous chromic acid does not.

topics.name: Carboxylic acids: acidity, derivatives, reduction, decarboxylation, and α-substitution
know: Carboxylic acids (RCOOH, suffix -oic acid) hydrogen-bond as dimers, giving high boiling points, and are the most acidic common organic group (pKa about 4–5) because the carboxylate's charge is delocalized over two oxygens. Electron-withdrawing substituents near the carboxyl (halogens, nitro groups) raise the acidity, and acids dissolve in aqueous bicarbonate as their salts.

Reactions at the carbonyl: with an alcohol and an acid catalyst they form esters (Fischer esterification, an equilibrium driven by removing water); an intramolecular ester is a lactone. With an amine (after activation, or on heating the ammonium salt) they form amides; the cyclic version is a lactam. Two acid molecules can condense to an anhydride. LiAlH₄ reduces an acid to a primary alcohol; NaBH₄ does not.

Decarboxylation: β-keto acids and malonic acids lose CO₂ on gentle heating through a cyclic transition state (the basis of the acetoacetic and malonic ester syntheses and of several metabolic steps); ordinary acids do not decarboxylate easily. Substitution at the α (2-) position: the Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky reaction (Br₂ with PBr₃) brominates the α-carbon, and the product can be converted to α-hydroxy or α-amino acids.
confusions: Esterification is reversible; the same acid catalyst with excess water hydrolyses the ester. Only acids with a second carbonyl two carbons away (β) decarboxylate readily.

topics.name: Acid derivatives: nucleophilic acyl substitution, relative reactivity, and strain
know: Carboxylic acid derivatives share the RCO–Z pattern: acid halides (-oyl chloride), anhydrides (-oic anhydride), esters (alkyl -oate), and amides (-amide). They react by nucleophilic acyl substitution: a nucleophile adds to the carbonyl to form a tetrahedral intermediate, which then expels the leaving group Z. Reactivity follows how good a leaving group Z is (a weaker base leaves more easily): acid chloride > anhydride > ester ≈ acid > amide. A more reactive derivative can be converted into any less reactive one, but not the reverse without activation.

Esters form from acid chlorides or anhydrides with alcohols, or by Fischer esterification, and are hydrolysed by aqueous acid (reversibly) or by base (saponification, irreversible because the carboxylate forms). Transesterification swaps the alkoxy group using another alcohol with acid or base catalysis (how biodiesel is made). Amides are the least reactive and need prolonged heating in strong acid or base to hydrolyse; amide resonance (the nitrogen lone pair delocalized into the carbonyl) explains that and also why the peptide bond is stable and planar.

Steric and electronic effects: bulky groups near the carbonyl slow attack, electron-withdrawing groups speed it. Ring strain makes cyclic derivatives more reactive: the four-membered β-lactam ring of penicillins and cephalosporins is so strained that it acylates the bacterial transpeptidase and shuts it down.
confusions: Base hydrolysis of an ester consumes one equivalent of hydroxide and gives a carboxylate, not the free acid, until the mixture is acidified. Because amides are more stable than esters, an acid chloride plus an amine gives an amide, but an amide plus an alcohol does not give an ester.

topics.name: Phenols, hydroquinones, and ubiquinones as two-electron redox centres
know: A phenol (an OH on an aromatic ring) is a weak acid (pKa about 10) that dissolves in aqueous NaOH but not in bicarbonate, and its ring is strongly activated toward electrophilic substitution. Phenols oxidize easily: 1,4-dihydroxybenzene (hydroquinone) is converted by mild oxidants to the 1,4-dione, p-benzoquinone, and the reverse reduction is just as easy, so the pair is a reversible two-electron, two-proton redox couple.

Ubiquinone (coenzyme Q) is a benzoquinone with a long isoprenoid tail that keeps it in the inner mitochondrial membrane. It accepts two electrons and two protons from complexes I and II to become ubiquinol and passes the electrons on to complex III; it can also carry one electron at a time as the semiquinone radical. Vitamin K and plastoquinone work the same way.

The antioxidant action of phenols such as vitamin E and the food preservative BHT comes from donating a hydrogen atom to a radical, leaving a resonance-stabilized phenoxyl radical that does little harm.
confusions: Phenols are more acidic than alcohols but less acidic than carboxylic acids, which is why extraction with bicarbonate and then hydroxide separates the three. Quinone/hydroquinone is a two-electron carrier; NAD⁺ takes a hydride, FAD can take electrons one at a time.

topics.name: Polycyclic and heterocyclic aromatic compounds in biology
know: Aromaticity needs a planar, fully conjugated ring with 4n + 2 π electrons (Hückel's rule). In pyridine the nitrogen's lone pair sits in an sp² orbital in the ring plane, outside the π system, so pyridine is a reasonable base (conjugate acid pKa about 5). In pyrrole the lone pair is part of the six-electron aromatic sextet, so pyrrole is a very weak base and its ring is electron-rich. Imidazole has one nitrogen of each kind; histidine's imidazole (pKa about 6) is a physiological buffer and a catalytic residue.

Biology runs on aromatic heterocycles: the purines (adenine, guanine; a pyrimidine fused to an imidazole) and pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine, uracil) of nucleic acids; the indole of tryptophan, serotonin, and melatonin; the porphyrin ring of heme and chlorophyll; the pyridinium of nicotinamide in NAD⁺ (reduced at C4 of the ring) and the flavin ring of FAD; thiamine (a thiazolium) and pyridoxal (vitamin B6).

Polycyclic aromatics (naphthalene, anthracene, benzo[a]pyrene) are fused benzene rings; some become carcinogens after metabolic activation to epoxides that alkylate DNA. The flat aromatic bases stack inside the DNA helix, and intercalating drugs are flat aromatics that slide between them.
confusions: Pyridine's nitrogen is basic; pyrrole's is not, because protonating it would destroy the aromaticity. Furan and thiophene are aromatic because one lone pair on the O or S counts toward the sextet.

categories.name: Thermodynamics and kinetics
categories.summary: Enzymes and the energy accounting of the cell, then the general rules behind them: the laws of thermodynamics, heat and enthalpy, free energy and phases, reaction rates, and equilibrium.

topics.name: Enzymes: classification, mechanism, and cofactors
know: Enzymes are protein catalysts (a few RNAs, the ribozymes, also catalyse) that speed a reaction by lowering its activation energy without changing the equilibrium or ΔG. Classes by reaction type: oxidoreductases (redox), transferases (move a group; kinases), hydrolases (cleave with water; proteases, lipases), lyases (break bonds without water or redox, often leaving a double bond or ring; run in the bond-forming direction they are often named synthases), isomerases (rearrange), ligases (join two molecules using ATP; DNA ligase), and translocases (move molecules across membranes).

The substrate binds the active site, a pocket whose shape and chemistry fit the substrate (specificity) and fit the transition state even better. Induced fit: binding reshapes the enzyme around the substrate. Catalytic strategies include acid–base catalysis by side chains, covalent intermediates (the serine proteases), metal ions, and holding the reactants in the right orientation and proximity.

Many enzymes need helpers, called cofactors: inorganic ions (Mg²⁺, Zn²⁺, Fe²⁺) or organic coenzymes, usually derived from water-soluble vitamins (NAD⁺ from niacin, FAD from riboflavin, coenzyme A from pantothenate, pyridoxal phosphate from B6, thiamine pyrophosphate from B1); a tightly bound one is a prosthetic group (heme). Apoenzyme plus cofactor makes the active holoenzyme.
confusions: An enzyme speeds the forward and reverse reactions equally; it changes how fast equilibrium is reached, not where it lies. Kinases add phosphate from ATP, phosphatases remove it by hydrolysis, phosphorylases break bonds using inorganic phosphate.

topics.name: Enzyme kinetics: Michaelis–Menten, Lineweaver–Burk, cooperativity, and conditions
know: At a fixed enzyme concentration the initial rate v₀ rises with substrate concentration and levels off at Vmax when every active site is occupied. Michaelis–Menten: v₀ = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]). Km is the substrate concentration that gives half of Vmax and reflects affinity (lower Km, tighter binding). Vmax = kcat[E]total, where kcat, the turnover number, is reactions per enzyme molecule per second, and kcat/Km measures catalytic efficiency. When [S] ≪ Km the rate is proportional to [S]; when [S] ≫ Km it is independent of [S] (saturation).
A Lineweaver–Burk (double-reciprocal) plot of 1/v₀ against 1/[S] is a straight line with y-intercept 1/Vmax, x-intercept −1/Km, and slope Km/Vmax, which makes the effect of an inhibitor easy to read.

Cooperativity: in multi-subunit enzymes (and hemoglobin) one subunit's binding changes the others' affinity, giving a sigmoidal rather than hyperbolic curve; a Hill coefficient above 1 means positive cooperativity. Local conditions matter: each enzyme has an optimal temperature and pH (pepsin near 2, trypsin near 8); rate rises with temperature until the enzyme unfolds, and pH changes the protonation of catalytic groups. Salt concentration and solvent also affect activity.
confusions: Km is not the enzyme concentration and not Vmax/2; it is the substrate concentration at which v₀ = Vmax/2. Doubling the enzyme doubles Vmax and leaves Km unchanged.

refs.label: OpenStax Biology 2e, 6.5 Enzymes

topics.name: Enzyme inhibition and regulation
know: Reversible inhibitors bind noncovalently. Competitive: binds the active site in competition with substrate, raises the apparent Km, leaves Vmax unchanged, and is overcome by more substrate (Lineweaver–Burk lines cross on the y-axis). Noncompetitive: binds a separate site whether or not substrate is bound, lowers Vmax, leaves Km unchanged (lines cross on the x-axis). Uncompetitive: binds only the enzyme–substrate complex and lowers both Vmax and Km (parallel lines). Mixed inhibition changes both. Irreversible inhibitors bond covalently (aspirin to cyclooxygenase, organophosphates to acetylcholinesterase, penicillin to transpeptidase).

Regulatory enzymes sit at committed steps. Allosteric enzymes have regulatory sites separate from the active site; effectors shift the balance between a low-activity (T) and a high-activity (R) conformation, giving sigmoidal kinetics. Feedback inhibition by a pathway's end product is the classic case: ATP inhibits phosphofructokinase-1 while AMP activates it.

Covalent modification: reversible phosphorylation by kinases and dephosphorylation by phosphatases switches enzymes on or off (glycogen phosphorylase is activated by phosphorylation, glycogen synthase inactivated); acetylation, methylation, and ubiquitination are others. Zymogens (proenzymes such as trypsinogen, pepsinogen, and prothrombin) are switched on irreversibly by proteolytic cleavage, and the amount of an enzyme is also set by transcription and degradation.
confusions: Only competitive inhibition is overcome by adding substrate. Noncompetitive lowers Vmax with Km unchanged; uncompetitive lowers both; the Lineweaver–Burk intercepts tell them apart.

topics.name: Bioenergetics: free energy, Keq, and ATP
know: The free-energy change decides whether a reaction can go: ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q, and at equilibrium ΔG = 0, so ΔG° = −RT ln Keq. Biochemists use ΔG°′ (standard conditions at pH 7). A reaction with a positive ΔG°′ still runs forward in the cell if the real concentrations make Q small enough (reactants kept high, products removed), which is how several steps of glycolysis proceed.

ATP hydrolysis to ADP and Pi has ΔG°′ ≈ −30.5 kJ/mol (about −7.3 kcal/mol) and about −50 to −60 kJ/mol at cellular concentrations, because the products relieve the charge repulsion between the phosphates, gain resonance stabilization, and are better solvated. Cells couple it to unfavourable reactions not by releasing heat but by group transfer: ATP donates a phosphoryl group to a substrate (making a phosphorylated intermediate) or to a protein (kinases), or an AMP group in activation steps, where the pyrophosphate released is hydrolysed to pull the step forward.

Phosphoryl-transfer potential: phosphoenolpyruvate and 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate release more free energy than ATP on hydrolysis, so they can make ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation; creatine phosphate buffers ATP in muscle; glucose 6-phosphate is lower on the scale. The ΔG°′ values of coupled reactions add.
confusions: ATP is not a long-term energy store, and its phosphoanhydride bonds are not unusually strong; energy is released because the products are more stable than ATP. ΔG°′ is a constant; ΔG depends on the actual concentrations.

topics.name: Biological oxidation–reduction: half-reactions, electron carriers, and flavoproteins
know: Biological oxidations move electrons from fuel molecules to oxygen in steps, each a redox pair written as a reduction half-reaction with a standard reduction potential E°′ (at pH 7). Electrons flow spontaneously from the pair with the more negative E°′ to the one with the more positive, and ΔG°′ = −nFΔE°′. From NAD⁺/NADH (E°′ ≈ −0.32 V) to O₂/H₂O (about +0.82 V) spans about 1.14 V, roughly 220 kJ per mole of NADH.

Soluble carriers: NAD⁺ accepts a hydride (two electrons and one proton) to become NADH, used mainly in catabolism; NADPH is the reductant for biosynthesis and antioxidant defence. Flavoproteins carry FAD or FMN, which can accept one or two electrons at a time (through a semiquinone) and stay bound to their enzymes (succinate dehydrogenase, acyl-CoA dehydrogenase); they feed electrons into the respiratory chain below NADH's level. Ubiquinone and the cytochromes (heme iron cycling between Fe³⁺ and Fe²⁺, one electron at a time) carry electrons within the membrane.

In organic terms, a carbon is oxidized when it gains bonds to oxygen or loses bonds to hydrogen (alcohol → aldehyde → acid) and reduced in the reverse direction. Count electrons: an NAD⁺-linked dehydrogenation removes two hydrogens from the substrate.
confusions: A more positive E°′ means a stronger electron acceptor; oxygen is the final acceptor because its potential is the most positive. NADH carries two electrons but only one of the two protons removed; FADH₂ carries both.

topics.name: Systems, state functions, and the laws of thermodynamics
know: A system is the part of the universe under study; the surroundings are everything else. State functions (internal energy U, enthalpy H, entropy S, free energy G, and P, V, T) depend only on the current state, not on the path; heat q and work w are not state functions. Zeroth law: two bodies each in thermal equilibrium with a third are in equilibrium with each other, which is what makes temperature a meaningful quantity.

First law: energy is conserved, ΔU = q + w, with q positive when heat enters the system and w positive when work is done on it (physics texts write ΔU = Q − W with W the work done by the system). The work of a gas is the area under its P–V curve; expansion at constant pressure does work PΔV. Isothermal: ΔU = 0, so heat in equals work out. Adiabatic: q = 0. Isochoric (constant volume): no work, so ΔU = q. A cycle returns to the same U.

Second law: in any spontaneous process the entropy of the universe increases (ΔS_system + ΔS_surroundings > 0). Entropy measures how many microscopic arrangements a state has (disorder, dispersal of energy), in J/K, and ΔS = q_rev/T for a reversible transfer. Entropy rises from solid to liquid to gas, with more moles of gas, with dissolving, with temperature, and with larger, more complex molecules. Heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold, and no engine can turn heat entirely into work. Third law: a perfect crystal at 0 K has zero entropy, so absolute entropies can be tabulated.
equations: w = -P\,\Delta V\ \text{(work done on a gas at constant pressure)}
confusions: Sign conventions differ: chemistry writes ΔU = q + w with w as work done on the system, physics writes ΔU = Q − W with W as work done by the system. A system's entropy can fall (water freezing) as long as the surroundings gain more.

topics.name: Heat capacity, calorimetry, heat transfer, and thermal expansion
know: Heat capacity C (J/K) is the heat that raises an object's temperature by 1 K; specific heat c (J/(g·K)) is per gram and molar heat capacity per mole, so q = mcΔT. Water's specific heat, 4.184 J/(g·K), is unusually high, which is why it buffers body and climate temperatures. During a phase change the temperature holds steady and q = mL (the latent heat).

Calorimetry measures heat by trapping it. In a coffee-cup (constant-pressure) calorimeter the heat released by a reaction warms the solution, q_reaction = −q_solution = −mcΔT, which gives ΔH directly. A bomb calorimeter (constant volume) measures ΔU and is used for food energy (1 nutritional Calorie = 1 kcal = 4184 J). When two bodies exchange heat, what one loses the other gains.

Heat transfer: conduction passes energy through contact by molecular collisions, at a rate kAΔT/d (metals conduct well, air and fat poorly); convection carries it by bulk fluid motion (blood bringing heat to the skin, warm air rising); radiation emits electromagnetic energy from any body above 0 K, at a rate growing as T⁴, with no medium needed. Evaporation also removes heat (sweating). Thermal expansion: most materials expand on heating, ΔL = αL₀ΔT for length and about 3α for volume; water is anomalous, densest at 4 °C.
confusions: A high specific heat means the temperature changes slowly for a given heat input. Latent heat is taken up at constant temperature, so steam at 100 °C delivers far more energy to skin than water at 100 °C.

topics.name: Enthalpy, heats of formation, Hess's law, and bond energies
know: Enthalpy H = U + PV; at constant pressure the heat of a reaction equals ΔH. Exothermic reactions release heat (ΔH < 0: combustion, neutralization, most bond-forming steps); endothermic reactions absorb it (ΔH > 0: melting, evaporation, dissolving ammonium nitrate). ΔH scales with the amount reacting and changes sign when the reaction is reversed.

The standard enthalpy of formation ΔH°f is the enthalpy change for making one mole of a compound from its elements in their standard states (1 bar, usually 25 °C); an element in its standard state has ΔH°f = 0. For any reaction ΔH°rxn = Σ ΔH°f(products) − Σ ΔH°f(reactants), each weighted by its coefficient. Standard heats of combustion and of neutralization are tabulated the same way.

Hess's law: because H is a state function, ΔH for an overall reaction is the sum of ΔH for any steps that add up to it (reverse a step to flip its sign, scale it to match the coefficients). Bond dissociation energy is the enthalpy to break one mole of a given bond in the gas phase, always positive; ΔH°rxn ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed), an estimate because tabulated values are averages.
confusions: Bond-energy sums run broken minus formed; formation-enthalpy sums run products minus reactants. Breaking a bond always costs energy; energy is released when a bond forms.

topics.name: Gibbs free energy, spontaneity, phase changes, and phase diagrams
know: Gibbs free energy combines both drives: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, with T in kelvin. ΔG < 0 means spontaneous (exergonic) in the forward direction, ΔG > 0 nonspontaneous (endergonic), ΔG = 0 at equilibrium. Four cases: ΔH < 0 with ΔS > 0 is spontaneous at every temperature; ΔH > 0 with ΔS < 0 never; ΔH < 0 with ΔS < 0 only at low temperature; ΔH > 0 with ΔS > 0 only at high temperature, with the crossover at T = ΔH/ΔS. ΔG° refers to standard states and gives K through ΔG° = −RT ln K; under actual conditions ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q.

Phase changes: melting (fusion) and vaporization are endothermic with positive ΔS, so they become spontaneous above the transition temperature, where ΔG = 0 and T = ΔH/ΔS. Water's heat of fusion is 334 J/g (6.01 kJ/mol) and its heat of vaporization 2260 J/g (40.7 kJ/mol); vaporization costs more because every intermolecular attraction must be broken. Vapour pressure rises with temperature, and a liquid boils when its vapour pressure reaches the external pressure, so water boils below 100 °C at altitude.

A phase diagram maps the stable phase against pressure and temperature: the solid–liquid, liquid–gas, and solid–gas lines meet at the triple point, where all three coexist, and the liquid–gas line ends at the critical point, beyond which there is only a supercritical fluid. Crossing the liquid–gas line is boiling or condensation, the solid–gas line sublimation or deposition. Water's solid–liquid line leans left (negative slope) because ice is less dense than liquid water, so pressure melts ice; for most substances it leans right. Spontaneous does not mean fast: ΔG says nothing about rate.
confusions: A negative ΔG means thermodynamically favourable, not fast (diamond turning to graphite is spontaneous). Use kelvin in ΔG = ΔH − TΔS and match the units: ΔH is usually in kJ, ΔS in J/K.

topics.name: Reaction rates, rate laws, reaction order, and the rate-determining step
know: Reaction rate is the change in concentration per unit time (M/s), defined to be positive and divided by the stoichiometric coefficient: for aA → bB, rate = −(1/a)Δ[A]/Δt = (1/b)Δ[B]/Δt. Rates depend on concentration, temperature, physical state and surface area, and catalysts.

The rate law, rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, is found by experiment, not read off the coefficients: compare initial rates in trials where one concentration changes (doubling [A] doubles the rate if first order, quadruples it if second, does nothing if zero order). The overall order is m + n and sets the units of k (s⁻¹ for first order, M⁻¹s⁻¹ for second, M/s for zero). Integrated forms: zero order [A] = [A]₀ − kt (a plot of [A] against t is linear); first order ln[A] = ln[A]₀ − kt (ln[A] against t is linear, and the half-life 0.693/k is constant); second order 1/[A] = 1/[A]₀ + kt (1/[A] against t is linear).

Most reactions occur through elementary steps, whose rate laws do follow their molecularity. The slowest step is rate-determining: the overall rate law contains the species in that step and any fast equilibria before it, with intermediates substituted out. A proposed mechanism must add up to the overall equation and match the measured rate law.
confusions: Orders come from data, not from the balanced equation (except for a single elementary step). A catalyst or intermediate can appear in the rate law for the slow step even though it is absent from the overall equation.

topics.name: Activation energy, energy profiles, Arrhenius, catalysts, and kinetic versus thermodynamic control
know: Collision theory: reactants must meet with at least the activation energy Ea and in the right orientation. The transition state (activated complex) is the highest-energy point along the reaction coordinate, and Ea is its height above the reactants. On an energy profile ΔH (or ΔG) is the gap between products and reactants, the forward and reverse activation energies differ by that gap, and each valley between peaks is an intermediate. Arrhenius: k = A·e^(−Ea/RT), so raising the temperature or lowering Ea speeds the reaction exponentially; a plot of ln k against 1/T is a line of slope −Ea/R.

A catalyst supplies a different pathway with a lower Ea (enzymes, acids, metal surfaces) and speeds the forward and reverse reactions equally. It is regenerated and does not change ΔG, ΔH, K, or the equilibrium position, only how fast equilibrium is reached.

Kinetic versus thermodynamic control: when two products are possible, the one with the lower activation barrier forms fastest (the kinetic product, favoured at low temperature, short times, and irreversible conditions), while the more stable one (the thermodynamic product, lower G) wins when the reaction is reversible and given time or heat to equilibrate. The classic case is HBr adding to 1,3-butadiene: at 0 °C the faster-formed 1,2-adduct dominates (about 71:29), at 40 °C the more stable 1,4-adduct (about 15:85).
confusions: A large negative ΔG does not imply a small Ea. Hammond postulate: a transition state resembles whichever species is closer to it in energy, so exothermic steps have early, reactant-like transition states.

topics.name: Chemical equilibrium: the equilibrium constant, Le Châtelier, and ΔG°
know: A reversible reaction reaches equilibrium when the forward and reverse rates are equal; concentrations then stop changing even though both reactions continue. Law of mass action: for aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, K = [C]^c[D]^d / ([A]^a[B]^b), with pure solids and liquids left out, and gases written as partial pressures (Kp) or concentrations (Kc, with Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn). K depends only on temperature. K ≫ 1 means products dominate, K ≪ 1 reactants. Reversing a reaction inverts K, multiplying its coefficients raises K to that power, and adding reactions multiplies their K values.

The reaction quotient Q uses the current concentrations in the same expression: Q < K and the reaction moves forward, Q > K backward, Q = K is equilibrium. Le Châtelier: a system at equilibrium shifts to partly undo a disturbance. Adding a reactant or removing a product shifts right; raising the pressure by shrinking the volume favours the side with fewer moles of gas; raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction (treat heat as a reactant of an endothermic reaction), and temperature is the only change that alters K itself. Adding an inert gas at constant volume, or a catalyst, leaves the position unchanged.

ΔG° = −RT ln K links thermodynamics to equilibrium: a negative ΔG° means K > 1. At 25 °C every −5.7 kJ/mol of ΔG° multiplies K by 10. For redox reactions the same K also connects to the standard cell potential (see galvanic cells).
confusions: A catalyst changes the rate, never K. Compressing a mixture with equal moles of gas on both sides does not shift it. Temperature is the only disturbance that changes K.

skills.name: Knowledge of Scientific Concepts and Principles
skills.what: Do you know the concept and can you recognize it in a new setting? These questions test recall and understanding of principles, relationships, and representations: a formula, a definition, a trend, a diagram.
skills.example: A question might describe a vessel narrowing and ask which quantity stays constant along it, expecting you to recognize the continuity principle for an incompressible fluid.

skills.name: Scientific Reasoning and Problem-solving
skills.what: Can you use the concept to work something out? These questions ask you to apply a principle to a situation in the passage, combine two ideas, run a calculation, or predict what changes when a variable changes.
skills.example: Given the radius and length of two tubes and the same pressure difference, a question might ask how many times greater the flow is in the wider one, expecting a Poiseuille's-law ratio rather than a memorized fact.

skills.name: Reasoning about the Design and Execution of Research
skills.what: Do you understand how the study in the passage was done, and what it can and cannot show? These questions ask about variables, controls, the purpose of a step in a procedure, sources of error, and whether a conclusion follows from the design.
skills.example: After a passage describing a calibration curve, a question might ask why the researchers measured a blank solution first, expecting you to identify it as the control for background absorbance.

skills.name: Data-based and Statistical Reasoning
skills.what: Can you read the data and judge what it supports? These questions ask you to interpret a figure or table, find a trend, estimate a value, compare error bars, and decide whether a difference is meaningful.
skills.example: Given a table of reaction rates at several concentrations, a question might ask for the order of the reaction with respect to one reactant, expecting you to spot that doubling it quadrupled the rate.

research_methods.name: Study designs
know: In an experiment the researcher sets the independent variable and measures the dependent one, with other factors held constant; random assignment to groups lets the result be read as causal. Observational designs (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional) measure what already varies and can show association but not causation on their own.
In the lab, a well-designed experiment changes one variable at a time, repeats each measurement (replicates), and includes controls.

research_methods.name: Variables and controls
know: Independent variable: what is manipulated. Dependent variable: what is measured. Controlled variables: held constant. A confounding variable changes along with the independent variable and offers a rival explanation for the result.

A negative control is a sample expected to show no effect (a blank, a vehicle-only sample, an untreated group); a positive control is one known to respond and proves the method works. A placebo controls for expectation; blinding keeps participants (single) or participants and researchers (double) from knowing who got what.

research_methods.name: Validity and reliability
know: Reliability is consistency: repeated measurements agree (precision). Validity is whether the measurement captures what it claims to (accuracy against the true value, in lab terms). A method can be reliable without being valid: a miscalibrated balance gives the same wrong mass every time.
Internal validity: the result is really due to the manipulated variable rather than a confounder. External validity: the finding generalizes beyond the sample and setting studied.

research_methods.name: Sampling and bias
know: A random sample gives every member of the population an equal chance of inclusion, so the sample resembles the population; larger samples make estimates more precise but do not fix a biased selection.

Selection bias comes from how participants or samples are chosen; measurement bias from a systematic error in the instrument or procedure (a consistently offset reading is systematic error, scatter around the true value is random error). Random error shrinks with more measurements; systematic error does not.

research_methods.name: Correlation and causation
know: A correlation (two variables move together) can arise from direct cause, reverse cause, a third variable driving both, or chance. Only a controlled experiment with random assignment can establish cause; a dose–response relationship and a plausible mechanism strengthen the case.
The correlation coefficient r runs from −1 to +1 and reports the strength and direction of a linear relationship; it says nothing about slope or cause.

research_methods.name: Descriptive statistics
know: Mean is the arithmetic average and is pulled by outliers; median is the middle value and resists them; mode is the most frequent value. In a right-skewed distribution the mean sits above the median; in a left-skewed one, below. In a normal distribution the three coincide and about 68% of values fall within one standard deviation of the mean, about 95% within two.

Range is max minus min; standard deviation measures spread around the mean; the standard error of the mean (SD divided by √n) shrinks as the sample grows and describes how precisely the mean is known.

research_methods.name: Reading graphs and tables
know: Check the axes first: what is plotted, in what units, and whether a scale is linear or logarithmic. On a log scale equal distances are equal ratios, so a straight line on a semi-log plot means exponential change and on a log-log plot means a power law.

The slope of a line has units (rise over run); extrapolating beyond the measured range is a guess. Error bars show variability or uncertainty; two means whose error bars overlap heavily (by more than about half their length) are unlikely to differ significantly.

research_methods.name: Significance and uncertainty
know: A p-value is the probability of seeing a difference at least as large as the one observed if there were really no effect; results are usually called significant when p < 0.05. A 95% confidence interval is the range that would contain the true value in 95% of repeated studies; an interval that includes zero (or a ratio of 1) is not significant.

A Type I error is calling an effect real when it is not (a false positive); a Type II error is missing a real effect (a false negative). Statistical power, the chance of detecting a real effect, rises with sample size and effect size. Significance is not the same as importance: a tiny difference can be significant with a large enough sample.

research_methods.name: Research ethics
know: Research on people requires informed consent (the person understands the purpose, procedures, risks, and the right to withdraw), review by an ethics board (an IRB in the US), privacy protection, and a favourable balance of benefit to risk; vulnerable groups get extra protection. Animal research requires justification, minimal numbers, and humane treatment under institutional oversight.
Data integrity: results are reported as obtained, outliers are removed only for a stated reason, conflicts of interest are disclosed, and work is described fully enough for others to repeat it.

math_toolkit.name: Scientific notation and exponents
know: Write numbers as a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10. To multiply, multiply the coefficients and add the exponents; to divide, divide and subtract. Keep the coefficient tidy by shifting a power of ten.
Negative exponents mean reciprocals (10⁻³ = 1/1000); a square root halves the exponent, so make the exponent even first.

math_toolkit.name: Logarithms: pH, pKa, decibels, half-lives
know: log x asks what power of 10 gives x, so log(10ⁿ) = n, log(ab) = log a + log b, and log(a/b) = log a − log b. Memorize log 2 ≈ 0.30, log 3 ≈ 0.48, log 5 ≈ 0.70, log 7 ≈ 0.85. Natural log: ln x = 2.303 log x, and ln 2 ≈ 0.693.

For [H⁺] = a × 10⁻ⁿ, pH = n − log a, so pH lies between n − 1 and n. Reverse it the same way: pH 4.7 means [H⁺] = 10⁻⁴·⁷ = 10⁰·³ × 10⁻⁵ ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁵ M. Decibels: a factor of 10 in intensity is 10 dB, a factor of 2 is about 3 dB.
math_toolkit.example: A solution with [H⁺] = 5 × 10⁻³ M has pH = 3 − log 5 = 3 − 0.70 = 2.3. A sound 500 times more intense than another is 10 log 500 = 10(2.70) = 27 dB louder.

math_toolkit.name: Units and dimensional analysis
know: Carry units through every step and cancel them like algebra; the answer's units check the setup. Convert with ratios equal to one (1000 mL / 1 L; 1 atm / 760 mmHg). When a unit is squared or cubed, the conversion factor is too (1 m² = 10⁴ cm²).
Common equivalents: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s², 1 J = 1 N·m = 1 kg·m²/s², 1 W = 1 J/s, 1 Pa = 1 N/m², 1 V = 1 J/C, 1 L·atm ≈ 101 J, 1 cal = 4.184 J, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
math_toolkit.example: A 70 kg person running at 3 m/s has KE = ½(70)(3)² = 315 kg·m²/s² = 315 J. To convert 2.5 L·atm to joules: 2.5 × 101 ≈ 250 J.

math_toolkit.name: Proportional reasoning
know: Most MCAT calculations are ratios. If y ∝ x, doubling x doubles y; if y ∝ x², doubling x quadruples y; if y ∝ 1/x², doubling x cuts y to one-quarter; if y ∝ x⁴ (Poiseuille), halving the radius divides flow by 16. Write the new value as the old one times the ratio raised to the right power, and skip the constants.
Percent change: new/old − 1. A 25% increase followed by a 20% decrease returns to the start (1.25 × 0.8 = 1).
math_toolkit.example: Coulomb's force at 3 times the distance is (1/3)² = 1/9 of the original. If a vessel's radius drops by 10% (ratio 0.9), flow at the same pressure falls to 0.9⁴ ≈ 0.66, about a third less.

math_toolkit.name: Estimation, rounding, and significant figures
know: Round to one or two significant figures before multiplying (9.8 → 10, 3.14 → 3, 101 → 100) and keep track of how much you rounded so you know which direction the true answer lies. Answer choices are usually far enough apart that a 10% estimate picks the right one.

Significant figures: a measurement's precision is set by its instrument; a product or quotient keeps the fewest significant figures of its inputs, a sum or difference keeps the fewest decimal places. Trailing zeros after a decimal point count; leading zeros never do.
math_toolkit.example: A 0.52 kg ball dropped from 9.8 m hits at v = √(2gh) ≈ √(2 × 10 × 10) = √200 ≈ 14 m/s (true value 13.9). 0.0320 g has three significant figures; 3200 g has two unless written 3.200 × 10³.

math_toolkit.name: Squares, square roots, and useful numbers
know: Know the squares to 15² and the roots √2 ≈ 1.4, √3 ≈ 1.7, √5 ≈ 2.2, √10 ≈ 3.2. For a root of a number that is not a perfect square, bracket it between neighbouring squares and interpolate. Fractions worth knowing as decimals: 1/3 ≈ 0.33, 1/6 ≈ 0.17, 1/7 ≈ 0.14, 1/8 = 0.125, 1/9 ≈ 0.11, 1/12 ≈ 0.083.
π ≈ 3.14, π² ≈ 10, e ≈ 2.72, and for small x, (1 + x)ⁿ ≈ 1 + nx.

math_toolkit.name: Trigonometry and the right-hand rule
know: For a right triangle, sin = opposite/hypotenuse, cos = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan = opposite/adjacent. Memorize: sin 0° = 0, sin 30° = 0.5, sin 45° ≈ 0.71, sin 60° ≈ 0.87, sin 90° = 1, and cos runs the same list backward; tan 45° = 1. sin²θ + cos²θ = 1. Inverse functions turn a ratio back into an angle.

Right-hand rule for cross products: point the fingers along the first vector, curl toward the second, and the thumb gives the result. For a positive charge moving in a magnetic field, fingers along v, curl to B, thumb along the force; reverse the force for a negative charge. For a current in a wire, the thumb along the current gives the field circling in the direction of the curled fingers.
math_toolkit.example: On a 30° incline the component of a 50 N weight along the slope is 50 sin 30° = 25 N and the normal force is 50 cos 30° ≈ 43 N.

math_toolkit.name: Vectors
know: Split a vector into perpendicular components (A cos θ along the axis it is measured from, A sin θ along the other), add components separately, then recombine with the Pythagorean theorem; the direction is tan⁻¹(y/x). Vectors at right angles never partly cancel.
Subtracting a vector means adding its reverse. The resultant of two equal vectors at 180° is zero; at 90° it is √2 times either; at 60° it is √3 times either.
math_toolkit.example: Forces of 3 N east and 4 N north give a resultant of 5 N at tan⁻¹(4/3) ≈ 53° north of east.

math_toolkit.name: Solving equations and simultaneous equations
know: Rearrange before substituting numbers so you can see which quantities cancel. Two unknowns need two equations: solve one for a variable and substitute, or add or subtract the equations to eliminate a variable. Circuit junctions and loops, conservation of momentum and energy, and mass balances all produce such pairs.
Check the result by plugging it back in, and check that it has the right sign and size for the physical situation.
math_toolkit.example: If x + y = 10 and x − y = 4, adding gives 2x = 14, so x = 7 and y = 3. Two resistors in parallel with total 2 Ω, one of which is 6 Ω: 1/2 − 1/6 = 1/3, so the other is 3 Ω.

math_toolkit.name: Reading linear, semi-log, and log-log graphs
know: A straight line on linear axes means y = mx + b: the slope has units and the intercept is the value at x = 0. On a semi-log plot (log y against x) a straight line means exponential growth or decay, and the slope is the rate constant over 2.303 (or the decay constant on a half-life plot). On a log-log plot a straight line means a power law y = kxⁿ and the slope is the exponent n.
Linearized forms let you read constants from a line: 1/v against 1/[S] (Lineweaver–Burk), ln k against 1/T (Arrhenius, slope −Ea/R), ln[A] against t (first-order kinetics, slope −k).
math_toolkit.example: On a plot of log(activity) against time, the line drops by one unit (a factor of 10) every 30 minutes; since 10 ≈ 2^3.3, the half-life is about 30/3.3 ≈ 9 minutes.

math_toolkit.name: Probability basics
know: The probability of two independent events both happening is the product of their probabilities; the probability of one or the other of two mutually exclusive events is the sum. The probability that something does not happen is 1 minus the probability that it does.
Expected count = probability × number of trials. Combinations (how many ways to choose k items from n) show up in genetics and in counting equivalent arrangements.
equations: P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B)\ \text{(mutually exclusive)}
math_toolkit.example: If each of three independent assays has a 90% chance of success, the chance all three succeed is 0.9³ ≈ 0.73, and the chance at least one fails is 0.27.

psych_soc.attribution: Organized according to the AAMC's What's on the MCAT Exam? outline. Descriptions are our own. See the official outline for the authoritative list.

glance.summary: This section tests introductory psychology, sociology, and the biology of behaviour as they bear on health: how people perceive and think, what drives behaviour and how it changes, how we see ourselves and others, and how social structure and inequality shape well-being. Passages often describe a study, so research methods and statistics carry extra weight here.
glance.math: Light arithmetic only: percentages, ratios, averages, reading tables and graphs, and the basic statistics of a study (mean, standard deviation, correlation, p-values). No calculator.
glance.scores_note: Scores in this app are percent correct. They are not MCAT scaled scores (118–132), which only AAMC's equating can produce.

concepts.name: Perceiving, thinking about, and reacting to the world
concepts.summary: Foundational Concept 6 (AAMC): the path from stimulus to experience. Sensation and perception, the cognitive processes of attention, memory, language, and thought, and the emotion and stress that follow.

categories.name: Sensing the environment
categories.summary: How stimuli become signals: thresholds and signal detection, the receptors and pathways of each sense, and the perceptual rules the brain uses to organize what it receives.

topics.name: Sensation, thresholds, Weber's law, and signal detection
know: Sensation is the detection of a stimulus by a receptor and its conversion into a neural signal (transduction); perception is the brain's interpretation of that signal. Psychophysics studies how physical stimulus intensity maps onto what we experience.

The absolute threshold is the weakest stimulus detected half the time; the difference threshold (just noticeable difference) is the smallest change in a stimulus that is noticed half the time. Weber's law: the change you can just detect scales with the starting intensity, so a bright light must change by more than a dim one before you notice.

Signal detection theory separates sensitivity from decision bias: a stimulus is either present or absent and you either report it or not, giving hits, misses, false alarms, and correct rejections. Expectations, motivation, and the cost of errors move the response criterion without changing sensitivity. Sensory adaptation is the fading of a response to an unchanging stimulus, which keeps attention on what is new.
equations: \dfrac{\Delta I}{I} = k\ \text{(Weber's law; } k \text{ depends on the sense)}
confusions: Subliminal stimuli fall below the absolute threshold for conscious report yet can still be processed; this is not the same as the persuasive 'subliminal messaging' of popular claims.

refs.label: OpenStax Psychology 2e, 5.1 Sensation versus Perception

topics.name: Sensory receptors and pathways
know: Receptor types are named for their stimulus: mechanoreceptors (touch, pressure, sound, balance), thermoreceptors, nociceptors (tissue damage, pain), photoreceptors (light), and chemoreceptors (taste, smell, blood chemistry). Each converts its stimulus into a receptor potential; if that reaches threshold, action potentials carry the message along a sensory neuron.

Most sensory pathways relay through the thalamus before reaching a dedicated area of cerebral cortex; smell is the exception, projecting first to the olfactory bulb and limbic structures. Stimulus intensity is coded by firing rate and by how many receptors respond; stimulus type is coded by which pathway is active (labeled lines).

Receptive fields and lateral inhibition sharpen contrast; some touch receptors adapt quickly (Meissner's and Pacinian corpuscles, which is why you stop feeling your clothes) while others, including pain receptors and some pressure receptors, adapt slowly.
confusions: Pain is not carried by overstimulated touch receptors; nociceptors are a separate population with their own fibres.

refs.label: OpenStax Biology 2e, 36.1 Sensory Processes
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 14.1 Sensory Perception

topics.name: Vision: the eye and visual processing
know: Light passes through the cornea (most of the focusing), the pupil (sized by the iris), and the lens (adjustable focusing, accommodation) to the retina. Rods are concentrated in the periphery, work in dim light, and carry no colour; cones are packed in the fovea, need bright light, and give colour and sharp detail. Photoreceptors signal bipolar cells, which signal ganglion cells whose axons form the optic nerve; where it leaves there are no receptors, the blind spot.

Pathway: optic nerve → optic chiasm, where fibres from the nasal half of each retina cross so that each hemisphere receives the opposite visual field → lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus → primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe. Colour: three cone types tuned to short, medium, and long wavelengths (trichromatic theory), followed by opponent channels (red–green, blue–yellow, black–white) that explain afterimages.

Visual processing runs in parallel: separate streams handle colour, form, motion, and depth at the same time, and feature-detector neurons respond to edges, orientations, and movement. The 'what' stream (ventral, to the temporal lobe) identifies objects; the 'where/how' stream (dorsal, to the parietal lobe) locates them and guides action.
confusions: Colour blindness is usually a cone pigment defect on the X chromosome, so it is far more common in males. The lens inverts the image; the brain, not the eye, turns it upright.

refs.label: OpenStax Psychology 2e, 5.3 Vision
OpenStax Biology 2e, 36.5 Vision

topics.name: Hearing: the ear and auditory processing
know: Sound waves are funnelled by the pinna down the auditory canal to the tympanic membrane (eardrum), whose vibration is passed through the three ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) to the oval window of the fluid-filled cochlea. Inside, the basilar membrane moves and bends the stereocilia of hair cells in the organ of Corti; bending opens ion channels, the hair cell depolarizes, and it releases neurotransmitter onto the auditory nerve.

Pitch is coded two ways: place theory (high frequencies peak near the stiff base of the basilar membrane, low frequencies near the apex) and temporal (frequency) theory (firing locked to the wave's rhythm for low frequencies). Loudness is coded by firing rate and the number of hair cells recruited. Sound is located by comparing timing and intensity between the two ears.

Pathway: auditory nerve → brainstem nuclei → inferior colliculus of the midbrain → medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus → primary auditory cortex in the temporal lobe. Conductive hearing loss blocks sound before the cochlea; sensorineural loss damages hair cells or the nerve (loud noise, ageing); mild to moderate loss is managed with hearing aids, and severe to profound loss may be treated with a cochlear implant, which stimulates the auditory nerve directly.
confusions: Hair cells are not neurons and do not regenerate in humans; that is why noise damage is permanent.

topics.name: Touch and pain, taste, smell, kinesthesis, and balance
know: Somatosensation covers touch, pressure, vibration, temperature, and pain from receptors in the skin and deeper tissues, mapped onto the somatosensory cortex of the parietal lobe with more cortex for the fingertips and lips than the back. Pain has sensory and emotional components; gate-control theory proposes that spinal interneurons can dampen pain signals (rubbing an injury helps), and descending signals and endorphins modulate it. Congenital insensitivity to pain shows why pain is protective.

Taste: chemoreceptors in taste buds respond to sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami (and perhaps fat); taste cells signal the gustatory cortex via cranial nerves. Smell: olfactory receptor neurons in the nasal epithelium bind odorants, project to the olfactory bulb, and from there directly to the olfactory cortex and limbic system, bypassing the thalamus, which is why odours are tied so tightly to memory and emotion. Pheromones are chemical signals between members of a species, detected in many mammals by the vomeronasal organ; their role in humans is uncertain.

The kinesthetic sense (proprioception) reports limb position and movement from muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs, and joint receptors. The vestibular sense reports head rotation (semicircular canals) and linear acceleration or tilt (utricle and saccule, with hair cells under otolith crystals); its conflict with vision causes motion sickness.
confusions: Much of what we call flavour is smell: with the nose blocked, foods are hard to tell apart beyond the basic tastes. Taste regions on the tongue ('taste map') are a myth; all basic tastes are detected across the tongue.

topics.name: Perception: bottom-up and top-down processing, Gestalt principles, depth and constancy
know: Bottom-up processing builds a perception from the sensory data; top-down processing uses expectations, context, and knowledge to shape it (reading a smudged word, hearing your name in noise). Perceptual sets and motivation bias what is seen.

Gestalt principles describe how the visual system groups elements: figure and ground, proximity, similarity, continuity, closure, and common fate; the overall rule is that we perceive the simplest, most regular form. Depth comes from binocular cues (retinal disparity, convergence) and monocular cues (relative size, interposition, linear perspective, texture gradient, relative height, light and shadow, motion parallax).

Perceptual constancies keep objects stable as the retinal image changes: size, shape, and colour or brightness constancy. Motion perception uses retinal movement, the apparent motion of sequential images (the phi phenomenon behind films), and comparison with self-motion. Illusions such as the Müller-Lyer arrows show the rules operating where they do not fit.
confusions: Two people can receive nearly the same sensory input yet perceive it differently, because expectations, experience, and attention shape top-down processing.

categories.name: Making sense of the environment
categories.summary: Cognition from the inside: attention, thinking and problem solving, intelligence, states of consciousness and drugs, memory and its failures, the biology of learning, and language.

topics.name: Selective and divided attention
know: Selective attention lets you focus on one stream of input while filtering the rest, as when you follow one voice at a party; unattended information is processed only shallowly, yet something salient such as your own name can break through (the cocktail-party effect). Filter models (Broadbent) and attenuation models (Treisman) differ on how much the unattended channel is processed.

Divided attention is attending to two tasks at once; it succeeds only when at least one task is practised enough to be automatic. Controlled processing is effortful and serial, automatic processing is fast and parallel, which is why conversation while driving in traffic degrades both.
Inattentional blindness (missing an obvious event while attending elsewhere) and change blindness show how little of a scene is actually encoded without attention.
confusions: Multitasking is rapid switching, not parallel attention; switching costs time and accuracy.

topics.name: Cognition and cognitive development
know: The information-processing model treats the mind like a computer: input is encoded, stored, processed, and retrieved, with limited capacity at each stage; concepts, schemas, and prototypes organize knowledge. Biological factors such as brain injury, sleep loss, nutrition, drugs, and ageing all change cognitive performance.

Piaget's stages: sensorimotor (birth to about 2; object permanence develops), preoperational (about 2–7; symbolic thought and language, but egocentrism and failure of conservation), concrete operational (about 7–11; conservation and logical reasoning about concrete things), formal operational (about 11 on; abstract and hypothetical reasoning). Children assimilate new experiences into existing schemas or accommodate the schemas.

Later work shows development is less stage-like than Piaget thought and shaped by culture: Vygotsky stressed social scaffolding and the zone of proximal development. In late adulthood, processing speed and fluid abilities decline while vocabulary and accumulated knowledge (crystallized intelligence) hold up; heredity and environment both contribute to cognitive development, and they interact.
confusions: Egocentrism in Piaget's sense means difficulty taking another's perspective, not selfishness.

refs.label: OpenStax Psychology 2e, 7.1 What Is Cognition?
OpenStax Psychology 2e, 9.2 Lifespan Theories
OpenStax Psychology 2e, 9.3 Stages of Development

topics.name: Problem solving, decision making, heuristics, and biases
know: Strategies: trial and error; algorithms (step-by-step procedures that always work but can be slow); heuristics (mental shortcuts that are fast but fallible); and insight, the sudden reorganization of a problem. Working backward and means–ends analysis break a goal into subgoals.

Barriers: mental set (sticking with a strategy that worked before), functional fixedness (seeing an object only in its usual role), and confirmation bias (seeking evidence that supports what you already believe). Framing changes choices even when the options are identical.

Common heuristics and biases: availability (judging frequency by how easily examples come to mind), representativeness (judging by resemblance to a prototype and ignoring base rates), anchoring (over-weighting the first number seen), hindsight bias, overconfidence (certainty beyond accuracy), and belief perseverance (holding a belief after its evidence is discredited).
confusions: A heuristic is not a mistake; it is a strategy that usually works and fails in predictable ways. The bias is the predictable failure.

refs.label: OpenStax Psychology 2e, 7.3 Problem Solving

topics.name: Intelligence: theories, measurement, heredity and environment
know: Theories: Spearman's general factor g underlying all abilities; Cattell's fluid intelligence (reasoning with new problems; peaks early) versus crystallized intelligence (accumulated knowledge; grows with age); Sternberg's triarchic view (analytical, creative, practical); Gardner's multiple intelligences; and emotional intelligence (perceiving and managing emotion). Creativity is divergent thinking, generating many possible answers.

Measurement: Binet's original scale led to IQ (originally mental age ÷ chronological age × 100); modern tests such as the Wechsler scales score by deviation from the mean of a standardization sample, with mean 100 and standard deviation 15, so about 68% of people score 85–115. A good test is reliable (consistent) and valid (measures what it claims); tests are standardized against a representative norm group.

Heredity and environment both matter: identical twins reared apart correlate more than fraternal twins reared together, giving heritability estimates around 0.5 or higher in adults, yet enrichment, schooling, and nutrition raise scores, and average scores rose across the twentieth century (the Flynn effect). Variation: intellectual disability is defined by IQ about two standard deviations below the mean together with deficits in adaptive functioning that begin in development; giftedness is roughly two standard deviations above. Stereotype threat and test bias can depress scores for some groups.
confusions: Heritability describes how much variation in a population is linked to genetic variation; it says nothing about how fixed an individual's intelligence is or about differences between groups raised in different environments.

topics.name: Consciousness, sleep, circadian rhythms, dreaming, and sleep disorders
know: Consciousness is being aware of what is happening inside you and around you; alertness is maintained by the brainstem reticular formation and is reflected in low-amplitude, high-frequency (beta) EEG activity, with alpha waves in relaxed wakefulness. Circadian rhythms of roughly 24 hours are set by the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus, which uses light information to time melatonin release from the pineal gland; jet lag and shift work are rhythm disruptions.

Sleep cycles through non-REM stages and REM about every 90 minutes. Stage N1: light sleep, theta waves. N2: sleep spindles and K-complexes. N3: slow-wave (delta) sleep, deepest and hardest to wake from, when sleepwalking and night terrors occur. REM: fast, wake-like EEG, rapid eye movements, vivid dreams, and muscle paralysis (atonia). N3 dominates early in the night and REM periods lengthen toward morning; total sleep and the share of N3 fall with age.

Why we sleep: proposed functions include restoration, energy conservation, memory consolidation, and clearance of metabolic waste; deprivation impairs attention, mood, immunity, and metabolism. Dream theories: Freud's wish fulfilment (manifest vs latent content), activation–synthesis (the cortex makes sense of random brainstem activity), and information-processing or consolidation views. Disorders: insomnia; sleep apnea (airway collapse, treated with positive airway pressure); narcolepsy (sudden REM intrusions, cataplexy, linked to loss of hypocretin/orexin); restless legs; parasomnias such as sleepwalking and REM sleep behaviour disorder (acting out dreams because atonia fails). Hypnosis is a state of focused attention and heightened suggestibility; meditation is trained attention that lowers arousal.
confusions: Dreams occur in non-REM sleep too, but REM dreams are longer and more vivid. Sleepwalking happens in N3, not during dreaming, because REM muscles are paralysed.

topics.name: Consciousness-altering drugs and the reward pathway
know: Depressants (alcohol, barbiturates, benzodiazepines) enhance GABA signalling and slow the nervous system, impairing judgement, coordination, and breathing at high doses. Stimulants raise alertness, heart rate, and blood pressure: cocaine, amphetamines, and methamphetamine boost dopamine (and norepinephrine) signalling, nicotine acts at acetylcholine receptors, and caffeine blocks adenosine receptors. Opioids (heroin, morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl) act at opioid receptors (the receptors for the body's own endorphins) to relieve pain and produce euphoria, and depress breathing. Hallucinogens (LSD and psilocybin, acting on serotonin receptors; cannabis through THC at cannabinoid receptors) alter perception and mood.

Addiction involves the mesolimbic reward pathway: dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area project to the nucleus accumbens, and drugs of abuse raise dopamine there far beyond natural rewards; with repeated use the system adapts, so more drug is needed for the same effect (tolerance) and stopping produces withdrawal.

Physical dependence (withdrawal symptoms) and psychological dependence (craving) can occur separately; substance use disorder is diagnosed by loss of control and continued use despite harm. Treatment combines medication (replacement or blocking agents, for example methadone or naltrexone) with behavioural therapy.
confusions: Tolerance and withdrawal alone do not define addiction; many prescribed drugs produce both without compulsive use.

topics.name: Memory: encoding and storage
know: Encoding converts information into a form memory can hold. Automatic processing handles time, space, and frequency without effort; effortful processing needs attention. Information can be encoded by meaning (semantic), by sound (acoustic), or by image (visual); semantic, deeper encoding lasts longest (levels of processing). Aids: elaborative rehearsal, chunking, mnemonics, imagery, relating material to yourself (self-reference effect), and spacing study sessions rather than cramming.

Storage runs through three systems. Sensory memory holds a raw copy for under a second (iconic) to a few seconds (echoic). Short-term memory holds about seven items (plus or minus two; newer estimates put it closer to four) for roughly 15–30 seconds without rehearsal; working memory is the active form, with a central executive directing a phonological loop and a visuospatial sketchpad. Long-term memory has no known limit and divides into explicit (declarative) memory, both episodic (events) and semantic (facts), and implicit memory, including procedural skills, priming, and conditioned responses.
Long-term knowledge is organized as semantic networks of linked concepts; activating one node spreads activation to related nodes, which is why a cue brings associated ideas to mind.
confusions: Rehearsal by rote repetition keeps information in short-term memory but transfers it poorly; linking it to meaning does the transferring.

refs.label: OpenStax Psychology 2e, 8.1 How Memory Functions
OpenStax Psychology 2e, 8.4 Ways to Enhance Memory

topics.name: Memory: retrieval, forgetting, and memory disorders
know: Retrieval takes three forms: recall (producing information without cues, as in an essay), recognition (identifying it among options, as in multiple choice), and relearning (material learned before is picked up faster). Retrieval cues, context (returning to the place of learning), and matching mood or physiological state (state-dependent memory) all help; the serial-position effect gives better recall of the first (primacy) and last (recency) items of a list. Emotional arousal strengthens memories through the amygdala, producing vivid but not always accurate flashbulb memories.

Forgetting: decay of unused traces; interference, either proactive (old learning blocks new) or retroactive (new learning blocks old); encoding failure; and retrieval failure such as the tip-of-the-tongue state. Memories are reconstructed at each retrieval, so suggestion and misinformation can alter them and source monitoring errors attribute a memory to the wrong origin; this is why eyewitness testimony can be confidently wrong.

Ageing mostly affects episodic memory and recall speed while semantic and procedural memory hold up. Alzheimer's disease destroys neurons, beginning in the hippocampus, with amyloid plaques and tau tangles, causing progressive memory loss; Korsakoff's syndrome, from thiamine deficiency usually in chronic alcohol use, causes severe amnesia with confabulation. Amnesia can be anterograde (cannot form new memories, as after hippocampal damage) or retrograde (loss of past memories).
confusions: Patients with hippocampal damage can still learn new motor skills: procedural memory depends on other structures (cerebellum, basal ganglia).

topics.name: Neural plasticity, long-term potentiation, and the biology of memory
know: Learning changes synapses: repeated activity strengthens connections (and unused ones weaken), new dendritic spines form, and in the hippocampus new neurons may be added in adulthood (still debated in humans). This plasticity is greatest in development but continues through life and underlies recovery after injury.

Long-term potentiation is the lasting increase in synaptic strength after brief high-frequency stimulation, best studied in the hippocampus: glutamate acting at NMDA receptors lets calcium into the postsynaptic cell, which adds AMPA receptors and enlarges the synapse. It is the leading cellular model for memory formation.

Memory systems map onto structures: the hippocampus forms new explicit memories and gradually consolidates them into cortical networks (which is why old memories survive hippocampal damage); the amygdala attaches emotion; the cerebellum handles conditioned motor responses; the basal ganglia support procedural learning.
confusions: Consolidation takes time, which is why sleep after learning improves recall and why a blow to the head erases the minutes before it.

topics.name: Language: development, influence on thought, and brain areas
know: Language is built from phonemes (sounds), morphemes (smallest meaningful units), words, and rules of grammar (syntax and semantics). Children babble, then produce single words near a year, two-word telegraphic speech from about 18 months, and grammar with overgeneralizations ('goed') soon after, in a similar sequence across cultures.

Theories of development: learning theory (Skinner: imitation and reinforcement), nativist theory (Chomsky: an innate language acquisition device and universal grammar, with a sensitive period in childhood), and interactionist theories (biological readiness plus social interaction, as in Vygotsky's view). The linguistic relativity (Sapir–Whorf) hypothesis holds that language shapes thought; the evidence supports a mild influence, for instance on colour discrimination and memory, not strict determinism.

Brain areas, usually in the left hemisphere: Broca's area in the frontal lobe produces speech (damage gives halting, effortful, telegraphic speech with intact comprehension), Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe handles comprehension (damage gives fluent but meaningless speech and poor understanding), and the arcuate fasciculus links them.
confusions: Broca's aphasia is a problem of production, not of understanding; the patient knows what they want to say.
