categories.name: Responding to the world
categories.summary: Emotion and stress: what they are made of, the competing theories of how they arise, the brain and body systems behind them, and how people cope.

topics.name: Emotion: components, universal emotions, and theories
know: An emotion has three components: a subjective, cognitive experience (feeling afraid), a physiological response (racing heart), and a behavioural expression (freezing, a facial expression). Emotions are adaptive: they prepare the body for action and communicate to others. A set of basic emotions (happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, and disgust) is recognized from facial expressions across cultures, although cultural display rules govern when expressions are shown.

Theories differ on the order of events. James–Lange: the bodily response comes first and the emotion is the perception of it (we feel afraid because we tremble). Cannon–Bard: the thalamus sends signals to the cortex and body at the same time, so feeling and arousal occur together and independently. Schachter–Singer two-factor theory: general arousal plus a cognitive label from the situation produces the specific emotion, so the same arousal can be read as fear or excitement.

Lazarus's cognitive appraisal view puts interpretation first; Zajonc argued some emotional reactions precede any appraisal. The facial-feedback hypothesis holds that making an expression nudges the feeling.
confusions: Cannon–Bard says arousal and emotion are simultaneous and separate; Schachter–Singer says arousal must be interpreted before it becomes a specific emotion.

refs.label: OpenStax Psychology 2e, 10.4 Emotion

topics.name: The biology of emotion: limbic system, autonomic nervous system, and physiological markers
know: The limbic system generates and colours emotion: the amygdala detects threat and attaches emotional significance to stimuli (fear conditioning; damage blunts fear), the hippocampus ties emotion to the memory of the context, and the hypothalamus drives the bodily response. The prefrontal cortex, especially its ventromedial part, regulates and evaluates emotional responses; damage there impairs decision making and emotional control.

Sensory information about a threat reaches the amygdala by a fast, crude route through the thalamus and by a slower, detailed route through the cortex, so the body can react before the situation is fully understood.

The autonomic nervous system provides the physiological signature: sympathetic activation raises heart rate, blood pressure, breathing, sweating (skin conductance), and pupil size and diverts blood to muscles; parasympathetic activity restores calm. These markers are measured in emotion research and in the polygraph, which detects arousal, not lying.
confusions: Different emotions share much of the same autonomic signature, which is why a polygraph cannot tell fear of being disbelieved from guilt.

topics.name: Stress: appraisal, stressors, responses, and coping
know: Stress is what happens when you judge a situation as taxing or dangerous and your mind and body react to that judgement. In Lazarus's model, primary appraisal asks whether an event is a threat, a loss, or a challenge, and secondary appraisal asks whether you have the resources to cope; the same event can be distress for one person and eustress for another. Stressor types range from cataclysmic events (disasters) and major life changes to chronic personal stressors (caregiving, poverty), daily hassles, and ambient stressors such as noise.

Physiological response: the sympathetic nervous system and adrenal medulla release adrenaline for the rapid fight-or-flight reaction, and the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis releases cortisol for a sustained response. Selye's general adaptation syndrome describes alarm, resistance, and, if the stressor continues, exhaustion, when immune function and health suffer. Emotional outcomes include anxiety, irritability, and depression; behavioural outcomes include poor sleep, substance use, and withdrawal from others.

Chronic stress is linked to cardiovascular disease, impaired immunity, slower wound healing, and worse memory. Coping can be problem-focused (change the stressor) or emotion-focused (change the reaction); exercise, relaxation and meditation, social support, perceived control, optimism, and religious or spiritual practice all buffer stress.
confusions: Cortisol is not 'bad': it mobilizes energy and dampens inflammation in the short term; the harm comes from chronically elevated levels.

concepts.summary: Foundational Concept 7 (AAMC): why people behave as they do and how behaviour changes. The biology of behaviour and individual psychology, the influence of groups and norms, and the learning and attitude processes behind change.

categories.name: Individual influences on behavior
categories.summary: The biology behind behaviour (nervous and endocrine systems, genes, development) and the individual psychology on top of it: personality, psychological disorders, motivation, and attitudes.

topics.name: The nervous system: neurons, divisions, and the spinal cord
know: Neurons receive input on dendrites, integrate it at the cell body, and send action potentials down the axon to synapses, where neurotransmitters cross to the next cell; glial cells support, insulate (myelin), and feed neurons. Sensory (afferent) neurons carry information in, motor (efferent) neurons carry commands out, and interneurons connect them. In a reflex arc, a sensory neuron synapses in the spinal cord, often on an interneuron, onto a motor neuron, so the withdrawal happens before the brain registers the pain.

The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord; the peripheral nervous system is everything else. The PNS divides into the somatic system (voluntary muscle, sensory input) and the autonomic system, whose sympathetic branch mobilizes the body (fight or flight: faster heart, dilated pupils, slowed digestion) and whose parasympathetic branch restores it (rest and digest).

The spinal cord relays signals between body and brain and runs reflexes on its own; its grey matter holds cell bodies and its white matter the ascending sensory and descending motor tracts, so damage at one level cuts off everything below it.
confusions: Sympathetic and parasympathetic branches are usually both active; behaviour reflects the balance, not a switch.

topics.name: The brain: forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain, lateralization, and methods of study
know: Hindbrain: the medulla controls breathing, heart rate, and blood pressure; the pons relays signals and helps regulate sleep; the cerebellum coordinates movement, balance, and procedural learning. Midbrain: the reticular formation governs arousal and alertness, the substantia nigra supplies dopamine for movement (lost in Parkinson's disease), and the tectum handles visual and auditory reflexes. Forebrain: the thalamus relays sensory input (except smell) to the cortex; the hypothalamus controls hunger, thirst, temperature, and the pituitary; the limbic system (amygdala, hippocampus) handles emotion and memory; the basal ganglia select and smooth movements; the cerebral cortex does perception, thought, language, and voluntary action.

The cortex has four lobes per hemisphere: frontal (planning, decision making, motor cortex, Broca's area; the prefrontal region matures last), parietal (somatosensory cortex, spatial attention), temporal (hearing, Wernicke's area, memory via the hippocampus beneath), and occipital (vision). The two hemispheres communicate through the corpus callosum; in most people the left is dominant for language and the right for spatial and face processing. Split-brain patients, whose callosum was cut, can name an object shown to the right visual field (left hemisphere) but can only indicate one shown to the left nonverbally, for instance by drawing it or picking it out with the left hand.

Methods: EEG records electrical activity with fine timing but coarse location; fMRI tracks blood oxygen to map active regions; PET traces a radioactive marker of metabolism or receptors; CT and MRI image structure; lesion studies (patients such as Phineas Gage) and transcranial magnetic stimulation link regions to functions.
confusions: Lateralization is relative: both hemispheres contribute to nearly every task, and the 'left-brained/right-brained personality' idea has no support.

topics.name: Neuronal communication and neurotransmitters' effects on behavior
know: At a synapse the action potential opens calcium channels, vesicles release neurotransmitter, and the transmitter binds receptors on the next cell to excite (depolarize) or inhibit (hyperpolarize) it; the signal ends by reuptake into the sending neuron or by enzymatic breakdown. A cell fires only if excitatory inputs summed over space and time reach threshold.

Major transmitters and their behavioural roles: acetylcholine (muscle contraction, attention, memory; depleted in Alzheimer's disease), dopamine (reward, motivation, movement; excess linked to schizophrenia, loss to Parkinson's), serotonin (mood, sleep, appetite; target of SSRIs), norepinephrine (alertness, arousal, stress), GABA (the main inhibitory transmitter; anxiety drugs enhance it), glutamate (the main excitatory transmitter; learning and memory), and endorphins (pain relief, pleasure).

Psychoactive drugs act as agonists (mimic or boost a transmitter), antagonists (block it), or reuptake inhibitors (prolong it); knowing which transmitter a drug affects predicts its effect on behaviour.
confusions: A transmitter is not inherently excitatory or inhibitory; the receptor it binds decides (acetylcholine excites skeletal muscle but slows the heart).

topics.name: The endocrine system and behavior
know: Endocrine glands release hormones into the blood, which act more slowly and more widely than neurotransmitters. The hypothalamus controls the pituitary, the 'master gland', which in turn directs the thyroid (metabolism and energy), adrenal glands (cortisol for stress and energy, adrenaline and noradrenaline for arousal), and gonads (testosterone, estrogen, and progesterone for sexual development and behaviour). The pancreas regulates blood glucose with insulin and glucagon, and the pineal gland releases melatonin.

Hormones shape behaviour: cortisol and adrenaline drive the stress response and affect memory and mood; testosterone supports sexual motivation in all sexes and shows only a weak association with aggression, mainly in men; oxytocin is involved in bonding, trust, and parental behaviour; thyroid disorders change energy and mood; growth hormone and the sex hormones organize puberty.

The nervous and endocrine systems are integrated by feedback loops: the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis raises cortisol under stress, and cortisol then suppresses further release; the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis regulates reproduction the same way.
confusions: The adrenal medulla (adrenaline, fast, neural control) and the adrenal cortex (cortisol, slower, hormonal control) are different tissues within one gland.

topics.name: Behavioral genetics: genes, temperament, heredity and environment
know: Behavioural genetics asks how much variation in a trait within a population tracks genetic variation. Twin studies (identical versus fraternal twins) and adoption studies separate heredity from shared environment; temperament, personality traits, intelligence, and vulnerability to many disorders are moderately heritable, and almost always polygenic rather than due to a single gene.

Genes and environment interact: a genotype may raise risk only under certain conditions (for instance, a stressful childhood), and the range of reaction describes the span of outcomes a genotype allows across environments. Epigenetic changes (such as DNA methylation) alter gene expression without changing the sequence and can be triggered by experience. Regulatory genes that switch other genes on and off underlie developmental timing and behaviour in animals, and genetically based behavioural variation exists in natural populations (for instance in foraging or migratory behaviour).

Traits and behaviours persist when they raise reproductive fitness; evolutionary psychology interprets fear of snakes, taste preferences, or mate preferences in those terms, though such explanations are hard to test directly.
confusions: A heritability of 0.5 does not mean half of a person's trait is genetic; it means half of the differences among people in that population are associated with genetic differences.

topics.name: Human physiological development: prenatal, motor, and adolescent
know: Prenatal development runs through the germinal period (fertilization to implantation, about two weeks), the embryonic period (weeks 3–8, when the organs form and the embryo is most vulnerable to teratogens such as alcohol, some drugs, and infections), and the fetal period (week 9 to birth, growth and maturation, with the brain developing rapidly in the last months).

Motor development follows reflexes (rooting, sucking, grasping, Moro) and proceeds in a predictable order, head to toe and centre outward, with milestones such as sitting around 6 months, crawling around 8–9, and walking around 12 months; the order is universal but the timing varies with individual and cultural factors.

Adolescence begins with puberty, driven by the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis: a growth spurt, development of primary and secondary sex characteristics, and menarche or first ejaculation. The brain keeps maturing: the limbic system develops ahead of the prefrontal cortex, which continues to mature into the mid-twenties, a mismatch often invoked to explain adolescent risk taking.
confusions: Puberty timing varies widely and has moved earlier in recent generations; early maturation carries different social consequences for girls and boys.

refs.label: OpenStax Psychology 2e, 9.3 Stages of Development

topics.name: Theories of personality and the situational approach
know: Psychoanalytic (Freud): personality arises from the conflict between the id (instinctual drives, pleasure principle), the ego (reality principle), and the superego (conscience), much of it unconscious, with defence mechanisms such as repression, denial, projection, displacement, rationalization, and sublimation; development passes through psychosexual stages (oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital) where fixation leaves its mark. Neo-Freudians (Adler, Erikson, Jung, Horney) kept the unconscious but emphasized social and cultural factors.

Humanistic (Maslow, Rogers): people strive toward self-actualization; Rogers held that unconditional positive regard allows the real self and ideal self to match (congruence). Trait theories describe stable dispositions: Eysenck's extraversion, neuroticism, and psychoticism, and the Big Five (openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism), which are stable across adulthood and partly heritable (the biological perspective). Behaviourists (Skinner) saw personality as learned patterns of reinforced behaviour.

Social-cognitive (Bandura): behaviour, personal factors, and environment shape one another (reciprocal determinism), and self-efficacy, the belief in one's ability to succeed, drives effort; Rotter's locus of control contrasts seeing outcomes as under one's control (internal) or due to luck and others (external). The situational approach (Mischel) notes that behaviour varies across situations more than trait theory predicts; the current view is interactionist, traits expressed differently in different settings.
confusions: Freud's theory is historically important, but most of its claims lack support in modern research; the Big Five and social-cognitive constructs have the strongest empirical support.

topics.name: Psychological disorders: approaches, classification, and major types
know: A psychological disorder involves disturbed thoughts, feelings, or behaviour that cause distress or impairment and are not simply culturally expected responses. The biomedical approach treats disorders as illnesses with biological causes and medical treatments; the biopsychosocial approach adds psychological and social causes and treatments. The diathesis–stress model says a predisposition becomes a disorder under stress. Classification uses the DSM-5 (criteria, no single cause assumed); in the United States more than one adult in five (23% in 2022, NIMH) has a diagnosable mental illness in a given year, with anxiety disorders the most common.

Major groups: anxiety disorders (specific phobia, social anxiety disorder, panic disorder, generalized anxiety disorder); obsessive-compulsive and related disorders (intrusive thoughts and ritual behaviours; body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding); trauma- and stressor-related disorders (PTSD: re-experiencing, avoidance, hyperarousal after a traumatic event); somatic symptom and related disorders (distressing physical symptoms with excessive health concern; illness anxiety; conversion); bipolar and related disorders (mania or hypomania alternating with depression); depressive disorders (major depressive disorder: depressed mood or loss of interest with sleep, appetite, energy, concentration, and worth changes for at least two weeks).

Schizophrenia: positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech and behaviour) and negative symptoms (flat affect, avolition, social withdrawal), typically beginning in late adolescence or early adulthood. Dissociative disorders (dissociative amnesia, depersonalization/derealization, dissociative identity disorder) involve disruptions of memory, identity, or awareness. Personality disorders are enduring, inflexible patterns (clusters: odd/eccentric such as paranoid and schizotypal; dramatic/erratic such as antisocial and borderline; anxious such as avoidant and obsessive-compulsive personality).
confusions: Schizophrenia is not 'split personality'; dissociative identity disorder is the diagnosis with multiple identities. Obsessive-compulsive disorder and obsessive-compulsive personality disorder are different diagnoses.

topics.name: Biological bases of nervous system disorders
know: Schizophrenia: strong heritability, excess dopamine signalling in some pathways (antipsychotics block dopamine D2 receptors), enlarged ventricles and reduced grey matter, and prenatal risk factors such as maternal infection; the dopamine hypothesis is incomplete because glutamate and other systems are also involved.

Depression: reduced monoamine (serotonin, norepinephrine) signalling is the classic model and the basis of antidepressants, together with an overactive stress axis (high cortisol), reduced hippocampal volume, and altered neural plasticity; genes raise vulnerability, and stress precipitates episodes.

Alzheimer's disease: accumulation of amyloid-β plaques and tau neurofibrillary tangles, loss of acetylcholine-producing neurons, and progressive atrophy beginning in the hippocampus; the APOE ε4 allele raises risk. Parkinson's disease: death of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra causes tremor, rigidity, and slowed movement, treated with the dopamine precursor L-dopa or deep brain stimulation. Stem-cell therapy aims to replace lost neurons (dopamine neurons in Parkinson's, for example) and is being tested, with challenges of integration, control of growth, and immune rejection.
confusions: A drug working on a transmitter does not prove that transmitter caused the disorder; the serotonin story of depression is a hypothesis, not an established cause.

topics.name: Motivation: instincts, drives, arousal, needs, and incentives
know: Motivation is what directs and energizes behaviour. Instinct theories (innate, species-typical behaviours) explain little human behaviour. Drive-reduction theory: a physiological need (hunger, thirst) creates a drive that pushes behaviour to restore homeostasis through negative feedback, as when low blood glucose prompts eating. Arousal theory: people seek an optimal level of arousal, and performance on a task peaks at a moderate level (the Yerkes–Dodson law, with the optimum lower for hard tasks).

Incentive theory adds the pull of external rewards; cognitive theories distinguish intrinsic motivation (the activity itself) from extrinsic (reward or punishment), and rewarding an already enjoyable activity can undermine intrinsic motivation (the overjustification effect). Need-based theories: Maslow's hierarchy (physiological, safety, belonging, esteem, self-actualization) and self-determination theory's needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness.

Biological and sociocultural motivators: hunger is regulated by the hypothalamus with signals such as ghrelin (hunger), leptin from fat (satiety), and blood glucose, and shaped by culture, learned preferences, and set point; sex drive depends on hormones (testosterone in both sexes) and on learning, culture, and relationships; substance addiction hijacks the reward system so that drug seeking outcompetes other goals.
confusions: Drive reduction cannot explain why people climb mountains or ride roller coasters; arousal and incentive theories were added for that.

topics.name: Attitudes and their link to behavior
know: An attitude is an evaluation of a person, object, or idea with three components: cognitive (beliefs), affective (feelings), and behavioural (tendency to act). Attitudes predict behaviour best when they are strong, specific to the behaviour, easily accessible, formed from direct experience, and when social pressure is weak.

Behaviour also shapes attitudes. The foot-in-the-door technique: agreeing to a small request makes a larger one more likely, because people act consistently with the self-image the first act created. Role playing: taking on a role changes attitudes to fit it, as in Zimbardo's prison simulation. Self-perception theory: when attitudes are weak, people infer them by watching their own behaviour.

Cognitive dissonance theory (Festinger): holding two inconsistent cognitions, or acting against one's attitude, produces discomfort that people reduce by changing the attitude, adding justifications, or minimizing the conflict; the effect is strongest when the behaviour was freely chosen and poorly rewarded (people paid one dollar to praise a dull task came to like it more than those paid twenty).
confusions: Dissonance reduction changes attitudes after the behaviour; persuasion changes attitudes before it. Both can run in the same episode.

categories.name: Social processes that influence human behavior
categories.summary: How other people change what we do: the mere presence of others, group decisions, the norms that define normal and deviant behaviour, and the socialization that teaches them.

topics.name: How the presence of others affects individual behavior
know: Social facilitation: an audience or co-actors improve performance on simple or well-learned tasks and worsen it on difficult or new ones, because arousal strengthens the dominant response. Social loafing: people exert less effort in a group when individual contributions are not identified; it shrinks when contributions are visible or the task matters to the person. Deindividuation: anonymity and group immersion loosen self-restraint and personal responsibility, as in crowds or online.

The bystander effect: the more witnesses to an emergency, the less likely any one of them is to help, through diffusion of responsibility and pluralistic ignorance (each reads the others' calm as evidence that nothing is wrong). Helping rises when a person is singled out or feels competent to act.

Conformity is adjusting behaviour or belief to match a group: in Asch's line-judging studies about a third of responses followed an obviously wrong majority, more with a unanimous group and less with one dissenter. Normative influence (wanting to fit in) and informational influence (believing others know better) both drive it; peer pressure is this influence from one's age group. Obedience is following a direct order from an authority: in Milgram's studies most participants delivered what they believed were severe shocks when an experimenter insisted, and obedience fell when the authority was distant, the victim was close, or another participant refused. Social control is the broader set of means, formal (laws, police) and informal (approval, ridicule), by which a society enforces its norms.
confusions: Conformity is to peers and often unspoken; obedience is to an authority's explicit command. Compliance (agreeing to a request) sits between them.

topics.name: Group decision-making: group polarization and groupthink
know: Group polarization: discussion among like-minded people pushes the group's average view further in the direction it already leaned, because members hear new arguments for their side and want to be seen as at least as committed as others. It explains why online communities and juries can end up more extreme than any member started.

Groupthink: a cohesive group's desire for harmony suppresses dissent and critical evaluation, producing poor decisions; symptoms include an illusion of invulnerability, self-censorship, pressure on dissenters, 'mindguards' who filter bad news, and an illusion of unanimity. It is more likely with a directive leader, isolation from outside views, and high stress from an external threat, and is countered by inviting criticism, assigning a devil's advocate, and seeking outside opinions.
Group size and structure matter: Sociologists note that dyads dissolve if one member leaves, triads allow coalitions, and larger groups become less intimate and more rule-governed.
confusions: Polarization shifts the group toward a more extreme version of its initial lean; it does not mean the group splits into two poles.

topics.name: Social norms, deviance, and collective behavior
know: Norms are a group's shared rules for behaviour, enforced by sanctions: positive (praise, promotion) or negative (ridicule, fines, prison), formal (written and officially enforced) or informal. Folkways are everyday customs whose violation draws only mild disapproval (table manners); mores are norms carrying moral weight (honesty, fidelity) whose violation provokes strong reaction; taboos are the most deeply held prohibitions (incest, cannibalism); laws are formally codified norms. Anomie (Durkheim) is normlessness, when rapid change or crisis leaves norms unclear and weakens social bonds.

Deviance is behaviour that violates norms and draws disapproval; it is relative to time, place, and audience. Perspectives: differential association (Sutherland: deviance is learned from the people one associates with); labeling theory (Becker: deviance is created when others apply the label; Lemert: primary deviance is the initial act, secondary deviance is the deviant identity taken on after being labeled); strain theory (Merton: a gap between culturally approved goals and the legitimate means to reach them produces conformity, innovation, ritualism, retreatism, or rebellion); and functionalist views (Durkheim: deviance clarifies norms and promotes unity).

Collective behaviour is relatively spontaneous, short-lived action by crowds or dispersed publics outside normal institutions: fads and fashions, crazes, mass hysteria and moral panics, rumours, and riots. Emergent-norm theory holds that crowds develop their own norms on the spot; value-added theory lists conditions (structural strain, a precipitating event, mobilization) that must accumulate.
confusions: Deviance is not the same as crime: much deviance is legal (unusual dress), and some crimes are widely tolerated (minor speeding).

topics.name: Socialization and its agents
know: Socialization is the lifelong process of learning a society's norms, values, roles, and skills, which is how culture is passed on and how a self is formed. Primary socialization happens in childhood, chiefly in the family; secondary socialization continues in school, work, and other settings; anticipatory socialization prepares for a future role; resocialization replaces old norms with new ones, most completely in total institutions such as prisons, the military, or boarding schools.

Agents: the family (the first and most influential, transmitting language, values, and class and ethnic identity); peers (especially in adolescence, teaching norms outside adult control); schools (the formal curriculum plus the hidden curriculum of punctuality, obedience, and competition); the workplace (occupational norms and roles); mass media and social media (models of behaviour and ideals, often idealized or stereotyped); and religion and government (rituals that mark life stages, laws that define adulthood).

Socialization differs by class, gender, and culture, and children are not passive: they select and reshape what they are taught. Cases of extreme isolation show that without social contact language and normal development fail.
confusions: Socialization is not only for children; adults are resocialized at every major role change (new job, parenthood, retirement, prison).

categories.name: Attitude and behavior change
categories.summary: How behaviour is learned and changed: habituation, classical and operant conditioning and what biology and cognition add to them, learning by observation, and the theories of how attitudes change.

topics.name: Habituation, dishabituation, and classical conditioning
know: Habituation is the simplest learning: a response to a repeated, harmless stimulus fades (you stop hearing the clock tick). Dishabituation is the return of the response when the stimulus changes or a new one appears. Both are non-associative, unlike sensitization, in which a strong stimulus makes responses to others larger.

Classical conditioning (Pavlov) pairs a neutral stimulus with an unconditioned stimulus that already produces an unconditioned response (food → salivation); after pairing, the now conditioned stimulus (a tone) produces a conditioned response (salivation) on its own. Acquisition works best when the conditioned stimulus comes shortly before the unconditioned one. Extinction is the fading of the response when the conditioned stimulus is repeatedly presented alone; spontaneous recovery is its return after a rest; generalization is responding to similar stimuli; discrimination is learning to respond only to the trained one.

Examples: fear conditioning (Watson's Little Albert), taste aversion, drug tolerance cued by surroundings, and the placebo response. Higher-order conditioning lets an established conditioned stimulus condition a new one.
confusions: Extinction is new learning that inhibits the response, not erasure; that is why the response can recover spontaneously or return in a new context.

topics.name: Operant conditioning: reinforcement, punishment, schedules, and biological limits
know: Operant conditioning (Skinner, building on Thorndike's law of effect) changes the frequency of a voluntary behaviour by its consequences. Reinforcement increases a behaviour: positive reinforcement adds something wanted (praise, food), negative reinforcement removes something unwanted (a seat belt alarm stops). Punishment decreases a behaviour: positive punishment adds something unpleasant, negative punishment removes something wanted (losing screen time). Primary reinforcers satisfy biological needs; secondary (conditioned) reinforcers such as money and grades gain value by association. Shaping reinforces successive approximations of a target behaviour; extinction follows when reinforcement stops.

Schedules: continuous reinforcement teaches fastest but extinguishes fastest; partial schedules are more resistant to extinction. Fixed-ratio (after a set number of responses: piecework) gives high rates with pauses after reward; variable-ratio (after an unpredictable number: slot machines) gives the highest, steadiest rates; fixed-interval (first response after a set time: a weekly quiz) gives a scallop of effort before the deadline; variable-interval (unpredictable time: checking email) gives a moderate, steady rate.

Escape learning ends an ongoing aversive stimulus; avoidance learning prevents it from starting, and both are maintained by negative reinforcement. Cognition matters: latent learning (Tolman's rats formed cognitive maps without reward) and insight show that learning can occur without immediate reinforcement. Biology limits conditioning: species are prepared to learn some associations (taste aversion forms after a single pairing with a long delay, Garcia effect) and not others, and trained animals drift back toward instinctive behaviours (instinctive drift).
confusions: Negative reinforcement is not punishment: it strengthens a behaviour by removing something aversive. Punishment suppresses a behaviour but does not teach a replacement, and it can model aggression.

topics.name: Observational learning, modeling, and mirror neurons
know: Observational (social) learning happens by watching others: in Bandura's Bobo doll studies children who watched an adult beat an inflatable doll imitated the aggression, especially when the model was rewarded (vicarious reinforcement) and less when the model was punished. The steps are attention, retention, reproduction, and motivation; models are more influential when they are similar, admired, or seen as successful.

Mirror neurons, first found in monkey premotor cortex, fire both when an animal performs an action and when it watches another perform it; related human systems are proposed to support imitation, understanding others' intentions, and feeling vicarious emotion (empathy), though their exact role is still debated. Watching pain or disgust in others activates some of the same brain regions as feeling it.

Applications: prosocial and antisocial behaviour, including media violence, are learned by modeling; observational learning explains how children acquire gender roles, health habits, and skills, and underlies treatments such as modeling for phobias.
confusions: Learning and performance are different: the children who saw the model punished had learned the aggression (they reproduced it when offered a reward) but did not perform it.

topics.name: Theories of attitude and behavior change
know: The elaboration likelihood model describes two routes to persuasion. The central route works through the quality of the arguments when the audience is motivated and able to think about the message; attitude change by this route is durable and predicts behaviour. The peripheral route works through cues such as an attractive or expert source, the number of arguments, or mood when the audience is distracted or uninvolved; its effects are weaker and shorter-lived.

Social cognitive theory (Bandura) holds that behaviour, personal factors (beliefs, expectations, self-efficacy), and environment all influence one another, and that people learn by observing outcomes for others; raising self-efficacy and showing successful models changes health behaviours.

Factors in attitude change: the message (two-sided and moderately discrepant messages, fear appeals that include a clear action), the source (credibility, attractiveness, similarity; the sleeper effect, when a message from a low-credibility source gains influence over time), the target (intelligence, self-esteem, age, need for cognition, prior attitude strength), and social factors (group norms, public commitment). Behaviour change itself changes attitudes through dissonance and self-perception.
confusions: A strong argument persuades only an audience that processes it; for a distracted audience a credible-looking source may matter more than the content.

concepts.summary: Foundational Concept 8 (AAMC): the self and social cognition. Identity and self-concept, how we explain and judge other people, and the processes of social interaction, from roles and groups to attraction and discrimination.

categories.name: Self-identity
categories.summary: Who we think we are: self-concept and its building blocks, the kinds of identity people hold, and the theories of how identity develops through social interaction and culture.

topics.name: Self-concept, self-esteem, self-efficacy, and locus of control
know: Self-concept is the set of beliefs a person holds about who they are, including roles, traits, abilities, and group memberships; self-identity is the sense of being a continuous, distinct person; social identity is the part of the self drawn from membership in groups (nationality, religion, profession, team). People hold multiple identities at once, and the salient one shifts with context.

Self-esteem is the evaluative part, how worthwhile one feels; it is shaped by comparison with others and by reflected appraisals and is linked to well-being, though high self-esteem is a result as much as a cause of success. Self-efficacy (Bandura) is the belief that one can carry out a specific task; Bandura named four sources: mastery experiences (the strongest), vicarious experience (seeing similar people succeed), verbal persuasion, and physiological and emotional states, including how arousal is interpreted; self-efficacy predicts effort and persistence. Locus of control (Rotter) is the general belief that outcomes depend on one's own actions (internal) or on luck, fate, and powerful others (external); an internal locus is associated with better health behaviours and achievement.
Types of identity include race and ethnicity, gender, age, sexual orientation, class, religion, and nationality; which ones are central varies among people and across the life course.
confusions: Self-esteem is global (am I worthwhile?); self-efficacy is task-specific (can I do this?). A person can have high self-esteem and low self-efficacy for mathematics.

topics.name: Formation of identity: developmental theories and social influences
know: Developmental theories: Freud's psychosexual stages (oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital) locate personality in early conflicts; Erikson's eight psychosocial stages each pose a crisis: trust versus mistrust (infancy), autonomy versus shame and doubt (toddler), initiative versus guilt (preschool), industry versus inferiority (school age), identity versus role confusion (adolescence), intimacy versus isolation (young adulthood), generativity versus stagnation (middle adulthood), and integrity versus despair (old age). Kohlberg's moral development runs from preconventional (punishment and reward) through conventional (approval, law and order) to postconventional (social contract, universal principles); Gilligan argued it undervalues an ethic of care. Gender identity develops from biology, social learning (reinforcement and modeling), and the child's own gender schemas; Marcia described identity statuses (diffusion, foreclosure, moratorium, achievement) in adolescence.

Social theories: Cooley's looking-glass self holds that we see ourselves as we imagine others see us; Mead's theory distinguishes the spontaneous 'I' from the socialized 'me' and describes children moving from imitation to the play stage (taking one role) to the game stage (taking many roles at once and grasping the generalized other, society's shared expectations). Role-taking, imitation of significant others, and reference groups (the groups we compare ourselves with, whether or not we belong) shape the self.

Culture and socialization set the content: individualist cultures emphasize independence and personal traits, collectivist cultures interdependence and group roles; family, school, media, and religion supply the identities on offer and the value placed on each.
confusions: Erikson's stages span the whole life, unlike Freud's; identity versus role confusion is the adolescent stage, not the only one.

categories.name: Social thinking
categories.summary: How we explain other people's behaviour and our own, where prejudice and stereotypes come from, and how expectations about groups become self-fulfilling.

topics.name: Attributing behavior to persons or situations
know: An attribution explains why someone acted: dispositional (internal: traits, ability, mood) or situational (external: circumstances, luck, pressure). The fundamental attribution error is overweighting disposition when explaining others' behaviour (the late colleague is lazy, not stuck in traffic); the actor–observer difference is explaining our own behaviour by the situation and others' by disposition; the self-serving bias credits our successes to ourselves and our failures to circumstances. The just-world hypothesis, the assumption that the world is fair so that misfortune must have been earned, leads to blaming victims.

Culture shapes attributions: people in individualist cultures make dispositional attributions more readily, while people in collectivist cultures weigh situations and relationships more; the fundamental attribution error is weaker in the latter.

Self-perception colours perception of others: the false consensus effect assumes others share our views, and projection assigns our own traits to them; perceptions of the environment (whether a setting is safe, competitive, or cooperative) frame how the same behaviour is read, and primacy effects and halo effects let a first impression or one good quality spread to everything else.
confusions: The self-serving bias and the fundamental attribution error point in opposite directions for the same bad outcome: my failure is the situation, yours is your character.

refs.label: OpenStax Psychology 2e, 12.1 What Is Social Psychology?

topics.name: Prejudice and bias: stereotypes, stigma, and ethnocentrism
know: Prejudice is a negative attitude toward a group and its members; a stereotype is the generalized belief (cognitive component) about what members are like; discrimination is the behaviour. Cognitive sources: categorizing people into in-groups and out-groups, seeing out-group members as all alike (out-group homogeneity), illusory correlations between a minority and rare behaviour, and confirmation bias that preserves the stereotype. Emotional sources: fear, frustration and scapegoating (blaming an out-group for one's troubles), and the self-esteem boost of favouring one's own group (social identity theory).

Sociological sources: power, prestige, and class. Dominant groups justify their position with beliefs about subordinate groups; conflict theory sees prejudice as a tool for protecting advantage, and competition for scarce resources (jobs, housing) sharpens it. Stigma (Goffman) is a mark that discredits a person in others' eyes, whether a physical attribute, a character blemish, or group membership, leading to exclusion and to the person's management of a 'spoiled identity'.

Ethnocentrism is judging other cultures by the standards of one's own and assuming one's own is superior; cultural relativism is understanding a culture's practices in its own terms, which is the stance of anthropology and of culturally competent medicine. Xenocentrism is the opposite preference for other cultures.
confusions: Stereotypes can be positive ('good at mathematics') and still harm, by denying individuality and adding pressure. Cultural relativism as a method of understanding does not require moral approval of every practice.

topics.name: Self-fulfilling prophecy and stereotype threat
know: A self-fulfilling prophecy is an expectation that causes the behaviour that confirms it: a teacher who expects a student to do well gives more attention and encouragement, and the student improves (Rosenthal and Jacobson's classroom study); the same mechanism has been shown in job interviews, where interviewers' expectations changed how candidates performed.

Stereotype threat is the anxiety that one may confirm a negative stereotype about one's group, which consumes working memory and lowers performance on exactly the task in question; in Steele and Aronson's studies, describing a test as a measure of ability widened the gap between Black and White students and describing it as non-diagnostic closed it; brief values-affirmation writing reduced a classroom achievement gap by roughly 40% in later field work, and the size of the effect varies across studies.
Both processes work without any intent to discriminate, which is why reducing them depends on changing situations and expectations, not only attitudes.
confusions: Stereotype threat is about the target's own performance under threat; the self-fulfilling prophecy is about how others' expectations change their treatment of the target. They can act together.

categories.name: Social interactions
categories.summary: The machinery of interaction: statuses, roles, groups, networks and organizations; how we present ourselves and read emotion; attraction, aggression, attachment, altruism and their biology; and discrimination.

topics.name: Status, roles, and groups
know: A status is a position in society; an ascribed status is assigned at birth or involuntarily (sex, age, race, being a daughter), an achieved status is earned (physician, graduate, parent by choice), and a master status (such as a disability or a prominent occupation) overshadows the others. A role is the set of expected behaviours attached to a status. Role conflict arises between the demands of two different statuses (employee and parent); role strain arises within one status (a resident who must be both learner and provider); role exit is the process of leaving a role that was central to identity, often with a new one taking its place.

Groups are people who interact and share a sense of belonging. Primary groups (family, close friends) are small, long-lasting, and valued for themselves; secondary groups (a class, a work team) are larger, impersonal, and goal-directed. In-groups are groups one belongs to and identifies with; out-groups are the ones outside, often viewed with suspicion. Group size changes dynamics: a dyad is the most intimate and fragile, a triad allows alliances and mediation, and larger groups become more stable but less personal and need leadership and rules.
Leadership can be instrumental (task-focused) or expressive (relationship-focused), with authoritarian, democratic, or laissez-faire styles.
confusions: Role conflict is between roles (two statuses); role strain is within one role (one status). An in-group need not be a primary group: fans of a team are an in-group but mostly strangers.

topics.name: Networks, formal organizations, and bureaucracy
know: A social network is the web of ties linking people and groups; strong ties (family, close friends) provide support, while weak ties (acquaintances) reach into other circles and are often more useful for finding jobs and information (the strength of weak ties). Social capital is the value of these ties: the help, information, and influence they can supply.

Formal organizations are large secondary groups set up to pursue explicit goals: normative (voluntary, joined for a cause), coercive (prisons, psychiatric commitment), and utilitarian (joined for pay or credentials, such as workplaces and universities). Weber's ideal bureaucracy has a hierarchy of authority, a clear division of labour, written rules, impersonality (rules applied without favouritism), and hiring and promotion by technical qualification; it is efficient at routine tasks but can be rigid and dehumanizing.

Perspectives on bureaucracy: the iron law of oligarchy (Michels) holds that even democratic organizations come to be run by a small elite; McDonaldization (Ritzer) describes the spread of efficiency, calculability, predictability, and control through technology from fast food to health care; 'red tape' is the everyday name for its dysfunctions.
confusions: Bureaucracy in sociology is a neutral description of an organizational form, not an insult; hospitals and universities are bureaucracies by this definition.

topics.name: Self-presentation: expressing and detecting emotion, impression management, and communication
know: Emotional expression is universal in its basic forms but shaped by display rules that say when and how much to show; cultures differ (collectivist cultures often mute negative expressions in public), and gender differences are real but small: on average girls and women show slightly more positive and internalizing emotion and read nonverbal cues somewhat better, while boys and men show slightly more externalizing emotion such as anger, with the differences depending on who is watching. Detection relies on facial expression, tone, posture, and context.

Impression management is the effort to control how others see us. Goffman's dramaturgical approach treats social life as theatre: on the front stage we perform a role for an audience, following a script and using props and setting; on the back stage we relax, rehearse, and drop the performance. People work to keep the two consistent and to repair a spoiled performance (face-saving).

Communication is verbal (words, and their tone and timing) and nonverbal (facial expression, eye contact, gestures, posture, distance, touch), with nonverbal cues carrying much of the emotional meaning and varying by culture, for instance in eye contact and personal space. Animal signals (pheromones, alarm calls, courtship and threat displays) are often reliable because they are costly to produce or hard to fake (the handicap principle), though bluffing occurs, as in displays that overstate fighting ability; human language differs in its open-ended grammar (productivity) and its ability to refer to absent things (displacement).
confusions: Goffman's 'performance' is not dishonesty; everyone manages impressions, and the back stage is where the same person behaves without an audience.

topics.name: Social behavior: attraction, aggression, attachment, altruism, and social support
know: Attraction grows with proximity (and the mere-exposure effect of familiarity), physical attractiveness, similarity of attitudes and background, and reciprocal liking; Sternberg's triangular theory describes love as combinations of intimacy, passion, and commitment, and the matching hypothesis notes that partners tend to be similar in attractiveness.

Aggression is behaviour intended to harm; it has biological roots (testosterone, with a modest effect, low serotonin, amygdala and prefrontal function, heritability), psychological triggers (frustration, provocation, pain, heat), and social learning (modeling, cultures of honour); hostile aggression is emotional, instrumental aggression is a means to an end. Attachment is the lasting emotional bond between infant and caregiver: Harlow's monkeys preferred a soft surrogate to a wire one that fed them, and Ainsworth's strange situation identified secure, avoidant, and resistant (ambivalent) patterns, to which Main and Solomon later added disorganized; the patterns track caregiver sensitivity and predict later relationships.

Altruism is helping at a cost to oneself; it is encouraged by empathy, by norms of reciprocity and social responsibility, and by having noticed, interpreted, and accepted responsibility for a need (the steps that the bystander effect interrupts). Social support, emotional, informational, and practical help from others, buffers stress and improves health outcomes.
confusions: Secure attachment is the most common pattern in most samples but not the only normal one; patterns also shift with caregiving and culture.

topics.name: Biological explanations of social behavior in animals
know: Behavioural ecology explains social behaviour by its contribution to reproductive success. Optimal foraging theory predicts that animals choose food and patches that maximize energy gained per unit of time and risk. Mating systems (monogamy, polygyny, polyandry, promiscuity) reflect how resources and parental care are distributed; mate choice (usually by the sex that invests more) favours traits signalling genetic quality or resources, and sexual selection can produce costly ornaments such as the peacock's tail.

Game theory models interactions whose payoff depends on what others do: the hawk–dove game explains stable mixtures of aggressive and peaceful strategies, and the prisoner's dilemma and tit-for-tat show how cooperation can evolve through reciprocal altruism among animals that meet repeatedly.

Altruism toward relatives is explained by inclusive fitness and kin selection (Hamilton's rule: help is favoured when the benefit to the relative, weighted by relatedness, exceeds the cost to the helper), which accounts for alarm calls, helpers at the nest, and sterile worker insects; reciprocal altruism explains help between non-relatives who can repay.
equations: rB > C\ \text{(Hamilton's rule: relatedness } r\text{, benefit } B\text{, cost } C\text{)}
confusions: Behaviour that benefits the group is not selected for the group's sake; most biologists explain apparent group-level altruism by kin selection or reciprocity, though multilevel-selection models remain debated.

topics.name: Discrimination: individual and institutional
know: Discrimination is unequal treatment of people because of their group membership. Individual discrimination is carried out by a person (a landlord refusing a tenant); institutional discrimination is built into the normal operation of organizations and laws, so that unequal outcomes persist without anyone intending them (hiring networks, lending rules, school funding tied to property taxes). Discrimination can be intentional or the side effect of neutral-looking policies.

Prejudice (attitude) and discrimination (behaviour) are related but separable: a prejudiced person may not act on it because of laws or norms, and an unprejudiced person may discriminate by following a biased rule; Merton's typology includes the unprejudiced discriminator and the prejudiced non-discriminator.

Power, prestige, and class make discrimination possible: groups with more resources set the rules and benefit from them, and discrimination in turn preserves their advantage; this is why racism and sexism are analysed as systems, not only as individual attitudes, and why health disparities persist across generations.
confusions: Institutional discrimination does not require prejudiced individuals; it can continue through routine procedures that nobody questions.

concepts.name: Cultural and social differences and well-being
concepts.summary: Foundational Concept 9 (AAMC): the structures people live inside. Sociological theory, the major institutions, culture, and the demographic make-up and change of societies.

categories.name: Understanding social structure
categories.summary: The sociologist's toolkit: the theoretical perspectives, the major social institutions (education, family, religion, government and economy, health and medicine), and culture.

topics.name: Theoretical approaches in sociology
know: Macrosociology studies large-scale structures and processes (institutions, class, population); microsociology studies face-to-face interaction. Functionalism (Durkheim, Parsons, Merton) sees society as a system of interdependent parts that each serve functions, manifest (intended) or latent (unintended), and treats dysfunction and anomie as breakdowns of that order. Conflict theory (Marx, later Weber and feminist and critical race theorists) sees society as groups competing for scarce resources, with institutions serving the powerful and change arising from struggle.

Symbolic interactionism (Mead, Blumer, Goffman) is micro: meaning is created in interaction through symbols and language, and the self and social reality are built from these shared meanings. Social constructionism holds that categories such as race, gender, and illness take their meaning from social agreement rather than from nature alone (the Thomas theorem, after W. I. and Dorothy Swaine Thomas: situations people define as real are real in their consequences).

Exchange theory and rational choice see interaction as exchanges in which people weigh costs and rewards and pursue their interests. Feminist theory analyses gender as a central axis of inequality and power across institutions, including how science and medicine have treated women's bodies and work.
confusions: Functionalism and conflict theory are both macro; symbolic interactionism is micro. A single phenomenon (education, say) is usually analysed through all three.

topics.name: Social institutions: education and family
know: Education transmits knowledge and culture, sorts people into occupations, and (functionalists add) builds social cohesion; conflict theorists stress that it reproduces inequality. The hidden curriculum is the unstated lessons schools teach, obedience, punctuality, competition, and class-specific expectations. Teacher expectancy (the Pygmalion effect) means expectations about students become self-fulfilling. Educational segregation and stratification: tracking, unequal funding, and residential segregation sort students by class and race into different-quality schooling with lasting effects on income and health.

The family is a group tied by blood, marriage, adoption, or commitment that cares for members and socializes children. Kinship may be traced through both parents (bilateral), the mother (matrilineal), or the father (patrilineal); nuclear and extended families, single-parent, blended, cohabiting, same-sex, and childfree families are all common forms. Marriage patterns include monogamy and polygamy (polygyny, polyandry); divorce rates roughly doubled between 1960 and a peak around 1980 and have fallen since; they vary with age at marriage, education, and economic stress, and children generally fare better in stable, low-conflict homes whatever the form.

Family violence includes child abuse and neglect, intimate-partner violence, and elder abuse, usually committed by a family member or other caregiver, under-reported, and more frequent under stress, isolation, and substance use; physicians are mandated reporters of child abuse in the United States.
confusions: The hidden curriculum is not secret; it is the ordinary discipline of schooling that is not in the syllabus.

topics.name: Social institutions: religion, government, and the economy
know: Religion, in Durkheim's classic definition, is a unified system of beliefs and practices relative to sacred things that binds its adherents into a moral community. Religiosity is the strength of belief and practice, measured by attendance, prayer, and importance of faith. Organizations range from the ecclesia (a state church) and denomination (established, mainstream) to the sect (a smaller, often breakaway group with intense commitment) and the cult or new religious movement (new, small, often secretive and controlling of members, viewed with suspicion). Religion and social change: modernization and secularization reduce religion's public role in many societies, while fundamentalism responds with a return to strict, literal doctrine; functionalists stress cohesion and meaning, conflict theorists stress religion's role in justifying inequality.

Government: Weber distinguished power (the ability to get one's way despite resistance) from authority (legitimate power), which may be traditional (custom, monarchy), charismatic (a leader's personal qualities), or rational-legal (law and office, as in bureaucracies). Forms of government include democracy, monarchy, oligarchy, and dictatorship or totalitarianism.

Economies organize production and distribution: capitalism (private ownership, markets, profit), socialism (collective ownership, planning), and the mixed economies of most countries; the division of labour grows with industrialization (Durkheim's shift from mechanical to organic solidarity), and the postindustrial economy is dominated by services and information work.
confusions: Charisma in Weber's sense is a source of legitimacy, not mere likeability; it tends to be unstable and is 'routinized' into traditional or legal authority after the leader.

topics.name: Social institutions: health and medicine
know: Medicalization is the process by which conditions once seen as normal variation or moral failing come to be defined and treated as medical problems (childbirth, alcoholism, attention problems, menopause); demedicalization runs the other way (the American Psychiatric Association stopped classifying homosexuality as a mental disorder in 1973). The sick role (Parsons): a sick person is excused from normal duties and not blamed for the illness, but must want to get well and seek and follow competent help; the role applies poorly to chronic and stigmatized conditions.

Health care delivery differs by system: the United States mixes private insurance, employer coverage, and public programmes (Medicare, Medicaid), leaving gaps in coverage and high costs; most high-income countries provide universal coverage through single-payer or regulated insurance. Delivery also depends on the professions (physicians' authority, the rise of other providers) and on institutions (hospitals, clinics, public health).

The illness experience is the patient's subjective side: symptoms and stigma are interpreted through culture and social position, chronic illness reshapes identity and daily life, and the same diagnosis is lived very differently across class and culture. Social epidemiology studies how health and disease are distributed across populations by class, race, gender, age, and place, and why: the social determinants of health.
confusions: Medicalization is neither simply good nor bad: it can bring treatment and relief from blame, and it can expand professional control and turn difference into disorder.

topics.name: Culture: elements, material and symbolic culture, change, and diffusion
know: Culture is the shared beliefs, values, norms, symbols, language, rituals, and practices of a group, learned and passed on. Material culture is the physical objects (tools, buildings, clothing); symbolic (nonmaterial) culture is the ideas, language, and norms. Language is the key symbol system, and the Sapir–Whorf hypothesis proposes it shapes thought. Values are shared ideas about what is good; norms are the rules that follow from them, and beliefs are what the group holds true.

Cultural change: culture lag (Ogburn) is the delay while nonmaterial culture catches up with technological change (laws lagging behind genetic testing or social media); innovation (discovery and invention) and diffusion (spread from one culture to another, now accelerated by media and migration) drive change. Culture shock is the disorientation of entering an unfamiliar culture. Subcultures hold distinct values within the larger culture (medical students, religious communities); countercultures oppose it. Mass media and popular culture are major carriers of culture today.

Contact between cultures produces assimilation (a minority adopts the dominant culture), multiculturalism (coexistence with respect for difference), pluralism, and sometimes amalgamation. Human culture itself has an evolutionary basis: the capacity for language, imitation, and cumulative learning allowed culture to become humans' main means of adaptation, and cultural practices such as dairying have in turn shaped human genes (lactase persistence); cooking may have done so too.
confusions: A subculture differs from the mainstream; a counterculture actively rejects it. Diffusion spreads elements between cultures; transmission passes culture within one across generations.

categories.name: Demographic characteristics and processes
categories.summary: Who makes up a society and how that changes: age, gender, race and ethnicity, immigration, and sexual orientation as social categories; then population change, social movements, globalization, and urbanization.

topics.name: Demographic structure: age, gender, race and ethnicity, immigration, and sexual orientation
know: Age: ageing is biological, but the life course (childhood, adolescence, adulthood, old age) is socially defined, with expectations attached to each stage. Age cohorts share birth years and historical experiences (the baby boomers); populations are ageing as fertility falls and longevity rises, raising the dependency ratio and the demand for care. The social significance of age includes ageism, retirement, and the varying status of elders across cultures.

Gender: sex refers to biological categories, gender to the social roles, behaviours, and identities a culture attaches to them; gender identity is a person's own sense, which may not match sex assigned at birth. Gender is socially constructed, learned through socialization, and performed; gender segregation appears in occupations (nursing versus engineering), pay, and spaces, and gender inequality shows in income, political representation, and unpaid care work.

Race is a social construction: categories based on visible traits have no consistent biological boundaries, yet racialization (assigning racial meaning to a group or practice) and racial formation (the historical creation and transformation of racial categories by law, policy, and conflict) make race real in its consequences. Ethnicity is shared culture, ancestry, or language. Immigration: patterns are driven by economic opportunity, family ties, and refuge; immigration status (citizen, permanent resident, visa holder, undocumented) shapes access to work, health care, and legal protection and intersects with race and ethnicity in how newcomers are received. Sexual orientation (heterosexual, homosexual, bisexual, asexual, and others) is a demographic category with its own history of stigma and legal change.
confusions: Sex, gender, gender identity, and sexual orientation are four different things; none can be inferred from another.

topics.name: Population change: theories, growth and decline, fertility, mortality, and migration
know: Malthus argued that population grows geometrically while food grows arithmetically, so famine, disease, and war would check it; technology and falling fertility have so far defeated that prediction, though neo-Malthusians apply it to resources and climate. Demographic transition theory describes four stages: high birth and death rates (stable), falling death rates with high births (rapid growth), falling birth rates (slowing growth), and low birth and death rates (stable or declining, with an ageing population); most high-income countries are in the last stage.

Measures: the crude birth rate and crude death rate are events per 1,000 people per year; the total fertility rate is the average number of children a woman would have at current age-specific rates (about 2.1 replaces a population); age-specific rates, infant mortality, and life expectancy track health. Population growth equals births minus deaths plus net migration. A population pyramid shows the age and sex structure: a wide base means a young, growing population; a narrow base and wide top, an ageing one. Projections extend current rates forward.

Migration is driven by push factors (poverty, war, persecution, disaster) and pull factors (jobs, safety, family, services); internal and international migration reshape both the places left and the places joined.
confusions: A country can have a high crude death rate simply because its population is old; age-specific rates separate the age structure from the risk of dying.

topics.name: Social movements, globalization, and urbanization
know: Social movements are organized, sustained efforts to promote or resist change. Relative deprivation theory says they arise when people feel deprived compared with others or with their expectations, not simply when they are poorest; resource mobilization theory stresses the money, leaders, networks, and media access a movement needs. Movements organize from informal groups to formal organizations (Blumer and Tilly's stages: emergence or preliminary, coalescence, bureaucratization or institutionalization, decline) and use strategies from petitions and lawsuits to protest, boycott, and civil disobedience; types include reform, revolutionary, religious, alternative, and resistance movements.

Globalization is the growing interconnection of economies, cultures, and governments, driven by communication technology, cheap transport, and economic interdependence (trade, multinational corporations, finance). Perspectives: it spreads prosperity and ideas (modernization view) or deepens inequality between core and peripheral countries (world-systems and dependency views); social changes include migration, cultural homogenization and backlash, civil unrest, and transnational terrorism.

Urbanization is the shift of population into cities, driven by industrialization and jobs; it concentrates both opportunity and problems (crowding, pollution, inequality). Suburbanization followed the car and highways, drawing wealth from city centres and causing urban decline; gentrification and urban renewal bring investment and higher-income residents back, raising rents and displacing long-time, often poorer, residents.
confusions: Relative deprivation explains why rising expectations can spark protest even as conditions improve; absolute hardship alone often produces resignation.

concepts.name: Social stratification, resources, and well-being
concepts.summary: Foundational Concept 10 (AAMC): inequality and its consequences. Where people live, class and mobility, poverty, and the resulting disparities in health and in health care.

categories.name: Social inequality
categories.summary: Where people stand and what it costs them: spatial inequality, social class and stratification, mobility and poverty, and the disparities in health and health care that follow.

topics.name: Spatial inequality: residential segregation, neighborhood safety, and environmental justice
know: Spatial inequality is the uneven distribution of resources and risks across places. Residential segregation by race and class, produced historically by law, lending practices (redlining), zoning, and private discrimination, concentrates poverty in some neighbourhoods and wealth in others, and it persists because of housing costs, school quality, and continued discrimination.

Neighbourhood conditions shape health directly: exposure to violence and fear limit outdoor activity and raise chronic stress; poor neighbourhoods have fewer grocery stores, parks, and clinics and more alcohol outlets and pollution; these effects hold even after individual income is taken into account.

Environmental justice concerns the unequal placement of environmental hazards (waste sites, highways, factories, lead pipes) near poor and minority communities and their unequal say in decisions; location therefore predicts exposure to asthma triggers, lead, heat, and flooding. Global inequality shows the same pattern between countries.
confusions: Segregation is not only a matter of choice; policies and markets created it and sustain it long after explicit discrimination was outlawed.

topics.name: Social class and stratification
know: Stratification is a society's ranking of people into layers with unequal access to wealth, power, and prestige. Social class is a group sharing economic position; socioeconomic status combines income, education, and occupation. Systems range from closed (caste, where position is ascribed) to open (class, where mobility is possible). Marx divided society by relation to the means of production (bourgeoisie and proletariat); Weber added status (prestige) and party (power) to economic class.

Class consciousness is awareness of one's class position and shared interests; false consciousness (Marx) is accepting beliefs that serve the dominant class against one's own interest. Cultural capital (Bourdieu) is the knowledge, tastes, and credentials valued by the dominant culture; social capital is the resources available through one's networks; both are passed from parents to children and so drive social reproduction, the persistence of class across generations. Power, privilege, and prestige are the three unequally distributed goods.

Intersectionality (Crenshaw) holds that class, race, gender, age, and other statuses combine to produce experiences of advantage or disadvantage that cannot be understood one axis at a time. The socioeconomic gradient in health is the finding that health improves at every step up the ladder, not only above a poverty line, through income, stress, control, and conditions of work and housing. Differences between countries account for a large share of global income inequality, alongside the inequality within countries.
confusions: Income (a flow) and wealth (accumulated assets) are different; wealth gaps between groups are far larger than income gaps and carry across generations.

topics.name: Social mobility and poverty
know: Social mobility is movement between positions in the stratification system. Intergenerational mobility compares a person's position with their parents'; intragenerational mobility is change within one's own lifetime. Vertical mobility moves up or down the ladder; horizontal mobility changes position without changing rank (one job for another at the same level). Structural mobility occurs when the whole economy shifts (industrialization creating middle-class jobs).

Meritocracy is a system in which position is earned by ability and effort; most societies claim it as an ideal, and sociologists measure how far reality falls short, since family wealth, schooling, and networks shape who gets ahead. Mobility in the United States is lower than its image suggests and lower than in several European countries.

Absolute poverty is lacking the resources for basic survival (food, shelter, clean water); relative poverty is being poor compared with the standard of one's society; official poverty lines are set by income thresholds that vary by family size. Social exclusion is being cut off from the institutions and relationships that make full participation possible, through segregation and isolation, and it compounds material poverty; the feminization of poverty refers to the rising share of the poor who are women and their children.
confusions: Upward mobility for some does not mean an open system: measure mobility by how strongly a child's position is predicted by the parents' position.

topics.name: Health disparities and health care disparities
know: Health disparities are systematic differences in health outcomes between groups: by class (lower income and education predict higher rates of heart disease, diabetes, infant mortality, and shorter life expectancy), by race and ethnicity (in the United States, Black Americans have higher infant and maternal mortality and lower life expectancy than White Americans, differences driven by social conditions and discrimination rather than biology), and by gender (women live longer but report more chronic illness and disability; men die earlier from injury, violence, and heart disease).

Health care disparities are differences in access to and quality of care: the uninsured and underinsured delay care and get less preventive care; rural areas have fewer providers; minority patients receive fewer recommended procedures and poorer pain management even with equal insurance, reflecting bias and system factors; women's symptoms, for instance of heart attack, are more often missed.

The social determinants of health (income, education, work, housing, neighbourhood, social support, and discrimination) explain more of the variation in health than medical care does, which is why reducing disparities involves policy as much as clinics; physicians still contribute through access, cultural competence, interpreters, and awareness of their own bias.
confusions: A health disparity is a difference in outcomes; a health care disparity is a difference in care. They reinforce each other but are measured separately.
